We’re a family-owned company, and we know a bed bug worry is stressful and private. We arrive discreetly, work efficiently, and treat your home with respect. Meet the family behind Coastal K9 →

How to know if you have bed bugs

Most people call us because something feels off — not because they have actually seen a bug. Bed bugs are nocturnal, flat enough to hide in a seam the width of a credit card, and expert at staying out of sight. By the time you spot a live one, the infestation is usually well established. These are the early warning signs our Aiken and CSRA clients notice first:

  • Small rusty or dark spots on sheets, mattress seams, or the box spring — digested blood left behind after feeding.
  • Itchy welts in a line or cluster, often on the arms, shoulders, neck, or legs, that appear overnight.
  • Tiny pale eggs or shed skins tucked into mattress piping, headboards, cracks, and baseboards.
  • A faint, sweet, musty odor in a room that will not go away.
  • Bites that keep coming back even after you have washed everything and changed detergents.

Any one of these is reason enough to schedule a professional inspection. The trouble with a do-it-yourself check is that bed bugs hide where you cannot easily look — inside wall voids, behind outlets, and under carpet edges — which is exactly where a trained detection dog excels. Book a K-9 bed bug inspection or call 803-226-3155.

K-9 detection vs. a traditional exterminator’s visual inspection

If you searched for a “pest control company” or “exterminator near me,” you may not realize there is a far more accurate option for bed bugs specifically. A conventional visual inspection relies on a technician’s eyes and usually covers only the areas a person can reach and see. A certified detection dog works entirely by scent — pinpointing live bed bugs and viable eggs behind walls, inside furniture, and in cracks no flashlight can reach.

Bed bugs are experts at hiding — in seams, cracks, outlets, and behind trim where a visual inspection easily misses them. The best time to check is before a problem grows. Frequently asked questions

How accurate are bed bug detection dogs?

Very accurate — but the number depends heavily on the team. In controlled University of Florida research (Pfiester, Koehler & Pereira, Journal of Economic Entomology, 2008), trained detection dogs indicated correctly on live bed bugs 97.5% of the time with no false positives, and were roughly 98% accurate locating live bugs in controlled hotel-room trials. Later field research found much wider variation between teams working real infestations, which is exactly why certification and ongoing training matter. Our teams are certified through NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA and train continuously to hold that standard.

Can dogs really smell bed bug eggs?

Yes. Viable eggs give off the same scent signature as live bugs, so a trained dog can alert on an infestation before those eggs hatch. That is what turns a small, contained problem into a spot treatment instead of a whole-home ordeal.

How long does a K9 bed bug inspection take?

A trained dog clears a typical room in a few minutes, and most single-family homes are finished in under an hour. A technician searching seam by seam with a flashlight takes far longer and still cannot reach inside wall voids or behind trim.

Do you treat bed bugs, or just find them?

Both. We locate the infestation with our detection dogs, build a targeted treatment plan around what we actually found, and can verify the result with a follow-up canine sweep. If you would prefer detection only — with no treatment relationship — we offer that as a standalone service. Just tell us when you call.

Do I really need an inspection before treatment?

Yes, and it is the core of our detection-before-treatment promise. Confirming where bed bugs are — and just as importantly, where they are not — means you do not pay to chemically treat rooms that were never infested. It also gives you a baseline to verify against once treatment is done.

Is the inspection discreet, and is it safe around kids and pets?

Yes to both. We arrive discreetly and work quickly and respectfully — bed bugs hitchhike into the cleanest homes and there is nothing to be embarrassed about. The inspection itself uses no chemicals or sprays, and our detection dogs are friendly, non-aggressive working dogs.

Can you inspect apartments, hotels, and commercial properties?

Yes. We work with homeowners, renters, landlords, hotels, multifamily communities, schools, and healthcare and senior-living facilities across the CSRA — with discreet scheduling and written documentation for property files.

What does a K9 bed bug inspection cost, and how soon can you come out?

Cost depends on the size and layout of the property, but a canine inspection is almost always cheaper than treating an entire home blind, because you only pay to treat confirmed hot spots. We offer same-week appointments in most cases across Aiken, Augusta, Columbia and the greater CSRA. Call 803-226-3155 for a no-obligation quote.

Bed bug inspections for medical & healthcare facilities

Hospitals, clinics, urgent-care and surgery centers, dialysis units, medical offices, and assisted-living and long-term-care facilities can’t afford to wait days for answers. One bed bug report can disrupt patient care, trigger a compliance review, and put a facility’s reputation on the line. Our canine teams run discreet, room-by-room inspections that clear or confirm suspected areas quickly, backed by written documentation your infection-control and facilities staff can file.

4-hour turnaround. For medical and healthcare facilities across Aiken and the CSRA, we offer a 4-hour response window—from your call to a documented inspection result—so you can act on the same shift, isolate a room if needed, and keep the rest of your facility running. Call 803-226-3155 and let us know it’s a medical facility so we can prioritize your inspection.

We provide canine bed bug detection across the CSRA and Midlands, including Aiken, North Augusta, Columbia, Lexington.

body:
Bed bug work is unforgiving in a way that most pest control is not. There is no partial credit. A treatment that kills 98 percent of a population and misses a few dozen cemented eggs behind a headboard has not reduced your problem — it has delayed it by about five weeks, which is roughly how long it takes an egg to become a breeding adult at indoor temperatures. Under laboratory conditions a bed bug population doubles about every thirteen days.

That is why this page is mostly about verification and follow-up rather than about products. The single most useful fact we can give you is the temperature difference between what kills an adult and what kills an egg, because every failed heat job in the country lives in that gap. If you also need to know whether a room, a floor or a building has bed bugs at all — before a lease turns over, after a guest complaint, or to clear a unit — that is a detection question, and our certified K-9 bed bug detection teams answer it. This page is the treatment.

118°FHeld for 71 to 90 minutes — the exposure bed bug eggs need. Adults die around 119°F on contact, which is why adult-based protocols fail
7 visitsAverage number of biweekly service visits per unit in the peer-reviewed program that achieved 92 percent elimination
88%Of 110 US bed bug populations carrying knockdown-resistance mutations against pyrethroids — the active ingredient in most store-bought sprays

What temperature actually kills bed bugs?

This is the technical core of the page and the number most protocols get wrong.

The controlled study is Kells and Goblirsch, published in Insects in 2011, and its method matters: the researchers used a slow temperature ramp deliberately simulating how a real room heats, rather than plunging insects into hot air. Step-function studies produce lower apparent lethal temperatures — which is exactly why lab numbers and field practice differ.

 AdultsEggs
Immediate lethal temperature48.3°C / 118.9°F54.8°C / 130.6°F
Sustained exposure at 113°F~95 minutes~428 minutes (7.1 hours)
Sustained exposure at 118.4°F—71.5 minutes

The authors' own recommendation for whole-room work is to hold 48°C (118.4°F) for 71.5 minutes, or to exceed 50°C (122°F). Virginia Tech's field guidance puts it at 118°F for 90 minutes for 100 percent egg mortality. The egg is the limiting factor. Any protocol built around the adult number fails, and it fails invisibly — the room looks clear for a month.

That is also why a field ambient target is typically around 135°F rather than 118°F. Ambient air temperature is not harborage temperature. Remote sensors go into cracks, crevices and the coldest anticipated locations to confirm those spots actually exceed the thermal death point, the heat is held at least sixty minutes past that, and a full job runs six to eight hours from setup to takedown.

Why do heat treatments fail?

Five documented reasons, and we would rather you know them before you buy heat from anyone, including us.

  • Heat sinks in older and remodeled buildings. Virginia Tech specifically flags that some structures — usually older remodeled buildings — have construction features that create heat sinks, and recommends supplemental insecticide in those areas. That describes a great deal of the housing stock in Aiken, Graniteville, Augusta and Columbia's older neighborhoods.
  • Thermal mass. Wall cavities, box spring interiors, stuffed furniture, book stacks and a heavy dresser pushed against an exterior wall all lag behind ambient air. Insulated items need extra time to equilibrate. A room can read 135°F while the core of a mattress is still well under lethal.
  • Bugs fleeing the gradient. This is no longer speculation. A 2024 paper in Scientific Reports found bed bugs release an alarm pheromone starting around 42°C — a temperature 83 percent of them survive — and that nearby bugs respond with frantic, rapid, directional movement. The authors warn directly that this may let insects relocate to thermally protected areas before lethal temperatures are reached. The countermeasure is air movement to flatten the gradient, plus a residual perimeter so anything fleeing a treated void crosses something that kills it.
  • No residual, at all. Virginia Tech states it plainly: heat treatment has no residual activity, which means bed bugs can reinfest the day after treatment. In an apartment building with an untreated neighbor, that is not hypothetical.
  • Sublethal heat is not control. Exposure in the 34 to 40°C range produces variable mortality and depresses fecundity for weeks. That is a real effect, and it is not a reason to call an underperforming heat job a success. We will not tell you it “still worked.”

The honest counterweight: bed bugs show very limited ability to evolve heat resistance — laboratory selection experiments plateaued after the fourth generation. Heat is not a resistance-selecting tool, and that is a genuine advantage over chemistry that no amount of resistance in the population can erode.

Why do store-bought sprays make it worse?

Two separate mechanisms, both documented, and both working against you at once.

Resistance. A 2010 study screened 110 US bed bug populations and found 88 percent carried target-site knockdown-resistance mutations in the sodium channel — V419L, L925I, or both. A single Richmond field strain sequenced in PLOS ONE showed roughly 5,200-fold resistance to deltamethrin and 111-fold to beta-cyfluthrin, driven by the kdr mutation plus multiple upregulated cytochrome P450s, carboxylesterases and a glutathione S-transferase — several independent mechanisms coexisting in one population. Some strains have also thickened their cuticle, slowing penetration.

The workaround chemistry is under pressure too. Romero and Anderson's 2016 study in the Journal of Medical Entomology measured neonicotinoid resistance ratios in field populations reaching 33,333-fold for acetamiprid, with hundreds-fold ratios for thiamethoxam, imidacloprid and dinotefuran. Resistance is population-specific — a Jersey City population remained susceptible to imidacloprid — which is precisely why a one-size-fits-all chemical protocol is inadequate.

Behavioral avoidance and dispersal. A 2009 study in the same journal found three of four bed bug strains significantly avoided deltamethrin-treated harborages and preferred untreated ones, and that sublethal contact increased locomotor activity — 58 percent of one strain was left wandering with poisoning symptoms rather than dying. Chlorfenapyr produced no such avoidance. What that means in a bedroom is that spraying a pyrethroid at the bed drives bugs out of the bed and into baseboards, adjoining rooms and, in an apartment, the neighbors — while killing very few of them. The same study found bugs would cross treated barriers to reach a heat source and feed, so pyrethroid “barriers” are not reliable either.

What actually works

  1. Inspection that takes real time

    The Rutgers program that achieved 92 percent elimination averaged 102 minutes per apartment for the initial inspection alone. Mattress and box spring seams, bed frame joints, headboard backs, nightstands, upholstered furniture seams, behind molding, loose wallpaper, cracks in hardwood, and in heavy infestations outlets and wall-to-ceiling junctions. A bed bug harbors in a crevice no wider than a toothpick, so the inspection is slow by necessity.

  2. Interceptors under every leg

    Passive pitfall monitors under bed and furniture legs are the highest-value tool in the entire job and they cost almost nothing. In systematic inspections of 2,372 apartments, brief visual inspection detected 72 percent of infestations while interceptors detected 89 percent — and about 49 percent of detected infestations were in units where the resident had no idea. Rutgers recommends 8 to 12 traps for a one-bedroom apartment, checked every one to two weeks. They stay down through the whole program and after it.

  3. Encasements on the mattress and box spring

    An encasement does not kill anything by itself. What it does is permanently remove the two largest harborages from play, turn the mattress into a smooth inspectable surface, and make throwing the bed away unnecessary. It has to stay on and stay intact — starvation inside a sealed encasement takes months at indoor temperatures, not weeks, and cheap vinyl tears.

  4. Steam, correctly

    Target 160 to 180°F at the surface, moving at 10 to 30 seconds per linear foot, with a triangular upholstery nozzle — a bare high-pressure nozzle blows live bugs off the surface and scatters them. Penetration is limited: roughly two and a half inches into a crack, less than an inch through fabric. Published data shows 100 percent egg mortality and 88 to 94 percent nymph and adult mortality. Steam goes first and dust goes after, once dry, because moisture measurably degrades dust performance.

  5. Silica gel — not diatomaceous earth

    A 2016 study in the Journal of Economic Entomology tested eight dusts three ways. In the discriminating assay — bugs briefly crossing a one-inch treated band — silica gel produced 100 percent mortality and every one of the other seven products, including 100 percent diatomaceous earth, produced 65 percent or less. Silica gel also transferred between insects, killing unexposed bugs at high rates; DE showed no comparable effect. The EPA notes bed bugs cannot become resistant to desiccants the way they do to other modes of action. Label rate matters, and pool-grade or food-grade DE carries a respiratory hazard the EPA warns about.

  6. Heat and targeted residual together

    Whole-room heat kills every life stage including eggs in a single session and penetrates furniture and mattress cores that no spray reaches. It has no residual. Targeted residual and dust give you the residual heat cannot. Rotating modes of action — and not repeating a pyrethroid that visibly failed — is the resistance answer. A field trial of a pyrethroid-plus-neonicotinoid combination produced a 98 percent reduction against 23 percent in untreated controls; chlorfenapyr has been shown effective across strains regardless of pyrethroid susceptibility.

  7. HEPA vacuuming, including after the bugs are dead

    Vacuuming quickly removes live and dead bugs and shed skins, though it cannot remove cemented eggs or bugs deep in cracks. Bags get sealed immediately and disposed of outside. There is a second reason to vacuum that most companies never mention: dust in infested homes carried an average of 54.6 micrograms of histamine per 100 mg, against under 2.5 in uninfested units in the same building — and a 2018 study found heat treatment that eradicated the bugs did not reduce histamine even three months later. Histamine is thermally stable. Physically removing the dust is the only thing that reduces it.

  8. Follow-up on a two-week cadence, and a real clearance standard

    Egg incubation runs five to ten days and egg-to-adult about 35 to 40 days at normal indoor temperature, which is exactly why a two-week recheck interval is correct and a six-week clean window is the right clearance standard. See the next section.

How many visits does it really take?

More than one, and we would rather say so up front than sell you a number we cannot hit.

Two peer-reviewed field programs give the honest answer. Cooper, Wang and Singh's community-wide program across four high-rise buildings and 358 apartments used biweekly service visits until elimination criteria were met, averaged seven service visits per successfully treated unit, and defined elimination as no bed bugs by interceptor catch, visual inspection and resident feedback across three consecutive visits spanning 42 days. The result was 92 percent elimination among treated apartments, a 98 percent reduction in mean counts, and a drop in building infestation rate from 15 percent to 2.2 percent over twelve months. A 2017 threshold-based study in Insects ran biweekly monitoring and treatment for up to 28 weeks, achieving 86 to 100 percent elimination depending on infestation level and method.

So when someone quotes you a one-visit guarantee, the question worth asking is what their clearance standard is. Ours is three consecutive clean checks over 42 days, with interceptors down the whole time. That is the standard the literature validated, and it is the one we hold ourselves to.

What does not work

  • Bug bombs. A 2012 study in the Journal of Economic Entomology tested three over-the-counter foggers against five field-collected populations and one susceptible lab strain. Field populations showed minimal mortality across all three products even after two hours of direct exposure. Only the susceptible lab strain approached full mortality, and only when it had no harborage available at all. The authors concluded foggers should not be recommended for bed bugs — no residual effect, and minimal if any penetration into typical harborage. Rutgers documents a case of nine foggers deployed in a single studio apartment with complete failure. The EPA also warns foggers carry fire and explosion risk.
  • Ultrasonic devices. Four commercial units tested in a 2012 study showed no significant difference in bed bug distribution against a no-sound control — neither repelled nor attracted.
  • “Natural” and essential-oil sprays. Rutgers researchers screened eleven products; only two exceeded 90 percent mortality, and only by direct spray on a visible insect. In the residual choice test — the realistic scenario, where bugs are hidden — the two best performers produced 1.7 percent and 10.0 percent mortality at ten days, against 90 percent for a conventional product under the same conditions. They also have little to no effect on eggs. A contact spray for a bug you can already see is the least useful moment in a bed bug job.
  • Diatomaceous earth on its own, moth balls, and rubbing alcohol. DE: 65 percent or less in the discriminating assay. Moth balls: under 50 percent of adults after a week, no effect on eggs. Rubbing alcohol: 50 percent maximum, and Rutgers explicitly recommends against it because the fire risk outweighs the minimal benefit. That is not theoretical — there are documented apartment fires started by people trying to kill bed bugs with alcohol.
  • Moving to the couch or the spare room. The most important “don't” on this page. Bed bugs follow host carbon dioxide and survive months without feeding. Moving where you sleep moves the infestation through the house. Keep sleeping in the treated, encased bed with interceptors under the legs — it keeps the population concentrated where it can be killed and measured.

How long can bed bugs survive without feeding?

Not a year, in your house. This is the most commonly misstated fact in the industry and it matters, because it is the basis for the worst advice people act on: “just move out for a while.”

A controlled starvation study at about 79°F measured mean survival by stage and strain. Susceptible strains ran roughly 90 to 128 days for later instars and adults. Pyrethroid-resistant strains — which is most modern field populations — died significantly faster, in the range of 28 to 73 days. The practical read is that at normal indoor temperatures, most stages die in roughly one to four months, with resistant field populations at the shorter end.

The “a year” figure comes from cold. University of Kentucky's guidance is one to four months in temperature-controlled buildings, but potentially a year or more at 55°F or below — an unheated vacant structure, a storage unit, an unconditioned outbuilding. So the answer to “can I just move out for a month and starve them?” is no, and vacating also redistributes them to wherever you go.

Do bed bugs spread disease?

No. The CDC's position is direct: bed bugs are not known to spread diseases to people. The documented effects are itching, sleep loss, occasional allergic reactions, secondary skin infection from scratching, and real anxiety and insomnia.

You will sometimes see a claim that bed bugs have been “implicated in 41 human diseases.” That is a historical association statement from older literature, not evidence of vector competence, and it should not be paraphrased as “they spread forty diseases.” There is laboratory work on Trypanosoma cruzi in bed bugs, and no epidemiological evidence of natural transmission to people. We will give you the CDC's answer, because it is the accurate one.

What is worth taking seriously is the psychological and financial cost, and the histamine residue described above. This is a pest that costs people sleep, dignity and money, and it deserves to be treated properly rather than dramatized.

How do you prepare for treatment?

Less than you have probably been told, and different depending on the method.

Before whole-room heat, these come out: pressurized and aerosol containers of any kind, including propane cylinders, butane lighters, spray paint and fire extinguishers; all pets, including fish and reptiles; all live plants; medications, vitamins and supplements; meltables such as candles, crayons, chocolate, cosmetics and vinyl records; flammables and solvents; firearms and live ammunition; and temperature-sensitive valuables such as oil paintings, glued wooden instruments, photographs and some antiques and veneers. Battery-powered devices, particularly lithium-ion, come out too.

What stays: furniture and clothing. Those are exactly the harborages the heat is meant to reach, and removing them removes the point of the treatment. That is the key difference from conventional prep, and it is the instruction people most often get backwards.

What not to do, in any scenario:

  • Do not bag up belongings and move them to another room, a car, a storage unit or a relative's house. Measured dispersal data shows marked bugs turning up in units neighboring five of six release apartments, with 92 percent of the adults that dispersed being female — and one mated female can found an entire new infestation. Moving your things is how one room becomes the whole house.
  • Do not throw out the mattress or box spring before treatment. Encasement preserves it, removes the harborage and makes it inspectable. Dragging an infested mattress through a hallway spreads bugs to every unit it passes. If something genuinely must go, the EPA's guidance is to slash the covers, remove the stuffing so it cannot be scavenged, mark it clearly, and arrange prompt pickup.
  • Do not spray over-the-counter pyrethroids before or between our visits, for both reasons in the resistance section above.
  • Do not deep-clean away all the evidence before the inspection. Fecal staining, cast skins and egg locations are the diagnostic data that drives where we treat.

One more thing worth saying to property managers: the Rutgers program that achieved 92 percent elimination in buildings housing elderly and disabled residents did not require residents to prepare their units at all. Staff performed decluttering assistance and supplied bags and laundry tokens. Heavy prep burdens pushed onto residents who physically cannot meet them are unnecessary for success and are a fair-housing exposure besides. A vendor who does the prep is solving a compliance problem, not just a labor one.

What about laundry?

The controlled numbers, from a 2010 study in the Journal of Economic Entomology, differ from the advice you will see most places:

  • Wash at 140°F on a 30-minute cycle: 100 percent mortality, all life stages including eggs.
  • Wash at 104°F: all adults and nymphs dead — but only 25 percent of eggs.
  • Dryer on hot for at least 30 minutes (roughly an eight-pound load): complete mortality, all stages. Ten minutes on hot killed only about 75 percent of nymphs and 85 percent of adults, and a cool cycle killed almost none.
  • Dry cleaning: complete mortality, all stages.

Common guidance says ten to twenty minutes in the dryer. The controlled data says ten minutes leaves 15 to 25 percent survivors. Use 30 minutes minimum on high heat. For items that cannot be washed, freezing works but the parameters are strict: 0°F for a minimum of about four days, and most domestic frost-free freezers cycle warmer than that — put a thermometer in yours before trusting it.

Bed bugs in apartments and multifamily housing

Treating one unit while the neighbors go untreated is a documented failure pattern, not an opinion.

A mark-release-recapture study across six apartments and 24 neighboring units recovered marked bugs in units neighboring five of the six release apartments within about two weeks, with movement of at least 2.5 metres from the sleeping area within units and some bugs crossing hallways more than twelve metres. Ninety-two percent of the adults that dispersed to neighboring units were female — already mated, and individually capable of starting a new infestation. Estimated populations ran from 2,433 to 14,291 bugs per apartment.

Against that, the building-wide approach produced 92 percent unit-level elimination and dropped the building infestation rate from 15 percent to 2.2 percent in a year. For a property manager in Columbia, Aiken, North Augusta or Augusta, the operational conclusion is that a complaint-driven, unit-by-unit response is a permanent expense and a building-wide program is a finite one. We scope it that way — see our multifamily and property management program.

Senior living deserves a specific mention: 57 percent of pest professionals nationally report treating bed bugs in nursing homes and assisted-care facilities, and the best-documented successful eradication program in the entire literature was run in senior and disabled high-rise housing. See our healthcare and senior living program.

Bed bugs in hotels, inns and short-term rentals

The legal picture in this two-state service area is not symmetrical, and it is worth knowing which side of the river you are on.

South Carolina has no bed-bug-specific statute. The 2024 EPA and NPMA compilation of state bed bug laws contains no entry for South Carolina. A 2013 bill that would have required hotel notice and landlord disclosure died in committee. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act at § 27-40-440 requires landlords to comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and to keep premises fit and habitable — but it contains no mention of pests, vermin or extermination, and neither does the tenant obligations section. Responsibility is therefore not statutorily assigned; it turns on the general habitability duty, the adopted local housing code and the lease. We would suggest checking your municipality's adopted property maintenance code rather than assuming.

Georgia has one enforceable rule, and it names bed bugs directly. Georgia Department of Public Health Rule 511-6-2-.13, covering tourist accommodations, requires that “effective and appropriate measures shall be taken to eliminate the presence of rodents and flies, roaches, bed bugs, and other insects on the premises.” The same rule requires restricted-use pesticides be applied only by licensed professionals, limits indoor fogging to licensed professionals operating an IPM program, and requires facilities to retain pesticide use records for at least 18 months documenting product, concentration, date, location, method, target pest and applicator. If you operate lodging in Augusta, Evans or Martinez, that recordkeeping requirement falls on you, and it is one of the things our service documentation is built to satisfy.

On liability generally, the case worth knowing is Mathias v. Accor Economy Lodging, decided by the Seventh Circuit in 2003. A downtown Chicago motel had a bed bug infestation management knew about for years; an exterminator had proposed treating all rooms for $500 and was refused; staff called the bugs “ticks” to avoid alarming guests; and a room marked “DO NOT RENT UNTIL TREATED” was rented anyway. The jury awarded $5,000 compensatory and $186,000 punitive per plaintiff, and the appellate court affirmed on willful and wanton conduct. The exposure was never the cost of treatment. It was the record showing they knew and did not act. Documented inspections and documented remediation are what that record looks like when it goes the other way. See our hotel and hospitality program.

What makes the CSRA and Midlands different?

February through April is our high-transience season, and it is unusual. The Aiken Triple Crown runs three consecutive March weekends — the Aiken Trials at the Historic Aiken Training Track, which draws over 10,000 spectators, the Aiken Spring Steeplechase, and Pacers and Polo at Whitney Polo Field — filling hotels, inns, guest cottages and barn apartments with out-of-state visitors and seasonal residents.

Then the Masters arrives in Augusta in April. The short-term rental surge around it is genuinely large: Masters week 2025 saw roughly $8.5 million in booked short-term rental revenue across April 7 to 13 alone, with more than 16,400 nights booked and an average daily rate of $514 against a normal month closer to $200. April 2024 generated $19.2 million for the month, against a typical Augusta month of $3 to 4 million. Thousands of private homes across Augusta, Evans, Martinez, North Augusta and Aiken become lodging for one week a year, hosting guests with luggage from all over the world — and then go back to being family homes, with none of the routine turnover inspection a hotel performs. The right windows are February and March for preventive inspection, and late April for detection and treatment.

August and January are the student-housing windows. The University of South Carolina's Columbia campus exceeded 40,000 students in fall 2025, including 7,829 new freshmen — the largest freshman class in its history, drawn from all 46 South Carolina counties and beyond. Combine an almost complete annual turnover of on- and off-campus housing with the dispersal data above, and August move-in is the operationally correct time to inspect Five Points, Olympia and Rosewood rentals rather than the correct time to discover a problem.

And a word about the “worst bed bug cities” lists. Neither Columbia nor Augusta appears on the 2025 Orkin ranking. That is not reassuring, because the list is built from one company's treatment volume in metro areas where it performed the most treatments — it measures market share, not incidence. A city served mostly by independent companies ranks low by construction. There is no scientific prevalence survey for South Carolina or the CSRA that we could find, and we are not going to invent one. What systematic inspection finds in multifamily housing generally is 12.3 percent of units infested, ranging from 3.8 to 29.5 percent by building, with about half of those residents unaware.

What is included in a bed bug service

  • Full inspection of beds, furniture, harborage and adjoining rooms, with findings photographed
  • Species and life-stage assessment, including whether eggs are present
  • Mattress and box spring encasements installed on the first visit
  • Interceptor monitors under bed and furniture legs, left in place through clearance
  • Steam applied at correct surface temperature and dwell, before any dust
  • Silica gel dust into harborage and voids at label rate
  • Whole-room heat where the situation calls for it, with remote sensors in the coldest locations
  • Targeted residual with rotated modes of action — not a repeated pyrethroid
  • HEPA vacuuming, including post-treatment for histamine and debris removal
  • Biweekly follow-up until three consecutive clean checks over 42 days
  • Written documentation suitable for a landlord, an insurer or a Georgia tourist-accommodation record

Where we work

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions is based in Windsor, South Carolina, and treats bed bugs across Aiken, North Augusta, Graniteville, Vaucluse, Warrenville, Beech Island, Edgefield, Columbia, Lexington, West Columbia, Cayce and Irmo, plus Augusta, Evans and Martinez in Georgia — homes, apartments, student rentals, hotels and inns, senior living communities and short-term rentals along the I-20 and I-26 corridors. Our vehicles and technicians can arrive unmarked where discretion matters. See all areas we serve.

Frequently asked questions

Can one treatment get rid of bed bugs?

Occasionally, for a very early, very contained infestation. Usually not. The peer-reviewed field programs that achieved 90 percent-plus elimination used biweekly visits and averaged about seven service visits per unit, with elimination defined as three consecutive clean checks over 42 days. The biology explains why: eggs incubate five to ten days and take 35 to 40 days to reach adulthood, so a two-week recheck interval and a six-week clean window are what the population dynamics require.

Should I throw away my mattress?

Almost never, and not before treatment. An encasement removes the harborage, preserves the mattress and makes it inspectable, and it costs a fraction of a replacement. Dragging an infested mattress through a hallway spreads bugs to every unit it passes, and buying a new one into an untreated room just gives them somewhere new to live. Disposal makes sense only for something like a heavily infested sofa that genuinely cannot be treated economically.

Is heat better than chemicals?

Heat is the strongest single knockdown tool and the only one that reliably kills eggs where they sit — and bed bugs show very limited capacity to evolve resistance to it. But it has zero residual, so reinfestation is possible the day after, and it cannot reach an untreated neighboring unit. Chemicals give residual but face 88 percent kdr resistance across US populations. The defensible answer is both, plus steam, silica gel, encasements and interceptor monitoring, with verification at the end.

Do I have to leave my home during treatment?

For whole-room heat, yes — along with pets, plants, medications, aerosols and anything meltable or flammable — typically for the working day, since a job runs six to eight hours from setup to takedown. For conventional treatment the re-entry interval is much shorter and depends on the products used; we will tell you exactly what it is before we start. What we will ask you not to do is sleep somewhere else afterward.

How did I get bed bugs?

Almost always travel or transported items — luggage, used furniture, a moving box, a guest, a hotel stay, a dorm move-in. It is not a cleanliness issue, and systematic inspections routinely find infestations in units where the resident had no idea. About half of the infestations found in one large apartment survey were in units whose residents did not know. We mention it because the shame around this pest keeps people from calling until the infestation is roughly three times more expensive to treat.

Why do I have bites but you found nothing?

Two possibilities and both are common. Bites are not diagnostic — many things bite, and reactions vary enormously between people, with some showing nothing at all. Or the population is genuinely there but very small: brief visual inspection detects about 72 percent of real infestations, while interceptors detect 89 percent over time. If we find nothing, we leave interceptors down and check again rather than declaring the room clear, and where certainty matters we can bring in a K-9 detection team.

Are the essential-oil products worth trying?

Not for a real infestation. Rutgers researchers screened eleven; only two exceeded 90 percent mortality, and only by directly spraying a bug you can already see. In the realistic test — residual, with bugs able to avoid treated surfaces — the best products produced 1.7 and 10 percent mortality at ten days. They also have little to no effect on eggs. If you want a non-chemical component that is actually supported, it is silica gel, steam, encasements and heat.

What is the difference between this and your K-9 bed bug detection?

Different questions. This page is treatment: kill the population, verify it is gone. K-9 detection answers whether bed bugs are present at all, and where — a point-in-time confirmation before a lease turns over, after a guest complaint, across a floor of rooms, or to clear a unit. Interceptors are the passive, weeks-long version of the same question. Most residential customers need treatment; hotels, property managers and anyone facing a dispute usually want both.

Do you work with landlords and tenants?

Yes, and we will document what we find and what we did for either side. South Carolina has no bed-bug-specific statute, so responsibility between landlord and tenant turns on the habitability duty, the local housing code and the lease — which means written, dated, photographed findings are worth a great deal when there is a disagreement. In Georgia, tourist accommodations have an explicit elimination duty and an 18-month pesticide recordkeeping requirement, and our reporting is built to satisfy it.

Can bed bugs live in a vacant unit for a year?

Only if it is cold. At normal indoor temperatures, controlled starvation studies put most stages at roughly one to four months — and pyrethroid-resistant field strains, which is most of them now, die faster than susceptible ones. The year-plus figure applies at about 55°F or below: an unheated vacant structure, a storage unit, an unconditioned outbuilding. Do not count on vacancy as a treatment.

title: Bed Bugs in Apartments: What Property Managers Need to Know
description: In a multifamily property, bed bugs are never really a single-unit problem — they're a building problem that happens to have been reported by one resident
h1: Bed Bugs in Apartments: What Property Managers Need to Know
body:
Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions  |  Windsor, SC  |  September 1, 2026

In a multifamily property, bed bugs are never really a single-unit problem — they’re a building problem that happens to have been reported by one resident. Bed bugs travel between units through wall voids, along utility and plumbing runs, and via shared laundry and hallways, which means that by the time one resident complains, the neighboring units are already the highest-risk units on the property. The property managers who handle this well do two things: they inspect surrounding units rather than just the reporting one, and they use a detection method that scales — because manually tearing apart dozens of units is not realistic.

How do bed bugs spread between apartment units?

Bed bugs move through the building’s own architecture. They travel through wall voids and along the penetrations that connect units — plumbing chases, electrical conduit, HVAC runs — and along baseboards and shared walls. They also move the way people do: through hallways, in shared laundry facilities, on furniture being moved in or out, and via maintenance and housekeeping equipment carried between units.

The practical consequence is that adjacency matters enormously. When one unit reports bed bugs, the units on either side, and the units directly above and below, are the most likely to be affected next — or already affected. A response that treats only the reporting unit and considers the matter closed is, in most cases, simply guaranteeing a second call in a few weeks from the unit next door.

Why does treating only the reporting unit fail?

Because you’re treating the unit that noticed, not necessarily the unit that started it or the units it has already reached. Bed bug infestations are frequently well established before anyone reports them — residents often don’t recognize the early signs, some people show no reaction to bites at all, and many residents delay reporting out of embarrassment or fear of being blamed or charged. So the reporting unit may be the second or third unit affected, not the first.

Treating that one unit while leaving the surrounding units unexamined pushes the problem around rather than solving it. Worse, treatment in one unit can drive bed bugs to move outward through wall voids into adjacent units, actively spreading the infestation. This is the single most expensive mistake in multifamily bed bug management, and it’s why the inspection footprint should always be wider than the complaint.

K9 INSIGHT  Treating only the unit that reported is the most expensive mistake in multifamily bed bug management — and treatment can actively drive bugs through wall voids into the units next door. Always inspect the adjacent units and the units above and below, as a default rather than an option.

How wide should the inspection footprint be?

At minimum, inspect the reporting unit plus the units sharing walls with it, and the units directly above and below. That’s the standard adjacency footprint, and it should be treated as the default rather than an optional extra. Depending on what those inspections turn up, the footprint may need to expand — if an adjacent unit is positive, its neighbors now warrant inspection too.

This is exactly where scale becomes the practical problem, and where K9 detection changes what’s feasible. Manually tearing apart six or eight units to inspect them properly is enormously time-consuming and disruptive to residents. A detection dog can clear a unit in minutes, which makes inspecting the full adjacency footprint — or sweeping an entire building — a realistic operational decision rather than a theoretical best practice you can’t actually afford to follow.

How should a property handle resident reporting?

The biggest obstacle to early detection in multifamily housing is that residents don’t report. They’re embarrassed, they worry they’ll be blamed, they fear they’ll be charged for treatment, or they worry about their lease. So they try to handle it themselves with store-bought sprays and foggers — which typically fail and often scatter bed bugs deeper into the structure and toward adjacent units — and by the time management finds out, a small problem has become a large, expensive, multi-unit one.

The fix is policy and culture. Make reporting easy and non-punitive, communicate clearly that bed bugs are not a cleanliness issue and residents won’t be shamed for reporting, and respond quickly and professionally when they do. A property where residents report early is a property where bed bugs stay contained and cheap. A property where residents hide the problem is one where you eventually treat a whole building.

What belongs in a multifamily bed bug policy?

A defensible policy should cover: how residents report (and an explicit statement that reporting is encouraged and non-punitive); the inspection protocol, including the adjacency footprint that will be inspected; who is responsible for what, including preparation requirements before treatment; the treatment approach and expected timeline; the verification step confirming treatment worked; and documentation of every inspection and action taken.

Documentation deserves particular emphasis. In multifamily housing, bed bug disputes with residents, and questions about landlord versus tenant responsibility, are common and can become contentious. A clear written policy plus a documented record of what was inspected, when, what was found, and what was done is what protects the property. Note that responsibility rules vary by jurisdiction and lease terms — for the specific legal obligations that apply to your property, that’s worth confirming with an attorney familiar with South Carolina landlord-tenant law.

Why does K9 detection make economic sense for a complex?

The economics are straightforward: the cost of inspecting is small, the cost of treating is large, and the cost of treating units that don’t need it — or missing units that do — is enormous. K9 detection lets you identify exactly which units have live activity, so you treat those and only those. On a property where a complaint might otherwise trigger a precautionary blanket treatment of a whole block of units, the savings are immediate and substantial.

There’s also a turnover and vacancy angle. Units out of service for treatment don’t produce revenue, and a complex with a reputation for bed bugs has a leasing problem. Proactive sweeps — at turnover, on a rotating schedule, or in response to a report — keep problems small, contained, and quiet. And as with hotels, the documented record of an active detection program is exactly what you want to have when a resident dispute or claim arises.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do bed bugs spread between apartments?

Through wall voids and along plumbing, electrical, and HVAC penetrations that connect units, along baseboards and shared walls, and through hallways, shared laundry, moved furniture, and maintenance equipment carried between units. That’s why adjacent units and the units above and below are the highest-risk units when one reports.

Should we inspect units next to a reported bed bug unit?

Yes — always, as a default. At minimum inspect the reporting unit plus the units sharing walls and the units directly above and below. If any of those are positive, expand the footprint further. Treating only the reporting unit typically guarantees another call from the unit next door in a few weeks.

Why is treating only the reporting unit a mistake?

Because the reporting unit may be the second or third unit affected, not the first, and treatment in one unit can actively drive bed bugs through wall voids into adjacent units. You end up pushing the problem around the building rather than solving it, which is the most expensive error in multifamily bed bug management.

Why don’t residents report bed bugs early?

Embarrassment, fear of being blamed or charged, and lease worries. So they try store-bought sprays and foggers, which usually fail and often scatter bed bugs deeper into the structure and toward neighboring units. By the time management learns of it, a small problem has become a large, multi-unit one.

How do we get residents to report sooner?

Make reporting easy and explicitly non-punitive, communicate clearly that bed bugs are not a cleanliness issue and no one will be shamed for reporting, and respond quickly and professionally. A property where residents report early keeps bed bugs contained and cheap; one where they hide it eventually treats a whole building.

What should a multifamily bed bug policy include?

How residents report and a non-punitive reporting statement; the inspection protocol including the adjacency footprint; responsibilities and preparation requirements; the treatment approach and timeline; a verification step confirming treatment worked; and documentation of every inspection and action. Responsibility rules vary by jurisdiction and lease, so confirm specifics with an attorney familiar with SC landlord-tenant law.

Does K9 detection save money on a large property?

Typically yes. Inspection is cheap; treatment is expensive. K9 detection identifies exactly which units have live activity so you treat those and only those, instead of blanket-treating a block of units precautionarily. It also reduces units out of service and protects the property’s leasing reputation.

Do you serve apartment complexes in South Carolina?

Yes. Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions provides K9 bed bug detection for apartment complexes and multifamily properties across Columbia, West Columbia, Aiken, Lexington, Cayce, Irmo, Charleston, Greenville, and surrounding areas. Call 803-226-3155 to discuss a program.

Need answers you can trust?

K9 bed bug detection for apartment complexes and multifamily properties across Columbia, Aiken, Lexington and South Carolina — inspect the full footprint, treat only what needs it.

Call  803-226-3155

Certified K9 teams • Honest recommendations • No scare tactics, no upselling

title: Bird Control in Aiken, SC
description: Bird control and exclusion for Aiken homes and businesses — netting, wire and ledge work that keeps pigeons, starlings and sparrows off your building.
h1: Bird Control in Aiken, SC

hero.eyebrow: AIKEN, SOUTH CAROLINA · BIRD CONTROL & EXCLUSION
hero.lead: Bird work in Aiken begins with identification, because the species decides the law. Rock pigeons, European starlings and house sparrows carry no federal protection. Almost every other bird on an Aiken roofline does, and so do its nest and eggs. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions builds exclusion first and treats deterrence as the supporting act.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Family-owned · Exclusion-first · Based in Windsor, a short drive from downtown Aiken

body:
Almost every bird call we take in Aiken arrives in the same shape. Something is roosting where it should not be, the droppings are past tolerance, and the caller wants it handled this week. The first question is not what to install. It is what bird that is. Federal law draws a hard line between three introduced species and everything else, and on the wrong side of it a nest clearance becomes an offence.

The second point: nothing you spray, hang or flash at a bird produces a permanent result. Birds are very good at working out which threats are real. What lasts is denying the perch, sealing the cavity and removing the food. That is the argument behind our bird control and exclusion service, applied here to a town with parapeted commercial blocks downtown, an unusual density of open barns, and a lot of industrial roof west and south of it.

1,106Bird species protected under the current Migratory Bird Treaty Act list at 50 CFR 10.13, revised at 88 FR 49310 effective 30 August 2023
232 daysFreeze-free window at the AIKEN 4 NE station, last spring freeze 22 March to first fall freeze 12 October
5,610Horses and ponies counted in Aiken County by the 2022 Census of Agriculture, across 1,132 farms

Which birds in Aiken may lawfully be touched, and which may not?

This is the point most bird control marketing skips. The Migratory Bird Treaty Act protects the species listed at 50 CFR 10.13, a list revised at 88 FR 49310, effective 30 August 2023, running to 1,106 species. Protection reaches the nest and the eggs, not only the adult, so once a protected species has an active nest on your parapet your options narrow sharply until that nest is finished. Three of the birds causing the most trouble on Aiken buildings are not on the list at all.

Rock pigeon

The ledge and parapet bird, and the one in the photograph above. Pigeons are excluded from treaty coverage as a human-introduced species rather than because their family was left out. See our pigeon profile.

European starling

A cavity nester, which is why starlings end up in soffits, gable vents and the gaps behind fascia boards. They are also the bird most likely to be standing in a feed bucket in an Aiken barn. Our European starling profile covers the cavity habit.

House sparrow

Small, tolerant of people, content to nest inside signage, light fittings and awning frames. Sparrows and starlings fall outside the treaties because their families were never covered — a different legal route, the same outcome. See the house sparrow profile.

Nearly everything else

American and fish crow, common and boat-tailed grackle, red-winged blackbird, brown-headed cowbird, the gulls, the egrets, Canada goose and the native swallows are all on the current list. Being handsome and familiar, several are the ones owners assume nobody cares about. That assumption is backwards.

Three federal provisions decide most of what happens next on a real job.

  • 50 CFR 21.100. No permit is required merely to scare or herd depredating migratory birds. Anyone selling you a permit to shoo birds has the rule the wrong way round.
  • 50 CFR 21.14. Any person may remove migratory birds from a building interior without a permit where they prevent normal use or create a health or safety risk. Handling must be humane, adhesive traps are prohibited, and the rule requires you to prevent reentry by patching holes or fitting exclusion devices. The federal government wrote exclusion into its own exemption.
  • 50 CFR 21.150. A depredation order for blackbirds, cowbirds, crows, grackles and magpies allows control without a federal permit where serious damage is occurring, non-lethal methods first each year. It does not extend to gulls, vultures, geese, herons, egrets or doves.

SCDNR issues depredation permits free of charge, valid thirty days and renewable, and notes that additional permits may be required for federally protected birds. Two layers, not one.

Why does exclusion outlast every deterrent you can buy?

Because a bird is not frightened by a thing. It is frightened by a consequence, and it stops being frightened when the consequence never arrives. Tape, plastic owls, sonic units and gels depend on a threat the property never carries out, and a flock works that out within weeks. Exclusion needs the bird to believe nothing. The ledge is occupiable or it is not.

The difference shows clearest on a cornice. A strip of repellent gel is fifteen minutes of labour, and pigeons learn to stand on its dried skin, or on the debris collecting over it, inside a season. A 45-degree ledge conversion is a fabricated slope in aluminium, stainless or polycarbonate that deletes the flat plane. One is a consumable; the other is permanent.

ApproachWhat it doesService life
Stainless spikesDenies landing on ledges, sills and sign tops; fails if debris builds a platformLong, if specified and cleaned
Post-and-wireUnstable perch on narrow ledges and railings; least intrusive on a historic facadeLong, with tension checks
45-degree ledge conversionRemoves the horizontal surface, so the perch stops existingPermanent
NettingEncloses courtyards, canopies, barn bays and equipment wellsLong, tensioned and inspected
Sealing soffits and ventsEnds starling and sparrow cavity nesting at source, which no perch deterrent touchesPermanent
Gels and pastesSurface discouragement; degrades, collects debris, gets learned aroundMonths
Sonic and visual scaresBrief displacement; habituation is documented across every deterrent classDays to weeks
Falconry patrolBreaks an entrenched flock’s habit of using the siteHolds while flown

What does Aiken’s building stock offer a bird?

The Laurens Street commercial blocks

Downtown sits on the original 1834 plan, wide streets divided by boulevards, the medians original to the plat. What matters for birds is above eye level: parapet copings, cornices, recessed sign bands and awning frame tops. Pigeons roost on parapets and loaf on awnings; sparrows nest inside the frames. Because the blocks are continuous, a displaced flock moves along the row, so we scope the run rather than the one address that called.

The Alley and outdoor dining

The Alley is a pedestrian lane of restaurants, rocking-chair seating and a taproom pouring forty-eight taps. Outdoor dining is a food source with a roof over it, and sparrows learn a patio faster than any other bird. Half the fix is exclusion above the seating, half is bin lids. See our restaurant and food service program.

Brick storefronts, churches and civic buildings

Masonry parapets, bell openings, louvred towers and deep window reveals. Appearance constrains the fix, so post-and-wire or a discreet slope beats a bank of spikes. Downtown holds South Carolina’s twelfth designated Cultural District, and Schofield and Parkway District anchors such as Friendship Baptist Church are where a visible install is the wrong answer.

Winter Colony houses and their outbuildings

Winter Colony Historic District I was National Register listed on 27 November 1984 and holds around thirty-five properties built between roughly 1882 and 1948, with large houses, outbuildings and stables on the tree-lined streets and unpaved roads of Highland Park Drive, Lancaster Street and Grace Avenue. Deep eaves, open porches, cupolas. The main house is rarely the problem. The carriage house and the stable are.

Warehouse and light industrial

Sage Mill industrial park, the Bridgestone plant at Graniteville and the Kimberly-Clark operation at Beech Island anchor a corridor of large-footprint buildings: high open bays, exposed purlins that read to a pigeon as a nesting shelf, dock doors open through the shift. Netting the bay and sealing the roofline is the job. See our warehouse and distribution program and, where product is exposed, our food processing program.

Campus and heavy industrial

USC Aiken passed 4,200 students in fall 2025 with residence halls full: covered walkways, breezeways, light structures, rooftop plant and food service. Twelve miles south, the Savannah River Site spreads across 310 square miles, and its pipe racks and transfer buildings pose the same problem as any steel estate. Campus work runs through our schools and student housing program.

Why does horse country change the problem?

A barn is, from a bird’s point of view, an unusually generous building. Warm, dry, open at both ends, structural ledges at every height, food on the floor. The 2022 Census of Agriculture counted 5,610 horses and ponies in Aiken County across 1,132 farms, alongside 4,057 acres of corn for grain. The equestrian half is concentrated tightly — the Aiken Training Track, the Steeplechase Racecourse, Whitney Field, Stable View, the Horse District and the 2,400-acre Three Runs Plantation.

  • Spilled grain. Sweet feed on an aisle floor is the most reliable starling and sparrow magnet on a horse property. Birds do not colonise barns because they are barns. They colonise them because feeding time is predictable.
  • Open structure. Bays open at the gable, unsealed soffits, hay lofts with no closure and exposed purlin runs give cavity nesters unlimited choice. Netting a run of bays beats any amount of work on individual perches.
  • Standing water. Troughs, wash racks and automatic waterers supply drinking and bathing water year-round, and bathing birds foul what the horses drink. Trough covers shift the picture faster than owners expect.
  • Competition at feed. Starlings work buckets, tubs and hay in flocks, take a share of the ration and foul the rest. Since starlings carry no federal protection, the constraints are physical rather than legal.

What about the barn swallows?

Barn swallows are native migratory birds. They sit on the protected list at 50 CFR 10.13, and that protection covers the nest and the eggs. The mud cup on the beam over your wash rack is not something you may simply scrape off in the breeding season, and no depredation order changes that — the order at 50 CFR 21.150 covers blackbirds, cowbirds, crows, grackles and magpies. Swallows are not on it.

That makes timing the plan rather than a convenience. Exclusion aimed at swallow-occupied structures belongs outside the nesting window, when nests are inactive. Once eggs or young are present, you wait. Preventing new nests from being started is a different act from destroying an active one, which is why we push barn clients toward the cool months instead of June.

We will not publish state nesting-window dates here, because we could not verify a South Carolina document that sets them and we are not going to invent dates carrying legal weight. At the site visit we confirm the position with the relevant federal and state wildlife offices for the species present. If a contractor quotes barn exclusion in nesting season without raising any of this, that is your answer about the contractor.

What do accumulated droppings actually do?

You will see claims that birds carry sixty or more diseases transmissible to humans. We could find no agency source for that figure, so we do not use it. Here is what is documented.

  • Histoplasmosis. Histoplasma lives in the environment, mainly across central and eastern states, and spreads in bird and bat droppings that mix into soil. The fungus grows in the droppings; the CDC does not describe birds as carriers. The risk is disturbing large accumulations in enclosed or poorly ventilated spaces — an attic, a disused loft, an old tower.
  • Cryptococcus neoformans. Present worldwide, with soil, bird droppings and decaying wood among its sources, and infections occurring overwhelmingly in people with weakened immune systems. Worth stating accurately at a healthcare site.
  • Uric acid corrosion. Droppings are acidic and attack what buildings are made of — painted metal, galvanised flashing, roofing membranes, HVAC casings, stone and mortar joints. On a historic facade that is a conservation problem, not a cleaning problem.
  • Blocked gutters, drains and scuppers. Nesting material and droppings block them, water backs up, and the water finds the structure. Aiken County averages 50.77 inches of precipitation a year on the 1991 to 2020 normals — a lot of water looking for the path a bird built.
  • Ectoparasites left behind. Bird mites and other nest arthropods do not leave with the bird. Pull a nest out of a soffit and do nothing else, and they disperse into the space looking for a host. Nest removal without treating and sealing the void is half a job.

Where does falconry fit, and where does it not?

Falconry abatement flies trained raptors on a planned patrol to break a flock’s habit of using a property. It changes a site’s risk profile. It does not eliminate a population.

Two controlled landfill study programmes in the UK are the best comparative evidence that exists. One flew trained falcons and hawks against gulls and corvids and found neither group eliminated all scavenging birds, though falcons reduced numbers more consistently. The wider programme ran forty trials over two years across six landfills against nine techniques and concluded that birds could not be eliminated, with habituation varying significantly by method.

Two more points for a quote comparison. There is no FAA approval scheme for falconry abatement or any other wildlife deterrent method, so a claim of federal approval describes something that does not exist. And no published study covers falconry at retail centres, campuses or equestrian venues. For an Aiken property, falconry is most defensible as a knockdown phase on an entrenched roost while exclusion goes in behind it. Our falconry bird abatement page sets out the permitting and the evidence in full. Geese are a separate discipline with their own federal control orders, handled through our Aiken goose control service.

When in the year should this work happen?

The calendar is a legal question before a convenience one. The AIKEN 4 NE station records a last spring freeze on 22 March and a first fall freeze on 12 October, giving 232 freeze-free days against a county mean annual temperature of 64.1 degrees F. A long mild season means a long breeding season, so the window for unrestricted work on buildings hosting protected species is narrow.

  • Late autumn through winter — the build window. October to February is when protected nests are inactive, barns are quieter, and netting, ledge conversion and soffit sealing proceed without a timing constraint. This is when exclusion goes in.
  • February and early March — before the season fills. The Aiken Triple Crown runs three consecutive March weekends. More than ten thousand spectators turn out for the Trials at the Historic Aiken Training Track, then come the Spring Steeplechase and Pacers & Polo at Whitney Polo Field. Work at a venue or an inn wants to be finished before it.
  • Spring — identification season. New nesting starts and the wrong decision is easiest to make. If a nest appears, the first action is to identify and photograph the species, not to remove it.
  • Summer — constrained. Protected nests are active and options narrow. Work on unprotected species and unoccupied structures continues, with deterrent maintenance and sanitation.

How does an exclusion job run?

  1. Identify the species and photograph the evidence

    Before anything is priced. Which birds, how many, where they roost as against where they feed and nest, and whether any nest is active. The species sets the legal envelope and the envelope sets the scope. This is also where we say if the answer is sanitation rather than hardware.

  2. Survey the structure, not the complaint

    Roof plane, parapet, cornice, sign band, soffit line, gable and ridge vents, exhausts, canopy frames and open bays. Birds use buildings as systems. Treating one ledge and leaving the soffit open moves the problem twenty feet and lets you believe you fixed it.

  3. Confirm the permitting position in writing

    Whether anything on site needs a federal permit or falls under a depredation order, whether an SCDNR permit is appropriate, and whether the calendar constrains the work. Where a protected species is involved we set out what is lawful, with the citation, so the position is on the record.

  4. Clean and remediate before installing

    Droppings and nest material come out first, with respiratory protection where accumulation is heavy and the space enclosed, and voids treated for the mites left behind. Netting over fouled surfaces traps the problem underneath, a common cause of a job that looks finished and is not.

  5. Install the physical work

    Netting, post-and-wire, spikes, ledge conversion, vent and soffit closure, and repair of the defects that let birds in. Fixings are chosen against the substrate: historic masonry, standing seam metal, EPDM and painted timber each want different treatment, and getting it wrong damages the building you were hired to protect. See our repairs and exclusion page.

  6. Fix the reason they came, then re-inspect

    Spilled feed, open bins, unlidded troughs, dock spillage, patio waste, standing water. This is the part most often declined and most often regretted. Then photographs, a written scope, and a scheduled return.

What is included?

  • Species identification and active-nest assessment before any pricing
  • Written statement of the permitting position, with citations
  • Dropping and nest removal, with treatment of ectoparasites in the void
  • Netting to courtyards, canopies, barn bays, parking structures and equipment wells
  • Spike, post-and-wire and 45-degree ledge conversion to ledges, sills and signage
  • Soffit, gable, ridge and exhaust vent sealing with correct hardware rather than expanding foam
  • Interior bird removal under the federal building-interior rule, entry sealed
  • Photographed before-and-after documentation for an inspector or insurer
  • Scheduled re-inspection of tension, fixings and debris

What will we not sell you?

  • Plastic owls, hawk silhouettes and reflective tape. They work briefly and then stop, because nothing follows the threat. The clearest example of habituation in the whole trade.
  • A nest knock-down without an identification. The species decides whether that is routine maintenance or a federal offence, and you cannot settle it with a squint from the ground.
  • An effectiveness percentage for falconry. No study supports one for any commercial setting, and the landfill work states plainly that birds could not be eliminated.

Who licenses this work in South Carolina?

Structural pest work in this state runs through the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation — the licensing body is the land-grant university, not a state agriculture department. The category is 7A, Industrial, Institutional, Structural and Health-Related Pest Control. A commercial firm needs a DPR business licence, a Designated Certified Applicator at every location, and general liability cover of at least $100,000 combined single limit.

Above that sits the federal wildlife layer, which pesticide licensing does not touch. Anything involving a species on the 50 CFR 10.13 list, including nest and eggs, is governed by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act and, where lethal action is contemplated, by a depredation permit or order.

Falconry adds a third layer, requiring a state falconry permit at the appropriate level plus the federal Special Purpose Abatement permit. South Carolina regulation is explicit that a Master Falconer may conduct abatement holding that federal permit, while a General Falconer may do so only as a sub-permittee, and SCDNR inspects facilities before a permit issues. If a vendor cannot say which layer each part of their proposal sits under, that is worth knowing before the scaffold goes up.

Which Aiken properties call us most?

Downtown retail and food service along Laurens Street and in The Alley, where the fix has to be invisible from the pavement. Lodging, from The Willcox, operating since 1898, through to the chain hotels on the highway corridors, where a fouled entrance canopy is a review problem before it is a maintenance one. Warehouse and light industrial along the Sage Mill corridor. Institutional buildings at USC Aiken and Aiken Technical College. Healthcare, where Aiken Regional Medical Centers runs 273 licensed acute-care beds and an immunocompromised population makes fouling a genuine concern. Multi-site scoping goes through our commercial programmes.

Residential calls cluster on starlings and sparrows in soffits and gable vents, and pigeons on a chimney or rear elevation. The city holds 15,345 housing units, much of the older stock carrying the open eaves and unscreened vents cavity nesters need. If you hear scratching above a ceiling rather than seeing birds outside, that may not be birds at all, and our Aiken K-9 rodent detection service settles it faster.

Where do we cover?

Our base is 320 Wendy Lane in Windsor, a short drive from the city. Regular coverage runs through downtown and the Laurens Street corridor, the Winter Colony districts and the Horse District, the Parkway District and Schofield, Virginia Acres, Crosland Park and Forest Heights, Woodside Plantation, Cedar Creek, Houndslake, the Kalmia developments and Three Runs Plantation, out to Montmorenci, Beech Island, New Ellenton and Jackson, and west into Horse Creek Valley at Graniteville, Vaucluse, Warrenville, Langley and Bath. Beyond the county we work North Augusta, Columbia and Lexington, and across the river into Augusta. The full list sits on our service areas page; if the question is bed bugs rather than birds, that is our Aiken K-9 bed bug detection page.

Frequently asked questions

Is it legal to remove a bird nest from my building in Aiken?

It depends entirely on the species. Rock pigeon, European starling and house sparrow nests carry no federal protection. Nests of species on the list at 50 CFR 10.13 are protected along with their eggs, and that list runs to 1,106 species. Several are hard to tell apart from the ground, so identification comes first. Photograph the nest and the adult bird and let us confirm.

Are barn swallows protected in South Carolina?

Yes. Barn swallows are native migratory birds on the federal protected list, and the protection covers the nest and eggs, not just the adult. No depredation order applies to them; the order at 50 CFR 21.150 covers blackbirds, cowbirds, crows, grackles and magpies only. So exclusion aimed at swallow structures belongs outside the nesting window, and preventing a nest is a different matter from destroying one.

Do bird spikes work, or do birds just nest between them?

They work on the surfaces they are designed for — ledges, sills, sign tops, pipe runs — and they fail when specified for the wrong surface, or when debris builds between the rows until it forms a platform. That is a specification and maintenance issue, not a defect in the method. On a wide parapet a ledge conversion is usually better, because it removes the flat plane instead of defending it.

Will falconry get rid of the pigeons on my building?

It will move them, and while it is flown it will keep them moving. It will not eliminate them. The two controlled landfill study programmes that form the best available evidence both concluded that birds could not be eliminated. For a single structure with a defined roost, exclusion is cheaper and permanent. Falconry earns its place on large, entrenched sites while the physical work goes in.

Does the FAA approve falconry for airfields?

No. It approves no wildlife deterrent method, because no such scheme exists. Any vendor claiming federal approval or certification is describing something that is not real. At an airfield, falconry operates as one contracted tool inside a biologist-led wildlife hazard management programme run under the airport’s own plan.

How dangerous are pigeon droppings in an old Aiken building?

The real risk is disturbing a large, long-standing accumulation in an enclosed, poorly ventilated space such as an attic, loft or tower. Histoplasma grows in droppings that mix into soil and is present across central and eastern states, which warrants respiratory protection and proper remediation. Droppings on an open car park do not carry the same exposure.

Birds keep getting into my warehouse. How fast can they come out?

The way in is usually dock doors held open, damaged personnel doors or gaps at the roofline. Rule 50 CFR 21.14 lets anyone remove migratory birds from a building interior without a permit where they prevent normal use or create a health or safety risk, with humane handling and no adhesive traps, and it requires the entry point to be closed afterwards. Sealing stops the repeat.

Starlings are eating my horses’ feed. What actually stops them?

Three things together. Feed discipline first: sweep spillage, lid the bins, shorten the window loose feed sits available. Then exclusion of the structure they nest in, meaning gable ends, soffits and open bays rather than individual perches. Then netting where a bay can be closed. Starlings carry no federal protection, so the constraint is structural.

Can exclusion go on a historic facade without damaging it?

Yes, but the fixing method matters more than the product. On historic masonry the aim is to fix into mortar joints rather than face brick or stone, to use non-staining stainless components, and to favour low-visibility systems such as post-and-wire over banks of spikes. Downtown Aiken and the Winter Colony districts both need that approach.

How soon can you look at a bird problem in Aiken?

Site visits are normally within the week from Windsor, and an interior bird in a plant or warehouse is urgent, because the regulation and the disruption point the same way. Installation is scheduled around species and season, which is why we steer barn owners toward the autumn and winter window.

Send us the building, a photograph of the birds if you have one, and what has already been tried. We will identify the species, tell you what the law allows for that species, and price the physical work that ends it — and if sanitation alone would fix it, we will say that instead. hero.lead: Downtown Columbia is a masonry city, and masonry produces ledges by the thousand. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions puts a name to the bird first, because federal law splits three introduced species from every native one, and then shuts the roost down with netting, wire and slope conversion rather than a product that wears off.
