body:
Ask a pigeon what it wants and the answer is dull: a flat surface wide enough to stand on, high enough to feel safe, with something edible within a short flight. Columbia supplies all three at a scale smaller Midlands towns do not. Stone cornices and string courses, parapeted flat roofs, deep porticos around the capitol complex, parking-deck beams, covered walkways, and a hospitality quarter where food waste leaves a building nightly.

Two questions govern every job here, and neither is which product to fit. Which bird do you have, because that decides what is lawful. And what part of the structure created the opportunity, because that is what has to change. Both sit at the centre of our bird control and exclusion service, worked out here for a capital city carrying seventeen National Register historic districts.

607Contributing buildings in the Melrose Heights–Oak Lawn–Fairview Historic District, the largest of Columbia’s districts — National Register reference 16000756, listed 2016
142,500 sq ftColumbia Metropolitan Convention Center, open since September 2004 and host to more than 8,000 events and 3.9 million visitors since
21,045Accommodation and Food Services jobs in Richland County, 9.5 percent of employment, on US Census employment-by-industry data

Which bird is standing on the ledge, and what does that decide?

Everything downstream. The Migratory Bird Treaty Act protects the species carried at 50 CFR 10.13, revised at 88 FR 49310 and effective 30 August 2023, now 1,106 birds, and protection extends to the nest and the eggs in it. Three of the birds fouling most Columbia buildings are absent from that list; a fourth group that looks just as ordinary is squarely on it.

Rock pigeon

The cornice bird, and the one photographed above. Its wider family sits inside the treaties, but the feral bird is excluded as a human import. More in our pigeon profile.

European starling

Starlings want a hole, not a shelf: louvred gable vents, lifted flashing, the void behind a fascia. Ledge spikes do nothing about any of that. Detail in the European starling profile.

House sparrow

Content to raise a brood inside an illuminated sign or a light housing. Sparrows sit outside the treaties for a reason unlike the pigeon’s: their family was never brought under them. See the house sparrow profile.

The birds people assume are fair game

Chimney swifts, swallows, purple martins, crows, grackles, blackbirds, cowbirds, herons, egrets, gulls and Canada geese are all listed, and several nest on exactly the old brick this city is full of.

Three federal provisions carry most of the weight.

  • 50 CFR 21.100. The text reads that “no permit is required merely to scare or herd depredating migratory birds.” Hazing is not a licensed act, and a pitch built on holding permission to frighten birds has the rule upside down.
  • 50 CFR 21.14. Anyone may take a migratory bird out of a building interior, unpermitted, when the bird stops the space being used normally or puts health and safety in question. Humane handling is required, glue traps are ruled out, and sealing the way in afterwards forms part of the exemption.
  • 50 CFR 21.150. A standing depredation order reaching blackbirds, cowbirds, crows, grackles and magpies where serious damage occurs, non-lethal measures attempted first in each calendar year. Its reach stops short of gulls, vultures, geese, herons and egrets.

SCDNR issues depredation permits free, valid thirty days and renewable, and warns that protected birds may require further authority.

What counts as a ledge in a city built out of masonry?

A pigeon needs a surface about as wide as its feet with a wall at its back; a starling needs a cavity the width of a fist. This is the downtown inventory.

Cornices, string courses and ornament

The projecting bands that give a masonry elevation its shadow lines are the most productive pigeon surface in the city, and statuary, clock surrounds and sign tops add small platforms that foul onto what the owner values most. Nothing announces it until the wall below stains.

Parapets and copings

A parapeted flat roof hands a flock a wind-sheltered perimeter with sightlines everywhere, and copings run wide and continuous, so treating one bay relocates the birds along the run.

Porticos, entablatures and columns

The capitol complex and the buildings around it are the classical end of the problem: columned porticos create sheltered runs at capital height, under an entablature no hose reaches.

Decks, walkways and the service side

Open-sided parking decks are the most under-treated bird structure downtown: beam flanges, ledger angles and light housings make excellent roosts, and the cars beneath take the result. Dock canopies, bay lintels, corral walls and rooftop condenser frames do the same over the point where waste leaves the building.

Why does exclusion outlive everything sold as an alternative?

Because deterrence is an argument with the bird and exclusion is not. Every repellent asks a flock to accept a threat the property never carries out, and pigeons test it daily. Exclusion makes no claim. The surface can be stood on, or it cannot.

Put the two side by side on a limestone string course. A bead of gel is finished once its skin hardens and grit settles into it, and on porous stone it leaves a residue long after the birds return. A fabricated 45-degree slope deletes the horizontal plane instead. One is a consumable; the other alters the building once.

MeasureWhere it belongs downtownHonest service life
45-degree slope conversionWide cornices, copings, string courses, sign topsAs long as the fabrication survives
Sealing soffits, gables and exhaustsStarling and sparrow cavities, which no perch product touchesPermanent, with hardware not foam
Tensioned nettingParking decks, light wells, plant enclosures, canopiesYears, given tension checks
Post-and-wireNarrow ledges, railings and ornament, where visibility is the constraintYears, if retensioned
Stainless spikeSills, pipe runs and lintels; fails when debris bridges the rowsLong, if cleaned
Falconry patrolLarge entrenched sites, as a knockdown phase alongside installationOnly while it is flown

None of it survives an unmanaged food source.

How is a contributing building different to work on?

A great deal, and it starts before anyone opens a toolbox. Seventeen National Register historic districts sit inside the city, and the contributing counts are not trivial. Melrose Heights–Oak Lawn–Fairview, a streetcar suburb with a concentration of “airplane” bungalow cottages, holds 607 contributing buildings. Elmwood Park, established by public auction in 1905 and filled out with brick bungalows in the 1920s and 1930s, holds 219 contributing of 279 homes. Forest Hills, mostly built after 1927, holds 215 contributing buildings, nine sites and one structure.

Waverly, Columbia’s first suburban development, built from about 1898 to 1925 and recognised by the National Park Service African American Civil Rights Network in February 2021, holds 132. Granby Mill Village, grouped around a Romanesque Revival mill of 1896 to 1897 with saltbox operatives’ houses, holds 97. Columbia Historic District I on Arsenal Hill holds nine, every one antebellum — few enough that an error on any of them is a permanent loss.

  • Attachment becomes a design question. Netting rides on a tensioned cable perimeter, and that perimeter has to land somewhere. On a contributing facade that means mortar joints and existing fixing points, never dressed stone or a moulded profile.
  • Adhesion is rarely the right tool. Glued spike bases and gel beads look non-invasive and behave otherwise, because the adhesive eventually has to come off. On soft brick and lime mortar the removal is the damage.
  • Reversibility is the test. If taking the system off in twenty years means grinding or solvent across an ornamental profile, it was the wrong specification.

The city maintains conservation districts and protection areas of its own, among them Cottontown/Bellevue, Elmwood Park, Granby, Melrose Heights/Oak Lawn, Oakwood Court and Wales Garden. We will not tell you what Columbia’s code requires of your elevation: we could not read that code from a desk, and we do not publish guesses about anything carrying legal weight. We confirm the review position with the city and the owner’s architect in writing first. A failed component is usually part of the story, which is where our repairs and exclusion work takes over.

Where do droppings stop being a nuisance and become a compliance problem?

At the point where they land on the path food travels. The Congaree Vista turned from warehousing into a restaurant, retail and hotel district in the late 1990s and early 2000s, and the Columbia Metropolitan Convention Center opened alongside it in September 2004 at 142,500 square feet, taking over 8,000 events and 3.9 million visitors since. Accommodation and food services accounts for 21,045 Richland County jobs, and all of it runs on loading docks, dumpster corrals and covered entries.

Those three surfaces turn birds into an inspection finding rather than an eyesore. A dock canopy with a roosting line above drops onto the pallets below, a corral wall perches a flock over open waste, and a covered entry turns a fouled soffit into a slick threshold. One correction is worth making, because plenty of competitor pages still have it wrong: since 1 July 2024 retail food establishments in South Carolina have been inspected by the South Carolina Department of Agriculture, not DHEC, which was split into the Department of Public Health and the Department of Environmental Services. SCDA covers roughly 24,000 establishments under SC Regulation 61-25.

Kitchen and dock work runs through our restaurant and food service program, guest-facing elevations through our hotel program, portfolios through our commercial programs.

What does a settled roost cost the building?

A figure circulates in this trade putting the number of human diseases spread by birds above sixty. We looked for an agency source behind it and there is not one, so it appears nowhere in our material. The documented harms are narrower and quite bad enough.

  • Histoplasmosis. Histoplasma grows in soil enriched by bird and bat droppings and is concentrated in the central and eastern United States. The CDC frames it as an organism of the environment rather than something a bird carries about with it. The exposure that matters is aerosolising an old deposit inside an enclosed, poorly ventilated space.
  • Cryptococcus neoformans. Distributed worldwide in soil, bird droppings and decaying wood, and causing disease almost entirely in people whose immune systems are already compromised. Real weight on a hospital campus, very little on a warehouse roof.
  • Uric acid attack on the fabric. Droppings are acidic: they etch painted and galvanised metal, degrade membranes, corrode HVAC casings and open mortar joints. On a contributing building that is irreversible loss of original material.
  • Blocked gutters, scuppers and drains. Nest material dams a scupper, water backs up over the upstand and goes into the structure. Richland County averages 47.75 to 48.11 inches of rain a year on the 1991 to 2020 normals.
  • Slip risk on a wet entry. Fresh droppings on smooth stone or polished concrete under a covered entrance are genuinely slippery, and that is where nobody looks down. This one turns up in an incident report rather than a laboratory.
  • The parasites left behind. Mites and the other arthropods living in nest material stay put once the birds have gone. Pull the material out of a soffit without treating the void, and they work inward looking for a new host.

What does a hospital campus need that a strip mall does not?

A different standard of evidence. Prisma Health Richland runs 641 beds plus 124 at the affiliated Heart Hospital, a Level I Trauma Center and a freestanding children’s hospital, and is the sole regional referral centre for the Midlands; health care is Richland County’s largest employment sector at 33,974 people. Work over an ambulance bay is sequenced around clinical access, remediation near air intakes needs containment agreed with facilities first, and the documentation has to be filable. Senior living carries the same profile and runs through our healthcare and senior living program.

What about chimney swifts and swallows on old brick?

They are the constraint owners discover too late. Chimney swifts and the native swallows are on the 50 CFR 10.13 list, and the protection covers the nest and the eggs, not only the adult. The depredation order at 50 CFR 21.150 does not reach them; it stops at blackbirds, cowbirds, crows, grackles and magpies. A disused masonry flue with swifts in it is not a chimney you may cap this week.

The distinction that keeps you lawful is between preventing a nest and destroying one. Capping, screening and netting an unoccupied structure ahead of the season is ordinary maintenance; over an active nest it is not. Columbia’s older districts and mill village stock offer the open flues and sheltered ornament these species have used for generations.

We do not print South Carolina nesting-window dates, because no state document fixing them could be verified and a date carrying federal consequences is not something to guess at. At survey we check with the office holding jurisdiction and write down what we are told.

Which products do we refuse to sell?

  • Plastic owls, rotating reflectors and holographic ribbon. A fortnight of displacement, then scenery. Habituation to deterrents carrying no consequence is the best-demonstrated effect in the field.
  • A nest knocked down before anyone identified the builder. The species is the whole difference between maintenance and a federal violation.
  • A percentage figure for falconry, or federal approval of it. No study produces a success rate for a commercial setting. No FAA approval scheme exists for falconry abatement, or for any wildlife deterrent method at all, so a vendor advertising one is describing a certification nobody issues.

Where does falconry honestly fit in a downtown program?

A falconry program flies a trained raptor over the site on a planned patrol until the flock no longer reads the place as safe ground. It shifts a site’s risk profile; it does not remove a population, and we will not describe it as though it does.

The evidence base is small and worth knowing. Baxter and Allan, in the Wildlife Society Bulletin in 2006, flew trained hybrid falcons and hawks at gulls and corvids on UK landfills; neither raptor group cleared every scavenging bird. The larger dataset from that programme ran forty trials over two years at six landfills against nine techniques, and its conclusion was blunt: “Birds could not be eliminated but numbers were reduced to different extents by different techniques.” Cook, Rushton, Allan and Baxter, in Environmental Management in 2008, found that methods carrying a genuine consequence lasted longest.

Translated to a Columbia block, falconry is rarely the right first purchase for one building with one roost, where exclusion costs less and does not stop the day the patrol ends. It earns its keep on a large entrenched site, as a knockdown phase while the physical work is built behind it. Permitting sits on our falconry bird abatement page.

Do the rivers change where birds go?

They organise the movement. The Congaree is formed in Columbia by the confluence of the Saluda and the Broad near the Piedmont fall line; the Columbia Canal, cut between 1820 and 1824 and rebuilt to reopen in 1891, runs alongside them, breached in the October 2015 flooding and still awaiting repair as of February 2024. The Three Rivers Greenway links riverfront parks on both banks. A corridor of water and cover through a city is a highway for anything with wings, so a riverside building rarely stays clear on work at that address alone, and we scope the elevation facing the corridor first. Waterfowl sit under their own federal control orders rather than ledge hardware, and go to our Columbia goose control service.

How does the calendar constrain the work?

Season is a legal question before a scheduling one. The state climatology office records a last spring freeze of 1 April and a first fall freeze of 13 October at Columbia Metropolitan Airport, 236 freeze-free days, while the Columbia University of SC station downtown records 26 February and 26 October for 261. That 25-day gap between two stations a few miles apart is the most defensible measure of Columbia’s urban warmth available. Longer warm season, longer breeding season, narrower window for unrestricted work.

  • Late autumn to late winter is when hardware goes up. With protected nests inactive, netting, slope conversion and cavity closure carry no timing argument.
  • Spring is identification season. New nesting begins and the costliest mistakes get made. Photograph the nest and the adult before touching anything.
  • August needs planning around. USC’s 2026 move-in runs early arrivals on 7 August and the full Move-In Day on 15 August, across 28 residence halls.
  • Summer is constrained wherever a protected species is present. Sanitation, survey and specification continue; the install waits for autumn.

What happens between the first call and the re-inspection?

  1. Confirm the species and the status of any nest

    Photographs of the birds, the fouling and any nest material, before a price exists. Which species, roughly how many, where they roost as distinct from where they feed, and whether anything is in use. The species fixes the legal envelope; the envelope fixes the scope.

  2. Map the envelope from the roof down

    Roof plane and plant deck, parapet and coping, cornice and string course, sign band, soffit line, ridge venting, canopy frames and deck beams. A bird treats a building as linked opportunities, so closing one and ignoring the rest redistributes the flock.

  3. Put the law and the calendar in writing

    Whether a federal permit is engaged, whether a depredation order reaches the species, whether SCDNR permitting applies, and what the season allows. Citations included.

  4. Remediate before anything is fixed to the building

    Material comes out first, with respiratory protection wherever the deposit is deep and the space poorly ventilated, and the void treated for mites.

  5. Specify fixings against the substrate

    Historic mortar, dressed stone, standing-seam metal, EPDM and precast concrete each want a different anchor, and the wrong one damages what we were hired to protect.

  6. Install, then remove the reason they came

    Netting, post-and-wire, spike, slope conversion and cavity closure, then bin lids, corral housekeeping and dock spillage. The second half is the recommendation most often declined and most regretted, and netting laid over unremediated fouling is how a job fails quietly.

What does the scope cover?

  • Identification of the species, and assessment of any active nest, ahead of pricing
  • A written statement of the federal and state position, citations attached
  • Tensioned netting to parking decks, light wells, plant enclosures and canopies
  • Slope conversion, post-and-wire and spike to cornices, copings, sills and signage
  • Cavity closure at soffits, gable louvres and exhausts, in hardware and not foam
  • Reversible mortar-joint fixings on contributing buildings, specified in advance
  • Removal of birds from a building interior under the federal rule, entry closed same visit
  • Before-and-after photography for an inspector, an insurer or a review board
  • A scheduled return to check tension, fixings and debris

Which institutional sites generate the most bird work here?

The ones with the most covered outdoor structure. The University of South Carolina enrolled 38,504 students on its Columbia campus in fall 2024 and operates 28 residence halls with 9,243 assignable beds, so roughly three quarters of the student body lives off campus. Breezeways, stair towers, covered walkways and rooftop plant are the recurring campus surfaces, handled through our schools and student housing program. The off-campus half is a landlord matter for our multifamily program — Columbia is a majority-renter city, 45.5 percent owner-occupied against 53,076 households.

Fort Jackson, annexed into the City of Columbia in October 1968, covers more than 52,000 acres with over 1,000 buildings and trains roughly 43,000 service members a year, an estate carrying every surface in this article several hundred times over. Public administration accounts for another 24,376 Richland County jobs, in the oldest and most ornamented buildings downtown.

Who regulates this work in South Carolina?

Structural pest control here is licensed through the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation, not the state agriculture department most people assume. The relevant licence category, 7A, covers industrial, institutional, structural and health-related work. Any firm doing it holds a DPR business licence, keeps a Designated Certified Applicator at every location, and carries general liability cover with a combined single limit of $100,000 or more.

Pesticide licensing does not touch the bird question, which is where most of the confusion in this trade lives. Every species named at 50 CFR 10.13 sits under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, together with its nest and eggs, and lethal action requires a depredation permit or an applicable order. Falconry occupies a third layer again: a state falconry permit at the right level alongside the federal Special Purpose Abatement permit, with South Carolina regulation letting a Master Falconer run abatement under it and a General Falconer act only as a sub-permittee. Where a proposal cannot place each line item on the correct layer, settle that before the lift is booked.

Where do we work around Columbia?

The base is 320 Wendy Lane in Windsor, and coverage runs across the city and the Midlands around it. Commercial calls concentrate downtown and in The Vista, along the Main Street blocks, around Arsenal Hill and out along the hospital corridors. Residential and small-commercial work runs through Shandon and Old Shandon, Rosewood, Heathwood, Forest Hills, Earlewood, Elmwood Park, Cottontown and Bellevue, Eau Claire, Hyatt Park, Historic Waverly, Wales Garden, Melrose, Druid Hills, Lake Katherine, Granby Hill and Olympia, University Hill, Seminary Ridge, Celia Saxon and Greenview, and across the rivers into Cayce and West Columbia. Beyond the city we take work in Lexington, Irmo, Aiken County and North Augusta, and our service areas page lists the rest.

Where the sound is scratching inside a ceiling void rather than birds on the parapet, it may not be birds at all, and our Columbia K-9 rodent detection service settles it faster than a torch and a hunch. Where the trouble is in bedrooms, start with our Columbia K-9 bed bug detection page.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a permit to chase pigeons off my building in Columbia?

No. Feral rock pigeons carry no protection under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, so no federal permit governs moving them or their nests. Even for protected species, 50 CFR 21.100 states that “no permit is required merely to scare or herd depredating migratory birds.” Permits attach to lethal take and raptor possession.

Our building is a contributing structure in a National Register district. Can it be netted?

Usually, but the specification changes. Netting rides on a tensioned cable perimeter, and on a contributing elevation those anchors belong in mortar joints and existing fixing points rather than dressed stone. Ask what the facade looks like when the system comes off in twenty years; that answer tells you whether it was specified well.

There are chimney swifts in a disused flue. What are our options?

Wait, then cap. Chimney swifts are native migratory birds on the 50 CFR 10.13 list, and the protection covers the nest and eggs. No depredation order reaches them, so clearing an active nest is unlawful. Preventing a nest is a different act from destroying one, which is why capping belongs outside the season.

Does Columbia have an ordinance about feeding birds downtown?

We do not know, and we will not invent an answer. The city’s code of ordinances sits on a platform we could not read reliably, and an unverified claim that no rule exists is as unhelpful as one saying a rule does. Ask the City of Columbia, or have your attorney check the code.

Who inspects restaurants in South Carolina now?

The South Carolina Department of Agriculture. Retail food inspection moved there on 1 July 2024, when DHEC was split into the Department of Public Health and the Department of Environmental Services. SCDA inspects roughly 24,000 establishments under SC Regulation 61-25, Grade A above 87. Copy still naming DHEC is out of date.

Will flying a hawk clear the birds off our parking deck?

It moves them while it is flown and does not eliminate them. The best comparative research available, forty trials over two years across six landfill sites, concluded that the birds could not be eliminated. On an open deck the durable answer is netting the beam bays and closing the light housings.

Starlings are nesting in the soffit of a rental house. Whose responsibility is that?

South Carolina statute is quieter here than people expect. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act at section 27-40-440 requires a landlord to keep the premises fit and habitable and to comply with codes materially affecting health and safety, but it never mentions pests, vermin or extermination, and section 27-40-510 is silent too. The lease decides.

How soon can somebody look at it?

Site visits from Windsor are normally inside the week, and a bird loose in a kitchen, food plant or clinical area gets priority, since the compliance exposure and the operational cost push in the same direction. Installation dates follow the species and the season, not our diary.

Stained stone and a ledge you keep washing?

Give us the building, a photograph of the birds where you have one, and a short history of what has been tried. You will get the species named, the legal position in writing, and a price for the work that ends the roost. Where the real answer is a bin lid and a pressure wash, that is what we will tell you. Bird exclusion for Columbia, the Vista and the Midlands, run out of Windsor, South Carolina.

title: Bird Control for Commercial Rooftops, Warehouses and Loading Docks
description: Commercial and industrial buildings are, from a pigeon's perspective, superb cliff habitat
h1: Bird Control for Commercial Rooftops, Warehouses and Loading Docks
body:
Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions  |  Windsor, SC  |  October 13, 2026

Commercial and industrial buildings are, from a pigeon’s perspective, superb cliff habitat — rooftops, rafters, beams, signage, HVAC equipment, and loading dock canopies provide exactly the elevated, sheltered ledges these birds evolved to nest on, with dumpsters and spilled product supplying the food. The result is droppings corroding your roof, contaminating product, clogging drains, and creating a health and compliance liability. The only thing that permanently solves it is physical exclusion — netting, spikes, wire, and structural bird-proofing correctly matched to each surface.

Why do birds target commercial buildings?

Because commercial architecture unintentionally reproduces cliff-and-ledge habitat at scale. Pigeons, starlings, and sparrows are looking for elevated, sheltered surfaces safe from ground predators, and a warehouse or distribution center offers hundreds of them: roof edges and parapets, rooftop HVAC units, structural beams and rafters, the underside of loading dock canopies, signage, light fixtures, and open bay doors leading to protected interior rafter space.

The food supply seals the deal. Dumpsters, waste compactors, spilled grain and product, food-service waste, and landscaping all provide reliable feeding, and in a distribution or food environment the volume can be substantial. Birds are also strongly site-faithful, returning to established roosts and nesting sites year after year, and existing droppings and scent attract more birds — which is why a bird problem on a commercial building compounds rather than fading.

What do bird droppings actually cost a commercial building?

Structurally, droppings are corrosive. They degrade roofing membranes, corrode metal, damage paint and stone, and shorten the life of expensive rooftop equipment — a roof that should last decades can be materially damaged by a sustained roosting problem. Nesting material clogs gutters, downspouts, and roof drains, which causes ponding and water intrusion, and packed nesting debris near lighting and electrical equipment is a genuine fire risk.

Operationally, droppings on loading docks, walkways, and entrances create slip hazards and liability exposure, and contaminate product and packaging moving through the dock — which in a food or pharmaceutical environment is a serious problem, not a cosmetic one. Then there’s the compliance dimension: for any facility under health-department oversight or third-party audit, bird activity and droppings are a finding, and a bad one.

K9 INSIGHT  The highest-value exclusion work is usually the least visible: sealing the gaps that let birds get into rafter space and voids. Interior nesting produces the worst contamination and the most expensive cleanup — and it’s the part a rooftop spike installation does nothing about.

Are bird droppings a genuine health risk?

They can be, and it’s worth taking seriously rather than dismissing. Accumulated bird droppings can support the growth of the fungus associated with histoplasmosis, and disturbing dried droppings — sweeping them, hosing them off, or working in a heavily fouled rooftop area — can aerosolize spores. Bird roosts are also associated with other pathogens and with ectoparasites like bird mites, which can migrate into a building when a nest is disturbed or abandoned.

The practical implication is about how cleanup is handled. Large accumulations of droppings should not be dry-swept or blasted off casually by maintenance staff without appropriate precautions; proper cleanup uses containment and protective equipment. For a facility manager, that means budgeting bird droppings as a controlled cleanup task rather than assuming somebody can just hose the dock down on a Saturday.

Which exclusion system fits which commercial surface?

Match the system to the surface — this is where most commercial bird jobs succeed or fail. Netting is for enclosing a volume: loading dock canopies, warehouse rafter space above open bays, courtyards, rooftop equipment areas, parking structures, and any space where birds are getting inside and nesting. Properly tensioned and fully sealed at the edges, it’s complete exclusion for that space, and it’s the workhorse of large commercial jobs.

Spikes suit narrow linear landing surfaces: ledges, parapets, beams, sills, signage tops, and light fixtures. Bird wire suits ledges and parapets where appearance matters — a customer-facing facade, a storefront, an office entrance. And structural bird-proofing closes the gaps and openings birds use to get into rafter space and voids in the first place, which is often the highest-value work of all because it stops the interior nesting that causes the worst contamination.

Why do scare devices and cleaning never solve it?

Because neither one makes the roosting surface unusable. Cleaning droppings removes the evidence but not the habitat; the birds return to the same beam that same evening. Scare devices — sonic units, distress calls, reflective deterrents, plastic owls and hawks — work briefly and then fail to habituation, exactly as they do with geese. Birds learn quickly that nothing bad ever follows the sound or the plastic predator, and they resume roosting, often within days.

This is the fundamental logic of bird control: you have to change the building, not try to change the birds’ minds. A ledge that cannot be landed on and a rafter space that cannot be entered produce permanent results, while a facility that relies on cleaning and scaring is signing up for a recurring cost with no end. Exclusion is capital spending that ends an operating cost.

When should commercial bird exclusion be installed?

Timing matters both legally and practically. Many bird species and their active nests carry legal protections, so exclusion work is best scheduled before nesting season begins or after young have fledged — installing netting over an active nest is both a legal problem and a practical one. If you already have nesting birds inside a rafter space, that needs to be assessed properly before work begins rather than after.

Practically, the argument for acting sooner is straightforward: an established roost gets worse and more expensive every season. The droppings accumulate, the corrosion progresses, more birds are attracted, and the eventual job now includes a substantial controlled cleanup before any exclusion can even be installed. Excluding before birds establish is dramatically cheaper than excluding after. If you’re seeing early bird activity on a building, that’s the moment to specify the work.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do pigeons keep coming back to our warehouse?

Because commercial buildings reproduce cliff-and-ledge habitat — roof edges, parapets, HVAC units, beams and rafters, dock canopies, signage — and dumpsters and spilled product supply food. Birds are strongly site-faithful and return to established roosts, and existing droppings and scent attract more birds, so the problem compounds.

What damage do bird droppings cause to a commercial building?

Droppings are corrosive: they degrade roofing membranes, corrode metal, damage paint and stone, and shorten the life of rooftop equipment. Nesting material clogs gutters and roof drains causing water intrusion, packed debris near lighting is a fire risk, and droppings on docks and walkways create slip hazards and contaminate product.

Are bird droppings a health risk to staff?

They can be. Accumulated droppings can support the fungus associated with histoplasmosis, and disturbing dried droppings can aerosolize spores. Roosts are also associated with other pathogens and with bird mites. Large accumulations shouldn’t be dry-swept or hosed off casually — proper cleanup uses containment and protective equipment.

Should we use netting or spikes on our building?

It depends on the surface. Netting encloses a volume — dock canopies, rafter space above open bays, courtyards, rooftop equipment areas, parking structures. Spikes suit narrow linear landing surfaces like ledges, parapets, beams, and signage. Using the wrong system for the surface is the most common reason bird-proofing fails.

Why don’t sonic devices and plastic owls work?

Habituation — the same reason they fail with geese. Birds learn quickly that nothing bad follows the sound or the plastic predator, and they resume roosting, often within days. Neither scaring nor cleaning makes the roosting surface unusable, so the birds return to the same beam that evening.

What’s the highest-value bird work on a commercial building?

Usually structural bird-proofing — sealing the gaps that let birds get into rafter space and interior voids. Interior nesting causes the worst contamination and the most expensive cleanup, and it’s exactly what a rooftop spike installation does nothing to address.

When should bird exclusion be installed?

Before nesting season begins, or after young have fledged — many bird species and their active nests carry legal protections, so installing over an active nest is both a legal and practical problem. Practically, an established roost gets worse and more expensive every season, so acting early is dramatically cheaper.

Do you install commercial bird exclusion in South Carolina?

Yes. Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions installs bird netting, spikes, wire systems, and structural bird-proofing for warehouses, distribution centers, rooftops, loading docks, and industrial facilities across Aiken, Columbia, Charleston, Greenville, Lexington, and surrounding areas. Call 803-226-3155.

Need answers you can trust?

Commercial bird exclusion — netting, spikes, wire, and structural bird-proofing — for warehouses, rooftops, loading docks, and industrial facilities across South Carolina.

Call  803-226-3155Certified K9 teams • Honest recommendations • No scare tactics, no upselling

h1: Bird Control in Lexington, SC

hero.eyebrow: LEXINGTON, SOUTH CAROLINA · BIRD CONTROL & EXCLUSION
hero.lead: Lexington is unusual. The town declared itself a bird sanctuary in its own code, in language broader than federal law, and that shapes how bird work should be approached inside the town limits. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions leads with exclusion here — netting, spikes, ledge geometry, sealed cavities — so birds never settle at all.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Family-owned · Exclusion-led · Working the Midlands from 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor

body:
Two facts set this town apart from anywhere else we take bird calls. One is a sentence in Title IX of the municipal code that protects birds more broadly than the Migratory Bird Treaty Act does, and names nest removal specifically. The other is that Lexington is young: the median housing unit in town dates from 2002, so the troublesome perches are canopy steel, sign boxes, rooftop screening and light standards, not weathered cornices.

Around it sits a county raising poultry at industrial scale, where starlings in a grow-out house are a feed bill and a biosecurity file rather than a stained wall. One discipline covers all three: name the species, read the rules for that address, then change the structure. That is our bird control and exclusion service.

1,106Bird species on the federal protected list at 50 CFR 10.13, as revised at 88 FR 49310 and effective 30 August 2023
7,065,868Broilers and other meat-type chickens inventoried in Lexington COUNTY by the 2022 USDA Census of Agriculture, alongside $331,830,000 in agricultural sales
2002Median year of construction for a housing unit inside the TOWN of Lexington, American Community Survey 2020–2024 five-year estimates, table B25035

Why does a bird job here begin with the town’s own code?

Because Lexington wrote a rule most municipalities never bothered with. Title IX, Chapter 91, section 91.06 is headed BIRD SANCTUARY; HUNTING BIRDS OR WILD FOWL PROHIBITED. The operative sentence reads: “It is unlawful to trap, hunt, shoot or attempt to shoot or molest in any manner any bird or wild fowl or to rob bird nests or wild fowl nests.” It arrived as Ordinance 285, passed on 1 April 1996.

  • No species list. The phrase is “any bird or wild fowl”. Federal law reaches a defined roster and leaves three introduced birds outside it; the town’s text prints no such carve-out.
  • Nests named directly. Robbing a nest is its own prohibited act, separate from anything done to a living bird — and nest clearance is our most common request.
  • A wide verb. “Molest in any manner” is not confined to killing or capture.
  • A real penalty. Section 91.99 sets up to $500 or thirty days, each day a separate offence.

Section 91.21 then adopts the Lexington County animal control ordinance by reference and provides that the county ordinance controls where the two conflict, most recently by Ordinance 2024-13, passed 7 October 2024.

Now the honest part. We are not offering a legal opinion on how the town interprets or enforces section 91.06, and nobody should take one from a contractor’s website. Anyone planning bird work inside the corporate limits should pull the current code and speak to the town first. Outside those limits the chapter does not apply.

What we will say is why this pushes our recommendation. Exclusion acts on the building, not on the bird. A slope fitted to a coping, mesh behind a sign, a gable louvre closed with hardware cloth — each prevents a bird establishing rather than doing anything to one already present. That is the durable answer anywhere, and here it also keeps the work furthest from the question the ordinance raises.

What does federal law protect, and where does the town’s line sit differently?

The Migratory Bird Treaty Act covers the species named at 50 CFR 10.13, revised at 88 FR 49310, effective 30 August 2023, now 1,106 birds. Protection travels to the nest and the eggs, which is why an active nest changes a project overnight. Five familiar birds sit outside it: rock pigeon, European starling, house sparrow, Eurasian collared-dove and mute swan. Almost everything else on a local roofline is in — gulls, crows, grackles, red-winged blackbird, brown-headed cowbird, Canada goose, cattle egret, great egret.

  • 50 CFR 21.100. The rule states that “no permit is required merely to scare or herd depredating migratory birds.” Federally, hazing is not a licensed activity.
  • 50 CFR 21.14. No permit is needed for anyone to remove a migratory bird trapped inside a building, where its presence stops the room being used as intended or puts health and safety in question. The bird must be handled humanely, glue boards are forbidden, and the same rule requires the entry to be patched or an exclusion device fitted so it cannot happen again.
  • 50 CFR 21.150. A depredation order for blackbirds, cowbirds, crows, grackles and magpies permits control without a federal permit where serious damage is under way, non-lethal methods first each year. Gulls, vultures, geese, herons and egrets fall outside it.

Here is the comparison that matters locally. Federal law gives an exit ramp on pigeons, starlings and house sparrows. The ordinance, on its face, does not, and it adds nest removal as a named act — a narrower envelope than a contractor working purely from the CFR would assume.

Which bird is actually up there?

Rock pigeon

The ledge specialist, and the bird photographed above. It wants a level surface about the width of its feet, a wall at its back and a short flight to food. More in our pigeon profile.

European starling

Starlings seek holes, not shelves, which is why spikes never solve a starling problem. They take gable louvres, lifted flashing, the void behind a fascia, an open sign box, the ventilation runs of a poultry house. Detail in our European starling profile.

House sparrow

Small, unbothered by people, content to raise a brood inside a light fitting, a canopy tube or a menu board frame. Sparrows sit outside the treaties by a different route than the pigeon: their family was never brought under them. See the house sparrow profile.

The natives that end the conversation

Barn swallows on a run-in shed, chimney swifts in a flue, killdeer on a flat gravel roof, crows and grackles in a parking lot. All federally listed, nest and eggs included.

Why does exclusion last when deterrence wears off?

A bird is not afraid of an object. It is afraid of an outcome, and it stops being afraid the moment the outcome stops arriving. Reflective tape, plastic raptors, sonic units and gels borrow credibility from a threat the property never delivers, and a flock audits that threat daily.

Exclusion asks the bird to believe nothing. A surface can be occupied or it cannot, and learning does not change geometry. Put the two on a parapet coping. A bead of gel takes fifteen minutes to lay and stops working once its skin cures or the birds stand on the crust. A fabricated 45-degree conversion in aluminium, stainless or polycarbonate deletes the flat plane instead. Gel is a line item you reorder; the slope is a change to the property.

MethodWhere it earns its place in LexingtonHow long it holds
Cavity closure at soffits, louvres and ventsStarling and sparrow nesting, untouched by any perch productPermanent, in hardware rather than foam
45-degree ledge conversionCopings, sign band tops, wide sills, canopy fascia returnsAs long as the fabrication lasts
Tensioned nettingLoading canopies, covered entries, plant screens, barn and poultry baysYears, with scheduled tension checks
Stainless spikeNarrow ledges, pipe runs, light standard heads, lintelsLong, unless debris bridges the rows
Post-and-wireSlim ledges and railings where the fix must stay invisibleYears, with retensioning

None of it survives an unmanaged food source. Hardware buys the structure; housekeeping buys the result.

What does a building put up after 2000 offer a bird?

More than owners expect, and this is the section most bird marketing omits, because it assumes every problem building is old. Of 10,348 housing units inside the corporate limits, 80.3 percent were built in 1990 or later and only 9.5 percent predate 1980. Town population reached 25,729 in the July 2025 estimate, up 8.9 percent since 2020 after 31.9 percent the previous decade. New structure has its own vocabulary of opportunities.

Covered entries and canopy steelwork

A drive-through canopy is a roof with no walls: ideal shelter for a pigeon, an ideal nest frame for a sparrow. Open-ended tube steel, C-channel with the web turned upward and the fascia return ledge foul first. Netting the underside beats defending every member.

Sign boxes and illuminated letters

An internally lit cabinet is warm, dry, dark and almost never inspected. Sparrows enter through the service gap or a failed gasket, and by the time anyone notices, the nest sits against a ballast.

Rooftop mechanical screening

Screening built to hide condensers from the street creates a sheltered corridor with a solid floor: one of the most productive pigeon roosts on a modern building, and one of the least visited.

Parking-lot light standards and walkway canopies

The head casting on a pole light and the run above a shopfront canopy foul onto surfaces customers use. Spike the standard, net the canopy, then deal with the trash corral drawing them back.

Loading canopies and dock roofs

A roosting line above a dock lands on pallets. Distribution work runs through our warehouse and distribution program, kitchens and dock lines through our restaurant and food service program.

Open venue structure

The Icehouse Amphitheater at 107 West Main Street is the clearest local example of a building offering birds everything and defending nothing. Ground was broken in 2015, the 900-seat venue opened in October 2016, a pavilion followed in 2021. Trusses, lighting bars and speaker mounts are perch, above seated people.

The residential side is a steady stream of subdivisions: the town’s status layer carries Barr Lake at 182 lots, River Ridge at 150, West of Main at 76 and Nightingale Hills at 66, plus phases of Sterling Bridge and Brookstone. Multifamily is 23.8 percent of the stock, where our multifamily and property management program gets called: breezeways, stair towers and dryer vents repeated across a property.

Institutional buildings drive the rest. Lexington County School District One operates 32 schools with 27,074 students on federal Common Core of Data figures, concentrating covered walkway structure above children; that runs through our schools and student housing program. Prysmian is expanding its plant at 700 Industrial Drive by $80 million, roughly 135 jobs, online around May 2028.

What are starlings doing inside a poultry house, and why is it not cosmetic?

Because the numbers are not cosmetic. The 2022 Census of Agriculture recorded 7,065,868 broilers and other meat-type chickens in Lexington COUNTY, across 822 farms and 79,450 acres, with $331,830,000 in products sold, 77 percent of it from livestock and poultry. The county ranks second in South Carolina for agricultural sales.

  • Feed removal. Starlings feed selectively and take the high-value fraction of a ration. A flock working pan lines through a winter is a shrink line, not an annoyance.
  • Biosecurity. A wild bird moving between houses, farms and a manure stack is a vector pathway every audit checklist asks about, and inspectors expect physical measures.
  • Structure and airflow. Nesting in ceiling voids and ventilation runs pulls insulation apart, blocks inlets and undermines the airflow the house was designed around.
  • The physical answer. Inlet and fan screening, closure at eave and gable, netting across open ends, door discipline, spillage cleared. Outside the town limits the constraint is engineering, not permitting.

Where product is processed rather than grown, documentation becomes part of the deliverable: that sits with our food processing and manufacturing program, and multi-site scoping with our commercial programs.

The small-scale version sits in back gardens all over town. Section 91.02 permits backyard chickens under limits: four birds maximum regardless of lot size, no roosters, a $20 permit from the Office of Planning, Building and Technology, rear yard only, structures 25 feet from any property line and reducible to 10 with a neighbour’s letter plus screening. It also requires the resident to provide sanitary waste disposal and pest control. That clause does real work, because an open feeder is a reliable starling magnet and the birds it draws do not stay in that yard.

What do years of droppings actually do?

A number gets passed around this industry putting the count of human diseases spread by birds above sixty. No agency publishes it, and we could not trace it to one, so it appears in nothing we write. What is documented is narrower.

  • Histoplasmosis. The fungus behind it lives in soil that droppings have enriched, most heavily through the central and eastern states. It is an environmental organism; the CDC does not describe birds as carrying it around. Exposure comes from stirring a deep old deposit into the air in a closed, unventilated room.
  • Uric acid attack. Droppings are acidic and work on materials continuously: painted and galvanised metal, single-ply membranes, HVAC casings, canopy panels. On a five-year-old building that becomes a warranty argument.
  • Blocked gutters and scuppers. Nest material dams a drainage path, water backs up over an upstand and finds the structure. The nearest published rainfall normals are Richland County’s next door, 47.75 to 48.11 inches a year on the 1991 to 2020 set.
  • Ectoparasites left behind. Mites and other nest arthropods do not depart with the birds. Pull a nest from a soffit and do nothing else, and they move inward through the ceiling seeking a new host.

Which popular fixes do we decline to sell?

  • Plastic owls, hawk silhouettes and holographic ribbon. A fortnight of displacement, then decoration. Habituation to a consequence-free deterrent is the best-demonstrated effect in the field.
  • A nest knocked down before anyone identified the builder. Federally the species is the difference between maintenance and a violation, and inside the town limits a second question sits on top of it.
  • An effectiveness percentage for falconry. No study produces one for a commercial site, and the best available research points the other way.
  • Federal approval of a deterrent method. No such scheme exists at the FAA, for raptor patrols or anything else, so a badge claiming one points at a certification that was never created.

Where does falconry fit in a town that calls itself a bird sanctuary?

Falconry abatement flies a trained raptor on a planned patrol until a flock stops reading a property as safe ground. It changes a site’s risk profile. It does not eliminate a population.

The evidence base is small and worth knowing before a patrol contract is signed. Two controlled programmes on United Kingdom landfills are the comparative work that exists. Falcons and hawks were put up against gulls and corvids; in neither case did the scavenging birds all leave. The wider programme tested nine techniques in forty trials at six sites over two seasons and reported that eliminating the birds proved impossible. Nothing published examines a shopping centre or a poultry farm.

Applied here, the recommendation is narrow. For one building with one roost, falconry is rarely the right purchase, because exclusion costs less and keeps working after the last visit. Its use is on a big site with a long-settled flock, breaking the habit while hardware goes in. There is also a local question: a patrol flown inside the corporate limits raises the same reading of section 91.06 as any other active method. Permitting sits on our falconry bird abatement page. Waterfowl are a separate discipline under their own federal control orders and belong with our Lexington goose control service.

When in the year should the hardware go up?

Season is a legal question before a scheduling one. There is no climate station inside the town, but the State Climatology Office publishes two in Lexington County that bracket it. LITTLE MOUNTAIN records a last spring freeze on 31 March and a first fall freeze on 20 October, 246 freeze-free days; PELION 4 NW records 21 March and 10 October, 226 days. A long warm season means a long breeding season, and a narrow window for unrestricted work where protected species are present.

  • Late autumn to late winter is the install window. Protected nests inactive, no timing argument against netting, ledge conversion or cavity closure, and the right season for a poultry house.
  • Late February and March is the last clean run. Preventive work on unoccupied structure finished before the season starts is ordinary maintenance; the same work three weeks later may not be.
  • Spring is identification season. New nesting begins and expensive decisions get made fastest. Photograph first, act second.
  • Summer is constrained. Where a protected species is nesting, options narrow. Survey and sanitation continue; installs wait.

How does the work run from the first phone call?

  1. Name the species and the status of any nest

    Pictures of the birds, the mess and any nest, taken before we talk money. What they are, how many, which surfaces they sleep on versus feed on, and whether a nest is currently occupied.

  2. Establish which rules apply at that address

    Inside the town limits or outside, which federal provisions are engaged, whether an SCDNR permit fits, what the calendar allows. Where section 91.06 is in play we quote it in writing and point you to the town, not to our reading of it.

  3. Survey the envelope, not the complaint

    Roof plane and plant screen, coping, canopy steel, sign cabinets, soffit line, gable venting, dock roofs, light standards. A flock reads the whole property, not the one ledge that generated the call, so a partial fix shifts the roost down the elevation.

  4. Clean and remediate first

    Droppings and nest material out before anything is fixed to the structure, with respiratory protection where the deposit is deep, and the void treated for mites.

  5. Specify fixings against the substrate

    Standing-seam metal, EIFS, precast panel, EPDM and masonry each want a different anchor, and a roof warranty is easy to void with the wrong screw. Failed components go to our repairs and exclusion work.

  6. Install, remove the attraction, then come back

    The hardware goes up, then the part clients skip: lids that close, corrals that get swept, feed not left in the open. Photographs, a written scope, and a return date already in the diary.

What is in the scope?

  • Species identification and active-nest assessment ahead of pricing
  • A written federal position with citations, plus the town code text where the address is in town
  • Removal of droppings and nest material, with the void treated for ectoparasites
  • Tensioned netting to canopies, covered entries, plant screens and poultry-house bays
  • Spike, post-and-wire and 45-degree slope conversion to copings, sills, sign bands and light standards
  • Cavity closure at soffits, louvres, ridge vents and exhausts, using screened hardware and never foam
  • Birds taken out of an occupied interior under the federal rule, with the way in shut before we leave
  • A scheduled re-inspection rather than an open-ended promise

Who licenses this work, and who answers the ordinance question?

In this state the licensing authority is a university. Clemson’s Department of Pesticide Regulation runs structural pest control, under category 7A: industrial, institutional, structural and health-related work. Firms operating commercially hold a DPR business licence, post a Designated Certified Applicator to each location, and carry general liability of $100,000 combined single limit or better.

Pesticide licensing says nothing about birds, and that gap is where most confusion in this trade lives. The wildlife layer is federal. Anything named at 50 CFR 10.13 falls under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, nest and eggs included, and killing one needs either a depredation permit or an order that covers it. Falconry forms a third layer: a state falconry permit at the right grade plus the federal Special Purpose – Abatement permit, which under South Carolina regulation a Master Falconer may work from while a General Falconer may act only as a sub-permittee.

The town layer is a fourth, and not ours to interpret. For section 91.06, for the chicken permit under section 91.02, and for anything else in Chapter 91, the Town of Lexington is the authority. In unincorporated Lexington County, county ordinances are enforced by the Sheriff’s Department code enforcement officers. If a contractor cannot say which layer each line of a proposal answers to, ask before the lift is booked.

Which properties around Lexington generate the most of this work?

Retail and food service first, because covered entries, drive-through canopies, illuminated signage and trash corrals cluster tightly on almost every site. Then schools, then multifamily, then industrial buildings with high open bays and dock doors held open through a shift. Agricultural buildings are their own category, and the county’s poultry sector means we see more of them here than in most places we work: barns, run-in sheds, feed rooms and grow-out houses each need a different closure strategy. Golden Hills Golf and Country Club at 100 Scotland Drive is the one verified golf property with a town address.

Residential calls concentrate on starlings and sparrows in gable vents, soffit returns and dryer vents, and pigeons on a chimney. If what you hear is scratching inside a ceiling void rather than birds visible outside, it may not be birds at all, and our Lexington K-9 rodent detection service settles that faster than a torch and a guess.

Where do we cover around Lexington?

We are based at 320 Wendy Lane in Windsor and work the Midlands from there. Around the town, regular coverage runs through the subdivisions on the town’s own map: Barr Lake, Bent Creek Plantation, Brookstone, Carriage Hills Lake, Cherokee Village, Coventry Lake, Creekside Farms, Gibson Forest, Golden Hills, Heritage Hills, Hope Ferry Plantation, Hunters Ridge, Laurel Falls, Madison Park, Mallard Lakes, Middlebrook, Nightingale Hills, Pilgrim Point, River Ridge, Shoal Creek, Sterling Bridge, Summerfield, Twelve Mile Ridge, Woodcreek and Woodside Farms.

We also work downtown along West Main Street, out toward Gibson Pond Park and Virginia Hylton Park, along the Fourteen Mile Creek corridor off North Lake Drive, and into the unincorporated county. Further afield we cover Irmo, Chapin, Cayce, West Columbia, Columbia, Aiken County and North Augusta; the full list is on our service areas page. Where the trouble is in bedrooms rather than on a roof, start with our Lexington K-9 bed bug detection page.

Frequently asked questions

Does the bird sanctuary ordinance mean nobody can do bird control in Lexington?

We will not give you a legal conclusion, because it is not ours to give. What we can do is show the text. Section 91.06 makes it unlawful to trap, hunt, shoot or molest in any manner any bird or wild fowl, or to rob bird nests, with a penalty of up to $500 or thirty days. Confirm the current code and the town’s position with the town. Meanwhile, exclusion changes your building rather than acting on a bird.

Federal law says pigeons are not protected. Does that settle it inside the town limits?

Not on its own. Rock pigeon, European starling and house sparrow are absent from the federal list at 50 CFR 10.13, so the Migratory Bird Treaty Act does not reach them. The town’s ordinance says “any bird or wild fowl” and prints no equivalent exception. Put that to the town before work is scheduled.

Can I take a nest off my own house?

Start by finding out what built it. If the species is on the federal list, nest and eggs are protected along with the adult, and 1,106 species are on it. Inside the corporate limits, section 91.06 separately names robbing bird nests as a prohibited act. Answer both questions before a ladder comes out.

Starlings are cleaning out the feeder in our chicken run. What helps?

Feed discipline first, because it is free: a treadle or covered feeder, feed lifted overnight, spillage swept, the bin sealed. Then close the coop with hardware cloth over vents and gaps. Section 91.02 already requires a permitted flock owner to provide pest control, alongside the four-bird cap.

Will flying a hawk clear the birds off our property for good?

No, and anyone promising that is selling past the evidence. Falconry moves birds while it is flown and shifts a site’s risk profile; it does not eliminate a population. The largest controlled programme, nine techniques across forty trials at six landfill sites, reported that eliminating the birds proved impossible. Nor has the FAA ever created an approval scheme for raptor patrols.

How dangerous is clearing out an attic full of droppings?

The exposure worth taking seriously is stirring a deep, long-settled deposit into the air in a closed space with no ventilation. The fungus behind histoplasmosis lives in soil that droppings have enriched, most heavily through the central and eastern states, so a loft clear-out calls for proper respiratory protection. An open car park is a different situation.

Our building is barely ten years old. Why do we have a bird problem?

Because age is not what birds respond to. They respond to geometry and shelter, and modern construction supplies both: rooftop screening, open-ended canopy tube steel, sign cabinets, walkway canopies, light standard heads. A building finished in 2016 can hold a settled roost within two seasons.

Do we need a permit just to scare birds off a roof?

Federally, no. The rule at 50 CFR 21.100 states that “no permit is required merely to scare or herd depredating migratory birds.” What needs permitting is killing a bird and keeping a raptor. Inside the town limits there is a separate question about how section 91.06 reads on active methods, and that one belongs to the town.

There are geese on the pond behind our building. Same job?

Same company, different discipline. Canada geese are federally protected and sit under their own control orders covering agricultural facilities, public health situations, airfields, and nests and eggs, so the permitting path looks nothing like a pigeon job. SCDNR puts the statewide resident population above 50,000.

Give us the address, a picture of the birds where you have one, and a line on what has already been attempted. Back comes the species, the federal position written down, the wording of the town chapter where your address falls inside it, and a figure for closing the roost. If a swept dock and a proper lid would do it, that is what you will be told. Bird exclusion across Lexington and the Midlands, from Windsor, South Carolina.

hero.lead: North Augusta sits on the bluff above the Savannah River, and its bird trouble gathers where the ledges are oldest and the food is easiest. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions names the species before quoting anything, works inside what federal law and the city code allow, then rebuilds the structure so the roost cannot re-form.
