h1: Falconry Bird Abatement for Casinos, Stadiums & Large Sites

hero.h1: Falconry Bird Abatement for Casinos, Stadiums & Large Sites
hero.lead: Falconry bird abatement uses trained raptors under a USFWS Special Purpose – Abatement permit to move gulls, pigeons, starlings, grackles and vultures off a property. It is silent, chemical-free and permitted for dispersal, not killing. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions runs abatement programs across South Carolina, Georgia and nationwide, paired with exclusion and food-source work.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · USFWS-permitted · Master Falconer on permit · SC, GA & nationwide deployment

body:
Most bird deterrents fail for the same reason: the bird works out that nothing actually happens. Cannons, distress calls, kites, reflective tape and pyrotechnics all rely on a threat that is never carried out, and a gull that has ignored a noise cannon for two weeks will ignore it for the rest of the season. A live raptor is different because the threat is real and occasionally reinforced, which is why it holds up far longer than acoustic and visual deterrents do.

We are going to be unusually direct on this page about what the evidence does and does not show, because this is an industry with a lot of invented statistics in it. There are only a handful of controlled falconry studies worldwide, mostly UK landfills and New Zealand vineyards, and every one of them reports reduction rather than elimination. If someone quotes you a 95 or 99 percent success rate for a casino or a stadium, they made it up. What falconry does well is break an entrenched flock's habit of using your property. What keeps them off afterward is exclusion and removing whatever brought them there.

0Protected birds our abatement permit authorizes us to kill. The federal form states it directly: an abatement permit does not authorize killing or injuring of birds or other wildlife
2 daysThe window in which any incidental take of a protected bird must be reported to the USFWS Regional Migratory Bird Permit Office
5 yearsMinimum records retention required under the permit — every bird, every acquisition, every activity

What is falconry bird abatement?

It is the use of trained, captive-bred raptors, flown by a licensed falconer on a planned patrol, to flush and haze nuisance bird flocks off a property. The birds you want gone are not caught or killed; they are made to feel that your rooftop, pool deck, loading dock or parking structure is a place where a predator hunts. Flocks relocate.

It is silent. It uses no pesticides, no pyrotechnics and no propane cannons, which is why it fits venues where noise and chemicals are not options — guest-facing resorts, hospitals, outdoor dining, stadium concourses and food plants. Handlers work in uniform, on agreed flight lanes, in patrol windows coordinated with your security and operations teams.

Because we also run an exclusion crew and a full commercial pest program, we can do the part that most falconry vendors cannot: fix the reason the birds were there. See our bird control and exclusion service and our repairs and exclusion work.

What permits does this actually require?

This section is worth reading closely, because almost every competitor page in this industry gets at least one of these points wrong, and a regulator can check every one of them.

  • The federal permit is USFWS Form 3-200-79, Special Purpose – Abatement, issued under 50 CFR 21.95. There is no CFR section called “the abatement regulations” — a 2015 proposed rule that would have created one was never finalized, and the word “abatement” is not even defined in the definitions section at 50 CFR 21.6. Abatement permits are special purpose permits. Anyone citing “abatement regulations” as their authority is describing something that does not exist.
  • Falconry itself is now at 50 CFR 21.82, not 21.29. Part 21 was reorganized effective 2022. You will still find 21.29 cited on competitor sites — and, remarkably, on some government pages that have not been updated. It is the single fastest way to tell whether a vendor's compliance material has been reviewed since 2022.
  • The permit is issued to individuals, not companies. A business name can be listed as a DBA, but no corporation holds an abatement permit. “Federally licensed company” is not a thing. Ours is held by our Master Falconer.
  • Eligibility is narrow. The holder must have a current, active state falconry permit at the Master Falconer level — which in South Carolina requires at least five years of practicing falconry with your own raptors at the General level. The raptors must be captive-bred and marked on the metatarsus with a seamless numbered USFWS band. And critically, the only raptors that may be used are those belonging to the permittee — you cannot fly borrowed or leased birds under a federal abatement permit.
  • Payment is expressly allowed, and only here. 50 CFR 21.82(f)(11)(ii) states that you may receive payment for providing abatement services if you have a Special Purpose Abatement permit. Falconry is otherwise a non-commercial activity — even conservation education programs are limited to cost recovery. Abatement is the one falconry-adjacent activity where a fee is permitted.
  • South Carolina authorizes it explicitly. SC Regulation 123-170 states that a Master Falconer may conduct abatement activities with a bird possessed for falconry if the falconer has a Special Purpose Abatement permit, that General Falconers may conduct abatement only as a sub-permittee, and that falconers may receive payment for abatement services with that permit. Facilities must pass an SCDNR inspection before a permit is granted.
  • Georgia works by incorporation. Georgia Rule 391-4-9-.07 requires falconry permittees to comply with the federal falconry standards as now or hereafter amended. Georgia has no rule text addressing abatement directly. We treat Georgia engagements as requiring their own confirmation with GA DNR's Special Permit Unit rather than assuming reciprocity, and we will tell a Georgia client exactly where that stands before we quote.
  • Nationwide means nationwide subject to state law. USFWS conditions the permit plainly: you may not conduct the authorized activities if doing so would violate the laws of the applicable state. Falconry permits are state-issued. Any vendor telling you a federal permit lets them operate in all fifty states is misreading their own permit. We deploy nationwide, and each engagement includes confirming authorization in that state.

Do the hawks kill the birds?

No, and the permit is explicit about it. The Form 3-200-79 language is worth quoting verbatim: “An abatement permit does not authorize killing or injuring of birds or other wildlife.” Programs are flown to move flocks off the property, not to catch them. Lethal take of a bird protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act requires a separate depredation permit or a depredation order — a different application, a different legal basis, and not what this service is.

There is a related point most vendors invert, and it is worth understanding because it tells you what you are actually buying. 50 CFR 21.100 states that no permit is required merely to scare or herd depredating migratory birds. Hazing protected birds is not itself a licensed activity. The abatement permit is required because we possess and commercially deploy MBTA-protected raptors — not because chasing gulls needs federal permission. When a competitor tells you “you need a permit to scare protected birds and we have it,” they have the regulation backwards.

Raptors are predators, and a bird flown at a live flock will occasionally catch something. When that happens to a protected species it is incidental take, and it must be reported to the Regional Migratory Bird Permit Office within two business days. We do that, every time, and we log it. Every acquisition and disposition of a raptor is filed on Form 3-186A, activity records are kept per bird, and records are retained for at least five years past permit expiration. If a vendor has never mentioned incidental take reporting to you, ask why.

Which birds are protected, and which are not?

This determines what is legally possible at your site, and the distinctions are finer than most people expect.

Not protected under the MBTA

Rock pigeon, European starling, house sparrow — plus Eurasian collared-dove and mute swan. A precision point worth knowing: pigeons and starlings are unprotected for different legal reasons. Pigeons belong to a family the treaties cover but are excluded as a human-introduced species. Starlings and house sparrows belong to families the treaties never covered at all. Competitors get this wrong constantly. Pigeon, starling and house sparrow profiles.

Protected — gulls

Laughing gull, ring-billed gull and herring gull are all on the current 50 CFR 10.13 list. Laughing gulls are the dominant Southeastern nuisance gull, breeding in South Carolina and Georgia salt marsh colonies and heavy at waterfront, marina, retail and stadium sites in spring and summer. Ring-billed gulls are the parking-lot gull and are a winter problem inland, driving most gull complaints from autumn through early spring.

Protected — corvids and blackbirds

American crow, fish crow, common grackle, boat-tailed grackle, red-winged blackbird and brown-headed cowbird are protected, but all fall under the depredation order now at 50 CFR 21.150, which allows control without a federal permit where they cause serious agricultural, health or structural damage — with non-lethal methods attempted first each year. Boat-tailed grackles are a coastal Carolina and Georgia specialty and are aggressive around outdoor dining and marinas.

Protected — vultures

Black and turkey vultures are protected and no depredation order covers them, so lethal take requires a full depredation permit. They are also a distinctive commercial problem: they roost on rooftops, cell towers, light stanchions and communications gear, and they damage EPDM roofing, pool covers, vehicle rubber trim and wiper blades, with heavy fecal loads. Non-lethal dispersal is the legally clean path, which is exactly why abatement suits them. Be aware that a vulture is a large soaring bird and flying at a vulture roost is a materially different operation from flying at gulls — we will tell you honestly what we would deploy and what to expect.

Protected — waterfowl and waders

Canada goose is protected, with a set of dedicated control orders covering airports and military airfields, agricultural facilities, public health situations, and nests and eggs. Resident geese on retail ponds, corporate campuses and golf courses are usually better handled through our dedicated Canada goose management program, with falconry as an escalation option. Cattle egret and great egret are protected and turn up at aquaculture, pasture-adjacent and retention-pond sites.

Birds already inside a building

A separate and very useful rule: 50 CFR 21.14 allows any person to remove migratory birds from a building interior without a permit where their presence prevents normal use or creates a health or safety risk. Humane handling is required, adhesive traps are prohibited, birds must be released immediately, and — importantly for warehouses and food plants — the rule itself requires you to prevent reentry by patching holes or installing bird exclusion devices. A sparrow in a distribution center is an exclusion job, not a falconry job.

What does the evidence actually show?

We would rather publish the real literature than a made-up number, so here is all of it.

Falcons outperform hawks on open-airspace flocking birds. Baxter and Allan, writing in the Wildlife Society Bulletin in 2006, flew trained hybrid falcons and hawks against gulls and corvids at UK landfills throughout daylight hours, seven days a week, for periods of seven to twelve weeks. Their conclusion: neither group eliminated all scavenging birds, but numbers were reduced more consistently by falcons than by hawks, and they recommended falcons as the more appropriate choice within an integrated bird management strategy.

The best comparative dataset that exists says nothing eliminates birds. The same researchers ran forty separate trials over two years across six UK landfills, comparing pyrotechnic rockets, helium kites, hawks, falcons, automated distress calls, hand-held distress calls, sound generators, blank-firing pistols and live rounds. Each trial ran twelve weeks or until birds stopped responding. Their conclusion, verbatim: “Birds could not be eliminated but numbers were reduced to different extents by different techniques. The success of various techniques also varied significantly in terms of habituation.” They hypothesized that combining techniques would improve results — which is precisely how we build programs.

Habituation is the real mechanism, and the honest version is more interesting than the marketing version. Cook, Rushton, Allan and Baxter, in Environmental Management in 2008, tested nine methods against three gull species across six landfills. Distress calls, falconry, and combinations of lethal and non-lethal ammunition produced the strongest initial deterrent effect — but the durable ones were the methods carrying real consequence. Non-consequential methods declined as birds habituated to repeated exposure without an actual threat. Note what that means: falconry's durability advantage comes from the raptor being a genuine, occasionally successful predator, not from merely looking like one. We are not going to tell you birds never habituate to a live raptor. We will tell you they habituate far more slowly, because the threat is real and gets reinforced.

The agricultural number, with its caveats attached. Kross, Tylianakis and Nelson, in Conservation Biology, studied New Zealand falcons introduced into vineyards and found a significant decrease in passerines and a 95 percent reduction in grapes removed relative to vineyards without falcons, with a 55 percent reduction in pecked grapes for one species, and modelled savings of US$234 per hectare for Sauvignon Blanc and $326 for Pinot Noir. Those are real published figures — and they come from New Zealand, from wild falcons establishing territory rather than a falconer flying trained birds on patrol, against a pest complex that is not ours. Quoting “falconry reduces bird damage 95 percent” without that framing would be misleading, so we do not.

What does not exist. There is no peer-reviewed US airport study quantifying strike reduction attributable to falconry. The FAA's own Wildlife Hazard Management at Airports manual mentions trained falcons in a single line, with no effectiveness data and no cost analysis, while habitat modification and exclusion get full chapters. There is no published study on falconry at casinos, resorts, stadiums, hospitals, retail centers, distribution centers, marinas or solar farms — none. There is no published dose-response on patrol frequency or program duration. Falconry is not FAA-approved, FAA-certified or USDA-certified, and no such designation exists. Any percentage you see attached to those settings on any company's website, including numbers that sound modest, is unsourced.

What falconry does not solve

Publishing this costs us some jobs. We would rather lose the ones we would have failed.

  1. It does not eliminate birds

    Two independent controlled studies say so explicitly. The deliverable is reduction and displacement, not eradication. If your requirement is zero birds, falconry is not the tool and no honest vendor will tell you otherwise.

  2. It does not work while the food stays

    Every study site was a landfill — the attractant remained, so the effect was suppression requiring continuous input. Open dumpsters, loading-dock spillage, outdoor dining, standing water, retention ponds and landscape fruit all have to be addressed, or you are paying us to fight your own site conditions indefinitely.

  3. It does not replace exclusion

    Netting, bird wire, ledge modification and sealed entry points are permanent. Falconry is a recurring service. Even the federal rule for interior birds requires patching holes and installing exclusion devices. The right sequence is usually knockdown by falconry while exclusion is installed, then a reduced maintenance patrol.

  4. It is the wrong tool for several situations

    Birds already on active nests — protected nests attract federal protection and entrenched nesters do not disperse well. Interior infestations. A single-structure pigeon problem that exclusion would solve permanently and more cheaply. Sites where the attractant cannot be reduced and the budget cannot sustain continuous patrols. And any situation where what the client actually needs is lethal control, which this permit does not authorize.

  5. It is weather-limited

    High winds, heavy rain, fog and extreme heat ground raptors. Coverage is not 24/7 and we will not pretend otherwise in a contract.

  6. Cost scales with patrol frequency

    And patrol frequency is the one variable the evidence says matters most. Both landfill studies flew birds daily, through all daylight hours, for seven to twelve weeks. Intermittent service is not what was tested. Event-day-only coverage manages the symptom during those hours and rarely relocates a resident flock.

Which raptors, and why?

Harris's hawk is the one species choice with genuine peer-reviewed backing behind it. Bednarz's 1988 paper in Science documented Harris's hawks in New Mexico forming hunting parties of two to six individuals in the non-breeding season, a behavior that improved capture success and let them take prey larger than themselves. They are the only North American raptor with documented cooperative group hunting, which is why they tolerate handling well, work in casts, and are the standard choice for structured, lower-airspace, guest-facing environments. That study documents wild social hunting, not abatement — we are not going to imply it tested our service.

Falcons — peregrine, gyr and saker hybrids, saker, lanner, barbary — are the open-airspace group, flown at gulls and pigeons over rooftops, landfills and large open sites. This is the one species-selection claim with head-to-head data behind it: falcons reduced gull and corvid numbers more consistently than hawks at UK landfills.

Smaller falcons such as aplomado and merlin are flown at small passerines — starlings, sparrows and small blackbird flocks — in tighter airspace. That mapping is real operational practice rather than published science, and we will describe it as our experience rather than dress it up as a study.

Eagles are not an abatement tool. Bald eagles are prohibited outright and golden eagles are excluded from the abatement permit. Eagles fall under an entirely separate permitting regime. If a vendor offers eagles for large sites, that is a compliance red flag.

How a program runs

  1. Site assessment

    We identify the species, count and map the flock, find where they roost versus where they feed, identify the attractants, and photograph the damage and the fouling. We tell you at this stage if we think exclusion or sanitation alone would solve it more cheaply, because a program built on the wrong diagnosis fails no matter how well it is flown.

  2. Scope, permits and coordination

    Written scope with a defined knockdown phase and a maintenance rate. Flight lanes and no-fly zones agreed with your venue. Patrol windows matched to target-species activity — dawn and dusk pressure for roosts, midday for feeding sites. Radio coordination with security and operations before each flight. Confirmation of state authorization for the site's jurisdiction. On airports, we operate as one contracted tool inside a biologist-led wildlife hazard management program, never as the program.

  3. Knockdown phase

    Consistent, frequent patrols — this is the phase where frequency does the work, and where thin coverage produces thin results. Telemetry on every bird, documented weather stand-down criteria, guest-corridor separation, and a documented response if a raptor is lost or a non-target animal is taken.

  4. Exclusion and source removal in parallel

    Netting, wire, ledge modification, sealed entry points, dumpster and spillage management, standing water. This is the part that makes the result durable, and it is why we prefer to run abatement inside a broader program rather than as a standalone patrol.

  5. Maintenance phase

    Reduced patrol frequency once the flock has relocated and the exclusion is in place, scaled to your season. For most Southeastern sites that means heavier coverage in the gull and vulture seasons and lighter coverage in between.

  6. Documentation

    Patrol logs, species counts against baseline, photographs, and USFWS-compliant records — every raptor, every acquisition and disposition, every activity, and every incidental take reported within two business days. If you are audited, inspected or challenged, the record is the deliverable.

Where falconry abatement makes sense

  • Casinos and resorts — pool decks, outdoor dining, valet and porte-cochère, where noise cannons and chemicals are unusable and guest optics matter
  • Stadiums and arenas — gulls and grackles working concourses and outdoor food service
  • Airports — as one contracted tool inside a 14 CFR 139.337 wildlife hazard management plan, never as the plan itself
  • Landfills and transfer stations — the one setting with real published data, and the one where daily flying was what was actually tested
  • Food processing and distribution — where FDA's Preventive Controls rule is the driver (see below)
  • Agriculture — vineyards, blueberry and pecan operations, with the New Zealand vineyard study as the only real evidence base
  • Marinas and waterfront — laughing gulls, boat-tailed grackles and herons
  • Hospitals and healthcare campuses — where an immunocompromised population makes fouling a genuine concern
  • Corporate campuses, retail centers and golf — resident geese, gull roosts and vulture perching on rooftop equipment
  • Warehouses and distribution centers — usually a combined interior-removal, exclusion and exterior-pressure job

What is the actual cost of a bird problem?

Aviation. The FAA reports about 19,700 wildlife strikes at 780 US airports in 2023, and roughly 292,000 reported strikes with civil aircraft between 1990 and 2023. Reported costs totalled $1.48 billion over that 34-year period, and adjusted for strikes where costs were not provided, losses could run as high as $300 million per year. Birds account for 97 percent of reported strikes. Waterfowl are only 4 percent of strikes but cause 27 percent of the damaging ones. We cite those figures because they are the FAA's own. We will not attach a falconry-attributable percentage to them, because no US study supports one.

Food facilities. This is the cleanest compliance hook there is, and it does not require inventing audit statistics. Under FDA's Preventive Controls rule, 21 CFR 117.3 defines “pest” to include birds — birds are legally pests in a food plant. And 21 CFR 117.35(c) states that pests must not be allowed in any area of a food plant, and that effective measures must be taken to exclude pests from manufacturing, processing, packing and holding areas. That is the regulation. We are not going to quote you AIB, SQF or BRCGS point deductions, because we have not verified them against the current standards and a wrong clause number in front of a QA manager is worse than saying nothing. See our food processing and manufacturing program and our warehouse and distribution program.

Health. Here too we are going to be more careful than the industry norm. You will see claims that birds carry 60 or more diseases transmissible to humans; we could find no agency source for that number or anything like it, so we do not use it. What the CDC actually says is narrower and worth stating correctly: Histoplasma lives in the environment, mainly in central and eastern states, and spreads in bird and bat droppings that mix in soil — the fungus grows in the droppings, and the CDC does not describe birds as carriers. Cryptococcus neoformans lives in the environment worldwide, with soil, bird dung and decaying wood among its sources, and infections occur overwhelmingly in people with weakened immune systems. Accumulated droppings are a legitimate reason to remediate. They are not a reason to frighten your staff.

The costs we see most often are more mundane and easier to price: sanitation labor and pressure-washing, slip hazards on fouled walkways and the liability that comes with them, product and packaging contamination, uric acid corrosion of roofing membranes and HVAC and painted metal, drains and gutters clogged with nesting material, fire risk from nests in signage and lighting, and guest complaints and review scores at hospitality and retail sites.

When should you start?

Before nesting, and the reason is legal as much as behavioral. MBTA protection extends to the nests and eggs of protected species. Once a protected bird has an active nest on your property, your options narrow considerably — the clean regulatory exception is 50 CFR 21.14 for birds inside a building, and everything outside a building interior becomes a different and more constrained analysis. Unprotected species — pigeon, starling, house sparrow — have no federal nest protection, which is one more reason species identification is the first step.

Behaviorally, a flock that is feeding at your site is far easier to move than a flock that has established a roost, and both are easier than birds that are nesting. We will not publish specific nesting-window dates for South Carolina and Georgia, because we could not verify a state-specific document and we are not going to guess at dates that carry legal weight. What we will do on your assessment is check the current guidance with USFWS Ecological Services and the relevant state nongame program for the species on your property, and tell you what window you are actually working in.

What we will not claim

We are putting this on the page deliberately, because you are going to compare vendors and it is easier to compare them against a list.

Common industry claimWhy it does not hold up
“Permitted under 50 CFR 21.29”Obsolete since the 2022 reorganization. Falconry is 21.82; the abatement permit is 21.95.
“Federally licensed company”Abatement permits are issued to individuals only. No company holds one.
“Our federal permit covers all 50 states”USFWS conditions the permit on compliance with applicable state law, and falconry permits are state-issued.
“FAA-approved” or “USDA-certified”No such designation exists. The FAA manual gives falconry one line with no effectiveness data.
“95% effective” / “eliminates nuisance birds”The two controlled landfill studies state that birds could not be eliminated.
“Birds never habituate to a live predator”Overstated. The research supports slower habituation because the threat is real and reinforced — not zero habituation.
“Permanent solution, one and done”Every study measured suppression under continuous daily flying at sites where the attractant remained.
“Birds carry 60+ diseases”No agency source exists for that figure or anything like it.
“Eagles available for large sites”Bald eagles are prohibited and golden eagles are excluded from the abatement permit.

Frequently asked questions

Is falconry bird abatement safe around guests, staff and pets?

Yes. Raptors are flown under a handler's direct control on planned lanes and are focused on the target flock, with agreed no-fly zones and guest-corridor separation, and patrol windows coordinated with your security team. Handlers work guest-facing venues in uniform. Falconry is silent and chemical-free, which is precisely why it suits properties where noise cannons, pyrotechnics and pesticides are not options.

Do the hawks kill the pest birds?

The goal is dispersal, not take. The federal permit states directly that an abatement permit does not authorize killing or injuring of birds or other wildlife. Programs are flown to move flocks off the property. Raptors are predators, so incidental captures do happen — and when a protected species is taken, we report it to the USFWS Regional Migratory Bird Permit Office within two business days and log it in the records we retain for five years.

How fast will we see results?

The only defensible timeline comes from the published landfill trials, which ran seven to twelve weeks of daily, all-daylight flying and measured reduction against a four-week pre-treatment baseline. How fast your site moves depends on whether it is a feeding site or an established roost, whether the food source is still there, flock size and species, the season relative to nesting, site openness, and above all patrol consistency. There is no published dose-response literature, so anyone guaranteeing results in a specific number of days is inventing it.

Can you provide abatement on event days only?

We can, but you should know what you are buying. Event-day-only coverage manages the symptom during those hours and rarely relocates a resident flock — the studies that produced measurable reduction flew birds daily for weeks. Venues that want birds gone rather than briefly displaced should fund a continuous knockdown phase first, then step down to event-day maintenance.

How is falconry priced?

By patrol hours and program length, driven by property size, number of zones, the species involved and how entrenched the flock is. Patrol frequency is the variable the evidence says matters most, so it is also the main cost driver. Pricing follows a site assessment and is issued as a written scope with a defined knockdown phase and a separate maintenance rate. We do not quote from a photograph.

Will this work on vultures?

Often, and it is frequently the only legally clean option, because no depredation order covers black or turkey vultures — lethal take requires a full depredation permit. Vultures roosting on rooftops, cell towers and light stanchions damage EPDM membranes, pool covers and vehicle rubber trim. Be aware that flying at a large soaring bird is a different operation from flying at gulls; we will tell you at assessment what we would deploy and what to expect.

Do we still need netting and spikes if we hire you?

Almost certainly, and we would rather say so before you sign. Falconry breaks a flock's habit of using your property; exclusion is what makes the change permanent. The federal rule for birds inside buildings actually requires patching holes and installing exclusion devices. The strongest programs run knockdown by falconry while exclusion is installed, then drop to maintenance patrols. We can do both parts — see our bird control and exclusion service.

Is falconry FAA-approved for airports?

No, and neither is anything else — there is no FAA approval scheme for wildlife deterrent methods. The FAA's Wildlife Hazard Management at Airports manual mentions trained falcons in a single line with no effectiveness data or cost analysis, while habitat modification and exclusion receive full chapters. At an airport we operate as one contracted tool inside a biologist-led wildlife hazard management program under the airport's own plan. Any vendor claiming FAA approval or certification is describing something that does not exist.

What about Canada geese?

Geese are protected but sit under a specific set of federal control orders covering airports and military airfields, agricultural facilities, public health situations, and nests and eggs. For retail ponds, corporate campuses and golf courses we usually lead with our dedicated Canada goose management program, which combines habitat modification, egg and nest work under the appropriate authorization, and dispersal — with falconry as an escalation option where the flock is entrenched.

Can you work outside South Carolina and Georgia?

Yes, and here is the honest framing. The federal abatement permit is federal, but USFWS conditions it on compliance with applicable state law, and falconry permits are issued by states. So we deploy nationwide subject to confirming the required authorization in each state, and that confirmation is part of the engagement rather than an assumption. For Georgia specifically, the state rule incorporates the federal falconry standards by reference and does not address abatement directly, so we confirm the position with GA DNR's Special Permit Unit for each engagement rather than assuming reciprocity.

Tell us the property, the species if you know it, and what has already been tried. We will assess the site, tell you whether falconry is the right tool — and if exclusion or sanitation would fix it more cheaply, we will say so. title: Food Plant Pest Control SC
description: K-9 rodent detection for food processing and manufacturing plants, built to satisfy FDA Preventive Controls and third-party audit programs.
h1: K-9 Rodent Detection for Food Processing & Manufacturing

hero.h1: K-9 Rodent Detection for Food Processing & Manufacturing
hero.lead: AIB, SQF, and customer audits leave no room for a pest finding. Our detection dogs pinpoint rodent activity before an auditor ever could — and document it thoroughly.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Certified K-9 teams · Family-owned · Serving the CSRA & Midlands

body:
In food processing and manufacturing, a single pest finding can jeopardize an audit score, a customer contract, a certification, or an entire production line. Auditors treat rodent evidence as a critical issue, and the cost of a failed audit dwarfs the cost of prevention. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions helps plants across the CSRA and Midlands stay audit-ready with canine rodent detection that pinpoints activity precisely and documents it the way auditors expect.

Detection-first is the right model for a regulated plant. Instead of relying on a bait-station log that proves rodents died, a detection dog finds active harborage in racking, voids, and utility runs before it becomes a finding — so you correct it proactively, on your schedule, rather than explaining it to an auditor after the fact.

½ inchA gap this small is all a rat needs to enter your plant
35+Diseases rodents can spread, according to the CDC
ZeroRodent evidence a food-safety audit will tolerate — so find it first

One finding can put an audit — and a contract — at risk

Food-safety audit schemes scrutinize pest management more closely than almost any other program, and for good reason: rodents in a processing environment threaten product safety, compliance, and consumer trust. A single droppings finding or a gnawed package during an audit can drop your score, trigger corrective action, or cost a certification a customer requires.

Detection dogs find active harborage in the places bait stations and visual checks miss — high in racking, deep in equipment and utility voids, and along structural runs — before it becomes an audit finding. That lets you correct proactively, document the correction, and walk into your next audit with evidence of a strong, trend-tracked program.

The pests we detect in food processing and manufacturing

Rodents drive audit findings, but processing environments face a broader pest profile we detect and help control:

Norway rats

Enter from below through foundations, docks, and utility penetrations, contaminating product and gnawing infrastructure. A half-inch gap is all they need.

House mice & roof rats

Squeeze through quarter-inch gaps and nest high in racking and voids. The most common audit-finding rodents in processing plants.

Stored-product pests

Beetles, weevils, and Indianmeal moths that infest ingredients and finished goods. We help pinpoint affected areas so lots are isolated quickly.

Cockroaches & birds

Roaches in warm equipment voids and birds entering open docks both generate audit deductions. We target harborage and provide humane exclusion.

The audit frameworks we build your program around

A processing plant answers to auditors and customers whose standards are exacting. Our program is built to strengthen your audit position:

  • AIB, SQF & BRCGS audits — Leading food-safety schemes weight pest management heavily. A single rodent finding can drop a score or threaten a certification. Detection helps you find and fix it first.
  • FSMA & HACCP — The Food Safety Modernization Act and HACCP require pest management as a documented prerequisite program. Our records slot directly into your food-safety plan.
  • Customer & brand audits — Retail and brand customers run their own audits and expect proactive, documented pest programs with trend data. Our reporting is built for them.
  • GMPs & sanitation — Good Manufacturing Practices treat pest evidence as a serious nonconformance. Detection and exclusion support a clean, compliant plant.

How our food processing and manufacturing K-9 program works

Every plant engagement follows a rigorous, documented workflow scheduled around production:

  1. Assess

    We map production, storage, utility, and dock areas and review your audit scheme, sanitation windows, and any prior findings.

  2. Detect

    A certified detection dog systematically screens the plant by scent, including the racking, equipment, and utility voids visual checks and bait logs miss.

  3. Map activity

    The handler confirms and maps exact harborage and travel routes, producing the activity map auditors and your team can act on.

  4. Exclude & treat

    We seal the structural gaps and penetrations rodents use and apply targeted control, timed to sanitation and off-shift windows.

  5. Verify

    A follow-up sweep confirms correction — the documented proof a re-audit or customer review requires.

  6. Document & monitor

    You receive audit-ready reporting with activity mapping and trends, on a monitoring cadence aligned to your audit cycle.

What our food processing and manufacturing program includes

  • Detection across production, storage & utility areas where rodents hide.
  • Structural exclusion to seal rodent entry points.
  • Pre-audit sweeps ahead of a scheduled AIB, SQF, or customer inspection.
  • Activity mapping and trend documentation over time.
  • Stored-product pest & bird service for ingredients and dock areas.
  • Scheduled monitoring aligned to your audit cycle and sanitation windows.
  • Off-shift scheduling so production is never disrupted.
  • Thorough, audit-ready reporting for your pest-management program records.

Why canine detection outperforms conventional pest control for food processing and manufacturing

A bait-station log proves rodents died — it does not prove your plant is clean. Here is why processors choose detection:

 Bait-station log onlyCoastal K-9 detection
What it showsWhere rodents diedWhere rodents are active
CoveragePerimeter stationsSystematic across the plant
Audit valueReactive recordProactive activity mapping and trends
Entry pointsUsually missedLocated and sealed with exclusion
TimingAfter a findingBefore the auditor arrives
Certification riskHigherLower, with documented prevention

Documentation that protects you

You receive detailed documentation — activity mapping, findings, corrective work, and trends — formatted to support AIB, SQF, BRCGS, FSMA, and customer audits.

A strong, proactive pest-detection record is exactly what auditors want to see, and it is what protects a certification and a contract. It demonstrates that your program finds and fixes issues before they become findings — the difference between passing and failing an audit.

Signs your plant needs a detection sweep

In a large plant, early rodent signs hide in the racking and voids. Schedule a sweep if you notice:

  • Droppings in production, storage, racking, or utility areas.
  • Gnaw marks or contamination on ingredients, packaging, or wiring.
  • Product or lot concerns flagged during sanitation or QA checks.
  • Grease marks and runways along structural runs and dock edges.
  • A prior audit finding you need to prevent from recurring.
  • An upcoming AIB, SQF, or customer audit you want to pass cleanly.

Serving food processing and manufacturing across the CSRA & Midlands

Coastal K-9 serves food-processing plants, co-packers, beverage and bakery operations, and manufacturers across the CSRA and Midlands, including the industrial corridors around Aiken, Graniteville, Augusta, and Grovetown along I-20, and the Columbia, Lexington, and West Columbia manufacturing hubs along I-26 and I-77.

As a local, family-owned company we schedule around production and sanitation windows and offer pre-audit and on-demand response — scaling from a single plant to a multi-site operation.

Why CSRA food and manufacturing plants choose Coastal K-9

Processing and manufacturing plants across the region choose Coastal K-9 because a detection dog finds what a bait-station log cannot, and because thorough, trend-tracked documentation strengthens their audit position and protects their certifications.

Our founder is FEMA-trained and NESDCA-certified, we are local and responsive, and every inspection is detection-first — targeted, documented, and built around the audits your business depends on.

Frequently asked questions

Can K-9 detection support our AIB or SQF audit?

Yes. Detection finds active rodent harborage precisely, and we document findings, corrective work, and trends in a format that supports AIB, SQF, BRCGS, FSMA, and customer audits.

Can you sweep before a scheduled audit?

Absolutely. Pre-audit sweeps let you find and correct any rodent activity before an auditor arrives, protecting your score and certification.

Do you work around production?

Yes. We schedule around your production and sanitation windows, including off-shift, so the line is never disrupted.

Do you seal entry points?

Yes. Detection is paired with structural exclusion to close the gaps and penetrations rodents use, making control lasting.

How is detection better than our bait-station program?

Bait stations show where rodents died at the perimeter; detection shows where they are active throughout the plant, including racking and voids — the proactive picture auditors want.

How much does plant pest detection cost?

It scales with facility size, audit cycle, and monitoring frequency, and is highly cost-effective against a failed audit or lost certification. Call 803-226-3155 for a quote.

Do you handle stored-product pests and birds?

Yes. Beyond rodents we help pinpoint stored-product pest activity in ingredients and finished goods and provide humane bird exclusion for dock areas.

How do the dogs find rodents in a large plant?

They alert to the scent of live rodents, urine, and nesting material, locating harborage deep in racking, equipment, and utility voids that visual checks and bait logs miss.

Do you provide trend documentation?

Yes. Recurring programs include activity mapping and trend reporting that demonstrate a proactive, improving program — exactly what auditors look for.

How often should we schedule?

Most plants align a monitoring cadence to their audit cycle — often monthly or quarterly — plus pre-audit sweeps and on-demand response.

How quickly can you respond to a finding?

We offer same-week response across the CSRA and prioritize active findings and upcoming audits.

What areas do you serve?

Food-processing and manufacturing facilities across Aiken, Graniteville, Augusta, Grovetown, Columbia, Lexington, and the greater CSRA and Midlands.

Related commercial programs

Warehouses & DistributionRestaurants & Food ServiceHealthcare & Senior LivingAll Commercial Programs

Schedule audit-ready K-9 rodent detection for your plant across the CSRA and Midlands.

title: Goose Control in Aiken, SC

h1: Goose Control in Aiken, SC

hero.eyebrow: AIKEN, SOUTH CAROLINA · CANADA GOOSE MANAGEMENT
hero.lead: Resident Canada geese settle where mown turf meets open water. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions works trained herding dogs on Aiken ponds, golf lakes and HOA basins, moving birds off the shoreline day after day until the flock relocates — then helping you change the ground so the site stops selecting for them.

body:
Almost every call about geese is described as a bird problem. It is not. It is a landscape problem that happens to have birds standing on it. A resident Canada goose is choosing your property against a short list of criteria, and once you know the list you can see why the pond behind one Aiken clubhouse is covered in droppings while a pond a mile away, the same size and age, has never held a goose.

The list is short grass to graze, an unobstructed view so the flock can watch for a predator, and water within a few steps to escape into. Mown turf running down to open water delivers all three — the geometry of a golf approach, a retention basin behind a subdivision, a campus quad with a stormwater pond, the lawn above a boat ramp. Geese did not invade those places. We built them, and the birds noticed.

50,000+SCDNR estimate of South Carolina’s resident Canada goose population, still increasing, concentrated in the Upper Coastal Plain, Piedmont and Foothills
4.9 ftAverage depth of Langley Pond across roughly 300 acres — shallow, warm and rimmed with mown park lawn
3,410 acresAudubon’s Silver Bluff Center & Sanctuary near Jackson, with about 50 acres of ponds and more than 200 recorded bird species

What is a resident Canada goose actually selecting for?

Short grass. Geese graze, and they prefer turf that is fertilised, irrigated and cut. The greener the sward, the higher the protein, and the more birds an acre carries.

Sightlines. A goose on the ground manages risk by watching. Open ground with nothing to hide a coyote behind reads as safe. Break the sightline and it stops reading that way, which is why a waterline you cannot see over beats any device you can buy.

Water within a few strides. Water is the escape route. A bird that must first cross forty feet of tall vegetation to reach it will not settle there.

A resident flock is not attracted to Aiken, or to your address. It is attracted to one arrangement of turf, view and water, a design decision that can be reversed. Our parent page on Canada goose management sets out the full method, and the species profile sits in our Canada goose library entry.

Why can nobody give you an Aiken goose count?

Because nobody has published one, and we will not invent one for a bigger number.

A statewide figure does exist. The South Carolina Department of Natural Resources puts the resident Canada goose population above 50,000 birds and describes it as increasing, with the largest concentrations in the Upper Coastal Plain, the Piedmont and the Foothills. Aiken County sits on the Sandhills belt at the top of the Upper Coastal Plain, so that distribution points our way. That is an inference from a sourced statewide number, and we label it as one rather than dress it up as a local census.

The load-bearing word is resident. These birds hatch here, nest here and stay year round. A goose that leaves in March is a photograph; a goose that stays through August is a maintenance line item. The AIKEN 4 NE station records a last spring freeze near 22 March, a first fall freeze near 12 October, and 232 freeze-free days — nothing that forces a bird to leave.

Which water around Aiken actually fits the pattern?

The county has plenty of surface water and very little documented waterfowl habitat.

Langley Pond

Roughly 300 acres of former Horse Creek mill impoundment near Burnettown and Langley, 19 feet at most and only 4.9 feet on average. It carries a 2,000-metre, eight-lane buoyed rowing course that hosted pre-Games training in 1996 and still runs winter regattas, and the park side adds a beach, bathhouse, fishing pier and free boat ramp. Shallow water with lawn running into it is textbook goose geometry, and the ramp and beach are where droppings become a public problem.

Audubon’s Silver Bluff Center & Sanctuary

3,410 acres at Jackson with 2.6 miles of Savannah River frontage, about 50 acres of ponds and wetlands, and more than 200 recorded bird species including waterfowl and wading birds. It is the county’s only site with documented waterfowl, and it is a sanctuary — we do not work it and would not propose to. It matters as context: a managed property nearby competes against genuinely good habitat.

Golf course water

Woodside Plantation holds five lakes alongside two eighteen-hole courses, The Reserve by Jack Nicklaus and Hollow Creek by Fuzzy Zoeller and Clyde Johnston. Houndslake runs three nine-hole layouts from Joe Lee’s 1974 design, and Cedar Creek is an Arthur Hills course through gently rolling sand hills and pine forests. Palmetto Golf Club dates to 1892, but we cannot document its water features and will not describe them. Nor will we name which club has a goose problem.

Subdivision and HOA water

Aiken has a long list of neighbourhoods whose names announce their water: Gem Lakes, Mallard Lake, Summer Lakes, Graylyn Lakes, Johnson Lake Estates. We cannot document how many ponds sit inside each, so we will not print a count. What is clear is that a retention basin is engineered for exactly what geese select — a broad shallow bowl, a mown verge, clear approach lines — and the basins from Aiken’s 2000s build-out are mature enough to hold established flocks.

What geese ignore

Horse Creek falls fast off the fall line through eight mill villages. Moving water in a wooded corridor is not goose habitat, and neither is Black Gum Pond in Hitchcock Woods, because 2,100 acres of closed canopy is the opposite of a sightline.

The Sand River, which is not a river

People send us the Sand River as a goose question and it never is one. It is a dry sand channel, not a stream. It runs only after heavy rain, can form quicksand when it does, and serves as the outlet for Aiken’s urban stormwater — which is why it has gullied Hitchcock Woods and why the city has built storage and retrofit projects to control it. A channel dry most of the year offers no escape water and no grazing.

What does a trained herding dog actually do out there?

A border collie worked on geese presents the posture of a stalking predator: head low, shoulders down, eyes fixed, moving in an arc. Prey animals read that as a hunt about to happen. The dog does not catch a goose, is not asked to, and a handler who allows contact with a protected migratory bird has turned lawful harassment into a federal problem. The birds lift, circle and settle elsewhere.

Repetition makes it work, not drama. One visit produces a spectacular thirty seconds and no lasting result — the flock returns next morning and the owner concludes dogs do not work. What changes behaviour is being moved off the same shoreline again and again, at unpredictable hours, until the site is written off as unsafe.

The published evidence worth knowing comes from gulls rather than geese. A 2008 study in Environmental Management tested nine deterrent methods against three gull species at six landfills and found that methods carrying real consequence held their effect, while methods with nothing behind them faded as birds habituated. We will not claim geese never habituate to a dog — that is an overstatement the industry makes constantly, and this study is why we avoid it. The decay is simply far slower than for anything inanimate, and the window it buys is what you spend on habitat.

Why do the cheap deterrents stop working?

Because a goose is a long-lived, social, observant animal that watches for threats all day, and every static device eventually files itself under scenery.

MethodWhat it doesWhy it fades
Plastic coyote or owl decoyAvoidance for a few days, sometimes weeksIt never moves, never approaches, never carries a consequence. Birds graze within a few feet of one by month’s end.
Reflective tape and flash deterrentsBrief startle on a bright, breezy dayNo threat is attached to the stimulus, and habituation is the documented outcome for non-consequential deterrents.
Propane cannons and noise makersClears a field briefly after each reportPredictable timing teaches the flock the schedule. Near housing or a school it generates complaints faster than results.
Feeding bans with no enforcementCorrect policy, no effectA sign changes nothing unless somebody actually asks people to stop. One household feeding bread can hold a flock by itself.
Herding dog plus habitat changeMoves the flock now and removes the reason it chose the siteThe dog’s effect decays slowly and needs maintenance. The habitat change does not decay at all.

None of these are frauds, and several have a narrow use inside a varied programme. The failure is selling one alone against an established flock.

What habitat changes hold after the dog goes home?

This is the only lever you control completely, and the one most people skip, because it changes how the property looks.

  • Let a vegetated buffer grow at the waterline. An unmown band of grass and native planting between turf and water removes the grazing surface and blocks the escape route at once. Geese dislike walking through cover tall enough to hide something.
  • Break the sightline with plantings. Shrub groupings, ornamental grasses and staggered small trees turn an open panorama into compartments. A goose that cannot see across the pond cannot post a lookout.
  • Steepen the bank where you can. A gentle turf slope into water is a ramp built for waterfowl. A rip-rap or boulder margin does not read as an exit.
  • Stop the feeding properly, not with signage. If your pond has a feeding culture, the buffer alone will not hold the line.
  • Reconsider fertiliser and irrigation nearest the water. The most attractive grass on the property is usually the last twenty yards before the water.
  • Accept the aesthetic trade. A manicured lawn running to a mirror of water is the most goose-attractive arrangement available. You can have that view, or a shoreline without droppings on it.

Where the buildings are the issue rather than the turf — roosting on a clubhouse roof, ledges above an entrance — that is bird exclusion, which is physical and permanent rather than behavioural.

Is it legal to run dogs at Canada geese?

Yes, and the reason is worth stating precisely, because this is where marketing copy gets loosest.

Canada geese are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, by name, at 50 CFR 10.13. That protection is real, not a technicality. What it prohibits is take — killing, capturing, possessing, or disturbing nests and eggs — not moving a bird along. The controlling language is 50 CFR 21.100: no permit is required merely to scare or herd depredating migratory birds. Harassment with a trained dog is exactly that. Now the boundaries.

  • Nests and eggs are a separate regulation. Destroying, oiling or addling nests and eggs falls under 50 CFR 21.162 and requires federal registration or authorisation. A vendor offering to quietly handle a nest is offering you a liability.
  • The general depredation order does not reach geese. 50 CFR 21.150 covers blackbirds, cowbirds, crows, grackles and magpies, and explicitly excludes geese, gulls, vultures, herons, egrets and doves. Anyone citing it at you over a goose has cited the wrong rule.
  • The resident goose control orders are narrow. Dedicated orders exist for airports and military airfields at 21.159, agricultural facilities at 21.165 and public health at 21.168, plus the Special Canada Goose Permit at 21.120, each with its own eligibility conditions. A golf course is not an airport.
  • State permits sit on top, not instead. SCDNR issues depredation permits free, valid 30 days and renewable, through its regional wildlife management and law enforcement offices, and notes that additional permits may be required for federally protected birds.

Contrast that with birds outside the Act. Rock pigeon, European starling and house sparrow are not protected at all — a legal difference with real operational consequences, which is why pigeons and European starlings are handled under an entirely different rule set from the geese on the same property.

When in the year does this matter most in Aiken?

  • Late winter, before pairing. The best time to start and the least glamorous. Birds have not committed to a nest site, and moving them now is far easier than later. With the last spring freeze near 22 March, late January into February is the window to establish a programme.
  • Nesting season, spring. Once a pair commits, harassment becomes less effective and more constrained: grazing birds can lawfully be moved, but the nest cannot be approached.
  • The summer molt. Canada geese drop their flight feathers once a year in summer and spend several weeks flightless. A flightless bird cannot leave, so harassment then pushes birds around on foot without giving them the option to relocate. We adjust rather than pretend otherwise, and this is when droppings accumulate fastest.
  • Late summer into autumn. Flight returns and birds re-evaluate the site, which makes this a strong window for intensive work. With the first fall freeze near 12 October and 232 freeze-free days, the grazing season runs long. The county averages 50.77 inches of rain on the 1991–2020 normals and a mean of 64.1°F, so the turf almost never stops.
  • Winter. Resident birds stay, migratory birds may add to the numbers, and shoreline planting is easiest in the dormant season.

How does a Coastal K-9 goose programme run?

  1. Site walk and habitat assessment first

    Before a dog comes out we walk the water with you and map what the birds use: loafing areas, grazing turf, entry and exit points, and where the sightlines run. This is also the honest conversation about whether the property will accept a changed shoreline.

  2. We agree the constraints

    Play schedules on a course, regatta dates at a water venue, pool hours on a campus, walking patterns in an HOA. Harassment must happen at unpredictable times, a scheduling problem best solved before it becomes a complaint.

  3. Intensive early visits

    The opening phase is frequent and deliberately irregular, because the flock has a routine and the objective is to make it unreliable. Frequency in the first weeks decides the outcome.

  4. The dog works, and never makes contact

    Handler and dog work the shoreline and loafing areas in a stalking approach. Birds lift and leave, the dog is recalled. Nothing is caught or cornered, and no nest is approached.

  5. We taper as use drops

    Visit frequency falls as the birds stop using the site. Here a property that did the habitat work separates from one that did not: the first tapers to maintenance, the second needs the dog indefinitely, because nothing has changed about why the birds came.

  6. Written recommendations and monitoring

    Buffer widths, plantings, grading opportunities, feeding policy and where to cut turf inputs, specific to your shoreline. Bird use is logged across the season, and most sites need a return push once a year as flight returns after the molt.

What is included

  • Initial site walk and a written habitat assessment of shoreline and adjacent turf
  • Scheduled non-lethal harassment visits with trained herding dogs, irregular by design
  • Handler-controlled work with no contact between dog and bird at any point
  • A logged record of goose use, so the trend is documented
  • Written habitat modification recommendations your grounds staff can act on
  • Guidance on where a federal or state permit is and is not required
  • Coordination with your superintendent, property manager or board
  • Seasonal return visits and a maintenance schedule once the flock moves
  • A clear statement of what we will not do — nests, eggs, take, or anything needing an authorisation we do not hold

What do golf courses and HOA ponds need that a back garden does not?

Scale, scheduling and a paper trail.

On a course the damage is not primarily aesthetic. Clemson Extension’s Savannah Valley District puts droppings from geese on small ponds at two to four pounds per bird per day, and notes that the birds compact soil and kill turf by overgrazing. Across a resident flock landing on greens, approaches and cart paths, that is a labour cost before it is anything else. Overgrazed turf on a bank also starts an erosion problem, and the soils here are quartz sand with rapid permeability — the Lakeland series through this belt is classified as excessively drained. Bare sand on a pond bank does not stay put.

An HOA faces a different pressure. The complaint arrives at a board meeting, the board has a fiduciary duty and no wildlife expertise, and the two loudest positions in the room are usually do something drastic and do nothing. A documented non-lethal programme with a written habitat plan answers both, and our HOA and golf course goose management programme is built around that. What we ask is honesty about the landscaping: a club that will not let a buffer grow is buying a permanent dog contract.

What about rowing venues, swim decks and walking paths?

Langley Pond is the clearest local example of the problem shape. A buoyed racing course brings crews to a launch area, and the park side has a beach, a fishing pier and a boat ramp. Each is a hard surface at the water’s edge with mown lawn behind it — a goose loafing area with a public use bolted onto it. Droppings on a ramp are a slip hazard, on a pool deck a complaint, and on a path they get tracked into cars and houses.

On water quality we will be careful, because this is a claim people overstate. Clemson Extension’s regional guidance reports that fecal bacteria counts in goose droppings run roughly 25 times those of human waste. That is a sourced statement about the material, not a statement that any particular Aiken water body has a bacterial exceedance — we found no published sampling for a specific local pond. What is fair: where people swim, launch boats or put hands in the water, waterfowl faeces concentrated on the shoreline is a legitimate consideration. Langley Pond does carry a state fish consumption advisory, which is a separate contaminant issue entirely.

Where else does this come up around Aiken?

Any property combining maintained lawn, a stormwater feature and foot traffic, which in a growing county means most institutional sites. USC Aiken exceeded 4,200 students in autumn 2025 with residence halls at capacity and more than 900 living on campus. Aiken Regional Medical Centers carries 273 licensed acute-care beds and over 1,200 employees, and a hospital entrance is not where anyone wants a slip hazard. The county school district runs 41 schools with nearly 23,000 students. Senior communities such as Cumberland Village deserve a mention, because a slip on a wet path is not theoretical at eighty. Where a goose issue sits alongside a rodent issue at the same pond edge, that is canine rodent detection.

Who regulates this work in South Carolina?

Two authorities, and neither is the one people expect. Wildlife sits with SCDNR at state level and the US Fish and Wildlife Service federally. SCDNR depredation permits are free, run 30 days, renew, and issue through the regional wildlife management and law enforcement offices, with the agency flagging that additional federal permits may be required for federally protected birds. Non-lethal harassment of the kind described here requires neither, under 50 CFR 21.100.

Pesticide work is a different regime. In South Carolina it runs through the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation rather than a state agriculture department, under category 7A, with a business licence, a Designated Certified Applicator at each location, and liability cover of at least $100,000 combined single limit. That governs chemical turf repellents, not running a dog. Across the river, structural work runs through the Georgia Department of Agriculture instead.

Where we work around Aiken

Our base is 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856, roughly twenty minutes from downtown Aiken. We cover the City of Aiken and its subdivisions — Woodside Plantation, Houndslake, Cedar Creek, Gem Lakes, the Kalmia developments, Three Runs Plantation, Summer Lakes and Mallard Lake — plus the Winter Colony districts, the Horse District, Schofield and the Parkway District, and the 1950s Savannah River Site subdivisions at Crosland Park, Virginia Acres and Forest Heights. Beyond the city we work Graniteville, Warrenville, Gloverville, Langley, Burnettown, Bath and Clearwater through the Horse Creek Valley, plus Montmorenci, Beech Island, Jackson and New Ellenton. See every area we serve.

Goose work also runs in North Augusta, Columbia and Lexington. Where a site needs a raptor rather than a herding dog — gulls and grackles at outdoor dining — that is falconry bird abatement. If the property also has a bed bug question, our Aiken canine bed bug work covers it.

Frequently asked questions

Will the dog hurt the geese?

No. A trained herding dog presents the posture of a stalking predator and is recalled before contact is possible. Nothing is caught, injured or cornered, and no nest is approached. That is a legal requirement as much as an ethical position: Canada geese are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, and this work is lawful without a permit because the birds are moved rather than touched.

How many visits will it take?

More than one, and that is the honest answer. A single visit moves the flock for a morning. Changing an established routine takes frequent, irregular visits across weeks, because what you are teaching is that the site is unreliable rather than dangerous on one particular Tuesday. Properties that modify the shoreline taper to maintenance. Properties that change nothing keep the dog indefinitely.

Do I need a permit to have geese moved off my property?

Not for non-lethal harassment. 50 CFR 21.100 states that no permit is required merely to scare or herd depredating migratory birds, and working a dog without contact sits inside that. Permits become relevant the moment anything touches a nest, an egg or a bird — those fall under separate provisions, including 50 CFR 21.162.

Can you addle eggs or remove nests for us?

Not as part of this service. Nest and egg work for resident Canada geese requires federal registration or authorisation under its own regulation, with its own reporting conditions. We would rather say plainly that it is outside our scope than take the job and improvise. If nest management is what a site genuinely needs, the route runs through the US Fish and Wildlife Service.

Why will a plastic coyote not do this for a tenth of the cost?

Because it never does anything. Geese are long-lived, social and observant, and a stimulus with no consequence behind it becomes background within days. The deterrent research is consistent: methods carrying a real consequence hold their effect, and methods that do not decay as birds habituate. Sold alone against an established flock, decoys fail.

Are the geese on my HOA pond even resident birds?

Almost certainly, if they are there in July. Resident Canada geese hatch, nest and live here year round rather than following a flyway schedule, and they are the population SCDNR puts above 50,000 statewide and calls increasing. Migratory birds may swell winter numbers, but the flock creating a summer maintenance problem is nearly always resident.

How much habitat change is enough?

Enough to break at least two of the three things the birds select for. A vegetated buffer at the waterline removes the grazing surface and the escape route at once, which makes it the highest-value single change. Add plantings that interrupt the view across the water and the site becomes genuinely uncomfortable. What is never enough is a device on a post with unchanged turf behind it.

Does this work in summer when the birds cannot fly?

It works differently, and we say so in advance. Canada geese drop their flight feathers once a year in summer and are flightless for several weeks. Harassment then moves birds around on foot but cannot offer them the option of leaving the property, so expectations have to be set accordingly. The strongest windows are late winter before pairing and late summer once flight has returned.

Can you clean up the droppings already on the ramp?

Clean-up is a separate trade and we will say if a site needs it, but the point of the programme is that it stops being a weekly line item. Clemson Extension’s regional figures put goose droppings on small ponds at two to four pounds per bird per day. What you spend on cleaning scales directly with how many birds stand on your shoreline.

Do you handle pigeons and starlings on the same site?

Yes, and it is a different job under a different rule set. Rock pigeon, European starling and house sparrow are not protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, so the constraints governing goose work do not apply. Structural birds are usually an exclusion problem rather than a harassment one — netting, ledge modification, sealing entry points. Our Aiken bird control and exclusion pages cover it.

We will walk the shoreline, tell you what the site is offering them, and give you a written plan pairing dog work with the habitat changes that make it stick.
