title: Goose Control in Columbia, SC
description: Humane Canada goose management in Columbia for retention ponds, corporate campuses, parks and golf courses, using trained herding dogs.
h1: Goose Control in Columbia, SC

hero.eyebrow: COLUMBIA, SOUTH CAROLINA · CANADA GOOSE MANAGEMENT
hero.lead: Three rivers meet in Columbia, and the geese that cause trouble here are almost never on them. They sit on campus, hospital and neighborhood ponds, where mown lawn runs down to still water. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions moves resident Canada geese off those shorelines with trained herding dogs, then reshapes the edge so the flock stops choosing it.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Family-owned · Non-lethal, and no bird is ever touched · Midlands work run out of Windsor, South Carolina

body:
The Broad and the Saluda meet in Columbia to form the Congaree, a river of roughly fifty-three miles that drains both watersheds before joining the Wateree to make the Santee. Very little of our goose work happens on that water. A river moves, and a current is not what a grazing bird wants underneath it. The calls come from ponds instead.

Ponds are what a capital city builds. Stormwater must be detained somewhere. A campus wants a water feature in a lawn, and an apartment community markets an amenity lake. Every one arrives with turf mown to the edge, and that detail, rather than anything peculiar about Columbia’s bird life, is why the phone rings.

50,000+SCDNR’s estimate of resident Canada geese in South Carolina — a statewide figure, still rising. No published Columbia count exists.
48,579 acresSurface area of Lake Murray, with 620 miles of shoreline across Lexington, Newberry, Richland and Saluda counties (SCDNR)
261 daysFreeze-free season at the Columbia University of SC station, 26 February to 26 October, against 236 days at Columbia Metro Airport (SC DNR State Climatology Office)

Why does a state capital produce so many goose calls?

Because government, higher education and healthcare all build the same landscape, and that landscape is what a resident Canada goose is shopping for.

Consider what the bird needs. It grazes, so it wants grass short, green and fertilised. It manages risk by watching, so it wants a long clear view and nothing nearby large enough to conceal a coyote. It escapes by swimming, so it wants water within a few strides. Assemble those three and you have described a detention basin behind an office park, a quad with a pond at its centre, an amenity lake at a leasing office, and the ground beside a cart path.

None of it was designed for waterfowl. It was designed for drainage, for a view from a window, for a photograph in a brochure. Geese read the site more literally than the designer did. Richland County’s two largest employment sectors are Health Care and Social Assistance at 33,974 jobs and Public Administration at 24,376 — 15.3 and 11.0 percent of county employment. Those are the industries that build campuses with ponds on them. The underlying method is set out on our parent page, Canada goose management; the biology sits in the Canada goose library entry.

Where is the water around Columbia, and which of it matters?

Plenty of surface water, and only a fraction of it in the shape geese select. What follows is geography, not an allegation. No source names a Columbia water body with a goose problem, we name no club, and we will not invent one. Harbison State Forest is the counter-example: closed canopy over Broad River bluffs that flood several times a year is the opposite of what a goose wants.

The confluence and the Columbia Canal

The Congaree begins where the Broad and Saluda meet near the Fall Line and runs about fifty-three miles as the outlet for both. Beside it lies the Columbia Canal, cut between 1820 and 1824, redesigned in 1888 and reopened in 1891 at roughly 3.5 miles. It was breached in the catastrophic flooding of early October 2015, and as of February 2024 the repair was still in planning despite funding approved in 2021.

Lake Murray, which is not a Columbia lake

SCDNR records Lake Murray at 48,579 surface acres with 620 miles of shoreline, spread across Lexington, Newberry, Richland and Saluda counties, impounded in the late 1920s behind a dam 1.6 miles long. It sits at the edge of the metro, not inside the city. Where a flock originated matters far less than what your own bank offers it.

Sesquicentennial State Park

A 30-acre fishing lake inside 1,419 acres of Sandhills park about twelve miles from downtown, with 12 miles of trails, created after Columbia’s 1936 sesquicentennial. Maintained shoreline plus heavy foot traffic turns a wildlife question into a housekeeping one.

The riverfront and the greenway

Riverfront Park sits on the Columbia side, and the City’s parks department pictures the diversion dam at its northern end. Across the water the Three Rivers Greenway threads through Cayce Riverwalk Park and the Timmerman Trail to the West Columbia Riverwalk Park and Amphitheater. The pattern is what counts: paved path, mown verge, open water, repeated for miles.

Institutional and HOA retention ponds

This is the day-to-day work, and the category with the least published information. No inventory of Columbia’s stormwater ponds, campus water features or association basins exists in any source we could reach, so we give no count and name no pond. What we can say is structural: a detention basin is a broad shallow bowl with graded turf banks and clear approach lines, which is goose habitat arrived at by accident.

Are the birds on your pond residents or migrants?

If they are still there in July, they are residents, and that one word changes the whole problem.

Resident Canada geese hatch, pair, nest, moult and winter inside a small home range, and will not solve anything by leaving in spring. SCDNR puts South Carolina’s resident population above 50,000 birds and calls it increasing, with the greatest concentrations reported for the Foothills, the Piedmont and the Upper Coastal Plain. Richland and Lexington Counties straddle the Fall Line between those regions, so the distribution points this way — an inference from a statewide number, labelled as one rather than a local census.

Climate explains why residency sticks. The state climatologist’s station normals give Columbia Metro Airport a last spring freeze of 1 April and a first fall freeze of 13 October, 236 freeze-free days. The Columbia University of SC station, downtown, records 26 February and 26 October — 261 days. That twenty-five day gap between two stations in one city is measured, not modelled. A long warm season and open water that rarely locks up gives a bird no reason to leave.

Which Columbia properties carry the most exposure?

The ones with the most maintained lawn, the most foot traffic and the least tolerance for a slip hazard — a short, heavily institutional list.

University campuses. USC enrolled 38,504 students on its Columbia campus in fall 2024, across more than 359 downtown acres, with roughly three quarters of them living off campus against 9,243 assignable beds. Two exposures overlap: institutional lawns, and the apartment communities absorbing everyone else. Columbia is a majority-renter city — 45.5 percent owner-occupied against 53,076 households — and rental communities compete on amenities, which often means a pond.

Hospital campuses. Prisma Health Richland operates 641 beds plus 124 at its affiliated Heart Hospital, and it is a Level I Trauma Center and the sole regional referral centre for the Midlands. An entrance, an ambulance approach and a walking loop are the last places for droppings underfoot.

Fort Jackson. More than 52,000 acres inside the city limits since annexation in 1968, training roughly 43,000 service members a year. We name it as scale, not a client.

The convention district. The Columbia Metropolitan Convention Center opened in September 2004 with 142,500 square feet, next to Colonial Life Arena in the Congaree Vista. Plazas, hardscape and event lawn near the river are where droppings stop being a grounds problem and become a guest-experience one.

Associations and clubs. A board carries a fiduciary duty, a complaint at a meeting and no wildlife background. That is the situation our HOA and golf course goose management work was designed around; multi-site portfolios go through commercial pest control.

What is the dog actually doing, and why does one visit fail?

The dog communicates one message: a predator is hunting here. A border collie worked on waterfowl drops its head below the shoulder line, fixes its eyes and moves in on an arc. Geese are prey animals with long memories for danger, and they read that shape without having to learn it.

Nothing is caught. The dog is not trained to make contact and is not permitted to, and a handler who allows it has converted lawful harassment into a federal problem. Recall discipline, and judgement about where birds are pushed, matter more than anything at the water’s edge.

Geese hold a daily routine, and a single visit interrupts one instance of it. The flock returns next morning, the manager concludes dogs are theatre, and the programme dies early. Behaviour changes through repetition across days and weeks, at hours the birds cannot anticipate, until the site stops reading as reliable. Frequency in the opening fortnight most predicts the outcome.

We will not tell you geese never habituate to a dog. That claim is common in this trade and it is an overstatement. A 2008 paper in Environmental Management tested nine deterrent techniques against three gull species across six landfills, and found methods backed by real consequence held up while methods without one faded. A live predator belongs in the first category, so the fade is gradual — gradual, not absent, and the time it wins you is time to spend on the shoreline.

Which deterrents underperform when they are the whole plan?

Nearly all of them, and the reason never varies. Geese live a long time, watch one another, and re-price risk continuously, so anything that threatens without ever delivering ends up as furniture.

What gets boughtWhat it deliversWhy it stops delivering
Coyote or owl statue at the bankSome avoidance for days, occasionally weeksIt has never once approached a bird. Give it a month and geese feed alongside it.
Reflective streamers and spinnersA brief startle in sun and windThe movement is random and consequence-free, so attention to it simply stops.
Bangers, sirens and sonic unitsOpen turf clears for a few minutes per firingFixed intervals teach the timetable, and near housing complaints arrive faster than results.
Grape-extract turf repellentLess grazing on treated grass while residue lastsRain and mowing take it off, and loafing birds still foul the pavement.
A feeding rule with nothing behind itSound policy, very little movementIt withdraws a supplement and leaves acres of forage. Your lawn is the meal.
Dog work paired with a rebuilt edgeRelocates the flock now, removes the reason it settledThe dog effect needs renewal. The change to the ground never needs repeating.

None of these are frauds, and rotating several slows habituation more than leaning on one. The failure is buying a single tool and expecting it to beat a settled flock.

How do you rebuild an edge so the result holds?

Habitat is the only lever an owner controls outright; everything else depends on a vendor or somebody’s compliance. Break two of the three things the bird came for and the site stops competing.

  • Leave the last band before the water uncut. Grass and native planting allowed to stand there erase the grazing surface and close the walk-out together. Nothing else here returns as much, and it costs less than any product, being labour you subtract rather than add.
  • Break the view into compartments. Grouped shrubs, ornamental grasses and staggered small trees replace one open panorama with several partial ones, and a flock unable to post a sentry treats the ground as risky.
  • Change the grade at the margin. A gentle turf slope into water is a boat ramp for waterfowl. Facing the edge with stone deletes the easy exit.
  • Pull the inputs back from the bank. The best forage on most properties is the last twenty yards of irrigated, fertilised turf before the water, and less nitrogen there means lower protein.
  • Treat the buffer as design, not neglect. Height and continuity are what matter biologically; a crisp mown edge behind the planting is what stops a board calling it a missed mowing.
  • Make the trade consciously. Nothing in Southeastern landscaping suits a goose better than clipped lawn meeting a flat sheet of water. That view and a clean bank are alternatives, not a package, and a property declining to pick one pays for visits forever.

Where birds are on the buildings instead of the grass — a parapet, a canopy, a ledge — the answer is hardware rather than behaviour. That is bird exclusion, covered further on our Columbia bird control page.

Should your property ban feeding, and what should you check first?

As a management principle, yes. Handouts concentrate birds exactly where people walk, and one determined household can undo everything else a board attempts. A written no-feeding rule in the covenants, backed by somebody willing to have the conversation, is worth having.

Two cautions come with it. The first is scope: bread and corn are a supplement, not the diet. Canada geese graze, and irrigated, fertilised lawn is high-protein forage available here most of the year. Ending the feeding removes a concentration point, but the food supply is the turf, and the turf is still there next morning.

The second is legal. We have not read the current City of Columbia code on feeding wildlife, so we do not tell you what it says in either direction — we would rather report that than guess. Anyone building a programme should check the current municipal code and their own HOA covenants, lease terms or campus policy. What governs a public park is frequently not what governs a private basin.

What does federal law actually permit here?

The Canada goose is a species the Migratory Bird Treaty Act covers, named at 50 CFR 10.13, and anyone who shrugs that off should worry you. The conduct barred is take — killing, capturing, possessing, or meddling with nests and eggs. Persuading a bird to stand somewhere else is none of those things. The governing text is 50 CFR 21.100, which says no permit is required "merely to scare or herd depredating migratory birds." A dog that never closes the distance works inside that provision. The edges are worth knowing exactly.

  • Nests and eggs answer to a separate rule. Addling, oiling or destroying them sits under 50 CFR 21.162, with federal registration or authorisation and reporting attached. A contractor who offers to deal with a nest discreetly is transferring liability to you, not absorbing it.
  • The general depredation order stops short of geese. The species named in 50 CFR 21.150 are magpies, grackles, crows, cowbirds and blackbirds. Doves, egrets, herons, vultures, gulls and geese are all excluded, so anyone citing that order at you over a goose has opened the wrong rule.
  • The resident goose control orders are deliberately narrow. Section 21.120 carries the Special Canada Goose Permit; 21.168 addresses public health; 21.165 covers agricultural facilities; 21.159 applies to airports and military airfields. A campus lawn answers to none of those descriptions.

Set that against the species the Act omits. Three birds routinely found on the same site — the rock pigeon, the European starling, the house sparrow — hold no federal status whatever, and the options open on them are correspondingly wider. Our pigeon and European starling profiles set out the difference. For gulls or grackles working an outdoor terrace, the usual answer is falconry bird abatement.

How does the goose year run in the Midlands?

  • Deep winter, before pairs commit. January and early February are the strongest and least popular time to begin. Nothing is defended yet, birds stay movable, and a programme started now shapes the breeding season.
  • Nesting, spring. Once a pair settles, the options shrink. Birds out grazing may still be moved lawfully; the nest itself is off limits. Beginning in this window means slower going, and we say so before the job starts.
  • The moult, early summer. Once each year the birds drop their flight feathers, and for several weeks afterward they cannot get airborne. A bird that cannot fly cannot leave, so harassment reshuffles the flock on foot rather than relocating it. Droppings accumulate fastest then, which is when most first calls arrive.
  • Late summer into autumn. Flight returns, the flock reassesses where it wants to live, and this is the most productive push of the year. Richland County averages 47.75 to 48.11 inches of rain and a mean of 66.5°F on the 1991–2020 normals, with about 76 days a year above 90°F against 30 on the coast.
  • Late autumn. With a first fall freeze near 13 October at the airport and 26 October downtown, growth carries on past the point most people expect. Dormant season is right for planting and grading, so the habitat work and the calendar line up.

What does a Coastal K-9 programme look like week by week?

  1. The water gets walked before any dog arrives

    We map how the flock uses the site: where it loafs, where it feeds, how it enters and leaves the water, what it can see from the bank, and which stretch generates complaints. This is also the candid conversation about whether the property will accept a changed edge.

  2. Constraints are settled up front

    Clinic hours, class changes, event dates in the Vista, pool schedules, peak trail use. Harassment must be unpredictable to the geese and predictable to your staff.

  3. Early visits cluster and vary

    The opening phase is deliberately frequent and irregular. The goal is not one impressive morning; it is making the flock’s routine unreliable enough that the site loses its appeal.

  4. Handler and dog work the edge, then stop short

    The dog works the loafing ground and the bank, birds lift and go, and the recall comes before anything closes. No bird is cornered, no nest is walked up on, and nothing is pushed toward traffic or a car park.

  5. Every visit goes on the record

    Counts, locations and behaviour are logged each time, so a board or facilities director has a trend line rather than competing impressions.

  6. Visits taper and the written plan takes over

    You receive buffer widths, planting options, grading opportunities, turf input changes and a feeding policy written for your bank. Most sites then need one renewed push a year, once flight returns after the moult.

What is included

  • Non-lethal harassment visits using trained herding dogs, scheduled irregularly on purpose
  • Work kept under handler control, with dog and bird never in contact
  • Shoreline recommendations written for a grounds crew or landscape contractor
  • Straight answers on which federal and state authorisations bear on your site
  • The boundaries stated in advance: no nests, no eggs, no take, nothing needing an authorisation we do not hold

What happens where droppings meet a public surface?

Clemson Extension’s Savannah Valley District reports that geese on small ponds produce two to four pounds of manure per bird each day, and that the birds compact soil and kill turf through overgrazing. Across a resident flock, that is a standing labour line. On a walking loop it travels into cars on shoe soles. On a pool deck or a plaza it is a complaint the same afternoon. On a cart path or boat ramp, wet and trodden, it is a slip exposure. Overgrazed bank turf then thins, and this is Sandhills country — quartz sand, the Lakeland series classified as excessively drained. Bare sand on a slope above water does not stay where it was put.

On water quality we are careful, because this is the claim the industry inflates hardest. Clemson Extension’s regional guidance puts faecal bacteria counts in goose droppings at roughly twenty-five times the level in human waste. Read that as a property of the material and nothing more. It does not establish that any pond, lake or river reach here exceeds a bacterial standard, and no published sampling for a specific local water body surfaced in our research, so none is cited here. The defensible version is smaller: droppings concentrated on a bank that people swim from, launch from or sit beside are worth managing.

Who licenses this work in South Carolina?

Two separate authorities, and neither is the one most people name first.

Start with wildlife. Administration of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act belongs to the US Fish and Wildlife Service. At state level SCDNR issues depredation permits at no cost, good for thirty days, renewable, out of its regional wildlife-management and law-enforcement offices, with a warning that federally protected species may require more. Herding without contact calls for neither permit, under 50 CFR 21.100.

Pesticides run through a different door. In this state the licensing authority for structural, institutional and health-related work is the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation, not an agriculture department. Under category 7A a firm holds a business licence, posts a Designated Certified Applicator at every location, and carries commercial general liability of $100,000 combined single limit or more, with no deductible above $1,000. That framework governs chemical turf repellents and structural work, not a dog, and a company that cannot explain the difference is not the one to hire.

Where we work in and around Columbia

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions operates from 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856; the Midlands is a straightforward run north. In the city we cover Shandon and Old Shandon, Rosewood, Heathwood, Forest Hills, Earlewood, Elmwood Park, Cottontown and Bellevue, Eau Claire, Hyatt Park, Arsenal Hill, Historic Waverly, Wales Garden, Melrose, Hollywood-Rose Hill, Sherwood Forest, Druid Hills, Kilbourne Park, Lake Katherine, Granby Hill, Olympia, The Vista, University Hill, Seminary Ridge, Grove Park, Tanglewood, Kings Grant, Historic Trenholm-Buchanan, Lincoln Park and Greenview. See every area we serve.

Outside the city limits we work the Richland County side toward Sesquicentennial and Harbison, and the Lexington County side through Cayce, West Columbia, Irmo and Lexington. Where a pond edge has a rodent issue alongside the waterfowl, that is canine rodent detection, and student housing, hotels and multifamily buildings are covered by our Columbia canine bed bug work.

Frequently asked questions

Did our geese come from Lake Murray?

Possibly, and it does not change the plan. Lake Murray covers 48,579 acres with 620 miles of shoreline across four counties, and sits at the edge of the metro rather than inside Columbia. Resident geese range locally and settle wherever the ground suits them. Chasing a flock’s origin is interesting; what your own shoreline offers is what produces a result.

How quickly should we expect to see fewer birds?

Movement usually shows inside the first fortnight, but the number that matters is how the site looks after two months. An established flock keeps a routine measured in seasons, and undoing it takes repetition at unpredictable hours until the ground stops feeling safe. Properties that also change the shoreline taper to maintenance; those that change nothing keep buying visits.

Do we need a permit before you start?

Not for non-lethal harassment. Under 50 CFR 21.100 no permit is required merely to scare or herd depredating migratory birds, and a dog that never touches a bird falls inside that. Permits become relevant the instant anything involves a nest, an egg, capture or take. If your situation calls for that route, it runs through the US Fish and Wildlife Service.

Can you work a hospital or campus pond without disrupting operations?

That is a scheduling problem and we treat it as one. Ambulance approaches, clinic hours, class changes and pool times are mapped before the first visit. Timing stays unpredictable to the geese while remaining fully known to your staff, and we agree in advance which directions birds may be pushed toward and which are off limits.

There is a nest on the island in our basin. Can you deal with it?

Not through this service. Anything done to a nest or its contents falls under 50 CFR 21.162, which carries its own registration or authorisation requirement. We would rather tell you it is outside our scope than improvise around a protected species. Harassment of grazing birds continues lawfully while a nest is active, provided the nest is left alone.

How wide does the unmown buffer need to be?

No honest answer is a single number, and we found no Columbia-specific prescription worth quoting. What governs the effect is height, density and continuity: vegetation tall enough that a goose cannot see over it, thick enough that walking through is unattractive, and unbroken enough that no gap exists. A buffer with a mown gap is a doorway, and the birds find it within a day.

Our board wants to try a laser or a drone first. What should we expect?

An initial response, then a decline, on the same logic that governs every other deterrent. Devices producing no consequence get reclassified as scenery by a long-lived, observant bird. These tools have a place inside a varied programme. Sold as the whole solution against a settled flock with unchanged turf, they disappoint.

Can you handle pigeons or starlings on the same site?

Yes, though it is a separate discipline. Neither species holds federal status, nor does the house sparrow, so none of the limits described above applies to them. Birds on structures are dealt with physically rather than behaviourally: netting, altered ledge angles, sealed openings. The dog plays no part in that work at all.

title: Goose Control for Golf Courses
description: A golf course is close to a purpose-built goose habitat: open water, wide expanses of short, fertilized, irrigated grass, clear sightlines, and no natural predators.
h1: Goose Control for Golf Courses: Protecting Greens, Playability, and Your Members’ Patience
body:
Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions  |  Windsor, SC  |  September 29, 2026

A golf course is close to a purpose-built goose habitat: open water, wide expanses of short, fertilized, irrigated grass, clear sightlines, and no natural predators. That’s why geese settle in and refuse to leave, and why decoys, noise makers, and repellents so reliably fail — none of them make the course feel genuinely dangerous. Trained working dogs do, because a real predator behaving like a predator is something geese cannot habituate to. For a course dealing with fouled greens, damaged turf, and member complaints, dog-based patrols are the humane approach that actually works.

Why are golf courses so attractive to geese?

Everything a Canada goose wants is on a golf course, arranged conveniently. They want open water for safety and roosting — you have ponds and water hazards. They want short, tender, nutrient-rich grass to graze — you spend enormous effort producing precisely that, fertilized and irrigated to a standard no natural meadow can match. They want clear sightlines so they can see predators approaching — fairways and greens deliver that perfectly.

Add the absence of meaningful predators, the general tolerance of people moving around at a distance, and in many cases members or guests feeding the birds, and you’ve created ideal habitat. Geese are also strongly site-faithful: once a flock has grazed and successfully nested on your course, they return year after year, and their goslings grow up regarding your course as home.

What do geese actually cost a golf course?

Start with the droppings, because the volume genuinely surprises people. A single goose produces a substantial amount of waste every day, and a resident flock of any size deposits an enormous quantity across greens, fairways, tees, cart paths, and clubhouse surrounds. That’s a direct labor cost in cleanup, it’s a playability problem on greens, and it’s a member-experience problem that generates complaints — nobody wants to putt through it or track it into the clubhouse.

Then there’s turf damage. Geese don’t just graze the grass, they pull at it and grub for roots, damaging the turf you’ve invested heavily in, and their concentrated grazing and trampling can degrade greens and tees. There are water-quality implications for ponds through nutrient loading, which can drive algae problems. And during nesting season, geese become aggressive — a defensive goose confronting a member or a child near a nest is a genuine liability concern, not a curiosity.

K9 INSIGHT  Schedule patrols for early morning and evening — that’s when geese are most active on the turf and when the course is quietest, so you disrupt the birds at peak effect without disrupting play. Superintendents consistently find this less intrusive to members than noise cannons ever were.

Why don’t the usual deterrents work on a course?

Habituation, and the scale of the property. Coyote decoys don’t move; geese work that out within days and go back to grazing beside them. Noise cannons and distress calls scare birds until it becomes clear nothing bad ever follows the sound, and on a golf course they also disturb the members you’re trying to keep happy. Reflective tape, flags, and balloons are visual clutter that stops working almost immediately and looks terrible on a well-presented course.

Chemical turf repellents can genuinely help, but on a course they’re expensive to apply across the necessary acreage, they wash off with irrigation and rain, and they need constant reapplication. And the drastic options — nest destruction or removal of birds — run into federal protections and, for a club with a public reputation and a membership, real optics problems. None of these methods changes the fundamental fact that the course feels safe to the geese.

How does a dog program work on a golf course?

Trained handlers work dogs across the property on a schedule, targeting the ponds, greens, fairways, and roosting areas the geese actually use, and working the birds with genuine predator behavior — stalking, pressuring, pushing them off the water and into flight. The birds cannot habituate to it, because it’s a real predator and it’s different every time. Over a program of consistent patrols, the geese conclude the course is not a safe place to spend their time and relocate on their own.

Practically, patrols are scheduled around play so they don’t interfere with members — typically early morning and evening when geese are most active on the turf and the course is quietest. The dogs never catch or harm the birds; the mechanism is disruption of the geese’s sense of safety, not violence. Course superintendents generally find the dogs are less disruptive to play and members than noise-based deterrents ever were.

Is it humane, and is it legal?

Yes to both, and that combination is a large part of why dog programs became the standard on golf courses, corporate campuses, and airports. The dogs harass and pressure the geese but do not catch or injure them — no bird is harmed, no nest destroyed, no goose killed. The geese simply decide the location isn’t worth it and leave. For a club that answers to a membership and a community, being able to say the program is entirely humane matters.

The legal picture reinforces this. Canada geese are protected under federal law, which sharply limits what may lawfully be done to the birds, their nests, and their eggs — which is exactly why humane, harassment-based methods are the standard, defensible approach. If you have questions about the specific regulations that apply to your property or situation, those are worth confirming with the relevant federal and South Carolina authorities; we can talk you through how the program works, but we’d always point you to the regulators on the legal specifics.

How long does it take, and will they come back?

Be skeptical of anyone promising a one-visit fix. Effective goose control is a program: consistent, repeated patrols over time until the flock genuinely relocates rather than simply being pushed to the far side of the property for an afternoon. How long depends on the size of the resident flock, how long they’ve been established, the season, and how much of the property they’re using — a long-entrenched flock takes more work than a newly arrived one.

And yes, geese will test the course again — they’re strongly site-faithful and they remember. That’s why ongoing or seasonal maintenance patrols are part of a realistic program, particularly around nesting season and during migration periods when new birds are prospecting for a place to settle. The course stays goose-free as long as it keeps feeling unsafe to them, which is precisely what maintenance patrols preserve.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do geese love golf courses so much?

Because a course provides everything they want: open water for safety, wide expanses of short fertilized irrigated grass for grazing, and clear sightlines to watch for predators — with no natural predators present. Geese are also site-faithful, returning year after year once they’ve grazed and nested successfully.

What damage do geese actually cause on a course?

Enormous quantities of droppings on greens, fairways, tees, cart paths and clubhouse surrounds — a cleanup cost, a playability problem, and a member-experience problem. Plus turf damage from grazing and grubbing at roots, water-quality issues in ponds from nutrient loading, and aggressive nesting-season behavior that creates liability concerns.

Why don’t coyote decoys or noise cannons work?

Habituation. Decoys don’t move, so geese work out within days that they’re harmless. Noise cannons and distress calls stop working once the birds learn nothing bad follows the sound — and they disturb the members you’re trying to keep happy. Nothing about these methods makes the course feel genuinely dangerous.

How do dogs get geese off a golf course?

Trained handlers work dogs across the ponds, greens, fairways, and roosting areas on a schedule, working the birds with genuine predator behavior. Geese can’t habituate to a real, unpredictable predator, so over consistent patrols they conclude the course isn’t safe and relocate on their own. The dogs never catch or harm the birds.

Will the dogs disrupt play?

Patrols are scheduled around play, typically early morning and evening when geese are most active on the turf and the course is quietest. Superintendents generally find dogs considerably less disruptive to members and play than noise-based deterrents like cannons and distress-call devices.

Is dog-based goose control humane and legal?

Yes. The dogs harass and pressure but never catch or injure the birds — no goose is harmed, no nest destroyed. Canada geese are protected under federal law, which limits what may be done to the birds, nests, and eggs, so humane harassment-based methods are the standard, defensible approach. Confirm specific regulations with the relevant authorities.

How long does it take to clear a course of geese?

It’s a program, not a single visit. Duration depends on the size of the resident flock, how long they’ve been established, the season, and how much of the property they use — an entrenched flock takes more work than newly arrived birds. Be skeptical of anyone promising a one-visit fix.

Will the geese come back?

They’ll test the course again — geese are site-faithful and they remember. That’s why ongoing or seasonal maintenance patrols are part of a realistic program, especially around nesting season and migration when new birds prospect for a place to settle. The course stays clear as long as it keeps feeling unsafe to them.

Need answers you can trust?

Humane, dog-based goose control for golf courses and clubs across South Carolina — protecting greens, playability, and your members’ experience.

Call  803-226-3155

title: Goose Control for HOAs, Parks, Schools and Corporate Campuses
description: Retention ponds, community lakes, campus lawns, and school fields are magnets for Canada geese — and once a flock settles in, the complaints start
h1: Goose Control for HOAs, Parks, Schools and Corporate Campuses
body:
Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions  |  Windsor, SC  |  October 6, 2026

Retention ponds, community lakes, campus lawns, and school fields are magnets for Canada geese — and once a flock settles in, the complaints start: droppings on walkways and playgrounds, fouled docks and beaches, aggressive birds during nesting season, and residents demanding that somebody do something. The difficulty for an HOA board, a facilities manager, or a school is that the obvious solutions are either ineffective (decoys, noise) or a public-relations disaster (anything that harms the birds). Dog-based goose control is the option that actually works and that you can defend to your residents, parents, and community.

Why do geese settle on retention ponds and campus lawns?

Because the modern developed landscape accidentally builds ideal goose habitat. A retention pond provides open water for safety and roosting. The surrounding mown, fertilized lawn provides exactly the short, tender grass geese prefer to graze. The open sightlines let them see predators coming. And there are no actual predators — just people, who geese quickly learn are harmless and who, in many communities, actively feed them.

Feeding is worth dwelling on, because it’s often the single biggest driver in residential and park settings and it’s entirely self-inflicted. Well-meaning residents feeding bread to the geese teaches the flock that this location is not merely safe but a food source, which anchors them permanently and grows the population. Any goose management program in a community setting has to address feeding, or it’s working against itself.

Why do geese become a real liability, not just a nuisance?

The droppings alone are a substantial sanitation problem — on sidewalks, playgrounds, athletic fields, docks, patios, and pool surrounds, in exactly the places where children play and residents walk. Beyond the cleanup burden, droppings on wet walkways create slip hazards, and they raise water-quality concerns in the pond itself through nutrient loading, which can drive algae blooms and degrade the amenity residents paid for.

The liability sharpens dramatically during nesting season. Geese defending a nest are genuinely aggressive, and they will confront residents, employees, children, and pets — hissing, charging, and sometimes striking. A nesting goose beside a playground, a school entrance, an apartment walkway, or an office door is a serious problem, and once a nest is established, your legal options for dealing with it narrow considerably because of federal protections. Preventing establishment is far easier than resolving it.

K9 INSIGHT  If residents are feeding the geese, no goose program will fully succeed — you’re offering a food reward while trying to convince the birds the site is dangerous. Signage and a clear community rule against feeding is the cheapest, highest-impact step an HOA or school can take.

Why is the PR dimension so important here?

In a community, a school, or a corporate campus, how you solve the goose problem is nearly as important as whether you solve it. Any approach that harms geese — or is even perceived to harm them — is likely to become a controversy: angry residents, upset parents, a viral social post, a board meeting you don’t enjoy. Geese are charismatic birds and people feel protective of them, even the same people complaining about the droppings.

This is precisely why dog-based control is such a strong fit for these settings. It’s genuinely humane — the dogs pressure and harass, but never catch or harm the birds, and no nests are destroyed. The geese simply choose to leave. That’s a program you can announce to residents, explain to parents, and defend publicly without difficulty, which is worth a great deal to a board or an administrator who has to live in the community afterward.

How does the program work in a community setting?

Handlers work trained dogs on a schedule at the areas the geese actually use — the pond, the shoreline, the lawns and fields they graze. The dogs work the birds with genuine predator behavior, pushing them off the water and turf. Because the threat is real and unpredictable, geese can’t habituate to it the way they do to decoys and noise makers, and after consistent patrols they relocate to somewhere that feels safer.

Patrols are scheduled to fit the community — typically early morning or evening when geese are most active and the property is quiet, avoiding busy periods, school hours, or events. It’s a low-visibility, low-disruption operation compared to the alternatives; you’re not firing noise cannons across a neighborhood or covering a park in plastic decoys and reflective tape.

What else does the community need to do?

Stop the feeding — and this genuinely requires a policy and communication, not just a hope. Signage, a clear HOA or facility rule, and an explanation to residents of *why* feeding harms the geese and the community (it anchors and grows the flock, concentrates droppings, creates aggressive birds, and degrades the pond) will do more than most people expect. A program that patrols the pond while residents keep feeding the birds is fighting itself.

Habitat modification helps too. Letting vegetation grow taller along the pond’s shoreline removes the clear sightlines geese require and makes the water’s edge less attractive, and it’s an easy, permanent, no-conflict change that supports the patrol program. Together — dogs making the site feel unsafe, no food reward, and less attractive shoreline habitat — the calculus for the geese shifts decisively, and they go somewhere better.

What should a board or facility manager expect?

Expect a program rather than a fix. Consistency over time is what convinces a flock to relocate, and how long depends on the size of the flock and how long they’ve been established. A flock that has nested on your pond for years takes more work than birds that showed up last month. Anyone promising to make the geese vanish in a single visit is overselling, and a board should be skeptical of that pitch.

Expect ongoing maintenance too. Geese are site-faithful and will test the property again, especially around nesting season and migration when new birds prospect for a place to settle. Seasonal or periodic maintenance patrols keep the site from being re-adopted. The realistic promise is a pond and lawns that geese have decided not to use — and that stay that way as long as the site keeps feeling unsafe to them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do geese take over retention ponds?

Because a retention pond plus mown, fertilized lawn accidentally recreates ideal goose habitat: open water for safety, short tender grass to graze, clear sightlines, and no predators. Residents feeding the birds compounds it enormously, teaching the flock the site is both safe and a food source, which anchors them permanently.

Are geese actually dangerous to residents or children?

During nesting season, yes — geese defending a nest are genuinely aggressive and will confront residents, employees, children, and pets, hissing, charging, and sometimes striking. A nest beside a playground, school entrance, or walkway is a serious liability concern, and federal protections narrow your options once a nest is established.

Why is dog-based control better for an HOA or school?

Because it works and it’s defensible. The dogs pressure and harass but never catch or harm the birds, and no nests are destroyed — the geese simply choose to leave. Any approach perceived as harming geese is likely to become a community controversy, so a genuinely humane program is one you can announce to residents and parents without difficulty.

Do we need to stop residents from feeding the geese?

Yes — and it needs a policy, signage, and communication, not just a hope. A program that patrols the pond while residents keep feeding the birds is fighting itself. Explaining why feeding harms the geese and the community (anchoring and growing the flock, droppings, aggression, pond degradation) is the cheapest high-impact step available.

What else can we do besides the dog patrols?

Habitat modification helps a lot. Letting vegetation grow taller along the pond shoreline removes the clear sightlines geese require and makes the water’s edge less attractive — an easy, permanent, no-conflict change that supports the patrol program. Combined with no food reward, the calculus shifts decisively.

How long before the geese leave?

It’s a program, not a single visit. Duration depends on flock size and how long they’ve been established — birds that have nested on your pond for years take more work than recent arrivals. Be skeptical of anyone promising the geese will vanish after one visit.

Will the geese come back?

They’ll test the property again — geese are site-faithful and remember. Seasonal or periodic maintenance patrols keep the site from being re-adopted, particularly around nesting season and migration when new birds prospect for somewhere to settle. The site stays clear as long as it keeps feeling unsafe to them.

Do you work with HOAs and schools in South Carolina?

Yes. Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions provides humane dog-based goose control for HOAs, community ponds, parks, schools, athletic fields, apartment complexes, and corporate campuses across Aiken, Columbia, Lexington, Charleston, Greenville, and surrounding areas. Call 803-226-3155.

Need answers you can trust?

title: Goose Control in Lexington, SC
description: Humane Canada goose management around Lexington and Lake Murray for HOA commons, golf courses and lakeside properties, using trained herding dogs.
h1: Goose Control in Lexington, SC

hero.eyebrow: LEXINGTON, SOUTH CAROLINA · CANADA GOOSE MANAGEMENT
hero.lead: Lake Murray hands Lexington 620 miles of shoreline, and a great deal of that edge is lawn cut straight to the water. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions puts trained herding dogs on resident Canada geese at lakefront lots, subdivision basins and club turf here, then reshapes the edge so the flock stops picking it.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Family-owned · Non-lethal, and no bird is touched · Lake Murray and the Midlands, run out of Windsor, South Carolina

body:
Two numbers carry most of the goose problem in this town. One is 620, the miles of shoreline SCDNR records for Lake Murray across Lexington, Newberry, Richland and Saluda counties. The other is 2002, the median year a housing unit inside the town of Lexington was built.

A very large reservoir and a very young suburb yield the same product: edge, where clipped grass meets standing water. Edge is what a resident Canada goose shops for. It is indifferent to a postcode or a set of covenants, and nearly every acre of what it wants here was built on purpose.

620 milesShoreline on Lake Murray, 48,579 surface acres averaging 41.5 feet deep, across four counties (SCDNR)
2002Median year a housing unit was built in the TOWN of Lexington, against 1993 for Lexington COUNTY (ACS 2020–2024, table B25035)
50,000+SCDNR’s estimate of resident Canada geese in South Carolina, statewide. No goose count has ever been published for Lexington.

How much lawn-to-water edge does this area really have?

More than anywhere else we work. SCDNR’s Lake Murray brochure gives 48,579 acres of surface water, 620 miles of shoreline, an average depth of 41.5 feet and a maximum near 200, across Lexington, Newberry, Richland and Saluda counties. The impoundment sits behind a dam 1.6 miles long and feeds the 205 MW Saluda hydroelectric station.

Shoreline length measures interface. Every mile is a mile where an upland owner decides what the last thirty feet before the water look like, and the customary answer is turf, mown short, running to a bulkhead or a sand edge with a dock beyond.

Most of that edge is neither town property nor public. Dominion Energy administers the reservoir under FERC Project No. 516, and the 360-foot contour marks normal maximum pool and, along much of the lake, the boundary between utility and upland owner. Of the public access sites the utility lists, two are labelled by county: the Park Site on the Lexington side at 17.9 acres, and the Dam Site on the Irmo side at 6.8. The method behind our work is on the parent page for Canada goose management, and the species account is in the Canada goose library entry.

What does a lakefront lot look like from the bird’s side?

Like a solved problem, which is exactly the difficulty. A grazing goose needs three conditions met at once. It eats grass, so it wants a sward short, green and preferably fertilized. It survives by watching, so it wants a view holding nothing large enough to hide a coyote. It escapes by swimming, so it wants water reachable in a few strides.

Now describe the standard Lake Murray lot. Lawn maintained to the top of a bulkhead, or to a shallow sandy margin. A dock or boat lift beyond it. No screening planting at the waterline, because screening blocks the view everybody paid for. Open water in front, and in the Midlands water that does not lock up in winter. All three conditions inside about thirty feet, which is why one house holds birds while a neighbor with a wooded bank and a rip-rap face never sees them on the ground. The dock compounds it, being a loafing platform with clear approaches on every side and instant escape underneath.

Why does a town built after 1990 hold so much of this habitat?

Because the drainage rules changed, and the drainage rules built the ponds. ACS tables for 2020 to 2024 put the town’s median year of construction at 2002, while Lexington County as a whole sits at 1993. Of the town’s 10,348 housing units, 80.3 percent went up in 1990 or later and only 9.5 percent predate 1980.

Subdivisions of that vintage arrive with engineered stormwater management, which here usually means a retention basin holding an amenity pond. Consider what a basin has to be: a broad shallow bowl, banks graded gently enough to mow safely, an unobstructed perimeter, a maintained turf apron. Nobody set out to build waterfowl habitat. The specification simply matches the bird’s requirements almost item for item.

The Town’s own GIS subdivision layer lists 93 named developments, and many announce their water: Barr Lake, Carriage Hills Lake, Coventry Lake, Mallard Lakes, Whiteford Lakes, Whisperlake, Lakeside at Woodcreek, Shoal Creek, Royal Creek, Bent Creek, Creekside Farms, Saluda Springs, Woodstream. No count of stormwater ponds inside the town limits was obtainable, so we print none rather than estimate one.

Which local water fits the pattern, and which does not?

What follows is geometry, not an accusation. No published source identifies a Lexington water body as having a goose problem, and we name no association or club as either a client or a complaint.

The Lake Murray shoreline

The main event and the least uniform. Coves with steep wooded banks hold almost nothing on the ground; cleared lots with turf to the bulkhead and a wide view generate the calls. Because the shoreline crosses four counties and much of it lies outside any municipal boundary, two neighbors a quarter mile apart can sit under different local rules.

Subdivision retention basins

The bulk of the day-to-day work, and a manufactured version of what the lake offers naturally: mown turf all the way round, a path, a bench, clear approach lines. Basins built in the 1990s and early 2000s are now mature enough to hold breeding, year-round flocks.

Gibson Pond Park and Old Mill Pond

Gibson Pond Park sits at 241 Gibson Road, where fishing runs under state rules, gas-powered watercraft are banned and swimming is prohibited. Old Mill Pond Trail runs from 711 East Main Street.

Twelve Mile Creek and Fourteen Mile Creek

Twelve Mile Creek is gauged: USGS station 02168810 at Lexington, hydrologic unit 03050109. Fourteen Mile Creek carries a 3,500-foot Town trail off North Lake Drive and Old Cherokee Road, and it floods. Both are poor goose ground, because moving water in a wooded corridor offers a grazing bird nothing it wants.

Golden Hills Golf and Country Club

One hundred Scotland Drive: eighteen holes, par 71, 6,426 yards. It is the single golf facility we could verify at a Lexington town address. We could not document its water features, so we describe none.

What we will not attach to this town

Timberlake Country Club is a genuine Lake Murray club, but its address is in Chapin, roughly eighteen road miles from downtown, so calling it a Lexington course would be wrong. Several neighborhood names that come up locally appear nowhere in the Town’s own 93-name layer, so we leave them out.

What is the dog doing, and why does one visit fail?

The dog delivers one signal: something is hunting here right now. Put a border collie on the bank and it flattens, fixes its gaze and comes in along an arc rather than head-on. That shape is the universal preamble to a predator’s rush, and prey species need no teaching to read it.

Contact is the line, and it is not a soft one. Closing the distance is neither trained nor tolerated, and a handler who lets it happen has converted a lawful push into a wildlife offence. The handler’s judgement about direction of travel matters more than anything the dog does, because birds have to be pushed toward open water and away from parking, occupied docks and traffic.

Timing is where expectations go wrong. Geese hold a routine measured in weeks and seasons, and a single visit interrupts one instance of it. Settled birds give way to sustained repetition instead, spread over weeks and timed so the flock can never predict it. Nor do we sell the line that a dog is immune to habituation, which the research does not support. Writing in Environmental Management in 2008, researchers ran nine deterrent methods at six landfill sites against three species of gull; the ones with genuine consequence behind them kept working, and the empty ones lost their grip. A live predator belongs in the first group, so the decline is slow rather than absent.

Which deterrents get bought first, and where do they run out?

Nearly all of them, for one reason. A goose lives a long time, watches its neighbours and re-prices risk continually, so anything that threatens without following through is eventually reclassified as furniture.

What gets triedWhat it buysWhere it runs out
Coyote or owl statue on the bankSome avoidance, days to a few weeksIt has never once taken a step toward a bird. Within a month geese feed in its shadow.
Flash tape, flags, spinnersA startle in bright, breezy conditionsMovement without consequence stops registering, and the tape looks tired by August.
Bangers, sirens, sonic unitsOpen ground clears for minutes per firingFixed intervals teach the timetable. At 6am in a subdivision you also meet the Town’s noise chapter.
A feeding rule and nothing elseCorrect policy, very little movementIt withdraws a snack and leaves acres of forage standing. The lawn is the meal.
Dog work plus a rebuilt waterlineRelocates the flock and deletes the reason it settledThe dog effect needs renewal. The change to the ground does not.

None of these are frauds, and rotating methods slows habituation. The failure is buying one and expecting it to beat a settled flock.

Does the town’s bird sanctuary ordinance change what is legal here?

It is a live question and it deserves a straight answer in two layers, federal first, local on top.

The federal layer. The Canada goose is protected by name under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act at 50 CFR 10.13. What the Act prohibits is take: killing, capturing, possessing, and interfering with nests and eggs. Persuading a bird to stand somewhere else is not take. That distinction is written into 50 CFR 21.100, which withholds any permit requirement from scaring or herding depredating migratory birds. A dog that never makes contact does not touch, injure or take a bird. Anything involving a nest, an egg, capture or removal is a separate regulation, principally 50 CFR 21.162, and needs federal authorization we do not hold.

The local layer. The Town of Lexington code contains § 91.06, headed bird sanctuary, making it unlawful to "trap, hunt, shoot or attempt to shoot or molest in any manner any bird or wild fowl or to rob bird nests or wild fowl nests." The general penalty at § 91.99 runs to $500 or thirty days, each day a separate offence. That provision is broader than the federal Act in two ways: it reaches birds the Act leaves out entirely, including rock pigeon, European starling and house sparrow, and it names nests directly.

  • We are not offering a legal opinion on § 91.06. How the Town reads "molest in any manner", and how it enforces the section, are questions for the Town and for your own attorney.
  • We claim no exemption, and we do not say the ordinance bans this work. No carve-out for professional waterfowl management was found in the Lexington code, and if somebody tells you one exists, ask for the section number. The opposite conclusion would be a legal opinion too, drawn in our own commercial interest.
  • Confirm the current code before anything starts. Anyone planning a goose programme inside the town limits should read the current text of Title IX, Chapter 91 and speak to the Town directly.
  • Two codes are in play, not one. Section 91.21 adopts the Lexington County animal control ordinance by reference and provides that where a Town provision conflicts, the County ordinance controls. The most recent adopting ordinance recorded is 2024-13, passed 7 October 2024.
  • Geography decides which layer applies. A retention basin inside the municipal boundary is in the town. Much of the Lake Murray shoreline is not, and answers instead to Dominion Energy under FERC Project No. 516.

If the code is uncertain, what always works?

Changing the ground. No ordinance restricts how tall you let the grass at your own waterline grow. Habitat is the one lever an owner controls outright, without depending on a vendor, a permit or anybody else’s compliance, and it is the only permanent change available.

  • Stop mowing the last band before the water. Leaving that strip in grass and native planting takes away the food and seals the exit at the same time. It costs less than any product, being work you subtract rather than add.
  • Plant to break the sightline. Grouped shrubs, ornamental grasses and staggered small trees convert one open panorama into partial views. A flock that cannot post a sentry treats the ground as risky.
  • Change the grade at the margin. A gentle turf slope into water is a launching ramp for waterfowl. Steepening it, or facing it with stone, deletes the easy exit.
  • Shrink the mown-turf-to-water interface itself. Measure how many linear feet of bank are cut to the edge, then set a reduction target.
  • Pull irrigation and fertilizer back from the bank. On most sites the richest feed is the final twenty yards of irrigated ground, and cutting nitrogen there drops the protein in precisely the sward they came for.
  • Treat the buffer as design. Biologically the requirement is height, density and continuity, and a gap works as a door geese find on the first day. Visually, native planting with a crisp mown edge behind it reads as landscape architecture rather than a missed cut.

Where birds are on the buildings instead, a clubhouse parapet or a ledge above an entry, the answer is hardware. That is bird exclusion, covered further on our Lexington bird control page.

What can an HOA board here actually get approved?

Less than the biology wants in year one, and more than most boards expect by year two. Somebody raises it at a meeting; the directors owe a duty of care and know nothing about waterfowl; and the room splits between people wanting something dramatic and people wanting it dropped. The quiet middle position, letting the grass grow at the pond, is the one that changes how the neighborhood looks, and boards approve budgets more readily than appearances.

Three things make approval likelier. Phase it, proposing one demonstration stretch of bank rather than the whole perimeter. Bring the log, because a documented record of bird numbers before and after answers both loud positions at once. And borrow the Town’s own language: Lexington’s land development regulations include an article stating that the Town encourages conservation subdivision design on all suitable land in and around the Town. Golf property runs on the same logic with playability as the extra constraint, and our HOA and golf course goose management work is built around those realities.

What do droppings cost on a dock, a ramp or a cart path?

Clemson Extension’s Savannah Valley District guidance puts geese on small ponds at two to four pounds of droppings per bird per day, and notes that the birds also compact soil and kill turf through overgrazing. A boat ramp or dock, wet and trodden, is a slip exposure. A cart path carries it onto shoes, and a pool deck produces a complaint the same afternoon. Overgrazed bank turf thins, which matters here: we sit in the Sandhills, on quartz sand, where the Lakeland soil series carries an excessively drained rating. Sand with a worn cover, tilted toward a pond, migrates.

Water quality is where we slow down, because no claim in this trade gets stretched further. Clemson Extension’s regional guidance reports fecal bacteria counts in goose droppings running roughly twenty-five times those in human waste. It does not establish that any pond, basin or stretch of Lake Murray shoreline exceeds a bacterial standard, and we found no published sampling data for a specific local water body, so none is cited. The defensible version is narrower and still useful: droppings concentrated where people swim, launch boats or set down children are worth managing.

How does the goose year run between the county’s two weather stations?

No climate station publishes normals for the town itself, so we use the two the State Climatology Office does publish inside Lexington County, and we label them.

  • January and February, before pairs commit. The strongest time to begin and the time almost nobody calls. Nothing is being defended and birds remain movable.
  • March into May, nesting. Once a pair sits, options narrow sharply. Grazing birds may still be moved lawfully; the nest is off limits and stays off limits. Little Mountain records a last spring freeze around 31 March, Pelion 4 NW around 21 March.
  • Early summer, the molt. Once each year the birds drop their primaries and go several weeks without the ability to fly. A flightless bird cannot accept an invitation to leave, so harassment then redistributes the flock on foot rather than relocating it.
  • Late summer into fall. Flight returns, the flock reconsiders where it wants to live, and this becomes the most productive push of the year. First fall freeze falls near 20 October at Little Mountain and 10 October at Pelion 4 NW, giving 246 and 226 freeze-free days respectively.
  • Winter. Residents stay, migrants may add to the numbers, and open water on a 48,579-acre reservoir does not ice over.

For temperature and rainfall the nearest published normals are the Columbia and Midlands set: 47.75 to 48.11 inches of precipitation and a mean of 66.5 degrees Fahrenheit on the 1991 to 2020 normals. Lexington sits roughly twelve miles from downtown Columbia, so we label those figures Columbia and Midlands rather than dressing them up as Lexington’s own.

How does a Coastal K-9 programme run here?

  1. The bank gets walked before any dog arrives

    Together we chart the way the birds use the place: grazing turf, loafing ground, walk-out points, sightlines, and which stretch generates complaints. On lake frontage we also want to know where your line sits relative to the 360-foot contour, because that decides who controls the ground you propose to plant.

  2. The local questions get settled first

    Municipal boundary or not, town park or private basin, association covenants, and what the Town tells you when you ask about Chapter 91.

  3. Constraints go into the schedule

    Tee times, pool hours, school traffic, peak trail use, event dates. Harassment must be unpredictable to the geese while staying predictable to your staff.

  4. Opening visits cluster and vary

    The first phase is frequent and deliberately irregular. One dramatic morning is not the aim. Wrecking the dependability of the flock’s day is.

  5. Numbers go on the record every visit

    Counts, locations and behaviour are logged each time, so you hold a trend line rather than competing recollections.

  6. Visits taper and the written plan takes over

    The document covers buffer depth, plant choices, where grading would pay, mowing and fertiliser changes, and a feeding rule fitted to your own water. Nearly every property wants one refresher season, timed to the return of flight.

What is included

  • A written habitat assessment covering the whole waterline and the ground behind it
  • Scheduled dog work, non-lethal throughout, with the timing kept deliberately erratic
  • Every visit run under handler control, with the dog kept clear of the birds
  • A season-long record of what was counted, where, and how the birds behaved
  • A measured baseline of how much of your bank is mown to the water, and a reduction target
  • Shoreline recommendations written so a grounds crew or landscaper can execute them
  • A written note of the local code questions to put to the Town before work begins
  • The limits stated up front: no nests, no eggs, no take, nothing requiring an authorization we do not hold

Who licenses this work in South Carolina?

Wildlife runs federal and state: administration of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act rests with the US Fish and Wildlife Service, while SCDNR hands out depredation permits free of charge, good for thirty days and renewable, from its regional offices. Neither is needed for the herding work set out above, per 50 CFR 21.100. These authorities stack rather than substitute, and none of them displaces a municipal provision.

Pesticide work is a wholly different regime. In this state, structural, institutional and health-related pest control is licensed by the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation rather than by a state agriculture department, under category 7A. That means a firm licence, a Designated Certified Applicator stationed at every location, and general liability cover no lower than $100,000 combined single limit. That framework governs chemical turf repellents and structural treatments, not a dog.

One distinction worth carrying. Rock pigeon, European starling and house sparrow hold no protection under the federal Act; the gap is spelled out in our pigeon and European starling profiles, and the Town’s § 91.06 language does not appear to carve those species out the way federal law does. Where gulls or grackles work an outdoor terrace, the tool is usually falconry bird abatement.

Where we work around Lexington

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions operates from 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856. Inside the town we work the subdivisions on the Town’s own list, among them Barr Lake, Bent Creek Plantation, Brookstone, Carriage Hills Lake, Carrington Place, Cherokee Village, Coventry Lake, Creekside Farms, Golden Hills, Hope Ferry Plantation, Lakeside at Woodcreek, Laurel Falls, Mallard Lakes, Nightingale Hills, Pilgrim Point, River Ridge, Royal Creek, Saluda Springs, Shoal Creek, Sterling Bridge, Twelve Mile Ridge, Whisperlake, Whiteford Lakes and Woodstream. See every area we cover.

Outside the town limits we work the Lake Murray shoreline on the Lexington County side, the Irmo and Chapin side of the lake, and the Cayce, West Columbia and Columbia end of the Midlands. Where a pond bank has a rodent problem alongside the waterfowl, that is canine rodent detection, and multifamily buildings, lakefront rentals and lodging are covered by our Lexington canine bed bug work.

Frequently asked questions

Does the bird sanctuary ordinance mean you cannot work in Lexington?

We will not answer that as a legal conclusion in either direction, because it is not ours to give. Section 91.06 makes it unlawful to trap, hunt, shoot or molest any bird or wild fowl, or to rob nests. How the Town interprets and enforces that language is a question for the Town and for your attorney. What we can say with certainty is that habitat modification is untouched by it.

Our lot is on the lake but outside the town limits. Which rules apply?

Different ones, and the difference is worth establishing before anything is scheduled. Municipal provisions apply inside the municipal boundary. Much of the Lake Murray shoreline sits outside it, under Dominion Energy’s administration of FERC Project No. 516, with the 360-foot contour as normal maximum pool and, along much of the lake, the property boundary. Federal migratory bird law applies everywhere regardless.

How many geese are there in Lexington?

Nobody has published a figure, and we will not manufacture one to make a page look authoritative. The only sourced number available is statewide: SCDNR puts the state’s resident Canada goose total past 50,000 and rising. That is a state figure, not a town or county one, and anyone quoting you a Lexington-specific count should be asked for the source.

Can you take a nest off our dock?

Not under this service. Nests and their contents are governed federally by 50 CFR 21.162, which brings registration or authorization and its own reporting duties. Saying so flatly beats improvising around a protected species. Birds out feeding can still be moved while a nest sits there, so long as nobody goes near it.

Our pond is small. Will a buffer really be enough?

On a small basin it is frequently the whole answer, because a small pond has proportionally more edge than open water, and edge is what you are changing. What governs the effect is height, density and continuity rather than width in feet: planting that stands above eye level for a goose, dense enough to discourage walking in, and carried right round without a break.

Why did the birds arrive only after our neighbourhood was finished?

Because the pond had to mature. A newly built basin has raw banks, thin turf and construction traffic. Give it a few seasons and it has established grass to the waterline, quiet, and a mowing contract keeping the sward short and green. Local stock is young, with a median build year of 2002 in the town, so many basins here reached that stage at roughly the same time.

How long before we see a difference?

Movement usually shows within the first two weeks, but the number that matters is what the bank looks like after two months. Birds that have lived somewhere for seasons only give it up after enough irregular pressure that the place stops feeling secure. Properties that also change the shoreline taper down to occasional maintenance. Properties that change nothing keep paying for the dog.

Can the dog work a public park or a town trail?

Anything on public ground is arranged with the Town rather than simply booked. Town parks open sunrise to sunset, prohibit hunting and trapping outright, and carry their own rules on dogs and use. Most of what we do is on private water, private basins and private lake frontage, where scheduling is between us and the owner.

hero.lead: North Augusta bans feeding waterfowl in its parks and on public land, and that ordinance is only half of an answer. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions works trained herding dogs at resident Canada geese on ponds, club turf and trail edges here, then rebuilds the waterline so the ground stops inviting the flock back.
