body:
Most of the Midlands is owned. Columbia is rented. Census QuickFacts puts owner occupancy in the city at 45.5 percent across 53,076 households, which leaves 54.5 percent of occupied homes in the hands of tenants, at a median gross rent of $1,204 a month against a median owner-occupied value of $264,300. That ratio explains more about bed bug pressure here than climate, soil or building age ever will.

Rented housing turns over. Turnover moves furniture, and furniture moves bed bugs. Add a university whose Columbia campus enrolled 38,504 students in fall 2024 against 9,243 assignable beds, and you get an annual, largely August-shaped churn of mattresses, futons, sofas and duffel bags. That is the mechanism, and everything below follows from it.

54.5%Of occupied Columbia homes are rented; owner occupancy is 45.5 percent across 53,076 households (US Census QuickFacts, ACS 2020–2024)
9,243Assignable USC on-campus beds in fall 2024, against 38,504 students enrolled on the Columbia campus (USC 2024 Annual Continuing Disclosure Report)
103.0%USC on-campus housing occupancy in fall 2022 — more residents than assignable beds (same report)

Why does Columbia’s housing market decide this?

Because the thing that carries bed bugs from address to address is a lease ending.

Run the census figures out and roughly 28,900 households inside the city limits are renters. Richland County adds 196,607 housing units and one number worth pausing on: 80 percent of residents lived in the same home twelve months earlier. One household in five moved. That is county-wide mobility rather than rental turnover, and we will not dress it up as the latter, but it is the only published mobility figure for this market.

A rented neighborhood hands this insect a fresh opportunity every time a unit changes hands, a sofa goes to the kerb, or somebody sublets a bedroom. Nothing about the residents differs. The traffic differs.

Detection and treatment also separate cleanly here. Establishing whether a unit is infested right now, before a tenant signs, is a different job from clearing one that already is. This page is the first; the second is bed bug treatment, and the parent page for canine work is K-9 bed bug detection.

How does a move cycle actually spread an infestation?

In four ordinary steps, none of which look dramatic while they happen.

Start with scale. USC runs 28 residence halls and 12 living-and-learning communities here. Capacity has climbed — 7,691 assignable beds in fall 2021, 9,243 by fall 2024 — but never approached the enrolment, and in fall 2022 the halls ran at 103.0 percent of assignable capacity. With 38,504 students on the Columbia campus in fall 2024, roughly three quarters of the student body sleeps elsewhere: a rented house in an old neighborhood, an apartment, a bedroom inside a subdivided single-family home.

Then compress the arrivals. For 2026, early move-in falls on 7 August and the full Move-In Day on 15 August, with arrival slots booked in 30-minute increments through the housing portal. Thousands of beds fill inside one weekend, and the off-campus market runs on the same calendar because leases are written to it.

Now the part people skip. At the other end of the year that population leaves, and what it leaves sits at the kerb: mattresses, box springs, futons, a couch four tenants have owned. USC does not publish hall closing dates on any page we could reach, so we will not quote a move-out week. The pattern is the point, not the date.

Four routes then do the work: curbside furniture carried into a new unit; a sublet where one room sees three occupants in a year; roommate turnover inside an intact lease, where nobody inspects anything; and shared walls, where an established population needs no moving truck. Our bed bug profile has the life cycle behind them.

Is any of this about cleanliness or income?

No. Not a bit of it, and the belief that it is does real damage in a city like this one.

Bed bugs feed on blood. Crumbs, dishes and laundry are irrelevant, because the only resource they need is a sleeping human. What raises risk is how many unfamiliar belongings arrive, and how often. A new-build apartment is exactly as habitable to them as a hundred-year-old bungalow.

We say this at the start of every job, because shame is the biggest cause of delay we meet. A tenant who thinks an infestation reflects on them waits, tries a supermarket spray, and tells nobody. By then it has had months to grow and, in an attached building, months to move next door.

What is a detection dog trained to smell, and how good is the evidence?

Live insects and viable eggs. Not staining, not shed skins, not a treatment that happened last spring.

That distinction is the whole commercial case for a dog. Visual inspection collects history: fecal spotting behind a headboard, cast skins in a seam, the occasional dead adult. That evidence sits there indefinitely, so it answers whether something ever happened in this room. A properly imprinted dog is scented to the living population, so its answer is present tense — the only tense of use to a landlord signing a tenant, a housing office turning a room, or a resident arguing with a manager.

Speed is the second difference, and it changes economics rather than accuracy. A trained team covers a bedroom in a couple of minutes with the bed left assembled, where a technician working visually has to take it apart. Across twenty units that is a whole day, which is why screening every unit becomes affordable when a full visual survey never does. It is also the only way to find the quiet ones, and systematic apartment surveys keep turning up infestations in homes whose occupants had reported nothing.

Kimberly Camera founded this company after more than twenty-eight years in scent detection, including FEMA Urban Search & Rescue work. Certifications are held through NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA, and we have published the canine research that does not flatter the industry on our detection accuracy page.

What will a dog not tell you?

  • How many there are. An alert marks where the odor is present. Six insects and six hundred produce the same alert.
  • How long they have been there. Nymph stages and staining density hint at it. Nothing measures it.
  • Anything reliable in a poor working environment. Heat, strong airflow, a tired dog, or a room another team has just worked will degrade a search. Those conditions get managed, not ignored.
  • A verdict without confirmation. Every alert gets a targeted look at the spot. Where it stays unclear, interceptor monitors go down and we return rather than issue a finding we cannot stand behind.
  • Which insect bit you. Bites are not diagnostic, reactions vary enormously between people, and other arthropods leave similar marks — our cat flea profile covers the commonest confusion.

Which Columbia neighborhoods change how an inspection runs?

Seventeen National Register historic districts sit inside the city limits, and their building stock behaves nothing like a 2015 apartment block. Age is not a moral failing; it is a harborage question. Plaster cracks, baseboards stand proud of the wall, floorboards separate, and a single-family house later split into four rented units has partitions nobody has opened in decades.

Melrose Heights–Oak Lawn–Fairview

The largest district by count, 607 contributing buildings, developed as a streetcar suburb outside the original city boundary in the first half of the twentieth century, with a documented concentration of airplane bungalow cottages. Modest houses, deep original millwork, many now rented. Inspecting one by eye is slow, which is where a dog earns its fee.

Historic Waverly

Columbia’s first suburban development: 132 contributing buildings from about 1898 to 1925, in Queen Anne, shotgun, American Foursquare and Craftsman forms. It became a community of African-American artisans, professionals and social reformers, and the National Park Service added it to the African American Civil Rights Network in February 2021. Those plans put beds against exterior walls and keep original door frames.

Elmwood Park and Old Shandon

Elmwood Park was laid out by public auction in 1905 and holds 219 contributing buildings out of 279, with brick bungalows filling in through the 1920s and 1930s. Old Shandon carries 42 contributing buildings from the 1890s to the 1950s. Both sit inside the university’s rental orbit, which is the operative fact for us.

Granby Mill Village and Olympia

The Granby mill went up in 1896 and 1897, and the district holds 97 contributing buildings — operatives’ houses on a New England saltbox model. Olympia’s mill village is listed separately. Small rooms, raised wood frame, original woodwork, and long-standing rental stock.

Forest Hills, Heathwood and the owner-occupied side

Forest Hills carries 215 contributing buildings, most built after 1927, in Tudor, Colonial and Spanish Colonial Revival. Larger houses, more guest rooms, easier access for treatment. Calls from this half of the city are usually anticipatory: family arriving, a room that was let out, a student home for the summer.

University Hill, The Vista and the apartment stock

The blocks nearest campus and the converted warehouse district between downtown and the Congaree. We will not name apartment communities or quote a unit count, because no verified multifamily inventory for Columbia was reachable. The relevant fact is structural: attached units share walls, voids and plumbing chases.

Every place named here comes from the city’s own neighborhood list or a National Register nomination. Where a district’s era or building count was not documented in a source we could read, it is not here.

What about the unit on the other side of the wall?

Very often it is the real answer, and treating one apartment while ignoring its neighbors is the most expensive mistake a Columbia owner can make.

The behaviour has been measured. Researchers marked bed bugs, released them into six apartments, then monitored twenty-four adjoining units. Inside roughly a fortnight, marked insects were recovered beside five of those six, some having crossed more than twelve metres of hallway. Of the adults that made those journeys, 92 percent were female and already mated.

The same research measured the alternative: a building-wide approach eliminated the insect from 92 percent of units and pulled one building’s infestation rate from 15 percent to 2.2 percent within a year. Responding only to complaints is a permanent operating cost with no end date; working the whole building is a project with a finish line. Canine screening makes the second option priceable, because it is the only method fast enough to look inside every unit rather than the ones that phoned in. That sequence is the backbone of our multifamily and property management program.

Under South Carolina law, whose problem is it?

Nobody’s, by statute. That is not a rhetorical flourish, and it is why documentation carries so much weight here.

Two landlord duties appear at section 27-40-440 of the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. One is meeting the building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety. The other is keeping the place fit to live in. Pests are not mentioned. Vermin are not mentioned. Extermination is not mentioned. Section 27-40-510, listing what a tenant must do, is silent too. No disclosure requirement, no response deadline, no rule about who pays.

So the question falls back onto the general habitability duty, local property maintenance provisions, and the lease. We are deliberately not going to characterise Columbia’s municipal code on rental pest responsibility in either direction: the city’s ordinances sit on a platform that would not return readable text to us, and an unverified negative misleads as much as an unverified positive.

What remains is evidence. When a tenant and a manager disagree about who brought what into a unit and when, the party holding a dated, independent, photographed record is in a far better position than the party holding a recollection. That cuts both ways, which is why we sell the report rather than the outcome; the argument is made in full on our independent canine detection page.

Which first attempts waste money?

  • Total-release foggers. Three retail foggers were tested in 2012 against five bed bug populations collected from occupied buildings, plus a laboratory strain with no resistance history. The Journal of Economic Entomology published the result: field populations showed minimal mortality after two hours of exposure, and the authors recommended against foggers entirely. The aerosol settles on surfaces; the insects are inside a seam.
  • Rubbing alcohol. It kills whatever it directly wets, then evaporates. It is also a flammable liquid being poured onto bedding by somebody frightened and short of sleep.
  • Retail pyrethroid sprays along the skirting. Resistance in field populations is documented and widespread, and these products repel as well as kill. Spraying a bed frame pushes survivors into wall voids, the next room and, in an attached building, the neighbor.
  • An encasement on its own. We fit them and recommend them, because they trap what is inside a mattress and make the surface inspectable. They do nothing about the headboard, nightstand, skirting board or armchair.
  • Leaving a unit empty over the summer. Strip the host out and most stages die within roughly one to four months at the temperature a conditioned apartment actually holds, with resistant strains fading faster still. The much-repeated twelve-month survival figure applies at around 55°F and below — an unheated store room, not a bedroom.

Heat or chemicals — which should a Columbia property use?

Usually both, and anybody insisting one is universally correct has not run enough of either.

FactorWhole-room heatConventional chemical
Effect on eggsLethal, provided the target temperature is reached at every point in the roomThe recognised weak point; follow-up visits are normally required
ResistanceNone possible. Temperature is a physical mechanismDocumented and common in field populations, particularly against pyrethroids
Common failureCold spots — wall voids, packed wardrobes, furniture against an exterior wallHarborage missed entirely, or tenant-applied product scattering the population
AfterwardsNo residual; the room can be reoccupied once it coolsResidual protection, which is why heat is normally paired with a perimeter product

The reliable programme is layered: heat or steam on concentrated harborage, a desiccant into voids nothing else reaches, encasements to make the bed inspectable, and interceptors under every leg. Proof of completion is three clean checks in a row over a forty-two day window. A unit treated and never re-checked has not been finished, only invoiced.

How does an inspection run in an occupied rental?

  1. We scope it on the phone first

    How many sleeping rooms, how many units, whether anyone is living in them, and whether you want a plain vehicle. For a building we also agree who gets told what when a unit comes back positive, because that decision goes badly if it is made in the corridor.

  2. Prepare by doing almost nothing

    No deep clean, no spraying, no bagging belongings, no pulling the bed apart. Each of those either erases the evidence we read or scatters the population before we see where it sits. If somebody has already sprayed, tell us.

  3. The team works a fixed pattern

    Perimeter, then the bed frame and box spring, then seating, nightstands and the floor-to-wall junction, at the same pace in every room. In a corridor building we read the door line as well, which screens a whole floor without opening every unit.

  4. Every alert gets confirmed

    A targeted visual check at the exact spot indicated. In an early infestation there may be almost nothing visible, which is precisely why a dog was worth bringing. If it is still unclear, we set interceptors and schedule a second visit.

  5. Findings and recommendation, kept apart

    Dated, photographed, unit by unit, with rooms that came back clear recorded as clear. What we found and what we would do about it are written as two different things, so the report stays useful to a third party and the treatment decision stays yours.

What is included in a Columbia inspection?

  • Certified handler and detection dog, imprinted on the living population, not residue
  • Room-by-room screening of sleeping areas, upholstered furniture and adjacent harborage
  • Door-line and corridor screening for apartment buildings and halls
  • Targeted visual confirmation at every alert location before anything is recommended
  • Dated, photographed findings covering clear rooms as well as positive ones
  • Common areas, laundry rooms, lounges and furnished model units in scope on request
  • Plain vehicle and plain clothes for guest-facing properties
  • Coordination with an existing vendor, or verification screening after somebody else has treated

Which Columbia institutions carry the most exposure?

Student housing, on and off campus. Twenty-eight residence halls, twelve living-and-learning communities, and a Greek Village of 20 facilities housing about 700 students. Fraternity and sorority life at USC spans 53 organisations and more than 30 percent of the student body, so the residential houses are a small part of a much larger network moving between addresses. Chapter houses combine bunked sleeping, heavy upholstered furniture, guests, and a summer when the building empties and refills. See our schools and student housing program.

Hotels and the convention trade. The Columbia Metropolitan Convention Center opened in September 2004 with 142,500 total square feet and has since hosted more than 8,000 events and welcomed 3.9 million visitors. Accommodation and Food Services employs 21,045 people in Richland County, 9.5 percent of county employment. We found no verified hotel or room count for Columbia and will not quote one, but the pattern needs no count: rooms turn over nightly, and exposure surfaces on a review site well before it surfaces as an invoice. See our hotels and hospitality program.

Healthcare and senior living. Health Care and Social Assistance is Richland County’s largest employment sector at 33,974 jobs, 15.3 percent of the total. Prisma Health Richland runs 641 beds plus 124 at the affiliated Heart Hospital, holds Level I Trauma Center designation, and is the sole regional referral centre for the Midlands. Belongings travel with patients between home, hospital and long-term care. In residential care, residents cannot always report a problem, skin reactions get misread, and rooms are densely furnished — the case for scheduled screening over complaint-driven response, made on our healthcare and senior living program page.

Fort Jackson. More than 52,000 acres, annexed into the City of Columbia in October 1968, training roughly 43,000 service members a year and employing close to 3,500 civilians. Any environment cycling tens of thousands of people through shared sleeping quarters is a high-throughput transient population, and that is how this insect moves. We have verified no incident there and are not implying one.

What does the screening calendar look like in a university city?

Here the academic calendar replaces the weather calendar, which is unusual for us. Columbia’s freeze dates are genuinely interesting — the state climatologist’s downtown campus station records 261 freeze-free days against 236 at the metro airport, a twenty-five day gap inside one city — and they say nothing whatsoever about this insect. A conditioned bedroom is the same temperature in January as in July.

  • July, before the leases turn. The moment to baseline units about to change hands. An empty unit is the only genuinely easy unit to work.
  • Early to mid August. USC’s 2026 early arrival is 7 August and the full Move-In Day is 15 August, with the off-campus market on the same rhythm. A screen immediately before occupancy fixes the condition of a unit at handover.
  • End of term. USC does not publish hall closing dates on the pages we could reach, so work to your own lease dates. Screen after the furniture leaves and before the next occupant arrives.
  • Around large events. Convention weekends fill rooms that were empty and empty them again. Spot-screening a sample between bookings is inexpensive; hearing about it from a guest is not.
  • Immediately on any dispute. A tenant reports bites, a resident’s family raises a concern, a buyer and seller disagree before closing. Book it the same week; what you are buying is the written finding.

Who licenses structural pest work in South Carolina?

Clemson University does, which catches almost everybody out. Structural pest control here is regulated by the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation rather than a state agriculture department, and the category is 7A, titled Industrial, Institutional, Structural and Health-Related Pest Control.

Three things are required of a commercial firm here. DPR issues the business licence. Each location must have its own Designated Certified Applicator. And the insurance floor is set in the rules: commercial general liability of $100,000 or more, combined single limit, with the deductible capped at $1,000. Fair questions to ask any vendor before they walk into an occupied building.

One related correction, because outdated copy is everywhere: retail food inspection here moved to the South Carolina Department of Agriculture on 1 July 2024, when DHEC was split in two. A company still telling a Columbia restaurant that DHEC will inspect it has not updated its material in two years. Our commercial program covers that work, and our German cockroach profile covers the pest that drives most food-service scores.

Where do we work around Columbia?

We are based at 320 Wendy Lane in Windsor and cover Columbia and the Midlands in full: Shandon and Old Shandon, Rosewood, Heathwood, Wales Garden, Forest Hills, Melrose and Hollywood-Rose Hill, Historic Waverly, Elmwood Park, Cottontown and Bellevue, Earlewood, Eau Claire, Hyatt Park, Arsenal Hill, University Hill, Seminary Ridge, The Vista, Granby Hill and Olympia, Whaley Street, Druid Hills, Kilbourne Park, Lake Katherine, Sherwood Forest, Booker Washington Heights, Celia Saxon, Lincoln Park, Greenview, Colonial Heights, Grove Park, Yorkshire and Tanglewood.

Across the rivers we work Cayce, West Columbia and the Riverwalk corridor, and out to Irmo, Lexington and Lake Murray. Our other Columbia pages cover K-9 rodent detection, bird control and goose control. See every area we serve.

Frequently asked questions

I am moving into a Columbia apartment in August. What should I do first?

Screen it before your furniture goes in, or within the first few days if that is not possible. An empty unit is quick to work, and the dated report establishes the condition of the apartment at handover. That document settles the later argument about whether a problem arrived with you or was already waiting.

Does everyone have to move out while you inspect?

No. Almost all of our residential work happens in occupied units with the residents at home. It is quiet work, the bed stays assembled, and residents usually sit in the next room. Secure any pets, keep food off the floor, and tell us if anything was sprayed recently.

A housemate brought a couch in off the kerb. Is that genuinely how this starts?

It is one of the commonest routes we see, and in a city with this much annual turnover it is a substantial one. Discarded upholstered furniture is often discarded for exactly this reason, and whoever put it out had no obligation to say so. If the item is already indoors, have it screened where it stands rather than dragging it back through a shared hallway.

Can my landlord make me pay for the treatment?

State law does not answer that, which surprises people. There is no bed-bug-specific statute in South Carolina, and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act never mentions pests or extermination in its landlord duties or its tenant duties. Responsibility depends on the general habitability obligation, on whatever local property maintenance code applies, and above all on the lease you signed.

The dog alerted but I cannot see anything. Was that a false alarm?

Possibly, and possibly the opposite. Early infestations regularly present with almost nothing visible, which is the whole reason a dog gets brought in, and it is why we confirm rather than declare. Where the picture stays unclear we place interceptor monitors and return. No detection team of any species is infallible, and one claiming to be should be avoided.

How many units in my building should be screened?

More than the one that complained. In the release study, marked insects reached units adjoining five of the six seeded apartments inside a fortnight, a few travelling over twelve metres, and mated females accounted for 92 percent of everything that moved. At minimum, screen the units either side, above and below.

Are residence halls and Greek houses handled differently?

The dog work is identical; the logistics are not. Institutional buildings need a scheduled window, a plan for how a positive room gets communicated, and a scope taking in lounges, study rooms and laundry areas rather than bedrooms alone. The right time is between occupancies, when the building is empty.

How quickly does a small problem become a large one?

Faster than the delay most people take before calling. Under laboratory conditions a population roughly doubles every thirteen days, and in a real apartment the limits are temperature and access to a host rather than anything the resident does. The cost of clearing a property climbs steeply with every week it goes unreported.

What do I actually receive at the end?

A dated, photographed record of every room or unit inspected, including the ones that came back clear, with the recommendation written separately from the findings so the document stays useful to a third party. With no statute assigning responsibility here, that record tends to outweigh everything else in the file once an argument starts.

title: How K9 Bed Bug Detection Works — And Why It Beats a Visual Inspection
description: A complete guide to K9 bed bug detection — how detection dogs work, how accurate they are, what an inspection looks like, and when to use one. By a NESDCA-certified handler.
h1: How K9 Bed Bug Detection Works — And Why It Beats a Visual Inspection

hero.h1: How K9 Bed Bug Detection Works — And Why It Beats a Visual Inspection
hero.lead: A trained detection dog can confirm live bed bugs in minutes — often catching an infestation weeks before a person would ever spot one. This complete guide explains how canine bed bug detection actually works, how accurate it is, what an inspection looks like, and exactly when it is the right call for your home or property.

body:
What this guide coversWhy bed bugs are so hard to findThe real cost of finding them lateHow a bed bug detection dog actually worksK9 detection vs. visual inspection: a direct comparisonHow accurate are bed bug dogs, really?When a K9 bed bug inspection is the right callWhat to expect during a K9 inspectionWhat happens after a confirmed alertHow to lower your risk of bed bugsEarly warning signs of bed bugsWhy certification and handler experience matterDetection before treatment — every time

Why bed bugs are so hard to find

Bed bugs are built to hide, and they are very good at it. Adults are only about the size of an apple seed, freshly hatched nymphs are nearly translucent, and the eggs — roughly a millimeter long and pearly white — are almost impossible to see against most surfaces. All three stages spend the vast majority of their lives tucked away in cracks and crevices, emerging mainly at night to feed.

Their preferred harborage reads like a list of places you cannot easily inspect: the piping and seams of a mattress, the joints of a bed frame, behind headboards, under loose baseboards, inside electrical outlets and switch plates, behind picture frames, in the folds of upholstered furniture, and along the tack strip where carpet meets the wall. In heavier infestations they spread outward into nightstands, dressers, cracks in the wall, and even into adjacent rooms through wall voids and shared utility runs.

This is the core problem with finding bed bugs by eye: a visual inspection can only assess what is visible on the surface. A person cannot see through a mattress seam, into a wall void, or behind a baseboard without dismantling the room. So unless the infestation is advanced enough to leave obvious signs out in the open, a visual-only inspection is essentially checking the small fraction of hiding places that happen to be exposed — and hoping the bugs chose one of them.

The real cost of finding them late

Bed bug infestations grow quietly. A single mated female can lay a few eggs a day, and under favorable conditions a small introduction can build into a serious problem over a matter of weeks — usually well before anyone notices a bug on the sheets. By the time you see live bugs in the open, the population has typically been established and breeding for some time, and it may already be spreading beyond the room where it started.

That delay is expensive in every direction. The infestation itself becomes larger and harder to treat, which raises the cost and the number of treatment visits. In a home, bugs can hitchhike into other rooms on clothing and belongings. In a hotel, a single flagged room can quietly seed its neighbors, and one guest review mentioning bed bugs can do damage that dwarfs the cost of the treatment. In multi-family housing, an unaddressed complaint can escalate into a habitability dispute.

Key takeaway

Early, accurate detection is the single biggest lever on how quickly, cheaply, and completely a bed bug problem gets resolved. Everything downstream — treatment cost, spread, reputation — flows from how early you catch it.

How a bed bug detection dog actually works

Detection dogs do not find bed bugs by sight. They find them by scent, and their noses operate on a level people struggle to imagine. Dogs have up to 300 million olfactory receptors, compared with roughly six million in humans, and they can effectively sample odor almost continuously as they breathe. This is the same biological capability that makes dogs the tool of choice for narcotics, explosives, and search-and-rescue work.

Trained to a specific target odor

A properly trained bed bug dog is conditioned to alert on one thing: the scent of live bed bugs and viable eggs. Just as importantly, the dog is trained to ignore what does not matter — dead bugs, cast skins, and old fecal staining. That distinction is critical, because a pile of dead bugs and shed shells is evidence of a past problem, not proof of an active one. A dog that alerts only on live activity tells you whether you have a problem right now.

A systematic search and a trained final response

On an inspection, the handler works the dog methodically around a room — along the perimeter, the bed, and the furniture — allowing the dog to sample the seams, cracks, and voids where bugs hide. When the dog detects live bed-bug odor, it gives a trained “final response,” usually a sit or a freeze focused on the source. A good handler reads that response, confirms the location, and marks it, so that any treatment is aimed precisely at where the bugs actually are rather than sprayed across the whole room on the chance that they might be there.

Key takeaway

A dog can screen a hotel room or apartment in a few minutes — far faster than a person doing a careful visual search, and with the ability to detect activity inside walls and furniture that a person simply cannot open up.

K9 detection vs. visual inspection: a direct comparison

Both approaches have their place, and a skilled inspector still matters — but for finding live bed bugs, especially early, the two are not close. Here is how they stack up on the factors that actually determine whether an infestation gets caught.

FactorVisual inspectionK9 detection
How it finds bugsSight — only what is visible on the surfaceScent — live bugs and viable eggs, including inside voids
Speed per room20–45 minutes for a thorough search2–5 minutes
Hidden harborageMissed unless furniture is dismantledDetected behind walls, baseboards, and furniture
Early / low-level infestationsFrequently missedRoutinely caught early
Post-treatment verificationHard to confirm absenceConfirms whether live activity remains

How accurate are bed bug dogs, really?

When the dog and handler are properly trained and actively maintained, canine scent detection is one of the most reliable tools available for finding live bed bugs, and it routinely detects infestations earlier than visual inspection can. But accuracy is not automatic — it is a product of training discipline, ongoing maintenance, and an honest handler. A dog that is not trained and proofed carefully, or a handler who over-reads the dog, will produce errors. That is exactly why third-party certification exists.

What drives real-world accuracy

  • Rigorous initial training to a clean target odor, with dead bugs and shells “proofed out”
  • Frequent, ongoing maintenance training so the dog stays sharp
  • A disciplined handler who confirms the source rather than assuming an alert
  • Independent certification that tests the team against known standards

Why certification is your assurance

At Coastal K9, our teams are certified through the National Entomology Scent Detection Canine Association (NESDCA) — the recognized standard for entomology scent-detection dogs — and led by a FEMA-trained handler with decades of working-dog experience. Certification is not a formality; it is the reason you can act on an alert with confidence.

When a K9 bed bug inspection is the right call

A canine inspection is not just for confirmed infestations. Because it is fast, accurate, and non-destructive, it is the right tool in a range of situations:

  • After a bite or a single sighting — to confirm whether you actually have bed bugs and, if so, exactly where
  • Multi-unit and hospitality properties — to screen many rooms or units quickly and discreetly
  • Real estate and move-in checks — to inspect a home or unit before you commit or move belongings in
  • Post-treatment verification — to confirm a treatment actually worked instead of guessing
  • Proactive, routine screening — for hotels, senior living, and apartments where catching an introduction early is far cheaper than chasing a spread

What to expect during a K9 inspection

If you have never seen a detection inspection, it is calmer and quicker than most people expect. Here is the typical flow:

Before the inspection

Minimal prep is needed, but a few things help the dog work: reduce clutter on the floor so the dog can move, turn off strong scent sources like plug-in air fresheners where possible, and keep other pets out of the area during the sweep. Your provider will tell you anything specific to your situation.

During the sweep

The handler works the dog systematically around each room. Most rooms take only a few minutes. When the dog alerts, the handler pauses to confirm the source, note the location, and, if useful, verify visually. You will often be able to watch the process, which is part of what makes canine inspection so reassuring — you can see the dog work the space.

After the inspection

You get a clear result: where live activity was detected, and where it was not. That map is what makes the next step efficient, whether that is a targeted treatment or simply peace of mind that the space is clear.

What happens after a confirmed alert

Finding the bugs is half the job; the other half is treating only what needs treating and then proving it worked. Once activity is confirmed, treatment is focused on the areas the dog identified and matched to the level of infestation. After treatment has had time to work, a follow-up canine sweep verifies whether any live activity remains — turning “we think it is gone” into “we confirmed it is gone.” That verification step is one of the most valuable and underused parts of a detection-driven program.

How to lower your risk of bed bugs

No prevention is perfect, because bed bugs travel on people and belongings — but a few habits meaningfully reduce your risk and help you catch problems early:

  • When traveling, check the mattress seams and headboard area before unpacking, and keep luggage off the bed and floor
  • Inspect secondhand furniture and clothing carefully before bringing them home
  • Use mattress and box-spring encasements to remove hiding places and make monitoring easier
  • Place interceptor monitors under bed and furniture legs to catch early activity
  • Act on the first sign — bites, spots, or a single bug — rather than waiting to be sure

Early warning signs of bed bugs

Between inspections, these are the signs worth watching for. Any one of them is a reason to consider a canine inspection to confirm what is really going on:

  • Small, itchy bites, often in a line or cluster, on skin exposed during sleep
  • Tiny rust- or blood-colored spots on sheets, pillowcases, or the mattress
  • Dark “ink dot” fecal specks along mattress seams, headboards, and baseboards
  • Pale, translucent shed skins (cast nymph shells) in cracks and seams
  • A sweet, musty odor in a heavily infested room
  • Live bugs — reddish-brown, flat, and apple-seed sized — in seams and crevices

Why certification and handler experience matter

It bears repeating because it is the whole ballgame: a detection dog is only as good as its training and its handler. The dog supplies an extraordinary nose; the certified handler supplies the discipline, interpretation, and accountability that turn an alert into a decision you can trust. That is why we hold our credentials through NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA, and ICRWDA, and why our programs are led by a founder who came into pest detection from FEMA Urban Search and Rescue canine work. When you hire a certified team, you are not just renting a nose — you are getting a professional who knows how to read it.

Detection before treatment — every time

Spraying an entire home “just in case” is expensive, unnecessary, and often ineffective, because it treats places pests are not and can miss the places they are. Confirming exactly where bugs are — and are not — makes treatment focused, faster, and cheaper, and gives you verification afterward that the problem is genuinely solved. That is the core of how we work and the reason for our name: detection before treatment, every time.

About the authorKimberly Camera is a FEMA-trained canine handler and founder of Coastal K9 Pest Solutions, with 28+ years of K9 detection experience and certifications through NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA, and ICRWDA. Read her full profile →

Frequently asked questions

Are bed bug detection dogs accurate?

Yes — when properly trained, maintained, and certified, detection dogs are highly accurate at finding live bed bugs and routinely catch infestations earlier than a visual inspection. Certification such as NESDCA is what ensures that accuracy is real.

How long does a K9 bed bug inspection take?

Usually only a few minutes per room. A dog clears a space far faster than a person performing a thorough visual search, and it can detect activity in places a visual inspection cannot reach.

Can a dog tell the difference between live and dead bed bugs?

A properly trained detection dog is conditioned to alert only on live bugs and viable eggs — not dead bugs or old shells — so an alert indicates an active infestation, not a past one.

How should I prepare for a canine bed bug inspection?

Reduce floor clutter so the dog can move, turn off strong scent sources like plug-in air fresheners where possible, and keep other pets out of the area during the sweep. Your provider will note anything specific to your situation.

Do you treat the bed bugs too, or just inspect?

Both. We confirm activity with the dog, treat the confirmed areas with a targeted plan, and then verify the treatment worked with a follow-up inspection.

Is a K9 inspection worth it for just one room?

Yes. A dog confirms whether bugs are present and how far they have spread, so you do not over-treat or miss a neighboring room. It is the fastest, most reliable way to know exactly what you are dealing with.

How often should hotels or apartments inspect for bed bugs?

A proactive rotation is most cost-effective, because catching an introduction early is far cheaper than treating a spread. The right frequency depends on turnover and history; we build it to the property.

Where does Coastal K9 offer bed bug inspections?

Across Aiken, the CSRA, and the South Carolina Midlands. See our service areas or call 803-226-3155.

title: Bed Bug Detection Lexington SC
description: Certified K-9 bed bug detection in Lexington and around Lake Murray — homes, short-term rentals and inns screened room by room, and discreetly.
h1: K-9 Bed Bug Detection in Lexington, SC

hero.eyebrow: LEXINGTON, SOUTH CAROLINA · CANINE BED BUG DETECTION
hero.h1: K-9 Bed Bug Detection in Lexington, SC
hero.lead: More than half the homes in the town of Lexington were built this century, and not one of them is protected by that. Bed bugs follow people, never build dates. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions screens Lexington houses, townhomes, apartments and lake properties using certified detection dogs, to settle one question: is anything alive in here now?
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Family-owned · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · Unmarked vehicle on request · Lexington County and the Midlands

body:
Lexington is a young town. The median housing unit inside the TOWN limits was built in 2002; across the COUNTY the median is 1993, nine years older. Of the town’s 10,348 housing units, 80.3 percent went up in 1990 or later, 57.5 percent since 2000, and only 9.5 percent date from before 1980. Population tracked the same curve: 17,870 residents in 2010, 23,568 in 2020, an estimated 25,729 in 2025.

Nearly every homeowner we meet here assumes newness buys them something. It does not. This insect has no relationship with the age of your drywall, your income or how often the house gets cleaned. Its one relationship is with human traffic, and traffic is what a fast-growing suburb makes more of every year.

2002Median year built for TOWN of Lexington housing, against 1993 for Lexington COUNTY (US Census ACS 2020–2024 5-year, table B25035)
80.3%Of the town’s 10,348 housing units were built in 1990 or later; just 9.5 percent predate 1980 (ACS 2020–2024 5-year, table B25034)
474Approved lots in four active town subdivisions alone — Barr Lake 3D and 3E at 182, River Ridge 150, West of Main 76, Nightingale Hills 66 (Town of Lexington GIS, Subdivision Status layer)

Is a house built in 2004 any safer than one built in 1954?

No. And that belief costs Lexington households more than any other idea in this trade.

A bed bug needs a host who sleeps somewhere predictable, a crevice within a few feet of that host, and a comfortable temperature. A 2004 house supplies all three. A sealed envelope and tight windows matter enormously for termites, rodents and ants, all of which must get in from outside. Bed bugs do not. They come through the front door, carried by the people who live there.

What newer construction changes is smaller than the marketing suggests. Fewer plaster cracks, fewer floorboard gaps, no layered wallpaper. Against that, a modern house holds more upholstered seating, more bedrooms and a guest room nobody enters for weeks. Harborage moved into the furniture.

Detection and treatment are separate jobs and we sell them separately. What is present today is this page and its parent, K-9 bed bug detection. Clearing a confirmed population is bed bug treatment.

What do the town’s own housing numbers say?

A suburb built for owners.

The TOWN records 9,778 households at 2.42 people each, 68.7 percent owner occupancy and a median owner-occupied value of $297,700. The COUNTY, larger and older, runs 77.4 percent owner-occupied at a median value of $234,500. Same census release, two geographies, labelled every time.

By type, the TOWN holds 6,661 single-family detached units — 64.4 percent of the stock — plus 653 attached single-unit homes, 2,461 units in buildings of five or more, and 300 mobile homes. Two homes in three are a detached house somebody owns, with several bedrooms and a great deal of furniture.

The pipeline keeps filling. The COUNTY issued 2,006 building permits in 2025, and the Town’s GIS lists twenty subdivisions under active planning or performance-bond status: Barr Lake 3D and 3E at 182 lots with 3C, 3G and 3J adding 61, River Ridge at 150, West of Main at 76, Nightingale Hills at 66, Sterling Bridge phases 6 through 10, Brookstone 1 and 2, and Riverside 1, 2A and 2B. New houses mean new arrivals, and arrivals bring the contents of an old house with them.

How does an insect with no wings reach a new subdivision?

Carried. Always carried. There is no second mechanism, and that is good news: a list of carriers is a list of things to inspect.

  • A suitcase. One night away, the bag on the bed, then home and unpacked onto the mattress. That is a large share of what we find in owner-occupied houses.
  • Used furniture. A dresser off a marketplace listing, a sofa from an estate sale, a bunk bed passed between families. Nobody selling furniture is obliged to say why they are selling it, and one delivery can seed a bedroom.
  • A child’s overnight stay. Sleepovers, travel teams, a week at a grandparent’s house. The sleeping bag comes home and goes on the bed. Badly under-recognised.
  • A college student home for the summer. A dorm room empties in May and lands in a Lexington bedroom the same afternoon. The one local pathway with a date attached.
  • A move. County economic development names Amazon, Dominion Energy South Carolina, Lexington Medical Center, Michelin and Nephron Pharmaceuticals among top employers, and Prysmian is expanding at 700 Industrial Drive with roughly 135 jobs online in May 2028. Every hire is a household on a truck.
  • A guest. Family in the spare room over a holiday, a contractor’s crew, an exchange student. The guest room is the least-inspected space in an American house.

Our bed bug library profile has the life cycle. None of those routes cares what year the house went up.

Does commuting to Columbia change your exposure?

It does, and it is the least discussed thing about living here.

The TOWN reports a mean travel time to work of 25.2 minutes, and sits about twelve miles west of downtown Columbia. A large share of the working population spends the day in another city. Harmless for almost every pest we handle; not harmless for this one, because a commuter is a set of belongings in motion for ten hours a day.

The scenarios are mundane. A bag under a desk in a building where somebody else has a problem at home. An adult child in a Columbia rental bringing laundry back on Sunday. That is how a house here acquires an infestation with no visitor ever setting foot in it. Columbia’s own version, driven by rental turnover and students, is on our Columbia detection page.

Why is a big house the hardest place to inspect by eye?

Because a visual inspection is a demolition job.

Done properly with a flashlight it means lifting every mattress, standing each box spring on end, pulling headboards off walls, tipping sofas and reading the floor-to-wall junction of every room. In a one-bedroom apartment that is an hour. In a five-bedroom house with a bonus room it is most of a day, and by room nine the technician starts skipping the second nightstand.

A certified detection dog inverts the economics. A trained team clears a bedroom in roughly two minutes with the bed still made, then moves on. That is why whole-house screening is a real product in a town of detached houses while a full visual survey is not. Speed is a claim about coverage, not accuracy, and coverage is where infestations get missed by everybody. A survey of 2,372 apartments found brief visual inspection detected about 72 percent of genuine infestations against 89 percent for passive interceptor monitors over time, with roughly half of everything found sitting in units whose occupants had reported nothing.

There is a second distinction. Visual evidence is history: spotting, cast skins and a dead adult persist long after a successful treatment. A properly imprinted dog is scented to live insects and viable eggs, which makes its answer present tense.

Kimberly Camera founded this company on more than twenty-eight years of scent detection, including FEMA Urban Search & Rescue work. Teams certify through NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA, and the research that does not flatter this industry sits on our detection accuracy page.

What can an alert not tell you?

A fair amount. Here it is, in the form people ask in a driveway.

The questionWhat a canine alert can answer
Is there a living population at this spot?Yes, subject to a confirming look at the exact location indicated. That is the purpose of the tool.
How many are there?Nothing. Eight insects and eight hundred produce the same behaviour.
How long has this been going on?Nothing measurable. Nymph stages and staining density are hints, not a clock.
Is the thing biting me a bed bug?Nothing. Bites are not diagnostic, and our cat flea profile covers the commonest mix-up.
Does the answer hold in a hot bonus room in August?Less well than it should. Heat, airflow and a tired dog all degrade a search, so we manage those conditions rather than pretend otherwise.

So every alert gets confirmed before anybody spends money. Where confirmation settles nothing, monitors are placed, a second visit is booked, and no finding is issued that we could not defend.

Which Lexington subdivisions change how the job runs?

The Town publishes its own GIS subdivision layer, listing 93 named subdivisions inside the town limits. Those records carry a name and, in five cases, a lot count and lot size. None carries a construction date, so we will not assign a decade to any neighborhood. They do support a grouping by build type.

Half-acre lots, larger floor plans

Carrington Place and Middlebrook are both recorded at half-acre lots, 45 and 41 lots respectively; Laurel Falls runs 40 lots at 0.35 acres. Bigger lots mean more sleeping rooms and more upholstered furniture, which is where a thorough visual inspection stops being affordable.

Compact detached subdivisions

Pilgrim Point is recorded at 50 lots on 0.17 acres, Shoal Creek at 74 lots on 0.23 acres, Cherokee Village at 0.11 acre lots. Less structure to hide in, which helps. Less room to arrange it, which does not: the bed often touches two walls.

Townhomes, villas and patio homes

Ashley Townhomes, Millcreek Townhomes, Palm Court Townhomes, Waverly Place Townhomes, Cross Creek Villas, Boardwalk Villas and Parkside Patio Homes are all on the Town’s list, and 653 town homes are attached single units. Attached housing is a different problem, because an established population needs no vehicle to reach the next address.

Apartment stock

2,461 units sit in buildings of five or more, 23.8 percent of the town’s housing. We will not name communities or quote an inventory, because no verified multifamily list for Lexington was reachable. Shared walls and shared laundry are enough.

The water-named neighborhoods

Barr Lake, Carriage Hills Lake, Coventry Lake, Lakeside at Woodcreek, Mallard Lakes and Whiteford Lakes are all in the Town layer, and Lake Murray sits immediately north. Water has nothing to do with bed bugs. Guests do, and water-facing property attracts them.

Subdivisions currently building out

Barr Lake, River Ridge, West of Main, Nightingale Hills, Sterling Bridge, Brookstone and Riverside all carry active status records. A new house is empty on handover day and holds a household’s existing furniture by the next weekend. That gap is the cheapest screening opportunity in town, and nobody uses it.

One correction while we are naming places. Golden Hills Golf & Country Club, 100 Scotland Drive, is the one club with a Lexington town address, and Golden Hills is also a subdivision name. Timberlake Country Club is real, but its address is Chapin.

Does a lake house need its own screen?

If strangers sleep in it, yes.

Lake Murray covers 48,579 acres with 620 miles of shoreline and an average depth of 41.5 feet, spanning Lexington, Newberry, Richland and Saluda counties. That much shoreline supports guest turnover: houses lent to relatives, weekends let out, a dock party where somebody stays over. No published count of short-term rentals on the lake exists as far as we could establish, so we will not quote one. A property that sleeps strangers and turns over with no housekeeping inspection is running hotel conditions without the hotel routine. The same logic covers a formal guest suite in town.

Which first moves make the problem worse?

A population roughly doubles every thirteen days in the laboratory, so weeks spent on the list below are expensive.

  • Total-release foggers. In 2012 researchers ran three over-the-counter foggers against a susceptible laboratory strain and against five populations taken out of infested buildings. Writing in the Journal of Economic Entomology, they found the field strains barely died after two full hours in the aerosol, and said the products should not be recommended for this pest. Fog settles on open surfaces. The insects sit inside a seam.
  • Retail pyrethroid sprays along the baseboards. Resistance is documented and widespread in populations collected from real buildings, and the products push insects away as much as they kill them. Spraying a bed frame in a two-story house drives survivors into the wall void, up the stud bay and into the room above.
  • Rubbing alcohol. It kills what it directly soaks, then evaporates. It is also a flammable liquid poured over bedding by somebody frightened and short of sleep.
  • Moving to the guest room or the sofa. The one we most want Lexington homeowners to stop doing. This insect orients to carbon dioxide and body heat, so moving the host moves the target. In a large house that turns one affected bedroom into three.
  • Throwing the mattress out first. The evidence leaves with it, the trip down the stairs seeds the route, and the replacement arrives into an untreated room. An encasement turns the same surface into something inspectable.
  • An encasement on its own. Useful, and we install them, but a cover seals a mattress and a box spring and stops there. Headboard, nightstand, baseboard and the armchair in the corner are all untouched.
  • Waiting out an empty house. Take the host away and, at the temperature a conditioned house is actually held, most stages are gone in roughly one to four months, with pyrethroid-resistant strains failing sooner. The year-without-feeding claim repeated everywhere applies at about 55 degrees Fahrenheit or below, which describes an unheated outbuilding rather than a bedroom.

Heat or chemical treatment — what is the honest comparison?

Both work, and both fail predictably. Anyone calling one universally right has not run enough of either.

QuestionWhole-room heatConventional chemical
What happens to the eggsKilled, so long as every point in the room genuinely reaches lethal temperatureThe acknowledged weak spot, which is why a return visit is normally scheduled
Can the population adapt to itNo. Temperature is physical and there is nothing to select forYes, and already has in field populations, particularly against pyrethroids
What is left behindNothing at all. Once the room cools it goes back into useSome residual, and that is the reason heat is normally backed by a perimeter product
How it fails in a house like thisCold spots — wall voids, a packed walk-in closet, a bonus room over an unconditioned garageHarborage missed outright, or a household product applied first that scattered the population
What it asks of the householdVacating for the day and removing candles, vinyl and anything with a low melting pointRe-entry intervals, label limits in occupied rooms, follow-up visits

What we recommend is a layered program: steam or heat where harborage concentrates, a desiccant pushed into the voids that nothing else reaches, covers on the mattress and box spring, and monitors under every leg so the result gets measured. Completion means three consecutive clean checks across forty-two days.

Can you come without a marked truck?

Yes, and it is asked for here more often than anywhere else we work.

Lexington’s residential geography is subdivisions with one entrance and neighbors who know each other’s vehicles. A liveried pest control truck in a driveway for two hours is a piece of public information. Nobody should feel that way about an insect that has nothing to do with how they keep house, but we are not going to lecture anyone about it. Plain vehicle, plain clothes, and a slot that avoids the school run.

A negative result goes in writing with no upsell attached, because we are not quoting the treatment. Where somebody else has to be told — a property manager, a buyer, an HOA board — we agree who says what before the visit, not in the driveway afterwards. The reasoning behind hiring a team with no treatment to sell is set out on our independent canine detection page.

How does a screen run in an occupied family home?

  1. We scope it on the phone

    How many sleeping rooms, whether there is a bonus room or a finished space over the garage, whether anyone is reacting to bites, and whether you want a plain vehicle. If a sale is involved, say so.

  2. Leave the house alone beforehand

    No deep clean, no aerosol, no bagging, no stripped beds. Each one erases the evidence we read or scatters the population. If anything has been sprayed already, say so.

  3. One pattern, every room

    Perimeter first, then bed frame and box spring, then chairs and sofas, nightstands, and the join between wall and floor. Same pace in every room, including the ones you are sure about. Secure pets first.

  4. Every alert gets a targeted look

    A visual check at the precise spot indicated, not a general hunt. Early on there is often nothing to see, which is why the dog was worth bringing. If it remains unclear, monitors go in and a second visit is scheduled.

  5. Findings and recommendation, kept apart

    Dated, photographed, room by room, and a room that came back clean is listed as clean. The findings and our advice about them are written as two different things, so the report keeps its value for a third party.

What comes with a Lexington inspection?

  • A certified handler and a dog imprinted on the odor of living insects and viable eggs
  • Whole-house screening: bedrooms, bonus rooms, guest suites, offices and every upholstered seat
  • Targeted visual confirmation at every alert before anything is recommended
  • Interceptor monitors and a scheduled return wherever the picture is unclear
  • Dated, photographed findings covering the clear rooms as well as the positive ones
  • Unmarked vehicle and plain clothes anywhere discretion matters
  • Verification screening after treatment, on the forty-two day schedule

Where does this matter beyond the family house?

Schools. Lexington County School District One enrolls 27,074 students across 32 schools with 2,083.80 full-time-equivalent teachers and a student-teacher ratio of 12.99, per federal Common Core of Data figures for 2024-25. Bed bugs do not establish in a classroom, because nobody sleeps there, but they are exchanged there on backpacks hung together. A school that finds one needs a targeted inspection and a calm letter. The district’s facilities study concluded in March 2026 with no approved new school and no published construction schedule, so nobody should imply otherwise. See our schools and student housing program.

Attached and multifamily property. Treating one unit and ignoring the neighbors is a documented failure pattern, not an opinion. In a mark-release-recapture study, marked insects released into six apartments turned up beside five of those six inside a fortnight, some crossing twelve metres of hallway, and 92 percent of the travellers were mated females able to found a population alone. The same work measured the alternative. Where a whole building was worked at once, 92 percent of units came clear, and one property’s infestation rate fell across twelve months from 15 percent down to 2.2 percent. Canine screening is what makes that second option costable. See our multifamily and property management program.

Senior living and care settings. Lexington Medical Center appears on the County’s own top-employer list. We could not verify a named assisted living or skilled nursing facility inside the town limits, so we will not list one. In residential care, residents cannot always report a problem, reactions get attributed elsewhere, and belongings travel between a private home, a hospital and a care room. Scheduled screening beats complaint-driven response there, as our healthcare and senior living program sets out. No verified Lexington hotel, bed bug count or municipal program exists either; we looked, so none is quoted.

What does South Carolina actually require?

Two answers, and the gap between them is the point.

On responsibility, the state is silent. No bed-bug-specific statute exists here. The landlord duties in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, at section 27-40-440, run to two things: compliance with building and housing codes where those codes materially bear on health and safety, and keeping the premises habitable. The word pest does not appear. Neither does vermin, nor extermination. Section 27-40-510, which lists what a tenant owes, says nothing about them either. So the matter turns on that general habitability duty, on whatever local property maintenance rules apply, and on the lease — which is to say it turns on who documented the condition of the property, and when.

On who may do the work, the state is specific. The regulator is not an agriculture department at all. Structural pest control in this state sits with the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation, which catches nearly everyone out. Category 7A is the one that applies, titled Industrial, Institutional, Structural and Health-Related Pest Control. Any commercial firm here carries three obligations: a Designated Certified Applicator posted at every location, a business license issued by DPR, and general liability cover of $100,000 or more as a combined single limit, with any deductible held under $1,000. Fair things to ask before somebody walks into your bedrooms.

Where do we work around Lexington?

Our base is 320 Wendy Lane in Windsor, and we cover the town along with the surrounding county. Inside the town that takes in Barr Lake, Bent Creek Plantation, Brookstone, Carrington Place, Cherokee Trail and Cherokee Village, Coventry Lake and Coventry Woods, Creekside Farms, Gibson Forest, Golden Hills, Heritage Hills, Hope Ferry Plantation, Hunters Ridge, Lakeside at Woodcreek, Laurel Falls, Madison Park, Mallard Lakes, Middlebrook, Nightingale Hills, Pilgrim Point, River Ridge, Riverside, Shoal Creek, Sterling Bridge, Summerfield, Tall Pines, Twelve Mile Ridge, Village Green Estates, Vintners Wood, Wellesley, Whiteford Lakes, Willowbrooke, Woodcreek and Woodstream, plus the townhome and villa communities and the apartment stock across town.

Beyond the town limits we work Cayce, West Columbia, Irmo, Chapin, Gilbert, Pelion and the Lake Murray shoreline, out to Columbia and the wider Midlands. The other Lexington pages are K-9 rodent detection, bird control and goose control. Every area we serve is listed here.

Frequently asked questions

Our house was built in 2016. Is an inspection even worth booking?

Yes, and the build year is no argument either way. They arrive on luggage, used furniture, a guest or a returning student, and a sealed modern envelope stops none of that. What a newer house changes is where they hide: less in cracked plaster, more in upholstery and bed frames.

Do you screen the whole house or only the bedrooms?

Whole house by default, because Lexington houses have too many places to sleep for a bedroom-only scope to be honest. That means bedrooms, the bonus room, any finished space over the garage, guest suites, a home office with a daybed, and the upholstered seating. Garages and recently delivered second-hand furniture go in on request.

Our son came home from college with his mattress and everything else. Should we worry?

Worried is the wrong word; deliberate is the right one. The May unload is one of very few pathways into a Lexington house with a date attached, and an entire apartment landing in one bedroom in an afternoon is worth screening. Best is before the load comes indoors.

Will the neighbors know why you are here?

Not unless you tell them. We come in an unmarked vehicle and plain clothes on request, we can take a slot that avoids the school run, and there is no signage of any kind. In a subdivision with one entrance that matters to people, and nobody has to explain to us why they asked.

We bought a dresser from an online listing. Can you check it before it comes inside?

Yes, and that is a good call. Leave it in the garage or on a hard-surfaced patio rather than carrying it through the house. Screening a single item is quick and costs far less than treating the bedroom it would otherwise have seeded. Unfinished joints, drawer runners and any fabric-covered underside are what matter.

The dog alerted where I cannot see a thing. Was that wrong?

Possibly, and possibly the opposite. Early populations are routinely invisible to the eye, which is exactly why a dog gets brought in and why we confirm rather than declare. Where the confirming look settles nothing, monitors go under the bed legs and we come back. No team, human or canine, is infallible.

We are renting a lake house for a week. What should we do?

Two minutes on arrival covers most of it. Leave the bags in the bathroom or on a hard floor rather than on a bed, lift a corner of each fitted sheet and read the mattress seam and piping, and check the headboard join. Coming home, launder everything on the hottest setting the fabric allows and run the dryer, because heat rather than water does the work.

What do we get when you are finished?

A record of every room screened, dated and photographed, with the rooms that came back clean listed alongside any that did not, and our advice written apart from the findings themselves. In a state that assigns nobody statutory responsibility for this insect, that document is frequently the strongest item in the file once people start disagreeing.

hero.h1: K-9 Bed Bug Detection in North Augusta, SC
hero.lead: Bed bugs travel with people, and North Augusta moves a great many people through a small footprint. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions runs certified detection dogs through hotels, apartments, rental turnovers and family homes here — live insects and viable eggs only, with dated written findings you can hand to somebody else.
