body:
Columbia does not have one rodent problem. It has four or five, layered on each other, and they do not answer to the same fix. A Main Street kitchen, a hospital dock, a bungalow from 1905 cut into four units and a student rental off campus each fail in a different place.

Which is the argument for finding before treating. A trap set in the wrong cavity catches nothing, and for three weeks nothing looks like progress. Trapping, baiting and structural repair belong to rat and mouse control. This page is the other half of the job, K-9 rodent detection.

21,045People employed in Accommodation and Food Services in Richland County, 9.5% of county employment (US Census employment-by-industry data)
54.5%Share of Columbia households that rent, against 53,076 households citywide (Census QuickFacts, ACS 2020–2024)
25 daysGap between the two Columbia freeze-date stations: 236 freeze-free days at Metro Airport, 261 at University of SC (SC DNR State Climatology Office)

Why does Columbia’s commercial core drive most of this work?

Health Care and Social Assistance is Richland County’s largest employment sector at 33,974 jobs, 15.3 percent of everyone employed here; Accommodation and Food Services follows at 21,045, or 9.5 percent. The two overlap physically in a compact downtown, and both run buildings that never fully shut.

One hospital runs a production kitchen, a receiving dock, linen handling, soiled-utility rooms and a waste compactor, all live at three in the morning. Prisma Health Richland carries 641 beds plus 124 at the affiliated Heart Hospital and is the Midlands’ Level I Trauma Center. There is no window in which somebody pulls equipment off a wall to look behind it, which shapes our healthcare and senior living program.

Food service is that problem shrunk down and repeated a few hundred times. Grease interceptors, dish pits, dry storage and shared refuse corrals behind buildings that back onto one another decide whether a whole block has rodents or one address does. In the Congaree Vista, much of it renovated warehouse space turned into shops and restaurants, party walls make a single-suite finding rare.

Volume arrives in bursts too: banquet catering at the 142,500-square-foot Columbia Metropolitan Convention Center, or Fort Jackson, 52,000-plus acres with about 3,500 civilian employees and 43,000 service members trained a year, annexed in 1968.

What does a detection dog give you, and what will it never give you?

One thing: location. Bait stations and traps sample, reporting only on animals that cross the twenty-odd points a person selected. A dog does not sample. Handler and dog move at walking pace along wall bases, floor junctions, equipment plinths, pipe chases and stacked goods, reading odor that escapes cavities no camera reaches, in occupied space, without cutting an exploratory opening in anybody’s drywall.

Now the part this industry leaves out. An indication marks where odor has collected, not where an animal is standing, and never how many there are. Odor drifts and settles at the bottom of a shaft, so three alerts on one wall may be one rodent or six. Nor can a dog name a species from scent; that comes from dropping shape and sign height.

A further limit, which we publish. Field validation for scent detection dogs is strongest in bed bug work and conservation biology; structural rodent detection has far thinner support. So no accuracy percentage appears anywhere on this page — we hunted for a study that would survive hostile questioning and found none. Reasoning on our canine scent detection accuracy page. Kimberly Camera, who founded this company, spent twenty-eight years in scent detection and came out of FEMA Urban Search & Rescue.

What happens to a 1905 house once it holds four tenants?

Seventeen National Register historic districts sit inside the city limits, and almost all the housing in them was built for one family per address. A large share now takes rent, by the unit or by the room, and that conversion is where the residential work lives.

Subdividing an old house means a second kitchen upstairs: supply lines, a drain, a gas run, a vent through the band joist, a mini-split line set through an exterior wall. Each job was done by a different trade in a different decade, and none were thinking about a mouse.

Foundations matter as much as plumbing. Pre-war Southern housing of this type characteristically rests on brick piers with a curtain wall between them over a vented crawl space — a regional pattern, not a Columbia statistic, since no source gives a slab-versus-crawl split for this county. A crawl space with a rusted vent covering and an original sill plate is where to start.

Granby Mill Village

Mill built in 1896 and 1897, with 97 contributing buildings and operatives’ housing on a New England saltbox model. Small footprints, low floor systems, porches enclosed and re-enclosed over a century. Shallow crawl spaces discourage inspection and reward harborage.

Melrose Heights–Oak Lawn–Fairview

At 607 contributing buildings, the largest district by count: a streetcar suburb with a concentration of airplane bungalow cottages. Deep eaves and mature street trees put the roofline within reach.

Elmwood Park, Waverly and Forest Hills

Elmwood Park counts 219 contributing homes of 279, platted by auction in 1905; Waverly holds 132 from about 1898 to 1925; Forest Hills has 215, most after 1927, with multi-gable roofs full of valleys. Shotgun and foursquare plans give long uninterrupted floor and ceiling runs.

Columbia Historic District I

Nine contributing buildings, all antebellum, on Arsenal Hill. In fabric of that age nothing gets cut or drilled speculatively, which is exactly where a non-destructive screen earns its fee.

Which of the three species is it, and how do you read the evidence?

The animal itself stays out of sight, so identification is forensic. Three commensal species live here, each on its own vertical plane, and calling the wrong one costs you two weeks.

SpeciesField marksWhere sign turns upWhat it changes
Norway ratBlunt muzzle, small ears, short tail; droppings to three-quarters of an inch, blunt endedGround plane — burrow mouths at slab edges, under stoops and dumpster padsBurrow work and sealing at grade lead. Needs water daily, and is wary enough of new objects to make pre-baiting mandatory
Roof ratPointed muzzle, big eyes, an ear long enough to fold over the eye; droppings near half an inch, taperedOverhead — attic insulation, top plates, ductwork, and the limbs and cables leading thereEverything moves to the roofline: soffit and gable vents, roof junctions, tree clearance
House mouseAbout half an ounce, oversized ears; droppings near a quarter inch, rice-shaped, scatteredEverywhere in small amounts — drawer backs, toe kicks, appliance cavities, dry atticsTrap density decides it. Home range is ten to thirty feet across, so two traps under a sink accomplish nothing

Species detail sits in our Norway rat, roof rat and house mouse profiles. Impostors come first, though. Flying squirrels nest in cavities and move after dark, which is why they get reported as rats, and the eastern gray squirrel is a game animal in this state. More in the pest library.

Why does the roof rat deserve extra attention in the older neighborhoods?

Because the streetcar suburbs were planted, and a century on the planting has grown into a road network. Honesty marker first: nobody publishes a roof rat survey for Columbia, so what follows describes habitat and behavior, not a population claim.

The behavior is well established. Roof rats climb by preference and nest above ground, travelling limbs, fence tops, cables and any continuous horizontal surface, with a documented US range across the lower East Coast and Gulf states. Canopy touching a roof is a bridge, and so is an overhead service drop. A porch roof tied in at a lower pitch is a staircase.

So a roof rat job barely resembles a Norway rat job, and nothing is solved at ground level. The productive work is at height: guarding gable and soffit vents, closing the junction where an addition meets the original box, capping chases at the top plate, cutting limbs off the roof. Sign is overhead too.

Do the rivers and the sewer network actually move rodents around?

They do, and the way to say so is carefully. Columbia sits where the Saluda and the Broad join to form the Congaree near the Fall Line, and the Congaree runs about 53 miles on to the Wateree. The Columbia Canal, dug between 1820 and 1824 and rebuilt by 1891, was breached in the catastrophic flooding of early October 2015; as of February 2024 the repair was still in planning.

What matters is not the water but the edge. A riparian corridor is a continuous strip of cover, food and moisture running through a built-up area, and Norway rats use it the way roof rats use branches. Flooding pushes burrowers off low ground onto whatever sits above it.

Buried infrastructure is the other half. The city entered a federal Clean Water Act consent decree on 10 September 2013, committing to rehabilitate the sanitary sewer system over twelve years at an estimated $750 million to address overflows. Good for a river, a temporary complication for rodent work: open trench, relined mains and replaced laterals disturb established burrow systems and push animals elsewhere. A missing cleanout cap, an unplugged lateral or a floor drain with a dried trap connects a sewer directly to a kitchen. What we will not give you is a rat count for those sewers, because nobody has one.

How small does an opening have to be before it counts?

Smaller than the number in your head. Coins are the shorthand: an opening the width of a dime admits a house mouse, one the width of a quarter admits a rat. Written as a specification, that is a quarter inch where mice are the target and half an inch where rats are. A door with half an inch of clearance beneath it, UC IPM points out, is a rat door.

The residential code reaches the same threshold from another direction. Section R408.2 of the International Residential Code holds the covering over an under-floor ventilation opening to a least dimension of a quarter inch, then names what satisfies it: cast-iron grilles, extruded brick vents, hardware cloth woven from 0.035-inch wire upward, perforated sheet metal at 0.070 inches, expanded metal at 0.047. A vent meeting that standard is doing exclusion for free; a rusted one is a defect and a doorway at the same time, and in the historic districts they are usually original.

  • Mesh: half-inch hardware cloth at 19 gauge against rats, quarter-inch at 24 gauge against mice, woven either way. Welded mesh separates at the joints under sustained gnawing.
  • Sheet metal: 24 gauge minimum, 22 where a surface takes abuse. Masonry patches want two inches of reinforced concrete or properly mortared brick.
  • Doors: threshold gap held to a quarter inch, with a sweep closing to an eighth at each corner, which is where sweeps fail and nobody checks.
  • Copper mesh: packing behind a rigid cap, never the barrier alone. Unlike steel wool it does not rust into a soft plug in one wet season.
  • The sill plate line: the highest-yield hour on any old Columbia house, because every water, waste, gas and refrigerant penetration ever installed crosses it.
  • Expanding foam: fine for air sealing, useless against teeth.

To stop burrowing structurally: a curtain wall 36 inches below grade, an L-footing returning a foot outward, or a two-foot gravel band. Our exclusion and repair crew builds to those figures.

Why is rodenticide the wrong opening move in a dense neighborhood?

Two reasons, and the first concerns animals you never meant to harm. Secondary poisoning is documented, not speculative. Cornell researchers writing in Ecotoxicology in 2022 screened 72 red-tailed hawks in New York and reported anticoagulant residue in 68 percent of them. USGS work on 40 barred owls from Oregon and Washington turned up at least one anticoagulant compound in 48 percent. Neither dataset is Southeastern, and we looked for regional raptor monitoring without success, so take both as evidence of a mechanism rather than local prevalence. Anticoagulants kill slowly. They leave a rodent alive and conspicuous for several days, which makes it the easiest thing a hawk, an owl or a household pet will find that week.

The second reason is selfish, and it explains why bait and detection do not mix. Poisoned animals die inside cavities and behind stored goods, which buys a fortnight of odor complaints and confirms nothing at all. Bait also wipes out the fresh sign a canine screen gets verified against.

None of that makes rodenticide illegitimate. In licensed hands it belongs outdoors, in numbered tamper-resistant housings drawn on a plan, once the envelope is understood. One consumer-side change is worth knowing: the EPA’s rodenticide risk mitigation decision took brodifacoum, bromadiolone, difenacoum and difethialone off the shelf for homeowners.

Which remedies should you stop paying for?

  • Ultrasonic and electronic repellers. The Federal Trade Commission took enforcement action against six companies from 1985 to 1997, and in May 2001 wrote to over sixty firms making or retailing ultrasonic pest devices. UC IPM puts it just as plainly: hardly any evidence supports sound, magnetism or vibration clearing an established mouse population.
  • Peppermint oil and botanical repellents. Nothing from an extension service or a regulator endorses peppermint oil in structural rodent work, and we did check, so we neither sell nor advise it. That is not a claim of disproof. It means nothing we would cite endorses it.
  • Unattended glue boards. Adults often sense a board and step around it, per UC IPM, so the tray collects juveniles while the breeding animals go untouched. Non-target lizards, snakes and songbirds end up stuck to them as well.
  • A single round of bait. Norway rats raise four to six litters annually, each of six to twelve young, and start breeding at roughly three months; house mice raise five to ten litters and start at six to ten weeks. One pair that survives, or one gap nobody closed, rebuilds the whole population inside a season.
  • The fire percentage in every rodent brochure. A number circulates in this trade assigning rodents some share of fires whose origin was never determined. We traced it to a state fact sheet that cites nobody, found nothing resembling it at the NFPA or the US Fire Administration, and therefore print no version of it. The defensible point needs no figure: incisors grow roughly five inches a year, and chewed wiring turns up constantly in an old infestation.

Does a longer warm season downtown change the rodent calendar?

It does, and the state climatologist’s own station data lets us show it rather than assert it. Columbia Metro Airport records a last spring freeze around 1 April, a first fall freeze around 13 October, 236 freeze-free days. Columbia University of SC, downtown, records 26 February and 26 October — 261 freeze-free days. That 25-day difference between two stations in one city is the closest thing to a measured urban warmth signal available without citing a heat-mapping study we could not verify exists. Rodents breed longer where it stays warmer.

Richland County averages a mean of 66.5 degrees F and about 76 days a year above 90. Heat cuts both ways: published work has Norway rat breeding peaking in spring and autumn, slowing through high summer, often halting in winter.

  1. Late February into April

    Downtown, freeze risk is over by the end of February, weeks ahead of the airport date, and the spring breeding peak arrives with it. Burrow entrances show along foundations before ground cover thickens.

  2. May through August

    Heat suppresses breeding while food outdoors is everywhere, so the pressure shifts outside: patio dining, refuse corrals, fruit trees. Interior calls fall away and people decide it fixed itself. It moved.

  3. September through November

    The annual spike. Cool nights and vanishing food outside coincide with autumn breeding, somewhere between the two first-freeze dates, and climbing rodents head for attics once the canopy opens up.

  4. December through February

    Whatever got in is obvious by now: noise overhead, droppings in a pantry, torn insulation, chewed cable. An occupied heated building is habitat all year, and winter does not pause breeding in one.

The sealing window is therefore August into early October: screen, then close, before the weather decides for you.

What can a Columbia renter actually do about it?

More than most tenants think, provided the documentation is right. In a majority-renter city this is a communication problem as much as a technical one. Columbia is 45.5 percent owner-occupied, so 54.5 percent of its 53,076 households rent, at a median gross rent of $1,204. Countywide, 80 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so roughly one household in five moves each year — and every turnover is a chance to inspect an empty unit that nobody takes.

The legal position, stated exactly: section 27-40-440 of South Carolina’s Residential Landlord and Tenant Act requires a landlord to meet housing codes materially affecting health and safety and to keep the premises fit and habitable. It never mentions pests, vermin or extermination, and section 27-40-510 on tenant obligations is silent too. No statutory deadline, no allocation of cost.

City requirements we will not summarize, because we could not read them. Columbia’s code sits on a platform that returned no usable text by any route we tried, and asserting that an ordinance exists, or that none does, would be invention.

Evidence fills that gap. A dated, photographed report naming where live activity is, identifying species from physical sign and listing the openings that must close turns an argument about noise into a document. It also settles the commonest dispute in a multi-unit building: shared cavities and plumbing chases connect units, so activity in your kitchen often starts two doors down. Hence our multifamily and property management program, and why some owners want an inspection from a firm that is not quoting the repair — see independent canine detection.

How does a screen run, from the phone call to the re-check?

  1. Scope agreed in advance

    Which structures and which floors, whether it is safe to enter an under-floor space, whether a kitchen has to be covered between services, and who gets the report.

  2. Outside on foot, before anything else

    Grade line, piers and curtain wall, stoops, crawl vents, weep holes, utility trenches, refuse enclosure, and every limb and cable reaching the roof, photographed first.

  3. The dog covers the structure

    A repeatable pattern across wall bases, floor junctions, cabinet kicks, chases, mechanical rooms and stored product. We stop before fatigue degrades the work, and decline conditions too hot for a dog.

  4. Human confirmation at every indication

    Targeted inspection wherever the dog alerted: rub marks, gnawing, urine staining, droppings, nest material, and where it helps a borescope pushed through a gap that is already there. Early activity leaves almost nothing visible, and that is the case a dog gets brought for.

  5. Species named, then mapped

    Dropping dimensions and end profile, sign height, grease marks and gnaw pattern fix the trap layout and the sealing order. You receive annotated photographs showing every opening that must close and the material that closes it.

  6. Clear, seal, re-screen

    Interior trapping runs first and envelope sealing follows, so nothing live is shut inside a wall. Then the dog works the building again.

What is included in a Columbia canine rodent inspection?

  • A certified handler and dog working a repeatable pattern, outside and in
  • Screening of wall voids, ceiling planes, chases, crawl spaces and stored product
  • Hand verification of every indication before anything is recommended
  • Species called from droppings and sign height, plus an entry-point map keyed to mesh, gauge and door-sweep specification
  • Harborage and sanitation findings, dated and photographed for an owner, a tenant, an insurer or an auditor
  • A re-screen once remediation is finished, no matter who carried the work out

Which Columbia operations need this on paper rather than just done?

Restaurants, bars and institutional kitchens. Get the regulator right, because much published advice has not caught up. Responsibility for inspecting retail food establishments in this state passed to the South Carolina Department of Agriculture on 1 July 2024, the day DHEC divided into the Department of Public Health and the Department of Environmental Services. SCDA covers roughly 24,000 establishments under SC Regulation 61-25, scoring out of 100, an A being anything above 87. Any competitor page still crediting DHEC tells you the year it was written. See restaurant and food service.

Hospitals, clinics and senior living. The county’s largest employment sector and the least forgiving place to work. Patient areas cannot be evacuated, product application is constrained, and the sensitive rooms cannot be disturbed: sterile processing, pharmacy, dietary, materials management. A canine screen applies nothing, which is why it fits.

Student housing and off-campus rentals. USC enrolled 38,504 students on the Columbia campus in fall 2024 against 9,243 assignable on-campus beds, putting roughly three quarters of the student body into private apartments and rented houses in the neighborhoods above. Add the late-night food economy serving them and kitchens, dumpsters and old buildings concentrate in a few blocks. See our schools and student housing program.

Hotels and banquet venues carry the same risk on one back-of-house spine of kitchen, store, dock and refuse handling, which is the shape our hotel and hospitality program is built around. Operators with several sites, or anyone answering to a customer audit, run on this identical methodology — see nationwide K-9 rodent detection — with a written program, a site drawing carrying uniquely numbered device locations, service reports and closed-out corrective actions. We quote no SQF, BRCGS or AIB clause numbers, because a wrong clause in front of a quality manager is worse than none.

Who is licensed to do rodent work in South Carolina?

Licensing sits where most people do not expect it. Applicators and pest control businesses answer to the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation — a land-grant university rather than a state agriculture department. Structural work falls under Category 7A: industrial, institutional, structural and health-related pest control.

A commercial firm must hold a DPR business license, designate a Certified Applicator at every location it works from, and carry general liability cover of at least $100,000 combined single limit with no deductible above $1,000. Ask any company in your building for both.

Which parts of the Midlands do we cover?

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · 803-226-3155 · Kim@ck9ps.com

Within the city we cover downtown and the Main Street corridor, the Congaree Vista, Arsenal Hill, University Hill, Shandon and Old Shandon, Rosewood, Heathwood, Forest Hills, Wales Garden, Melrose, Elmwood Park, Cottontown and Bellevue, Earlewood, Eau Claire, Hyatt Park, Historic Waverly, Druid Hills, Kilbourne Park, Lake Katherine, Granby Hill, Olympia, Whaley Street, Celia Saxon, Lincoln Park and Greenview. Beyond the limits we work Cayce, West Columbia, Irmo, Lexington and the Fort Jackson side of town. See every area we serve.

Buildings here rarely need one thing only. K-9 bed bug detection in Columbia covers lodging, student turnover and senior living; bird control in Columbia handles roosting on roofs, ledges and signage; goose control in Columbia addresses pond and turf pressure.

Frequently asked questions

If the dog alerts three times, does that mean three rats?

No. An alert marks a concentration of odor, and odor travels. It moves on air currents, pools in low points and leaks from a cavity some distance from where the animal sits, so several alerts on one wall are often one animal. Numbers come later, from trap catch.

Can you screen a working kitchen without shutting it down?

Usually. Nothing is applied on a detection visit, so no exclusion period applies and no room has to be cleared of food or people. We work between services or after close, and settle in advance how a finding inside a production area gets passed to your manager.

DHEC does not exist any more. Who scores my restaurant now?

The South Carolina Department of Agriculture. Retail food inspection moved there on 1 July 2024, when DHEC was split into the Department of Public Health and the Department of Environmental Services. SCDA inspects around 24,000 establishments under SC Regulation 61-25, on a 100-point scale where above 87 earns an A.

I rent half of an old house. Is this the landlord’s problem or mine?

Legally it is less clear than it should be. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act obliges a landlord to keep premises fit and habitable, but section 27-40-440 never mentions pests, and the tenant obligations section is silent. In practice what moves a landlord is a dated, photographed, independent report.

Will the dog work a crawl space under a pier foundation?

Often from outside first. A crawl space leaks odor continuously through its vents and hatch, so a dog can usually read it from the perimeter. If the space is dry, tall enough and safe, the team goes in. If it is not, a technician crawls it with a light and a camera and works only the points the dog marked.

Something runs across my ceiling after dark. Is that automatically a rat?

No, and identifying it first saves money. Southern flying squirrels are nocturnal cavity nesters and sound almost identical through a ceiling, and eastern gray squirrels are a game species with separate handling rules. Timing helps: squirrels are loudest at dawn and dusk. We confirm from droppings, never from noise.

Why does this page not carry an accuracy percentage?

Because we could not find a study behind one. Canine detection has genuine published validation in bed bug work and conservation research; rodent detection inside structures has far less. Borrowing a figure from a different application and target odor would be marketing dressed as science.

Do you do the repairs, or only tell me where the problem is?

Both, and deliberately separate. Detection yields the map; rat and mouse control covers trapping and clearance; the repair crew builds exclusion to the dimensions set out above. One contractor suits some clients. Others would rather the inspection stayed independent of whoever prices the repair.

h1: K-9 Rodent Detection in Lexington, SC

hero.h1: K-9 Rodent Detection in Lexington, SC
hero.lead: Lexington sits inside a poultry county with a brand-new town wrapped around it, and rodent pressure follows the feed. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions runs a certified detection dog through barns, feed rooms, lakeshore outbuildings and post-2000 subdivision houses to mark where live activity actually sits, then hands over the map.

body:
Two very different buildings generate most of the rodent calls we take around Lexington. One is a feed and equipment building on a farm, where the thing being protected is the thing the rodents came for. The other is a house finished after 2000, whose owner was told new construction does not get rodents, and who is now in a garage listening to something move above the ceiling.

Neither is solved by guessing which cavity to open. This page is detection; trapping, baiting and structural repair live on rat and mouse control under the wider rodent control service.

7,065,868Broilers and other meat-type chickens counted in Lexington COUNTY by the 2022 Census of Agriculture (USDA NASS county profile)
2002Median year built for housing in the TOWN of Lexington; Lexington COUNTY’s median is 1993 (ACS 2020–2024, table B25035)
620 milesLake Murray shoreline, across 48,579 surface acres in four counties, average depth 41.5 feet (SCDNR)

Why does a poultry county change what a rodent inspection has to cover?

Because the largest concentration of rodent food here is not in anybody’s kitchen. It is in feed bins, delivery augers, litter packs and the ground beneath a feed line.

The 2022 Census of Agriculture puts 822 farms and 79,450 acres of farmland in Lexington County, selling $331,830,000 of product that year, second in South Carolina for total agricultural sales. Seventy-seven percent of that money came from livestock, poultry and their products, and the number explaining the rest is 7,065,868 broilers and other meat-type chickens. Row crops are there too, at 9,189 acres of forage and 4,457 of cotton.

So the productive surfaces are rarely the ones a homeowner would name: bin skirts and boot pits, the underside of auger runs, the seam where a sidewall curtain meets the foundation, the cool room, the generator shed, the pallet of bagged feed nobody has moved since spring. A dog reads all of that at walking pace. For growers and elevators under customer audit, the same methodology runs through agriculture and grain handling.

What can a nose do here that a bait station cannot?

Stations and traps answer one narrow question: did an animal cross this exact spot since the last service. Everything between the devices goes unmeasured, and on a farm that is most of the volume.

Detection inverts that. Handler and dog move along wall bases, slab edges, machine plinths, chases and stacked goods, and the dog responds to odor leaving cavities nobody has opened. Nothing is applied and no exploratory hole gets cut on a hunch.

Here is the part we insist on printing. An indication gives a place, not a headcount. Odor pools at the bottom of a chase, so an alert can sit several feet from the animal producing it. Scent will not name the species either. That call is made later, from physical sign.

One more limit, published rather than buried. Scent-dog field trials are numerous for bed bugs and sparse for commensal rodents in structures, so you will find no hit rate quoted here. We hunted for a study that would hold up to hostile questioning and came away without one. The argument is on our canine scent detection accuracy page. This company was founded by Kimberly Camera, twenty-eight years into scent detection work and formerly with FEMA Urban Search & Rescue.

Does keeping four hens in a back yard make this your problem?

The Town of Lexington has answered that in its own code, and the answer is yes.

Section 91.02 permits backyard chickens with conditions: four birds maximum however large the lot, no roosters, a $20 permit from the Office of Planning, Building and Technology, rear yard only, and any structure at least 25 feet from a property line, reducible to 10 feet with a neighbor letter and screening. In the same passage, the resident is required to provide proper disposal of sanitary waste and pest control.

That clause is not decoration. A sack of layer feed in a garage, an open bin beside a coop and scratch grain on bare soil amount to a small feed operation dropped into a subdivision. The same ordinance keeps horses, hogs and cows 250 feet from a residence and barns 500 feet; chickens got the pest-control clause.

Note also that section 91.21 adopts the Lexington County animal control ordinance by reference, and where the two conflict the county ordinance governs. The latest amendment is Ordinance 2024-13, adopted 7 October 2024.

A flock is easy enough to make rodent-hostile: feed in a hard-sided bin with a latching lid, feeders up at dusk, run floor and coop skirt closed with quarter-inch hardware cloth. Chicken wire keeps a hawk out. It does not slow a rat.

If the houses are this new, why are rodents getting in?

Label the geography before the number, because the two Lexingtons are not the same place. The TOWN’s median year of construction is 2002; the COUNTY’s is 1993. Of the town’s 10,348 housing units, 80.3 percent were built in 1990 or later, 57.5 percent in 2000 or later, only 9.5 percent before 1980. Town population went from 17,870 in 2010 to an estimated 25,729 in 2025.

People assume young stock means tight stock. It does not. New construction fails in a short, predictable set of places, and because the housing is uniform the same defect repeats down a street.

  • Garage door corner seals. The bottom seal compresses across the middle and lifts at both ends, leaving a triangle at each jamb. It is the opening we photograph most in post-2000 houses here.
  • Utility penetrations at the slab edge. Water, waste, gas, service entrance and the refrigerant line set all cross one band, each drilled by a different trade.
  • Weep holes in brick veneer. Required for drainage, so filling them is not an option. Stainless or copper inserts keep the drainage path and close the doorway.
  • Soffit returns. Where a gable meets the main box, the soffit dead-ends into a void that often opens into the attic behind the fascia.
  • Builder-grade exterior doors. More than a quarter inch of clearance underneath is an entrance, and new-house sweeps are usually adequate at the middle and open at the corners.
  • Trench backfill and stoop edges. Loose fill along a service trench is the easiest digging on the lot, and Sandhills quartz sand neither waterlogs nor collapses around a burrow.

None of it is a builder scandal, and all of it is fixable in an afternoon once somebody marks the openings. Our repair crew closes to specification.

What happens when the next phase breaks ground behind you?

You inherit the neighbors, through nothing you did.

The town’s own GIS subdivision status layer shows how much ground is moving. Barr Lake phases 3D and 3E carry 182 lots between them. River Ridge is recorded at 150 lots, West of Main at 76, Nightingale Hills at 66. Sterling Bridge is working through phases six to ten at 26, 16, 25, 25 and 65. Brookstone one and two add 51 and 53, and Riverside runs through phases one, 2A and 2B. Countywide, 2,006 residential building permits were issued in 2025.

When a grader strips forty acres, everything living in that cover relocates within a day or two. Burrow systems along a fence line or a drainage swale get opened or buried, and the animals do not disperse evenly. They move to the nearest structure with food and harborage: the finished phase next door.

The signature is unmistakable: a street of five-year-old houses with no history of trouble starts generating calls, clustered on the side facing the work. It is also the cheapest moment to seal.

Which of the three species is it, and what does each one leave?

The animal itself stays out of view, so the call gets made from what it leaves behind. Three commensal species share these buildings, each on its own vertical plane, and naming the wrong one costs you a fortnight.

SpeciesField marksWhere the sign turns up hereWhat it dictates
Norway ratHeavy build, blunt nose, small ears, a tail that falls short of head plus body; droppings up to three-quarters of an inch, ends squared offAt grade — burrow mouths at slab edges and stoops, under feed bins and shedsGrade-level sealing and burrow work lead. It drinks daily and shies from new objects, so a device must sit unused for days
Roof ratSlender, sharp nose, prominent eyes, an ear that folds forward past it; droppings around half an inch, both ends drawn to a pointOverhead — loft floors, top plates, duct runs, batt insulation, and the limbs and cables leading up to themThe whole job moves up: gable and soffit vents, chase caps, canopy cut off the roof
House mouseHalf an ounce, ears large for the head; droppings near a quarter inch, rice-shaped, scattered not piledSmall amounts in many places — drawer backs, toe kicks, appliance cavities, tack trunks, dry atticsTrap density decides it. Needs no free water; home range of ten to thirty feet, so two traps under a sink do nothing

Detail sits in the Norway rat, roof rat and house mouse profiles. Rule out the impostors first. A southern flying squirrel nests in cavities and moves after dark, so it lands on the phone as a rat almost every time, and the eastern gray squirrel is game in this state with separate rules. Our pest library has the rest.

The shortcut on a farm: sign on a feed room floor points at Norway, sign along a truss chord at roof rat, a light scatter everywhere at mice. Height settles more arguments than size does.

Does a lakeshore address change the job?

It changes the inventory. A house on the water is rarely one building, and the outbuildings are where the work is.

Lake Murray covers 48,579 acres with 620 miles of shoreline across Lexington, Newberry, Richland and Saluda counties, averaging 41.5 feet deep, and its 1.6-mile dam feeds the 205 MW Saluda hydroelectric station. Along much of that shore the normal maximum pool sits at the 360-foot contour, frequently the boundary between Dominion Energy and the upland owner, under FERC Project No. 516 and a Shoreline Management Plan first developed in 1975. What you may build on the water is not a town decision.

A lakeside property therefore accumulates structures a house inspection never touches: a boathouse loft, a dockbox holding rope and dog food, a pump house, a detached garage with a boat in it. Each has a low floor system, an unfinished ceiling and nobody looking inside for months. Frontage also guarantees permanent drinking water, which matters for the Norway rat, and shoreline canopy supplies the routes a roof rat prefers.

Inland, the creek corridors do the same work. Twelve Mile Creek runs through Lexington with USGS gauging station 02168810 on it, in hydrologic unit 03050109, and the Twelve Mile Ridge subdivision takes its name from it. Fourteen Mile Creek carries a 3,500-foot town trail off North Lake Drive and Old Cherokee Road. A riparian strip is unbroken cover, water and food running through developed ground, and burrowers travel it the way climbers travel branches.

How small does a gap have to be before it counts?

Smaller than instinct suggests. The coin version is worth memorizing: a house mouse passes an opening about the width of a dime, a rat one about the width of a quarter. As a specification, seal anything over a quarter inch for mice and over half an inch for rats. UC IPM puts it bluntly — a half-inch gap beneath a door is a rat door.

The building code lands on that same quarter inch by a different route. Under IRC R408.2, whatever covers an under-floor ventilation opening may not exceed a quarter inch in its least dimension, and the acceptable materials are listed out: 0.070-inch perforated sheet metal, 0.047 expanded metal, cast-iron grating, extruded brick vents, or hardware cloth woven from 0.035-inch wire upward. A compliant vent excludes rodents for free. A rusted one is simultaneously a defect and a door.

  • Against rats: half-inch hardware cloth, 19 gauge, woven. Welded mesh opens at the joints under repeated gnawing.
  • Against mice: quarter-inch hardware cloth, 24 gauge, again woven.
  • Sheet metal: 24 gauge for pipe and wall barriers, 22 gauge where a surface takes abuse.
  • Doors: a quarter inch maximum at the threshold, and a sweep that still shuts to an eighth of an inch out at the jambs, since the jamb end is what gives way.
  • Copper mesh: stuffing to sit behind a hard cap, not the cap itself. It has one advantage over steel wool, which rusts loose inside a season.
  • Sill plate and band joist: the highest-yield hour on any building here, because every service crossed that line.
  • Expanding foam: an air seal and nothing more. Teeth pass through it without slowing.

Digging gets stopped structurally by one of three published details: a below-grade curtain wall taken down three feet, a footing with a twelve-inch outward return, or a two-foot band of gravel at the perimeter.

Why is bait the wrong opening move around poultry and feed?

Two reasons, and the first is everything on the property that is not a rat.

Secondary poisoning has been measured, not merely argued. A 2022 Ecotoxicology paper out of Cornell reported anticoagulant residue in 68 percent of the 72 red-tailed hawks it screened in New York. Separate USGS sampling of 40 barred owls returned at least one anticoagulant compound in 48 percent. Neither study is from this region, and our search for Southeastern raptor monitoring turned up nothing, so read those numbers as proof the pathway is real, not as a rate for this county. On farmland the pathway is what counts: an anticoagulant kills over days, and a rodent dying slowly is the slowest thing on the property. A hawk takes it. So does a barn cat.

The second reason is that bait destroys your own evidence. A poisoned rat does not oblige you by dying in the aisle. It dies inside a wall, under a litter pack or six bales into a stack, and you get a fortnight of odor and no confirmation.

None of that makes rodenticide illegitimate. Used by a licensed applicator after the envelope is understood, it sits outside in tamper-resistant housings that are numbered on a drawing and serviced on a record. Worth knowing on the consumer side: the EPA rodenticide risk mitigation decision pulled the second-generation anticoagulants — brodifacoum, bromadiolone, difenacoum, difethialone — out of homeowner products, and pellet formulations are off the consumer shelf as well.

Which rodent remedies are worth nothing?

  • Ultrasonic and electronic repellers. Between 1985 and 1997 the Federal Trade Commission took enforcement action against six companies over these products; in May 2001 it sent warning letters to over sixty firms making or selling them. UC IPM says the same thing without the litigation: almost nothing in the evidence base shows noise, magnets or vibration emptying a building of established mice.
  • Peppermint oil and botanical repellents. We searched for an extension service or regulator endorsing peppermint oil in structural rodent work and came up empty, so we neither sell nor recommend it. We are not asserting it has been disproven, which is a separate statement. We are saying nothing citable backs it.
  • Glue boards left down and forgotten. Grown animals often sense the board and walk around the edge of it, per UC IPM, which leaves you a tray of juveniles and an untouched breeding population. Lizards, snakes and small birds end up stuck on them too.
  • One round of bait and nothing after. A Norway rat runs four to six litters annually at six to twelve young each and is breeding by three months old; a house mouse runs five to ten litters and is breeding between six and ten weeks. Leave one pair alive, or one hole open, and the season replaces everything you killed.
  • Chicken wire on a coop or a crawl vent. Poultry netting was designed to contain birds, not exclude rodents, and the mesh is far too coarse for either target. Woven hardware cloth is the cheapest upgrade on a residential lot.

The gnawing fact worth citing is anatomical: incisors grow roughly five inches a year and must be worn down continuously, which is why chewed wiring and stripped insulation are routine findings.

When does rodent pressure arrive in Lexington County?

Two SC State Climatology Office freeze stations sit inside the county and they disagree by twenty days. Little Mountain records a last spring freeze around 31 March, a first fall freeze around 20 October, 246 freeze-free days. Pelion 4 NW records 21 March and 10 October, for 226. The town lies between them, with no station of its own. The nearest published temperature and rainfall normals are the Columbia and Midlands set, roughly 47.75 to 48.11 inches a year on a mean of 66.5 degrees F, and they are cited here as Midlands figures rather than Lexington ones.

A long frost-free season means outdoor food and cover persist most of the year. It does not mean breeding never stops. Published work puts the Norway rat reproductive peaks in spring and again in fall, with a summer lull and frequently a winter halt.

  1. Late February into April

    The spring reproductive peak, landing as fields are worked and feed movement picks up. Burrow entrances along foundations and bin skirts become visible before ground cover thickens over them.

  2. May through August

    Summer heat slows reproduction just as outdoor food peaks, so the pressure moves outside onto gardens, spilled feed and refuse. Calls about indoor noise dry up, and owners decide the problem went away by itself. It changed address.

  3. September through November

    The yearly peak. The autumn breeding surge arrives alongside colder nights and disappearing food outdoors, somewhere between the two county freeze dates, and roof rats start moving into lofts and attics as leaf cover drops away.

  4. December through February

    Whatever got in is obvious — overhead noise, droppings behind a pantry, shredded insulation, chewed cable. Poultry houses are heated by design, so they never get a quiet season.

The sealing window here runs from August into early October. Screen, then close, while the timing is still yours.

How does a canine screen run here, from the first call?

  1. Scope settled on the phone

    Which structures and levels, whether birds are in the houses, whether a feed room can be quiet for an hour, and who gets the report.

  2. The outside, on foot, first

    Grade line, slab edge, stoops, garage door corners, weep holes, utility trenches, bin pads, and every limb and service drop reaching a roof. Sign gets photographed before the dog leaves the vehicle.

  3. The dog works the structure

    One consistent search pattern over wall bases, floor lines, machine bases, pipe chases, plant rooms and product on pallets. A tired dog gets pulled off the job, and we will not run one in heat that is unsafe for it.

  4. Every indication verified by hand

    Targeted inspection at each alert — droppings, urine staining, grease marks, gnawing, nest material, and a borescope through an existing opening.

  5. Species called from physical evidence

    Dropping dimensions and end profile, the height sign appears at, gnaw pattern. That fixes trap layout and the order openings close in.

  6. Map, clear, seal, re-screen

    You get an annotated photo set: each opening to be closed, and the material and gauge that closes it. Trapping indoors precedes sealing the envelope, so nothing alive gets shut into a cavity. The dog then covers the building a second time.

What does a Lexington canine rodent screen include?

  • A certified handler and dog on one repeatable search pattern, inside and out
  • Photographed exterior survey of grade line, slab edge, roofline, weep holes and utility penetrations
  • Indoor coverage of stud cavities, ceiling planes, pipe chases, machine bases and palletized goods
  • Barns, feed rooms, bins, coops, boathouses and detached garages within the agreed scope
  • Hand confirmation of every canine indication before a single recommendation is made
  • An entry-point map keyed to mesh size, gauge and door-sweep specification
  • Harborage and sanitation findings: spilled feed, storage practice, vegetation contact, refuse
  • Written, dated, photographed findings for an owner, an insurer or an auditor
  • A re-screen after the work is finished, regardless of who carried it out

Which Lexington operations need this documented rather than merely done?

Poultry, grain and feed handling. Anyone facing a customer audit needs the written program, the drawing with uniquely numbered device positions, dated service records and corrective actions closed out on paper. A canine screen feeds that file the thing auditors press hardest on: a specific location, photographed, with the evidence beside it. The same program runs nationally through nationwide K-9 rodent detection. We will not recite an SQF, BRCGS or AIB clause number, since citing the wrong one does more damage than citing none.

Industrial and distribution space. Prysmian is putting $80 million into its facility at 700 Industrial Drive in Lexington for FlexRibbon fiber-optic cable, roughly 135 new jobs, online in May 2028. At county level the economic development office lists Amazon, Dominion Energy South Carolina, House of Raeford, Lexington Medical Center, Michelin, Nephron Pharmaceuticals, Shaw Industries and Southeastern Freight Lines among its largest employers. Deep racking is the point at which looking with your eyes stops telling you anything — see our warehouse and distribution program.

Schools. Lexington County School District One enrolls 27,074 students across 32 schools, with 2,083.80 full-time-equivalent teachers and a ratio of 12.99, in a locale NCES calls large suburban. Cafeterias, receiving docks, kitchen line voids and portable classrooms have to be inspected without applying anything around children. See our schools and student housing program.

Food service. Know who scores you, because a lot of advice online is out of date. Since 1 July 2024 the retail food program in this state belongs to the South Carolina Department of Agriculture, not DHEC. Roughly 24,000 establishments fall under it, inspected against SC Regulation 61-25 on a hundred-point scale, with an A awarded above 87. See restaurant and food service.

Apartments and managed communities. Nearly a quarter of the town’s housing sits in buildings of five units or more, where a shared cavity is a corridor rather than a boundary — our multifamily program covers that, and some owners want an inspector who is not pricing the repair, which is the argument on our independent canine detection page.

Who is actually allowed to do this work here?

Not where most people look for it. Licensing of applicators and pest control businesses in South Carolina runs through Clemson University, specifically its Department of Pesticide Regulation, rather than through any state agriculture department.

The credential is Category 7A, covering industrial, institutional, structural and health-related pest control. A commercial firm also needs a DPR business license, a Designated Certified Applicator named for every location it works out of, and general liability insurance at a combined single limit of $100,000 or better with the deductible held under $1,000. Ask to see both. A legitimate firm produces them in a minute.

Where in and around Lexington do we work?

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · 803-226-3155 · Kim@ck9ps.com

Inside the town we cover the Main Street blocks around the Icehouse Amphitheater at 107 West Main, plus Virginia Hylton Park, Gibson Pond and the subdivisions named in the town’s own GIS: Barr Lake, Bent Creek, Brookstone, Cherokee Village, Coventry Lake, Gibson Forest, Golden Hills, Heritage Hills, Hope Ferry Plantation, Hunters Ridge, Lakeside at Woodcreek, Laurel Falls, Mallard Lakes, Middlebrook, Nightingale Hills, Pilgrim Point, River Ridge, Riverside, Shoal Creek, Sterling Bridge, Twelve Mile Ridge, Whiteford Lakes and Woodside Farms. Golden Hills Golf & Country Club on Scotland Drive sits in the middle of it.

Beyond the town limits we work the Lake Murray shoreline and the Dominion access areas, Dreher Island, the Lower Saluda at Saluda Shoals Park, and out toward Irmo, Chapin, Cayce, West Columbia and Pelion. See every area we serve.

Properties here seldom need one service only. K-9 bed bug detection in Lexington covers lodging and rental turnover; bird control in Lexington handles roosting on ledges and signage; goose control in Lexington addresses pond and shoreline pressure.

Frequently asked questions

Can the dog tell me how many rats I have?

No, and any company saying otherwise is selling something it cannot deliver. A detection dog reports location and live activity. Odor drifts and settles low in a cavity, so an alert marks a concentration of scent, not an animal at that address.

Can you work a poultry house with birds in it?

Usually the surrounding structures rather than the occupied house itself, planned with you beforehand. Feed rooms, bin pads, cool rooms, generator sheds and building perimeters are where the useful findings sit. Nothing is applied on a detection visit, so no exclusion period applies and no product goes near feed or birds.

My house was built in 2006. Should it really have rodents?

Age predicts far less than people assume. New construction fails in a short, repeatable list of places: garage door seal corners, utility penetrations at the slab edge, open weep holes, soffit returns, and the clearance under a builder-grade door. Because the stock is uniform, one defect repeats down a street.

They started clearing land behind my subdivision. Is that connected?

Very likely. Grading strips cover and opens burrow systems within a day, and displaced animals head for the nearest structure offering food and harborage. The tell is several neighbors on one side of the street reporting activity within weeks of each other. Sealing first costs far less.

Do I have to unstack the feed room first?

Please leave it alone. A cluttered room is the argument for hiring a dog, not something to fix before one arrives. Breaking the stack down spreads odor around, wipes out runways and takes away the physical evidence we need to verify an alert. An aisle wide enough to walk is the only preparation required.

Does the town chicken ordinance really require me to do pest control?

Section 91.02 of the Town of Lexington code permits up to four hens, no roosters, on a $20 permit in a rear yard with a 25-foot setback, and states that the resident must provide proper disposal of sanitary waste and pest control. Section 91.21 also adopts the county animal control ordinance by reference, and the county version governs where the two conflict.

Will the dog work a boathouse or a dock?

Yes, and those structures are frequently where the finding is. A boathouse loft, a dockbox holding rope and food and a pump house all combine a low floor system, an open ceiling and months with nobody looking inside. Shoreline structures fall under FERC Project No. 516 rather than the town, so repairs need the permitting path checked.

Why does this page carry no accuracy percentage?

Because no study we would stand behind supports one. There is real published validation for detection dogs in bed bug work and in conservation fieldwork. For commensal rodents inside buildings there is far less, and lifting a percentage from an unrelated target odor and a different environment is marketing dressed up as evidence.

Do you carry out the repairs, or only find the problem?

Both, and deliberately kept apart. Detection produces the map and the species call. Trapping and clearance belong to rat and mouse control, and the exclusion crew builds to the figures above, then re-screens. Some clients want one contractor end to end; others want the inspection independent of whoever prices it.
