title: Rodent Detection, N Augusta
description: Certified K-9 rodent detection in North Augusta — we locate live rodent activity inside walls and crawl spaces, then seal the entry points for good.
h1: K-9 Rodent Detection in North Augusta, SC

hero.eyebrow: NORTH AUGUSTA, SC · CANINE RODENT DETECTION
hero.h1: K-9 Rodent Detection in North Augusta, SC
hero.lead: A certified detection dog from Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions covers a North Augusta property and pinpoints where live rodent activity actually is — under seventy-year-old floor systems, behind cabinet runs, above apartment ceilings, inside riverfront storerooms. You get mapped, photographed locations instead of another month of guessing.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Family-owned · Evidence first, demolition last · Based in Windsor, working the Savannah River line

body:
North Augusta grew up twice. A land company bought about 5,600 acres in 1890, the city incorporated on 11 April 1906, and the Savannah River Plant build-out then quadrupled the population. That second wave is still standing and still occupied, which is why so many rodent calls here sound identical: a noise overhead after dark, droppings behind the range, weeks of moving snap traps from one guess to the next.

Guessing is the expensive part. A trap set in the wrong void records nothing, which reads, wrongly, as good news. Trapping and repair belong to rat and mouse control; detection sits under K-9 rodent detection.

17.4%Share of North Augusta housing units built in the 1950s — 2,213 of 12,694, the city’s largest single decade (ACS 2023 5-year, DP04)
1986Median year a North Augusta structure was built (US Census, ACS 2023 5-year, table B25035)
13.2%Housing units vacant citywide, including a 12.6% rental vacancy rate (ACS 2023 5-year, DP04)

Why does a Savannah River Plant-era house leak rodents?

Because it has had seventy years of trades cutting holes in it, and nobody was thinking about mice on any of those days.

Of 12,694 housing units, the 1950s account for 2,213 — 17.4 percent, the largest decade on the record. The 2000s sit almost level at 17.1 percent. Everything predating 1950 totals 672 units, just 5.3 percent, while post-2000 building is 32.2 percent. The median structure dates to 1986 and 69 percent of units are single-family detached. The shape is a barbell, with a thin trough in between.

Our inspections concentrate in the older half, and the reason is not the walls. Walls rarely fail. What fails is everything passing through them. Count the penetrations on a 1953 house: original supply and drain, original electrical service, a gas line, then a refrigerant line set, a dryer vent, cable, an irrigation feed. Each was cut through a rim joist or sill plate by somebody solving a different problem and closed, if at all, with whatever was on the truck.

One figure we will not give you, because nobody has it: what share of local houses sit on crawl space rather than slab. No published source reports that split for this city or county. The single citable number is national — NAHB puts the South Atlantic division at 85.7 percent slab — and it describes 2024 new construction only. We look at your foundation and tell you what it is.

What can a detection dog tell you, and what will it never tell you?

It tells you where. Smaller than the claim this industry usually makes, and more useful than it sounds.

Traps and stations are sampling devices. They report only on animals crossing the fifteen or twenty points a human chose, so a rodent that never crosses one is invisible to the programme. A dog is not sampling. Handler and dog cover perimeter walls, floor junctions, cabinet kicks, chases and stacked product at walking pace, reading odor that leaves cavities the eye cannot enter — in occupied space, without cutting an exploratory hole.

Now the boundaries. An indication marks a concentration of odor, not an animal at an address, and never a census. Odor pools and settles at the low point of a chase, so two indications do not mean two rats. Nor does a dog name the species.

A further limit, published rather than buried. Peer-reviewed field validation for canine scent detection is deepest in bed bug work and conservation detection; structural rodent detection has far less behind it. So we attach no accuracy percentage here, having found no study we would defend in front of a sceptical client. The company was founded by Kimberly Camera, who brings twenty-eight years in scent detection plus a FEMA Urban Search & Rescue background, and the argument is laid out on our canine scent detection accuracy page.

Which North Augusta subdivisions do we end up in, and what does the era mean?

The city’s planning GIS carries roughly three hundred recorded plats. Names we work in and around include Hammond Hills, Crystal Lake, Pinehurst, Knollwood, Walnut Grove, Wando Woodlands, Butlers Mill, Martintowne, Foxglove, Windtree, Bergen Place, Sudlow Hills, Hampton Terrace, The Summit, The Rapids, Rivernorth, Hammonds Ferry and Leyland Place, plus the bird-named villages of Lakes and Streams — Swan Lake Village, Robin Lake and Bluebird Lake Village.

Two caveats. That layer covers the city and surrounding areas, so some plats sit in unincorporated Aiken County. And it carries book and page, not recording dates, so we will not attach a build decade to a name we cannot date. Hammond’s Ferry is a documented 2000s development by LeylandAlliance; the Hampton Terrace name descends from a 1903 hotel that burned in 1916. Otherwise we date the house by looking at it.

The mid-century cohort

Original sill plates carrying seven decades of re-cut service penetrations. Under-floor vents are often original louvres, rusted past the quarter-inch limit the code sets, and kitchens remodelled twice leave abandoned pipe stubs behind toe kicks.

The 1960s through 1990s middle

Roughly 37 percent of the stock. The vulnerable line moves upward: gable and soffit vents, roof-to-wall junctions where an addition meets the original box, attic air handlers whose condensate lines open into the ceiling plane.

The post-2000 third

Nearly a third of the city is twenty-first-century and the envelopes are tighter. That is not immunity. Recurring failures are garage door corner seals, weep holes with no rodent guards, and trench backfill that never consolidated.

How is the Georgia Avenue and Butler Avenue district a different problem?

Because it is old in a way almost nothing else here is, and because there is very little of it.

The district joined the National Register on 5 April 1984 under reference 84002017, covering roughly thirty acres along Georgia Avenue, Butler Avenue, Observatory Avenue and Martintown Road, on a hill overlooking Augusta, Georgia. The nomination counts sixteen properties — thirteen contributing buildings, one cemetery, three non-contributing structures — with a period of significance from about 1859 to about 1930 and most erected between 1903 and 1907. Named examples include Star of Edgefield, an 1859 red brick house with a two-tier veranda on iron posts, and Palmetto Lodge of 1903, Tudor Revival with half-timbering in the ends of a multi-gable roof.

Only 5.3 percent of the city’s housing predates 1950, so this is a small number of buildings doing something the rest of the stock does not. A multi-gable roof is a set of valleys and junctions, each a route for a climbing animal, and outbuildings turn a single address into a four-building job.

What we will not do is describe the Georgia Avenue commercial block. That nomination is a residential document; it lists commercial among present uses but gives no build dates or construction type for the storefronts, and no other source we found does either. Anyone stating confidently what those buildings are made of is guessing.

Which rodent is it, and how do you read what it leaves?

You will almost never see the animal, so identification is forensic. Three commensal species occur here, they occupy different vertical planes, and calling the wrong one costs you a fortnight.

EvidenceNorway ratRoof ratHouse mouse
DroppingsUp to three-quarters of an inch, blunt endsAbout half an inch, tapered to pointsAround a quarter inch, rice-grain, scattered
BodyBlunt muzzle, small ears, tail shorter than the bodyPointed muzzle, big eyes, ear folds over the eye, long tailHalf an ounce, large ears for its size
Where sign isFloor line, slab edge, burrow mouths, under stoopsDuctwork, top plates, attic insulation, raftersEverywhere in small amounts — drawers, toe kicks
WaterNeeds free water dailyNeeds free waterNeeds none, which is how it survives a dry attic
RangeWide-ranging, neophobic; pre-baiting is not optionalArboreal; travels limbs, fence tops, cablingHome range ten to thirty feet across
What it changesGround plane sealing, burrow workRoofline sealing, soffit and vent workTrap density — many traps close together

Details sit in the Norway rat profile, the roof rat profile and the house mouse profile. Rule out impostors first: attic noise proves an animal, not a rodent. Southern flying squirrels are nocturnal cavity nesters reported as rats constantly, and eastern gray squirrels are a game species with their own handling rules. More in the pest library.

What does Fall Line sand do to a burrow?

Augusta is the fall line city of the Savannah River, which puts North Augusta on that boundary and inside the Sandhills belt — the uppermost coastal plain, covering about twelve percent of South Carolina.

The soils are deep quartz sands. USDA-NRCS classifies the Lakeland series as thermic, coated Typic Quartzipsamments. Translated: excessively drained, permeability from rapid to very rapid, upwards of eighty inches of sand, clay hardpans somewhere beneath that. Rainwater does not linger; the county averages 50.77 inches a year and most goes straight down.

For a burrowing rat that is close to ideal ground. Treat the next line as professional observation rather than published finding, because nobody has measured Norway rat burrowing in Sandhills soil: these burrows stay serviceable all year, so an open hole beside a stoop in February is usually current.

Where digging must be stopped structurally, the specification is settled. Three details each stop a digging rat at a foundation: a curtain wall carried thirty-six inches or more below grade, an L-footing returning about twelve inches outward, or coarse gravel laid in a band two feet wide. Our exclusion and repair crew builds to those dimensions.

How big does a gap have to be before it matters?

Smaller than almost anyone expects. Coins make the useful mental picture. A dime-sized hole admits a house mouse; a quarter-sized one admits a rat. As a specification, close anything wider than a quarter inch where mice are in play, half an inch for rats. UC IPM notes that a rat will get under a door with a half-inch gap beneath it.

The code arrives at the same place from another direction. Under IRC section R408.2, the covering on a crawl space vent must hold its least dimension to a quarter inch or under. The code then names what satisfies that: perforated sheet metal from 0.070 inches, expanded metal from 0.047, cast-iron grating, and hardware cloth woven from wire of 0.035 inches upward. A vent still meeting that standard is already a barrier; a rusted one is a code defect and a doorway at once.

  • Hardware cloth against rats: half-inch mesh, 19 gauge, woven rather than welded — welded joints are where cheap mesh gives way.
  • Hardware cloth against mice: quarter-inch mesh, 24 gauge, woven.
  • Sheet metal: 24 gauge or heavier on wall and pipe barriers, 22 gauge where it takes abuse.
  • Doors: a quarter-inch threshold gap at most, with a sweep closing to an eighth of an inch at both corners, which is where sweeps fail.
  • Copper mesh: packing behind a hard cap, never the barrier itself. It does not rust the way steel wool does.
  • Sill plate and band joist: the highest-yield line on any older house here.
  • Expanding foam: an air seal. It stops draughts and stops nothing with incisors.

Why is rodenticide the wrong opening move?

Two reasons. The first involves animals you never meant to poison. Secondary poisoning is documented rather than theoretical. Cornell researchers reporting in Ecotoxicology in 2022 recovered anticoagulant residue from 68 percent of the 72 New York red-tailed hawks they examined. USGS work on 40 barred owls in the Pacific Northwest returned at least one anticoagulant in 48 percent of the birds. Both are out of region, and we looked for Southeastern raptor monitoring without finding any, so we offer them as evidence of a mechanism rather than a local prevalence figure. A poisoned rodent does not die quickly. It becomes slow and exposed for days, and a slow rodent is the easiest meal available to a hawk, an owl or your own dog.

The second reason is that bait destroys your evidence. A poisoned rat dies in a wall cavity or deep in stored product, and you get a fortnight of odor and confirmation of nothing. None of that makes rodenticide illegitimate. Handled by a licensed applicator it goes outside, in locked tamper-resistant housings that carry numbers and appear on a drawing, and it goes out after the envelope is understood.

What is being sold to you that does not work?

Naming these is the fastest way to stop somebody wasting a season.

Ultrasonic and electronic repellers

Six companies faced Federal Trade Commission enforcement between 1985 and 1997, and in May 2001 the Commission followed with warning letters to over sixty makers and sellers of ultrasonic pest devices. UC IPM is blunt on the point: almost no evidence supports sound, magnetic or vibrational gadgets clearing a settled mouse population.

Peppermint oil and botanicals

Nothing from an extension service or a regulator backs peppermint oil as a structural rodent repellent, and we did look, so it is not something we sell or advise. That is not the same as calling it disproven. It means no source we would cite endorses it.

Glue boards left down and forgotten

Adults frequently sense a glue board and walk around it, per UC IPM, leaving a tray of juveniles while the animals doing the breeding go untouched. Non-target lizards, snakes and small birds get caught too.

One round of bait, then nothing

A Norway rat delivers four to six litters annually, six to twelve young apiece, and is breeding by month three. Mice manage five to ten litters and breed at six to ten weeks. One surviving pair rebuilds the whole population inside a season.

Sanitation on its own

Necessary and insufficient. Even first-rate housekeeping will not remove a house mouse population, and the trade’s standard handbook says so plainly. Cleaning does not close a building.

The fire percentage you have read

A widely circulated figure attributing a share of fires of unknown origin to rodents runs through this industry. The trail ends at a state fact sheet that cites nobody, and neither the NFPA nor the US Fire Administration carries anything resembling it, so the number stays off this page. Incisors grow roughly five inches a year and gnawing is compulsory; that is enough.

How does the rodent year run in the CSRA?

The published normals frame it. AIKEN 4 NE, the nearest official station, records a last spring freeze around 22 March, a first fall freeze around 12 October and 232 freeze-free days, on a county mean of 64.1°F. Outdoor food and cover therefore persist most of the calendar. It does not follow that breeding runs unbroken outdoors. Published work puts two Norway rat peaks on the calendar, one in spring and one in autumn, with a lull through the heat and a frequent winter halt.

  1. Late February into April

    The spring peak, opening around that 22 March freeze date. Burrow entrances along foundations reappear before the grass thickens, which makes these the best weeks of the year for an exterior survey.

  2. May through August

    Heat suppresses breeding while outdoor food is everywhere, so the pressure shifts outdoors: fallen fruit, spilled seed, pet bowls, dumpster pads, patio dining. Interior complaints fall away and people conclude it resolved itself. It went outside.

  3. September through November

    The annual spike. Autumn breeding meets cooling nights and the collapse of outdoor food around the 12 October freeze date, and climbing rodents move into attics as the canopy thins.

  4. December through February

    Whatever got in is now unmistakable: ceiling noise, pantry droppings, shredded insulation, gnawed wire. A heated building with harborage is a year-round habitat.

August into early October is therefore the window here for a screen followed by sealing.

Do vacancy rates and the greeneway corridor actually matter?

Both do, and both deserve stating carefully rather than dramatically.

Start with vacancy, which nobody thinks about. Of 12,694 housing units, 1,679 are vacant — 13.2 percent, against a rental vacancy rate of 12.6 percent. An empty unit is unheated, unmonitored and unswept, with nobody to notice droppings, and in a duplex or townhouse row the wall cavity it shares with an occupied unit is a corridor rather than a barrier.

Then the linear corridors. The North Augusta Greeneway runs over seven miles of paved trail along an abandoned railroad alignment, named for Mayor Thomas W. Greene, who served from 1985 to 1997. It reaches from Pisgah Road to Riverside Boulevard near the River Golf Club, with a 1.5-mile extension through the Crystal Lake area to the riverfront. A continuous vegetated edge with reliable cover is a travel lane for wildlife. Label that as what it is, a habitat argument: no agency publishes rodent counts for this city, and we are not inventing any.

The code does give one hard, citable sanitation rule. Section 5-16 requires that manure, urine, soiled straw and other animal refuse not accumulate more than 24 hours, held in leakproof and flyproof receptacles with tight-fitting covers, cleaned daily. Chapter 5 Article IV, adopted 17 May 2010, separately bars feeding wild animals and waterfowl in city parks and on other publicly owned land, counting each day a separate offence, though it reaches public land only. Where the pressure is birds or waterfowl, see bird control in North Augusta and goose control in North Augusta.

Which North Augusta businesses need this documented rather than merely done?

Here is a claim we will not make. We could not verify a single warehouse, distribution centre or manufacturing plant physically inside North Augusta. Regional names get attached to this city constantly and should not be: Kimberly-Clark operates at Beech Island, Bridgestone’s plant is at Graniteville, Textron is in Augusta, Georgia. The commercial rodent story here is food service, lodging, retail, offices and apartments.

Restaurants, bars and event food service. Riverside Village is a roughly 30-to-35-acre, approximately $200 million mixed-use development at the 13th Street Bridge; it broke ground as Project Jackson in May 2017 and holds restaurants, a brewery, an amphitheatre, apartments and offices. City-owned SRP Park opened beside it on 12 April 2018, seats 4,782 and holds up to 10,000 for larger events — concession space that runs hard in short bursts, then sits idle. Know who inspects you. Since 1 July 2024 the agency scoring South Carolina retail food establishments has been the Department of Agriculture rather than DHEC, working a hundred-point sheet on which anything above 87 earns an A.

Lodging. The Crowne Plaza North Augusta at 1060 Center Street opened in January 2019 inside Riverside Village: five storeys, 180 guest rooms and suites, 11,000 square feet of meeting space and a 5,400-square-foot ballroom. That shape puts kitchens, banquet storage, loading and refuse handling on one back-of-house spine, which is the geometry a canine screen covers fastest. See our hotel and hospitality programme.

Apartments, offices and retail. Multifamily of all sizes totals roughly 2,475 units, about 19.5 percent of the stock, and in a connected building a rodent problem in one stack is a building problem misfiled as a tenant problem — the basis of our multifamily programme. The plat record also carries Interchange Business Park, Martintown Professional Office Park and Merovan Business Center, where shared plenums and refuse enclosures mean a finding in one suite is rarely confined to it. Multi-site operators get the same methodology through nationwide K-9 rodent detection, and we quote no SQF or BRCGS clause numbers, because citing the wrong clause to a quality manager is worse than citing none.

How does a canine rodent inspection actually run?

  1. Scope settled before the van leaves

    Which buildings and levels, whether a crawl space is safe to enter, whether a kitchen needs us between services, and who receives the report.

  2. Exterior survey on foot, first

    Perimeter and grade line, slab edge, stoops, garage door corners, utility trenches, refuse enclosure, weep holes, vents, and every line or limb reaching the roof. Burrows and gnaw damage are photographed first.

  3. The dog works the structure

    Handler and dog cover walls, floor junctions, cabinet kicks, chases, mechanical spaces and stored product in a consistent pattern. A tired dog is a useless dog, so we stop short of that, decline conditions too hot for safe work, and will not follow another handler through a freshly scented building.

  4. Every indication confirmed by hand

    Targeted inspection at the point indicated — droppings, urine staining, rub marks, gnawing, nesting material, and where needed a borescope through an existing gap rather than a fresh hole. Early or light activity leaves almost nothing visible, and that scarcity of sign is exactly the case a dog was brought for.

  5. Species called from the evidence

    Dropping size and end profile, height of the sign, runway grease marks, gnaw pattern. That fixes trap layout and the order sealing happens in.

  6. Map, clear, seal, re-screen

    You receive marked-up photographs: each opening that has to be shut, alongside the material and dimension that shuts it. Interior trapping comes down first and envelope sealing follows, in that order, so no live animal is shut into a cavity. The dog then re-screens.

What does a North Augusta canine rodent inspection include?

  • Certified handler and detection dog, working to a repeatable pattern
  • Exterior perimeter, grade line, roofline, vent and utility survey, photographed
  • Interior screening of wall voids, ceiling planes, chases and cabinet runs
  • Crawl space and under-floor assessment where conditions allow entry
  • Hand confirmation of every indication before a recommendation is written
  • Species identification from droppings, runway height and gnaw evidence
  • Entry-point map keyed to mesh, gauge, door-sweep and masonry specifications
  • Harborage and sanitation findings against the 24-hour city refuse standard
  • Dated, photographed findings for an owner, tenant, insurer or auditor
  • Post-remediation re-screening, whether the repairs were ours or not

Who is licensed to do this work on each bank of the river?

The Savannah River is a licensing boundary as well as a state line, and North Augusta sits on the South Carolina side of it.

South Carolina vests licensing in the Department of Pesticide Regulation at Clemson University. A land-grant institution holding that authority, instead of a state agriculture department, surprises nearly everybody who asks. Structural work sits in Category 7A, and a firm must hold a DPR business licence, name a Designated Certified Applicator at each location, and carry general liability of $100,000 combined single limit or better.

In Georgia, which matters the moment a portfolio crosses the bridge into Augusta, the regulator is the Georgia Department of Agriculture, acting through its Structural Pest Division alongside the Structural Pest Control Commission, whose authority comes from O.C.G.A. section 43-45. Household Pest Control is the operative category, and its rule text is unusually exact about scope: mammals fall outside it, apart from commensal rodents and squirrels.

Where do we work in and around North Augusta?

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · 803-226-3155 · Kim@ck9ps.com. We are an Aiken County company working an Aiken County city, which is why same-week scheduling is normal rather than exceptional.

Inside the city we cover the Georgia Avenue and Butler Avenue corridor, Martintown Road, the Five Notch and Knox Avenue side of town, Riverside Village and Hammond’s Ferry, the Crystal Lake area and the greeneway corridor, and the residential belt through Hammond Hills, Pinehurst, Knollwood, Walnut Grove, Butlers Mill, Wando Woodlands, The Summit and The Rapids. Beyond the limits we work Belvedere, Clearwater, Bath, Beech Island, Jackson, Graniteville, Warrenville, Vaucluse and on into Aiken. See every area we serve. Properties here often need more than one line of work, and K-9 bed bug detection in North Augusta covers lodging, apartments and turnover units.

Frequently asked questions

Can the dog work a crawl space, or does somebody have to go under the house?

Both, in that order. A dog can often read a crawl space from the access hatch and the vent line, because odor leaves it continuously. Where the space is dry and safe, handler and dog work it directly. Where it is not, a technician goes under with a light and a camera and works the points indicated.

My house is from the 1950s. Is that a real problem or a sales line?

A real pattern. The 1950s is the largest construction decade here at 17.4 percent of housing units, and the issue is age rather than build quality. Seventy years of plumbing, electrical, gas and HVAC work means seventy years of holes cut through the sill line. A house can be sound and still be open in nine places.

Do I need to empty cabinets or move stored product before you arrive?

Please do not. Clutter is the reason to bring a dog, not an obstacle to it. Pulling a pantry apart scatters odor, disturbs runways and destroys the fresh sign we use to confirm an indication by hand. One thing does help: switch off strong fans nearby.

Will an indication tell me whether it is rats or mice?

Not by itself. The dog reports location and live activity; it does not name species from odor, and anyone claiming otherwise is overstating the method. Species gets called at the confirmation step, from dropping size, the height sign appears at, and gnaw pattern.

Is anything applied during the inspection? We have a cat and a dog.

Nothing is applied. A detection visit is a handler, a dog on lead and a camera, which is the practical argument for leading with detection rather than product. We ask that resident animals be shut in another room, mainly to keep both dogs relaxed and the scent picture clean.

My apartment manager blames the neighbouring unit. Is that plausible?

Frequently yes, and it is testable rather than a matter of opinion. Shared wall cavities, ceiling plenums and plumbing chases connect units, so activity often originates two doors away. With rental vacancy at 12.6 percent citywide, an empty adjoining unit is a strong candidate.

Should I put bait down while I wait for the appointment?

We would rather you did not, and the reason benefits you. Bait sends animals into voids to die, which produces odor with no confirmation and degrades the fresh sign we use to verify what the dog finds. Snap traps in a safe location are fine.

Do you carry out the repairs, or only the finding?

Both, and deliberately separate. Detection produces the map. Rat and mouse control handles trapping, and our repair crew builds exclusion to the mesh and gauge specifications above. Some clients want one contractor; others want the inspection independent of whoever quotes the work.

Why will you not publish an accuracy percentage for this service?

Because we found no structural rodent detection study we would be prepared to defend. Canine detection has solid field validation in bed bug work; rodent detection inside buildings has much less. Borrowing a number from a different application would be dishonest. The reasoning is on our independent detection page.

title: K9 vs. Visual Bed Bug Inspection: Which One Actually Finds the Bugs?
description: A certified detection dog works from scent, so it can find live bed bugs concealed inside furniture, walls, and seams that no visual inspection can reach.
h1: K9 vs. Visual Bed Bug Inspection: Which One Actually Finds the Bugs?
body:
Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions  |  Windsor, SC  |  July 21, 2026

The honest answer is that both methods have a place — but they are not equivalent, and the difference matters most in exactly the situation where it counts: a small, early, hidden infestation. A visual inspection can only find what a person can see, which means it reliably catches heavy, established infestations and routinely misses light ones. A certified detection dog works from scent, so it can find live bed bugs concealed inside furniture, walls, and seams that no visual inspection can reach. If you need to know whether bed bugs are present at all, the dog is the far more sensitive tool.

What can a visual inspection actually find?

A skilled human inspector examines the places bed bugs are known to hide: mattress and box spring seams, bed frames, headboards, nightstands, baseboards, outlet covers, and furniture joints. In a heavy infestation, this works — there will be live bugs, shed skins, dark fecal spotting, and eggs visible in the obvious harborage. A thorough visual inspection of a single room by an experienced person is genuinely useful and can absolutely confirm a bed bug problem when the infestation is established.

The limitation is structural, not a matter of effort: a visual inspection cannot see inside a wall void, deep inside a piece of furniture, or into a crevice too tight to reach. Bed bugs are flat and specifically evolved to occupy exactly those spaces. So when the population is small — which is when you most want to catch it — the bugs may be entirely concealed, and a careful inspector can honestly report finding nothing while an infestation is quietly building.

Where does visual inspection fail most often?

Visual inspection fails most predictably in three situations. The first is an early or light infestation, where only a few bugs are present and all of them are hidden. The second is a large or multi-unit property — a hotel, an apartment building, a healthcare facility — where the sheer volume of rooms makes a thorough manual teardown of every unit impractical, so inspections get rushed and shallow. The third is verifying a treatment, where a small number of survivors can easily evade visual detection for weeks.

There’s also the false-reassurance problem, which is the most costly failure mode. When a visual inspection turns up nothing, people naturally conclude they don’t have bed bugs — but the only thing actually established is that nothing was visible. The infestation continues to grow, spreads to more rooms or units, and becomes dramatically more expensive to eliminate by the time it becomes obvious.

K9 INSIGHT  A negative visual inspection tells you nothing was visible — not that you’re bed bug free. That false reassurance is what lets small infestations grow into expensive ones. When the stakes are high or the evidence is unclear, that’s exactly when a detection dog earns its keep.

What does a detection dog add?

A detection dog changes the problem from “what can we see” to “what can we smell,” which removes the accessibility limitation entirely. The dog detects the odor of live bed bugs and viable eggs escaping from inside walls, seams, and furniture, so concealment doesn’t defeat it. That gives you sensitivity at the early stage where visual inspection is weakest, and it means a negative result from a strong K9 team carries far more weight than a negative visual inspection.

The dog also brings speed and pinpoint location. It can clear a room in minutes and, when it alerts, it identifies exactly where the odor is strongest — which room, which piece of furniture, which corner. That’s what makes targeted treatment possible instead of blanket-treating a whole property, and it’s why K9 inspection scales to hotels and apartment complexes in a way manual inspection simply cannot.

Is a dog inspection more expensive?

A K9 inspection is typically a specialized service with its own cost, but the more useful question is what it saves. Treatment is the expensive part of a bed bug problem — not inspection — and the two biggest ways people waste money are treating rooms that don’t need it and failing to find the rooms that do. Pinpointing exactly where activity is concentrated means treating two units instead of ten, or one bedroom instead of a whole house.

For commercial properties, the math is even more lopsided. The cost of a K9 inspection sweep is small against the cost of an outbreak spreading through a hotel or apartment complex, the cost of unnecessary blanket treatment, the downtime of units out of service, and the reputational damage of a guest or resident bed bug complaint. Catching an infestation early is almost always the cheapest outcome available.

When is a visual inspection enough?

We’ll be straight with you: you don’t always need a dog. If you have an obvious, heavy infestation — live bugs visible on the mattress, clear fecal spotting, shed skins — you don’t need a dog to confirm what’s already plainly in front of you. At that point you need treatment, not detection. A visual inspection is also perfectly adequate for a quick check of a single, uncluttered room where you’re just looking for obvious signs.

K9 detection earns its value when the answer is genuinely uncertain: an early or suspected infestation, unexplained bites with no visible evidence, verifying a treatment, checking many rooms efficiently, or needing documented confidence before making an expensive decision. That’s where the dog does something a person fundamentally cannot.

So which should you choose?

Choose based on the question you’re trying to answer. If the question is “do I have bed bugs and where exactly are they?” — especially when nothing is visibly obvious — a certified detection dog is the more sensitive and more efficient tool, and it will give you a far more trustworthy negative result. If the question is “how bad is this obvious infestation and how do we treat it?” you’re already past detection.

In practice the two methods work best together: the dog finds and pinpoints, and a thorough visual confirmation follows up at the alert location. That’s how we work — the dog identifies the zones, and the findings are documented clearly so you know exactly what you’re dealing with and can treat with confidence rather than guessing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a bed bug dog better than a human inspector?

For finding hidden or early infestations, yes — significantly. A human can only find what’s visible, while a dog detects the odor of live bed bugs concealed inside walls, seams, and furniture. For an obvious, heavy infestation that’s already visible, you don’t need a dog to confirm it; you need treatment.

Why did my visual inspection find nothing when I’m still getting bitten?

Because visual inspection only reveals what’s accessible to the eye, and bed bugs are flat, nocturnal, and evolved to hide in places you can’t see — wall voids, deep furniture joints, tight crevices. A light infestation can be entirely concealed. A negative visual inspection doesn’t rule out bed bugs; a K9 inspection is far more sensitive.

Are K9 bed bug inspections worth the cost?

Usually, because inspection isn’t the expensive part — treatment is. Pinpointing exactly which rooms have live activity means treating one bedroom instead of a whole house, or two units instead of ten. For hotels and apartments, the cost of a K9 sweep is small against an outbreak, unnecessary blanket treatment, and downtime.

Can a dog find bed bugs a person can’t?

Yes. Because the dog works from scent rather than sight, concealment doesn’t defeat it. It detects odor escaping from inside mattress seams, bed frames, furniture joints, baseboards, outlets, and wall voids, which is precisely where early infestations hide from visual inspection.

How fast is a K9 inspection compared to a visual one?

A dog can typically clear a room in minutes, while a thorough manual teardown inspection of the same room takes far longer. That speed advantage is why K9 detection scales to hotels, apartment complexes, and healthcare facilities where many rooms must be checked, and where manual inspection of every unit is impractical.

Can a dog verify that my bed bug treatment worked?

Yes, and it’s one of the strongest uses. Confirming success with visual inspection alone is unreliable, because a few surviving bugs can hide for weeks before the population rebounds. A follow-up K9 inspection gives a much more trustworthy answer about whether the infestation is actually eliminated.

Do you use both methods together?

Yes. In practice they complement each other: the dog detects and pinpoints the zones of live activity, and a focused visual confirmation follows up at the alert location. You get clear documentation of what was found and where, so treatment can be targeted with confidence.

Do you offer K9 bed bug inspections in South Carolina?

Yes. Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions serves Aiken, Columbia, West Columbia, Lexington, Cayce, Irmo, Graniteville, Edgefield, Charleston, Greenville, and surrounding areas, for homes, hotels, apartments, healthcare facilities, and commercial properties. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule an inspection.

Need answers you can trust?

Certified K9 bed bug detection across Aiken, Columbia, and South Carolina — accurate answers and clear documentation, with no upselling.

Call  803-226-3155

Certified K9 teams • Honest recommendations • No scare tactics, no upselling

h1: Media & Press

hero.lead: Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions is a family-owned canine detection and pest management company based in Windsor, South Carolina. Founder Kimberly Camera talks to journalists, podcasters and industry media about scent-detection dogs — what the published research actually supports, and where the honest limits of the work sit.

body:
Most pest control coverage runs into the same wall: everyone in the industry has a claim, and very few of those claims come with a citation. Kim Camera came to this work from an unusual direction — more than 28 years in scent detection, canine work for FEMA Urban Search & Rescue, wildlife tagging, and falconry — and she is comfortable saying on the record when the evidence for something is thin.

That is the reason producers keep calling, and it is the reason this page exists. Below you will find every published appearance, the subjects Kim can speak to in detail, copy-ready biographies at three lengths, and a plain list of the industry claims she will not repeat on air. If you are working to a deadline, the fast-facts table has everything you need to fact-check a mention.

Published appearances

Three pieces are published and publicly available: an article Kim wrote for Pest Control Technology and two interviews. Each is linked to its original host rather than re-hosted here.

Article · Written by Kim

Kim Camera Reflects on ‘the Heart of the Industry’

Pest Control Technology · PCT Magazine · 18 September 2026

In a piece she wrote for PCT, Kim tells the story of Iggy Pop, a puppy who fought through parvo in our kennel, washed out of the working-dog program, and found a home through BASF’s Liz Dunbar and Desiree Straubinger and the volunteers at Greyhounds in Motion. It is a look at how dogs are evaluated for detection work — and at the people in pest control who give their time to causes like rescue.

Read on PCT
Podcast · Episode 13

Beyond the Pest — Kim Camera

Pest Control Technology · PCT Radio Network · 1 July 2026

Mike Thome and Jen Sweeney-Ingram of UPMTC talk with Kim about arriving in pest control after a career in wildlife tagging, falconry and canine work for FEMA Urban Search & Rescue. The conversation covers running detection dogs against heavy rodent populations, and how the family business grew into bed bug detection and nuisance wildlife work across the country.

Listen on PCT Watch on YouTube
Video Episode

Canines to the Rescue

Pest Posse TV

A sit-down on the daily reality of scent work: how a dog is handled through a building, the order the rooms get covered in, and what separates a useful indication from a guess. Kim walks through the process behind a rodent detection or bed bug inspection and the lessons that only come from years of running the same dogs on real jobs.

Watch on Pest Posse TV

What Kim can speak to

These are subjects she works in daily and can discuss with specifics rather than generalities. If your angle is not here, ask anyway — the answer may simply be that it falls outside what she would claim expertise in.

How a detection dog is actually validated

The difference between a dog that has been trained and a team that has been certified and tested to a published standard, and why the distinction matters to a customer.

Bed bug detection in occupied buildings

Screening a room in roughly two minutes, why a visual sweep misses eggs and early activity, and what a handler does when a dog indicates on a wall shared with the next unit.

Where the rodent evidence stops

Structural rodent detection does not have the published field validation that bed bug detection has. Kim will say so on the record rather than quote a number nobody can source.

Exclusion before chemistry

Why sealing a building beats another round of bait, what secondary poisoning does to raptors and pets, and how an exclusion-first programme is priced and sold.

Falconry and bird abatement

What a flown bird genuinely does to a site’s risk profile, what two controlled landfill studies found, and why the effectiveness figures circulating in the trade press do not hold up.

Multi-site and audit-driven programmes

Running canine detection across distribution networks and food plants, and what documentation an auditor is actually looking for.

Disaster and search work

Canine work for FEMA Urban Search & Rescue, and how that training transfers — and does not transfer — to commercial pest detection.

Building a family detection business

Going from a specialised skill to a working company, including the parts that were harder than expected.

The claims Kim will not make on air

This is unusual to publish, and it is deliberate. Several figures circulate freely in pest control marketing that we have not been able to source. If an interviewer offers one of these as a premise, expect it to be corrected rather than accepted.

  • That rodents cause 20 to 25 percent of fires of unknown origin. The figure traces back to an uncited state fact sheet. Neither the NFPA nor the US Fire Administration supports it.
  • That birds carry more than 60 diseases. No agency source exists for that number.
  • That falconry abatement is 95 percent effective, or FAA-approved. Two controlled landfill studies state plainly that birds could not be eliminated, and there is no FAA approval scheme for abatement falconry.
  • That bed bugs survive a year without feeding. That holds below roughly 55°F. At normal indoor temperatures it is closer to one to four months, and pyrethroid-resistant strains die sooner.
  • That brown recluse spiders are common in South Carolina. Forty-four verified specimens statewide between 1953 and 2004, against 738 physician diagnoses in 2004 alone.
  • Any canine accuracy percentage for structural rodent detection. The field studies that exist for bed bug detection have no rodent equivalent.

Biographies, ready to copy

Three lengths, all cleared for publication. Please use the hyphenated company name, Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions, in body copy.

Short — 40 words

Kimberly Camera is the founder of Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions in Windsor, South Carolina. She has spent more than 28 years in scent detection, including canine work for FEMA Urban Search & Rescue, and runs certified detection teams for bed bugs, rodents and wildlife.

Medium — 90 words

Kimberly Camera founded Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions, a family-owned canine detection and pest management company based in Windsor, South Carolina. She came to pest control after more than 28 years in scent detection, including canine work for FEMA Urban Search & Rescue, wildlife tagging and falconry. Her teams hold NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA credentials and work on bed bug and rodent detection locally across the CSRA and Midlands, and nationwide on multi-site commercial programmes. She is a recipient of the NPMA Impact Award.

Long — 200 words

Kimberly Camera is the founder of Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions, a family-owned canine detection and pest management company based in Windsor, South Carolina. She spent more than 28 years in scent detection before entering pest control, including canine work for FEMA Urban Search & Rescue, wildlife tagging, and falconry — a background that shaped how she runs the company today. Her detection teams hold NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA credentials and screen for bed bugs, rodents and nuisance wildlife in homes, hotels, apartment buildings, warehouses, food plants and institutional facilities. Locally the company works across the Central Savannah River Area and the South Carolina Midlands; nationally it runs canine rodent detection programmes for multi-site operators. Camera is a recipient of the NPMA Impact Award. Her public position is that detection is only useful when it is honest: she publishes what the research supports, states where it stops, and corrects industry claims that cannot be sourced — including several that are commercially convenient for her own company. She is available for interviews on canine scent detection, exclusion-first pest management, bird and falconry abatement, and the practical realities of running working dogs as a small business.

Fast facts for producers and editors

Company nameCoastal K-9 & Pest Solutions
SpokespersonKimberly Camera, founder
Headquarters320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, South Carolina 29856
Phone803-226-3155
EmailKim@ck9ps.com

Canine certificationsNESDCA, WDDO, CPDA, ICRWDA
RecognitionRecipient of the NPMA Impact Award. Detail on awards and recognition.

Formats to dateAudio podcast and recorded video interview
Images and b-rollTell us what you need and we will send what we have. Please do not lift images from this site without asking first.
Best contact methodPhone or email. Kim is often in the field, so email with your deadline in the subject line gets the fastest answer.

How to book an interview

  1. Send the angle, not just the ask

    Tell us what the story is actually about and who the audience is. It lets Kim prepare specifics instead of generalities, and it lets us tell you honestly if someone else would serve you better.

  2. Include your deadline

    Put it in the subject line. Field work runs long and a recording window that looks open on Monday may not be open on Wednesday.

  3. Tell us the format and the length

    Audio, video, live or recorded, and roughly how long. If you want a dog on camera, say so early — that is a scheduling and animal-welfare question, not a logistics one.

  4. Send the premise you plan to open with

    If it rests on a statistic, we will check it before recording. That is not an obstacle; it is the reason the interview will hold up afterwards.

A note on filmed demonstrations

We are glad to show the work, and we will not stage it. A detection dog indicates on target odour that is actually present, and a handler who cues a dog to indicate on a clean room is teaching that dog to lie for the rest of its working life. If a filmed demonstration is part of your plan, we will set up a genuine search with a known target so the footage shows a real find. What we will not do is fake an alert for the camera, and any company that agrees to is telling you something about how it works when nobody is filming.

Frequently asked questions

Who should we contact for an interview request?

Kimberly Camera directly, at Kim@ck9ps.com or 803-226-3155. She is the founder and the spokesperson, and there is no press office in between. Email tends to be faster than a call because she is frequently on site with a dog.

Will Kim give an accuracy percentage for detection dogs?

For bed bug detection she will discuss the published field research and what it does and does not establish. For structural rodent detection she will not quote a percentage, because the field validation that exists for bed bug work has no rodent equivalent. Saying so is more useful to your audience than a number nobody can trace.

Can we film a dog working?

Ask, and be prepared for the answer to depend on the dog rather than the schedule. Working dogs have limits on heat, duration and handling by strangers, and those come first. If a shoot is possible we will build a real search with a genuine target rather than pretend for the camera.

What makes this different from any other pest control company?

Two things. The detection work is certified rather than self-declared, and the company publishes the limits of its own methods. The list of claims Kim will not make on air is on this page, and several of those claims would help sell her services if she were willing to repeat them.

Does Coastal K-9 work outside South Carolina?

Yes. Local detection and treatment work runs across the CSRA and the Midlands. Canine rodent detection is offered nationwide, mostly for multi-site commercial operators who need consistent documentation across locations. Details are on the nationwide rodent detection pages.

May we reuse the photographs on this website?

Please ask first. Most images are of the company’s own dogs and handlers and we are usually happy to license them for editorial use, but a few are stock and we cannot pass those on. Tell us the outlet and the context and we will sort out what you can use.

Is Kim willing to be quoted correcting an industry claim?

Yes, and she is used to it. If your reporting has turned up a figure that sounds too clean, send it over. Where we can source it we will say so; where we cannot, she will explain what the evidence actually shows and why the number persists anyway.

What is the correct way to write the company name?

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions, with the hyphen, in body copy. The registered legal string is Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions without it, which is why both spellings appear in different places. Either is defensible; the hyphenated form is preferred in editorial text.

h1: K-9 Bed Bug & Rodent Detection for Multifamily & Property Management

hero.h1: K-9 Bed Bug & Rodent Detection for Multifamily & Property Management
hero.lead: Bed bugs and rodents spread unit to unit — and residents talk. Our detection dogs pinpoint exactly which units are affected so you treat precisely, document everything, and protect the whole community.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Certified K-9 teams · Family-owned · Serving the CSRA & Midlands

body:
For apartment communities, condos, student housing, and rental portfolios, a bed bug or rodent report in a single unit is really a warning about the whole building. Pests do not respect lease lines — they move through shared walls, plumbing chases, and outlets. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions helps property managers across the CSRA and Midlands get ahead of that spread with canine detection that finds exactly which units are affected.

The result is a program that saves money and protects you legally: you treat only the units that actually have activity, you resolve issues before they become a building-wide crisis or a code complaint, and you keep a defensible, unit-by-unit record for lease files, turnover charges, and resident disputes.

Up to 95%Bed bug detection accuracy of trained dogs in controlled studies
¼ inchA gap this small is all a house mouse needs to get inside
500+Eggs one female bed bug can lay, spreading unit to unit

One report is rarely just one unit

Bed bugs and rodents travel. Bed bugs move between units through wall voids, baseboards, and outlet gaps, and they hitch rides on belongings and even maintenance carts. Rodents follow plumbing chases and utility runs from one apartment to the next. Treating only the reported unit almost guarantees a callback, because the source is still active next door.

A detection dog changes the math. It can sweep the reported unit and its neighbors — above, below, and on either side — and confirm where activity actually exists. That mapping means you solve the problem once instead of chasing it for months, and you avoid the expense and resident frustration of treating an entire building blind.

The pests we detect in multifamily housing

Multifamily properties face a specific set of pests that spread between units and generate resident complaints. Our programs target the ones that matter most:

Bed bugs

The most disruptive multifamily pest. We detect live bugs and viable eggs by scent in the reported unit and every adjacent unit, mapping the true extent before you treat.

Rodents (rats & mice)

Travel through shared walls, chases, and common areas. We locate active harborage and pair detection with exclusion to seal entry points for good.

German cockroaches

Spread rapidly through kitchens and shared plumbing between units. We identify harborage so treatment is targeted rather than building-wide.

Occasional invaders

Ants, spiders, and other pests that drive resident complaints in ground-floor and exterior units, handled as part of a full-property program.

The standards and regulations we build your program around

A multifamily pest program has to satisfy housing law, ownership, and residents at the same time. Ours is built around accuracy, consistency, and documentation:

  • Warranty of habitability & housing codes — Landlords are generally responsible for maintaining habitable, pest-free units. Documented detection and prompt treatment show you met that duty.
  • Fair-housing & consistent response — A defined, documented program means every resident and every unit is handled the same way — important for fair and consistent treatment across a community.
  • HUD, NSPIRE & REAC inspections — For subsidized and HUD-assisted properties, pest evidence costs inspection points. Proactive detection and records help you pass and stay compliant.
  • Lease & turnover documentation — Unit-by-unit records support turnover charges, security-deposit decisions, and resident disputes with defensible, professional evidence.

How our multifamily communities K-9 program works

Every multifamily engagement follows a clear, documented workflow so you always know the true scope:

  1. Assess

    We review the complaint, the unit stack, and any history to plan which units to screen — the reported unit plus its neighbors.

  2. Detect

    A certified detection dog screens the reported and adjacent units by scent, clearing each in minutes with minimal resident disruption.

  3. Map the scope

    The handler confirms live activity and maps exactly which units are affected — and, just as importantly, which are not.

  4. Targeted treatment

    Only confirmed units are treated, and rodent findings are paired with exclusion to seal shared-wall and chase entry points.

  5. Verify

    A follow-up canine sweep confirms a unit is clear before you close the ticket or turn it for the next resident.

  6. Document & schedule

    You receive a unit-by-unit record for your files, and we can set recurring turnover and common-area sweeps to keep the community ahead of problems.

What our multifamily communities program includes

  • Complaint-driven inspections of the reported unit and all adjacent units.
  • Move-out & turnover sweeps to confirm a unit is clear before the next lease.
  • Rodent detection & exclusion for shared walls, utility chases, and common areas.
  • Building-wide surveys when you need to establish the true scope.
  • Cockroach & common-invader service for kitchens and ground-floor units.
  • Post-treatment verification to close out a unit with confidence.
  • Resident-friendly scheduling and notice support to minimize disruption.
  • Unit-by-unit documentation for lease files, disputes, and ownership reporting.

Why canine detection outperforms conventional pest control for multifamily communities

Treating a multifamily pest problem the old way is expensive and rarely works the first time. Here is the difference detection makes:

 Conventional exterminatorCoastal K-9 detection
ScopeOften treats whole building blindConfirms exactly which units are affected
CallbacksCommon, because the source is missedRare, because the source is mapped and treated
CostPay to treat every unitPay to treat only affected units
Rodent entry pointsFrequently missedLocated and sealed with exclusion
Resident disruptionRepeated whole-building treatmentsQuiet, targeted, unit-by-unit
DocumentationMinimalUnit-by-unit record for disputes

Documentation that protects you

Every inspection produces a unit-by-unit record: what was screened, what was found, what was treated, and what was verified clear. In multifamily, that documentation is worth as much as the treatment itself.

It protects you in tenant disputes and turnover-charge questions, supports security-deposit decisions, satisfies ownership and HUD reporting, and demonstrates a consistent, proactive program — the professional paper trail a reactive spray service cannot provide.

Signs a unit — or a building — needs a sweep

Screen early. A single detection sweep is far cheaper than a building-wide infestation. Watch for:

  • Resident bite reports — itchy welts in lines or clusters appearing overnight.
  • Blood or rust spots and shed skins in mattress seams, headboards, and baseboards.
  • Droppings or gnaw marks in units, cabinets, or common areas.
  • Scratching or scurrying sounds in shared walls or ceilings at night.
  • Repeat complaints in the same stack of stacked or adjacent units.
  • Turnover — every move-out is a chance to catch a problem before the next resident inherits it.

Serving multifamily communities across the CSRA & Midlands

Coastal K-9 serves apartment communities, condominiums, HOAs, student and workforce housing, and single-family rental portfolios across the CSRA and Midlands — Aiken, Augusta, North Augusta, Evans, Martinez, Grovetown, Columbia, Lexington, and Irmo, along the I-20 and I-26 corridors.

As a local, family-owned company, we offer same-week response for active resident complaints and can build a recurring turnover-and-common-area program sized to your portfolio, whether you manage one community or many.

Why CSRA property managers choose Coastal K-9

Property managers across the region choose Coastal K-9 because unit-by-unit detection is simply better business: you treat only what is affected, resolve problems before they escalate to a code complaint or a review, and hold a defensible record for every unit. Our founder is FEMA-trained and NESDCA-certified, and every inspection is detection-first.

We are local and responsive — not a national call center — and we understand that in multifamily, a fast, quiet, well-documented response protects both your residents and your bottom line.

Frequently asked questions

A resident reported bed bugs — do you have to inspect the whole building?

Not necessarily. We inspect the reported unit and its immediate neighbors first, since that is where bed bugs spread. That confirms the true scope so you treat only what is affected instead of the entire building.

Can you inspect units between tenants?

Yes. Move-out and turnover sweeps are one of the most valuable uses of detection — confirming a unit is clear before the next resident moves in prevents inherited problems and disputes.

Do you handle rodents too, not just bed bugs?

Yes. Multifamily buildings are prone to rodents traveling through shared walls and utility chases. We detect active harborage and pair it with exclusion to seal entry points for good.

Will inspections disturb my residents?

Minimal disruption. A detection dog works a unit in minutes, the process is chemical-free, and we schedule around residents with proper notice.

Do you provide documentation for disputes and turnover charges?

Yes. You receive a unit-by-unit record of every inspection, which is invaluable for lease files, turnover charges, security-deposit decisions, and resident disputes.

How much does multifamily pest detection cost?

It depends on the number of units and how often you schedule, but detection-first is almost always cheaper than treating a whole building blind and dealing with callbacks. Call 803-226-3155 for a portfolio quote.

Who is responsible for bed bugs, the landlord or the tenant?

Responsibility varies by lease and local law, but landlords generally must maintain habitable units. A documented detection-and-treatment record protects you either way by showing a prompt, professional response.

How accurate are the detection dogs?

In controlled studies, trained bed bug dogs have detected live bugs with accuracy as high as 95% — far better than a visual-only inspection across many units.

Can bed bugs spread through walls between apartments?

Yes. They travel through wall voids, outlet gaps, and shared baseboards, which is exactly why we always screen the units adjacent to any confirmed report.

Do you treat, or only detect?

Both. We detect to pinpoint the problem, then provide targeted treatment and, for rodents, exclusion — and we verify the unit is clear afterward.

How quickly can you respond to a complaint?

We offer same-week response across the CSRA and prioritize active resident complaints so a unit can be confirmed or cleared quickly.

What areas do you serve?

Apartment communities and rental portfolios across Aiken, Augusta, North Augusta, Columbia, Lexington, Evans, Martinez, and the greater CSRA and Midlands.

Related commercial programs

Hotels & HospitalityHealthcare & Senior LivingSchools & Student HousingAll Commercial Programs

Solve it by the unit, not the building.

Schedule unit-by-unit K-9 detection for your community across the CSRA and Midlands.

Call 803-226-3155Request an Inspection

h1: Nationwide K9 Rodent Detection for Commercial Facilities

hero.h1: Nationwide K9 Rodent Detection for Commercial Facilities

body:
Nationwide · Commercial & Industrial

Certified detection dogs locate active rodent harborage and burrow systems that device maps, trend reports, and visual inspection cannot find — deployed nationwide for food processing, agriculture, warehousing, and multi-site operators.

Request a Site AssessmentCall 803-226-3155

What is K9 rodent detection?

K9 rodent detection uses certified scent-detection dogs to locate live rodent activity, nesting harborage, and burrow systems inside and around a commercial facility. Unlike bait stations and traps — which record rodents only after they are caught — a detection dog identifies where rodents are actively living, including concealed voids, plugged burrow entrances, and harborage behind product or equipment. For facilities under GFSI or AIB audit, that turns a reactive monitoring program into a targeted corrective action.

Your trend report is a record of what you caught. It is not a map of what you have.

If you manage pest control in a regulated facility, you already run the program the standards ask for: a site-specific risk assessment, a numbered device map that reconciles to the floor, weekly interior checks, exterior stations on schedule, and twelve months of trended logs with corrective actions closed out.

That program is built to answer one question: did we catch anything? It is not built to answer the question your auditor asks when the trend line ticks up: where are they coming from?

A device map records captures. It cannot tell you there is an established Norway rat burrow system forty feet off the receiving dock with three concealed bolt holes under a pallet stack. It cannot tell you which of the eleven burrow openings along your fence line are active. It cannot tell you the “occasional activity” in your dry-goods area traces back to a wall void nobody has opened since the building went up. That is what a detection dog does — it works the scent of live rodents and active harborage, not the aftermath.

Why bait and gas treatments fail on established burrow systems

A completed Norway rat burrow typically has a primary entrance plus one or two escape holes — “bolt holes” — often hidden under vegetation or debris and lightly plugged with soil from the inside. They are built to be invisible.

If you bait or gas the entrance you can see and the system has two openings you cannot, the colony relocates through an exit you never found and re-establishes twenty feet away. The treatment worked. The mapping didn’t. Detection dogs work the scent, not the visible opening — and mapping the full system before treatment is the difference between eliminating a colony and chasing it around your property for two years.

What we do on site

  1. Pre-deployment review. Before we arrive we review your device map, the last twelve months of trend data, any open corrective actions, and your audit scheme — looking for the gap between where your program says activity is and where it is likely originating.
  2. Canine sweep. Our teams work the interior and exterior perimeter systematically — production and non-production areas, storage, voids, utility penetrations, exterior grade, and the full property line. The dog covers ground and volume a technician with a flashlight cannot, and works product-dense and equipment-dense areas where visual inspection is effectively blind.
  3. Confirmation and mapping. Every canine alert is confirmed by the handler and documented — location, evidence found, photographs, and where it sits relative to your existing device map. Alerts that cannot be confirmed are logged as unconfirmed, not counted as findings.
  4. Findings report. You receive a written report structured for your auditor: numbered findings tied to facility locations, photographic evidence, a distinction between active and inactive harborage, and recommended corrective actions in priority order — with a firm turnaround we commit to during the pre-deployment review.
  5. Treatment and coordination. Where you want us to act on what we find, we deliver full detection-through-treatment — self-performed in states where we hold licensure, and coordinated with your licensed provider or our vetted local partners on multi-state and larger programs. Prefer to keep treatment with your current vendor? We also deliver detection and documentation only.
  6. Verification sweep. After corrective action we return and re-run the sweep, giving you documented evidence the finding was closed — which is what the auditor wants and what a service log alone cannot demonstrate.

Where we deploy

We serve commercial clients across the United States and currently support more than 15 companies nationally with large-scale rodent detection and mitigation, including complex Norway rat burrow systems that conventional programs have not resolved. Our specialization is facilities where rodent pressure is constant, documentation is non-negotiable, and precision matters more than volume:

K9 rodent detection for food processing plants — built around SQF, BRCGS, FSSC 22000 and AIB requirements, where a single major non-conformance in the pest section can cost a certification grade and the retail contracts behind it.

Agricultural and grain facility detection — bulk product, structural voids, and constant ingress make grain storage, feed mills, and ag operations among the hardest environments to inspect visually.

Norway rat burrow detection and mitigation — mapping full burrow systems, including concealed bolt holes, before any treatment is applied.

Multi-site detection programs — one methodology and one reporting standard across every location in a portfolio, so results are comparable site to site.

In New York City and Long Island, our detection work runs alongside Graduate Pest Control, a second-generation firm founded in 1983 with an entomologist on staff. Kim trained Hugo and Mia, the detection dogs on Graduate’s canine program, and the two teams work accounts together.

Why the handler matters more than the dog

Published research on scent-detection dogs shows a wide gap between controlled and field conditions. In University of Florida research, trained dogs indicated correctly at very high rates under controlled conditions; later field studies of multiple teams working real infestations found substantially more variation. That gap is not about the dogs — it is about handler skill, blind-testing discipline, and whether a team maintains certification or lets it lapse.

Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions is led by founder Kimberly Camera, who came out of FEMA Urban Search & Rescue canine work and has spent 28+ years in scent detection. Our teams hold certification through NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA and train continuously to maintain it. When you are putting a detection finding into an audit file, the credential behind it is the finding’s defensibility.

Detection you can defend. See the research behind canine scent detection and how we verify every alert on our detection accuracy page.

Your vendor manages a monitoring and control program — devices, service intervals, logs, trending. That tells you what has been caught. We locate where rodents are actively living. The two are complementary, and we work alongside existing vendors regularly.

title: Grain & Ag Rodent Detection
description: Certified detection dogs locate rodent harborage across grain storage, feed mills and agricultural facilities where bait stations alone never finish.
h1: K9 Rodent Detection for Agricultural & Grain Operations

hero.h1: K9 Rodent Detection for Agricultural & Grain Operations

body:
Nationwide · Agriculture, Grain & Feed

Bulk product, structural voids, and constant ingress make grain storage, feed mills, and agricultural facilities among the hardest environments in the industry to inspect visually.

Call 803-226-3155Nationwide rodent detection

Why is rodent control so difficult in grain and feed facilities?

Because the product is the food source, the harborage, and the visual obstruction simultaneously. Bulk grain, feed, and stored commodities give rodents unlimited food and unlimited cover in the same space, while conveyors, legs, pits, and elevator structures create voids that cannot be inspected. Add continuous truck and rail ingress and seasonal pressure from surrounding fields, and monitoring devices around the perimeter of a space cannot tell you what is living inside it.

What makes these facilities different

In a food plant, product is contained and rodents are looking for a way to it. In a grain operation, they are already in it. Three conditions compound:

Unlimited harborage inside the commodity.

Rodents nest in bulk product. Devices placed around the room monitor traffic; they do not detect a population living inside the pile.

Structural voids by design.

Boot pits, elevator legs, conveyor housings, tunnel systems, and headhouse structures are impossible to visually inspect at any meaningful depth and are precisely where established populations settle.

Seasonal exterior pressure.

Harvest and cold weather drive migration off surrounding ground. A perimeter that holds in July fails in October, and burrow systems establish along foundations, pads, and bin bases.

Where FSMA fits

Facilities under FDA and FSMA preventive controls, and those audited against GFSI schemes or AIB standards, carry the same documentation burden as any food manufacturer — risk assessment, device mapping, activity records, trending, and corrective actions with demonstrated closure. Rodent contamination remains a leading driver of FDA enforcement action in stored-commodity settings. Our findings reports are structured to drop into that documentation set; see audit-ready documentation and verification for report structure.

Devices count traffic. They do not find populations.

A monitoring network measures rodents moving through the spaces where devices sit. In an environment where the commodity itself is both food and shelter, a substantial population can live and breed without ever crossing a device in meaningful numbers.

This is why grain facilities so often see a modest, stable capture trend alongside recurring contamination and gnaw damage. The trend is not wrong — it is just measuring the wrong thing. A detection sweep searches the harborage directly.

How we work a grain operation

  1. Exterior and bin-pad survey. Foundations, bin bases, equipment slabs, rail and truck approaches, and grounds — prime Norway rat burrow locations, worked before harvest intake and ahead of the first cold snap.
  2. Interior and structural voids. Boot pits, elevator legs, conveyor housings, tunnels, and headhouse structures — the voids where established populations settle and visual inspection cannot reach.
  3. Commodity odor mapping. The dog works live rodent odor emanating from the commodity and surrounding structure, showing where the population is concentrated so remediation is targeted rather than facility-wide.
  4. Confirmation and documentation. Every alert handler-confirmed, photographed, and located, with combustible-dust and confined-space protocols coordinated in advance.
  5. Findings report and verification. An auditor-ready report that drops into your FSMA and GFSI documentation, followed by a verification sweep after remediation.

Frequently asked questions

Can a dog work around bulk grain and dust?

Yes. Detection dogs work in dusty, odor-heavy environments routinely. We coordinate on dust levels, combustible dust protocols, and confined-space restrictions before arrival, and we schedule around loading and unloading where required.

Can you detect rodents living inside a grain pile?

We detect live rodent odor emanating from the commodity and surrounding structure. That tells you where the population is concentrated so remediation is targeted, rather than treating the whole facility uniformly.

When is the best time to schedule?

Before harvest intake and again ahead of the first cold snap. Those are the two windows where exterior populations move and where finding established harborage early prevents it from being sealed inside with the commodity.

Do you handle burrow systems around bins and pads?

Yes — that is one of our core capabilities. Bin pads, foundations, and equipment slabs are prime Norway rat burrow locations. See our Norway rat burrow detection and mitigation page.

Do you work with our current provider, or replace them?

Either. Most of our agricultural work is detection and documentation delivered to the operator and their existing provider, but where you want treatment closed out we self-perform where licensed or coordinate with vetted local partners.

title: Audit-Ready Rodent Records
description: Device maps, service records, trend analysis and corrective actions — the rodent documentation package a third-party auditor actually asks to see.
h1: Audit-Ready Documentation & Verification
body:
Nationwide · Compliance & Verification

Findings mapped, dated, photographed, and tied to corrective actions you can defend standing on the floor next to the auditor.

Call 803-226-3155Nationwide rodent detection

What documentation do auditors expect from a pest program?

At minimum: a site-specific pest risk assessment, a numbered device map matching physical placement, twelve months of service and activity records, trend analysis, corrective action records with evidence of closure, applicator licensing and product documentation, and proof the program is reviewed and adjusted. Auditors are assessing the system behind the service, not just whether logs are filled in. Untracked paper logs and verbal walk-throughs generate findings because they cannot demonstrate the program is managed on a defensible schedule.

Why most corrective actions close weakly

A corrective action has three parts an auditor cares about: what caused it, what you did, and how you know it worked.

Most pest corrective actions are strong on the middle part and thin on the other two. “Increased service frequency and added four devices” documents an action. It does not establish root cause, and it does not demonstrate the condition was actually eliminated. The next audit cycle re-opens the same finding.

Detection produces evidence for the two weak parts. A canine sweep locating an active wall void establishes root cause with photographic support. A post-remediation verification sweep documents that the void is no longer active. Between them, the corrective action closes on evidence rather than assertion.

“No activity recorded” and “no activity present” are different claims

Your trend data supports the first. Only a search supports the second.

That distinction is exactly what an auditor is probing when they ask how you know a condition was resolved. A verification sweep lets you answer with a documented search rather than the absence of a capture — which is the difference between a closed finding and a repeat finding.

What our reports contain

  1. Numbered findings tied to named facility locations and cross-referenced to your existing device map.
  2. Photographic evidence at each finding, dated and location-tagged.
  3. Active-versus-inactive classification, so treatment scope is defensible.
  4. Handler confirmation status — confirmed findings and unconfirmed alerts are recorded separately and never merged.
  5. Prioritized corrective-action recommendations, sequenced by risk.
  6. Team credentials — certifying bodies and current certification status, so the finding’s provenance is documented.
  7. Verification sweep results where a follow-up has been performed, delivered in a format you can attach directly to your food safety management system without reformatting.

Frequently asked questions

Will an auditor accept a third-party canine detection report?

Auditors accept documented evidence from qualified parties. What makes a report credible is the same thing that makes any record credible: a named, credentialed inspector, dated findings, location specificity, photographic support, and a clear methodology. Our reports carry all of that, including certification status for the team that performed the work. Ask any vendor for a sample report before engaging.

Can you work to our existing document control format?

In most cases yes. Tell us your template and numbering conventions during the pre-deployment review.

Do you provide documentation for insurance or litigation?

We provide factual inspection reports. What they are used for afterward is your call. Tell us in advance if a report may be used in a legal or claims context so it is scoped and worded appropriately from the start.

How long should we retain detection reports?

Follow your scheme’s retention requirement for pest records — twelve months of service history is a common floor, and most facilities retain longer. Treat detection reports as part of the pest file, not as separate correspondence.
