body:
Beech Island is not a town and it is not an island. The Census Bureau first drew it as a place in 2020, counting 1,421 residents across 4.9 square miles — about 321 per square mile, the thinnest spread of the Aiken County communities we serve. The name is a worn-down Beech Highland, which describes the ground: high land above the Savannah River bottom.

What makes it unusual for our trade is the mix. Inside those few square miles sit a very large manufacturing and distribution operation, a natural gas generating station, five National Register properties, an agricultural club meeting monthly since 1856, and farm ground that grew cotton, corn and soybeans long before the industry came. A programme built for one half is wrong for the other.

1.1M sq ftAnnounced addition at the plant at 246 Old Jackson Highway, inside an expansion of over $200 million, operating from the second quarter of 2027 (Office of the Governor of South Carolina, May 2025)
138,479 acresLand in farms across Aiken COUNTY, in 1,132 farms, led by forage at 14,447 acres and cotton at 8,093 (2022 Census of Agriculture). A county figure, not a local one
42%Share of Aiken COUNTY housing units older than forty years (SRSCRO Regional Housing Study for the Aiken–Augusta area, September 2025, page 14). No reliable town-level figure exists and we will not estimate one

What does general pest control cover out here, and what do we not sell?

Our general pest control programme is ants, cockroaches, spiders, silverfish, occasional invaders and the exclusion that stops the repeat. Three specialisms sit alongside it: rodent detection, trapping and sealing; bed bug detection and treatment; and cockroach work split by species.

Now the part most companies leave vague. Termite work is not on our list, nor CL-100 reports, nor bonds, nor mosquito or lawn programmes. Where a crawl space shows what reads as wood-destroying insect damage, we photograph it and say so. Pointing at something is not offering to treat it.

Why does one unincorporated community carry two separate pest problems?

Because two land uses sit side by side with no transition, and each generates a different animal.

The industrial side. Kimberly-Clark’s facility at 246 Old Jackson Highway opened in 1968 and is described by the Governor’s office as the company’s largest manufacturing plant in the world; the 2025 announcement adds over 1.1 million square feet and more than 150 jobs, bringing manufacturing and distribution, in the state’s phrase, under one automated roof. The Dominion Energy natural gas plant at Urquhart Station is here too.

Read that as a technician. Industry at that format means dock doors open for hours, trailers against seals that do not quite meet, palletised packaging stacked to walls, and a building that never fully goes dark. Around it sits a haulage and supplier economy of smaller yards and warehouses, and those are the buildings that phone us. None of this says we hold that contract. We do not, and naming a plant is not naming a client.

The farm side. Aiken County still reports 1,132 farms across 138,479 acres, with about 9,085 cattle and 5,610 horses. The institution for that history is the Beech Island Agricultural Club, organised on 5 January 1856 by Governor James H. Hammond and eleven other farmers for what the state marker calls the diffusion of agricultural knowledge; monthly meetings and barbecues have been held almost without interruption since. A club keeping a monthly calendar for a century and three-quarters is not a museum exhibit. It is evidence that this is still farmed country.

Farm ground produces a different animal. Cutting and harvest push rodents toward the nearest structure, and feed rooms, tack rooms and equipment barns hold grain, seed and nesting material with nobody in them for days. Warehouse work is the envelope and the dock line. Farm work is outbuildings first, house second.

How does dock rodent pressure differ from a farmhouse call?

The species overlap. Almost nothing else does, which is why one price list for both would be dishonest.

Warehouse and light industrialFarmstead and rural residential
What pulls them inStanding product, cardboard and pallet voids, compactors, floor drains, warmthStored feed, spilled grain, animal bowls, brush and equipment piles
Where sign turns upWall-to-floor junctions behind racking, atop stacked loads, along conduit, inside pallet stringersRafters and lofts, feed bin lids, shed insulation, under stoops and slab edges
What changes in our workMapped stations, numbered device list, sealing sequenced around production, written findings each visitOutbuildings screened first, house second, indoor trapping, non-target risk assessed first
Where it is written upWarehouse and distribution, or food processingRodent detection and control

Three commensal species, three different jobs — which one is in your building?

The animal is rarely seen, so naming it is forensic work. Name the wrong one and every trap goes to the wrong height.

Norway rat

The ground-plane animal, and usually what a dock or a farm has. Its droppings reach three-quarters of an inch and the ends are squared off rather than pointed. It digs, so look for open holes at slab edges, under stoops and at the base of feed bins. New objects genuinely worry it, and a trap set overnight can be walked around for days. See the Norway rat profile.

Roof rat

The climber. Droppings about half an inch, tapered, and the sign sits high — rafters, top plates, ductwork, the tops of stacked loads. On rural lots the route in is vegetation: an untrimmed limb, a fence line, a vine on a gable. Seal the ground, ignore the roofline, and you have solved nothing.

House mouse

Rice-grain droppings around a quarter inch, scattered rather than piled. It needs no free water, which is why a dry barn loft suits it. Its whole home range can be ten to thirty feet across, so sign clusters tightly and traps go close together and in numbers. See the house mouse profile.

Two cautions. Ceiling noise proves an animal, not a rodent; cavity-nesting squirrels get reported as rats constantly. And a dog reports where live activity is, never which species — that gets called by hand, from dropping size, the height of the sign, rub marks and gnaw pattern.

Why is rodenticide the wrong opening move around farms, dogs and barn cats?

Two reasons, and the first is the one that matters on a property with animals on it.

Anticoagulant baits do not kill quickly. A rodent that has fed goes slow and disoriented for days before it dies, which makes it the easiest prey on the place, and whatever eats it takes a share of the dose. That is secondary poisoning, and the literature is not ambiguous about it. Cornell researchers writing in Ecotoxicology in 2022 screened 72 New York red-tailed hawks and recovered anticoagulant residue from 68 percent of them; a USGS survey put 48 percent of 40 Pacific Northwest barred owls positive for at least one compound. Neither is a Southeastern dataset, none turned up when we looked, and we will not imply a local figure. The mechanism travels even where the data does not. Barn cats, working dogs and the hawks hunting your field edges are all on the receiving end.

The second reason is practical. A baited animal dies inside a wall cavity or deep in a hay stack, which buys you two weeks of smell and no evidence at all. None of that makes rodenticide illegitimate. A licensed applicator puts it outside, in secured housings, each one numbered against a site plan, and only after the envelope has been read.

German or American cockroach, and why does that answer change the job?

Because one is a delivery problem and the other a drainage problem, and treating either like the other wastes a season.

German cockroach

Half to five-eighths of an inch, tan, two dark stripes running back from the head on nymphs and adults alike. The University of Georgia puts it in the obligate indoor category, never to rarely recorded outdoors. It does not walk in from a field. It is carried in — cardboard, delivery cartons, used appliances, bags moved between kitchens — and where this much palletised carton stock moves, that vector is not academic. The female carries a case of thirty to forty eggs for about two weeks, which is why they survive most contact sprays. See the German cockroach profile.

American cockroach

Reddish-brown, running from an inch and a half up to two, with a pale band edging the shield behind its head. It lives in sewers, storm drains, crawl spaces and mulch beds, and is commoner in commercial buildings than houses. LSU AgCenter notes it passes three-millimetre openings and that older buildings with degraded seals are especially open to it. Find these at two in the morning by a floor drain and the work is drains, grease interceptors, sump lids and mulch depth.

Chemistry alone has a poor record against the first: published work found total-release foggers essentially ineffective against resistant German cockroach populations. Assessing the population beats the label on the can. Both species sit under cockroach control.

What does a canine bed bug screen answer that a walk-through does not?

It answers the question eyesight is worst at: is there anything here at all, in a room where nothing is visible yet.

The published figures are unflattering. Across 2,372 apartments in 43 buildings, brief visual inspection caught 72 percent of infestations against 89 percent for interceptor monitors left down, and about 49 percent of those found sat in units where the resident had no idea. An infestation nobody notices is one still spreading.

Locally that matters for turnover and travel. Rural properties with rental cottages, farm-labour housing and short-let rooms see a trickle of luggage rather than a hotel’s flood, and the early low-level case is what a walk-through misses. A dog covers a room or a row of units at walking pace, reading odor from seams nobody can open, and gives a location rather than a count. We publish no accuracy percentage for our own work, because presenting a laboratory number as a field result would be dishonest. Treatment follows under bed bug control.

What does exclusion look like with a tape measure in hand?

Sealing is the only part of this work still paying after we drive away, and it gets specified in fractions of an inch, not adjectives.

  • The two numbers: a quarter inch is the mouse threshold, half an inch the rat threshold, and anything at or above those closes. In coins: a dime passes a mouse, a quarter passes a rat.
  • Crawl space vents: residential code section R408.2 caps the covering’s least dimension at a quarter inch and lists what satisfies it — perforated sheet metal at 0.070 inches and up, expanded metal at 0.047 and up, hardware cloth once the wire reaches 0.035. A rusted vent is a code defect and an entrance in one.
  • Mesh: for rats, hardware cloth at half-inch openings in 19 gauge; for mice, drop the opening to a quarter inch and the wire to 24. Buy woven — cheap welded mesh fails at the joints.
  • Barn and shed doors: the usual failure is a door dropped on its hinges that no longer meets the jamb. A 24-gauge kick plate along the lower eighteen inches, plus a threshold that actually contacts, fixes more rural rodent problems than any product does.
  • Dock doors and levelers: the corners of a sectional door and the pit beneath a leveler stay open all day. Check both with a torch from inside, door down.
  • Digging at a footing: a curtain wall thirty-six inches below grade, an L-footing returning twelve inches outward, or a two-foot gravel band. Shallower is a delay, not a barrier.
  • Feed and seed: metal bins with latching lids, nothing in paper sacks on a floor, and an eighteen-inch inspection lane along the wall so sign shows before it is a population.

Carpentry sits with our exclusion and repair work, kept separate from inspection so nobody diagnoses a problem they also quote to build.

What documentation does a commercial account here actually get?

Rural industrial sites get audited to the same standards as urban ones, and auditors want paper, not reassurance.

  • A site drawing with every exterior station and interior device numbered and placed
  • A dated record per visit: what was inspected, found and done
  • Photographs of each opening recommended for sealing, with the material and dimension that closes it
  • Product records: material, concentration, location, target pest, method, applicator

What we will not do is quote a food-safety clause number at you. Schemes revise their codes, and citing the wrong one to a quality manager is worse than citing none. Tell us which scheme holds you and we write the record to satisfy whoever is asking. Structure is on the commercial pest control page.

Who is licensed to work each bank of the Savannah River?

The river below Beech Island is a state line, and the far bank is Georgia. That matters more than people expect, because the two states put pest licensing in completely different places.

South Carolina vests it in the Department of Pesticide Regulation at Clemson University, not a state agriculture department, which surprises nearly everyone who asks. Structural work is Category 7A, defined to cover industrial, institutional, structural and health-related pest control. Holding it means a DPR business licence, a Designated Certified Applicator based at the location, and evidence of financial responsibility on file. Small animal work is a separate category, 12C.

Georgia, across the water, runs through the Department of Agriculture’s Structural Pest Division with the Structural Pest Control Commission, under O.C.G.A. section 43-45. Its Household Pest Control category is unusually precise: it covers pests entering, nesting in or invading structures, and excludes mammals apart from commensal rodents and squirrels. Buildings on both banks need two credentials, not one.

Where do we work around Beech Island?

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · 803-226-3155 · Kim@ck9ps.com. An Aiken County firm. Its founder, Kimberly Camera, has twenty-eight years behind her in scent detection, including canine deployment with FEMA Urban Search & Rescue.

Locally we cover the Old Jackson Highway corridor, Williston Road on U.S. 278 past Spann Hammond Road, Redcliffe Road and the Double Springs Road side. Redcliffe Plantation State Historic Site occupies 369 acres at 181 Redcliffe Road, one of five National Register listings here with Fort Moore–Savano Town Site, The Cedars, Zubly Cemetery and Oakland Plantation. Buildings of that age are their own category of work: mortised sills, outbuildings, openings cut before anyone specified a mesh size.

Beyond here we work Jackson to the south, North Augusta upriver, and Windsor, where we are based. See every area we cover, or tell us what the building is doing and we will say whether it is our work or somebody else’s.

Frequently asked questions

We have barn cats and two working dogs. Can you treat without putting them at risk?

Yes, and it changes the sequence rather than the outcome. Trapping goes indoors where animals cannot reach it, exterior bait if used at all goes in locked tamper-resistant housings, and the durable result comes from sealing. We ask where every animal sleeps, feeds and hunts before anything is placed.

Does being unincorporated change anything for a business here?

It removes a layer rather than adding one. No town council, no municipal pest ordinance, no city inspection regime — county and state requirements are what apply. For a commercial account the effect is that your documentation gets written for your own auditor or insurer.

Rodents appear in the barn every autumn after harvest. Is that inevitable?

The pressure is. The entry is not. Cutting and harvest displace rodents toward whatever structure stands closest, and what decides whether they settle is latched metal feed bins, doors that close square, and a clear inspection lane along the walls.

Can a detection dog work around stacked pallets and stored product?

That is the situation it is best in. Odor keeps leaving a stack whether or not anyone can see into it. Please do not tidy or shift stock beforehand: moving product scatters odor and destroys the fresh sign we use to confirm by hand.

Do you handle termites, or a CL-100 for a sale?

Neither one. Termite treatment, wood infestation reports and bonds all sit outside what we sell, so a closing needs a firm certified for that document. If other work takes us into your crawl space and we see damage or a moisture condition, we photograph it for the right contractor.

Is a house on high ground safer than one down toward the river?

Different, not safer. High ground drains fast through sandy soil, which suits burrowing rats and keeps their burrows serviceable year-round. The lower, poorly drained pockets hold moisture, which favours American cockroaches. Elevation shifts which problem you get rather than removing one.

Two kinds of building, one phone number

A dock door that never quite seals, or a feed room filling with droppings — the first step is the same. Somebody who knows the difference walks the property and writes down what is there. Serving Beech Island from Windsor, South Carolina.

Roughly one home in three in this town is standing empty. Read that as a line in a demographic table and you will misread every pest problem here.

An unoccupied structure is four things at once: unheated, unmaintained, undisturbed and unwatched. What each of those favors does not stay put.

30.7%Of housing units here stand vacant, the highest share on our outlying list; Barnwell County runs 18.2 percent (ACS five-year, DP04)
294Manufactured homes, 28.0 percent of all units and the largest town share we work with; the county runs 32.8 percent (ACS five-year, B25024)
±190Margin of error on the 1,051-unit housing estimate, so county figures carry anything load-bearing here (Census Reporter)

What is on the list here, and what is not?

  • Ants, both outdoor nests foraging in and colonies already inside a wall
  • Cockroaches, German and American. See cockroach control
  • Spiders and occasional invaders — silverfish, crickets, ground beetles
  • Rodents — canine detection, trapping, and the carpentry that decides whether they return. See rodent control
  • Bed bugs, screened by a certified detection dog. See bed bug control
  • Sealing work — skirting, vents, sweeps, floor penetrations, belly repair. See exclusion and repairs

The boundary matters as much as the list. No termite treatment, no CL-100 letters, no fumigation, no mosquito or lawn work. The rest sits under general pest control.

What does a thirty percent vacancy rate do to the house you live in?

It parks a permanent supply beside a temporary solution.

Nobody heats an empty building, so the inside tracks the weather instead of fighting it. Nobody runs a tap, so P-traps dry and the drain line opens into the room. Nobody replaces a fallen skirting panel. And nobody walks through, the part people underestimate: rodents and roaches expand hard without disturbance, and a building no one enters holds numbers an occupied house never reaches.

That structure then behaves as a source. A house mouse may never leave the building it was born in. A Norway rat covers a hundred feet or more of ditch bank and fence line for food, and American cockroaches shift along the ground whenever weather pushes them. Your bin sits inside that radius.

So, honestly: treating your home alone will not hold while the property next door produces animals faster than we remove them. What exclusion buys is that your house stops being the easiest destination on the block.

What can you honestly do about a building you do not own?

Not treat it. We work a property only with its owner’s authorization. Where one owner holds both parcels the empty one can be serviced too, and that is the version that gets solved. Otherwise the work sits on your side.

  1. Close your own envelope

    Every opening measured rather than eyeballed. It is the only part of this under your control, and the part that moves the outcome most.

  2. Strip the approach and the reward

    Shrubs off the wall, firewood off the ground, grass cut at the fence line, pet food in overnight, bins latched. Rodents travel under cover and hesitate at open ground.

  3. Monitor at the boundary

    Non-toxic monitors facing the vacant property show which way pressure runs while everything is still outside. The unsecured structure itself is a matter for the town, not us.

Why does bait alone stop working where the source never stops?

Bait is a subtraction. It removes individuals well and cannot close the route they came by. Run rodent stations along a boundary with a continuously producing property behind it and you have built a feeding station: consumption stays high month after month, which reads as control and is really an uninterrupted supply. Gel bait for German cockroaches has the same ceiling. So the order is exclusion, then reduction, then monitoring: chemistry lasts weeks, mesh over a vent lasts years.

What makes a manufactured home a different building to work?

Twenty-eight percent of the housing here is manufactured. These are ordinary homes, no harder to keep clear than any other, but built to a different logic, and a site-built checklist walks past the five places that decide the job.

Skirting is a fence, not a wall

Skirting closes the gap between chassis and ground, but it is a light panel in a track. Panels pop at a corner, take a knock from a mower, or stand clear of uneven ground. The federal installation standard wants the space below ventilated, so openings belong there by design; molded louver inserts stop nothing. We back each with quarter-inch hardware cloth and trench the bottom edge.

The bottom board is the real floor

Under the joists runs the belly wrap: a poly membrane holding insulation up and moisture out, and the only continuous barrier between ground and floor cavity. Rodents open it; so do crews who slit it for plumbing access and never patch it. Torn, it sags, holds damp and turns into nesting material a foot below the carpet.

The marriage line on a double-wide

Two halves joined on site meet along a seam running the length of the home, gasketed at the ridge and capped outside, never inspected by a factory as a finished assembly. Gaskets take a compression set, the cap lifts, and the rim joists rarely close cleanly at the gables. Those ends are a classic mouse entry.

Floor penetrations and the crossover duct

Water, drain and gas come up through the deck rather than in from the side, cut generously so the plumbing lands. A quarter-inch annulus at a tub drain or toilet flange is a rodent route and a roach route both. Multi-section homes add the crossover duct, a flexible run looping underneath to feed the second half; off its collar it opens the underside straight into your registers.

Piers, pads and an open frame

The home stands on dry-stacked block piers on load-bearing pads, held by anchors and straps. None of that seals at ground level: the perimeter is open by design and skirting closes it, so the space below is only as tight as its weakest panel.

How do you keep rodents out of a home standing on piers?

With a tape measure. The numbers are small and not negotiable.

  • A house mouse needs about a quarter of an inch. If a pencil shaft passes, so does a mouse. Gaps are held to that, not to whether they look like a hole.
  • A Norway rat needs about half an inch and enlarges anything smaller. Incisors grow continuously and cut vinyl, foam and soft mortar without slowing.
  • Quarter-inch galvanized hardware cloth behind every skirting opening and over the access hatch. Insect screen is not an exclusion material.
  • Copper or stainless mesh packed in, then sealed. Mesh fills the annulus at a floor penetration and sealant caps it. Foam alone is a chew toy.
  • The skirting-to-ground line. A panel resting on uneven ground leaves a gap along its whole length, which is why this fault rarely looks like a neat round hole.

Detection comes first. We run certified dogs to find where activity is rather than reason backwards from droppings in one cupboard, and we publish no accuracy percentage for rodent detection in buildings: the field validation for such a number does not exist. Published trials are on bed bugs. See the Norway rat profile.

German or American cockroach — which one is in the house?

The difference here separates a problem the block handed you from one your plumbing did.

 German cockroachAmerican cockroach
What it isHalf an inch, tan, two dark bars behind the head. Indoors only, with no outdoor population worth the name in this stateAn inch and a half or more, glossy reddish brown. Outdoors by preference — under skirting, in the belly cavity, in drain lines
How it arrivedCarried in: a box, a used appliance, a load of furnitureWalked in: a floor penetration, a dried trap, an open skirting panel
What an empty house next door meansLittle, unless things physically move between the two buildingsA great deal — a vacant home with torn belly wrap is permanent habitat

Life cycles sit in the German cockroach profile and the American cockroach profile. A note for anyone already spraying: repellent aerosols drive German cockroaches deeper into wall voids and adjoining rooms, so the colony regrows out of range of the can.

How do you screen a small home for bed bugs?

With a dog first, and the reason is tense. A visual inspection finds evidence — fecal spotting, cast skins, a dead insect in a seam — and evidence is durable. Staining behind a headboard can outlast a successful treatment by years: proof of history, not of a live problem. A well-imprinted dog works to the odor of living insects and viable eggs, so it reports the room as it is now.

The limits get published too. An alert marks scent at one location. It puts no number on the insects and no age on the problem, so we confirm each visually. Kimberly Camera founded this company after twenty-eight-plus years in scent detection, and our teams certify through NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA.

What license should a Blackville pest company be holding?

Licensing runs through the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation, not a state agriculture department — a land-grant university holds the register here, which surprises most people. Category 7A covers industrial, institutional, structural and health-related work, and any legitimate firm keeps a Designated Certified Applicator at every location.

Three Blackville places, and one correction

God’s Acre Healing Springs, north of town, was deeded to Almighty God by Lute Boylston and stands open to anyone; the 1944 deed date repeated all over the internet is one we could not confirm, so we omit it. Barnwell State Park, 307 acres and Civilian Conservation Corps built, carries a Blackville address at 223 State Park Road. And the Clemson University Edisto Research and Education Center sits at 64 Research Road, its published program areas including Entomology and Plant Pathology. We have no relationship with Clemson. We raise it because applied insect science happens here as routine.

And the correction: Blackville has no National Register listings, so a page advertising a historic district in this town invented it.

Who else do we cover on this stretch of US 78?

From 320 Wendy Lane in Windsor, on the same US 78 corridor: Williston, whose ZIP adjoins 29817; Barnwell, nine miles down SC 3; Salley northwest; Orangeburg east. Full list on service areas.

Frequently asked questions

The house beside mine has been empty for years. Can you just treat it?

Not without its owner’s authorization, and we will not pretend otherwise to win a job. What we can do is make your building the harder target: seal the envelope to measured standards, clear the approach, and monitor that boundary so pressure shows up before anything is indoors.

Do you need to get underneath my home to inspect it?

We need access to the space below, which usually means opening a skirting panel or the hatch rather than crawling its length. Most of what matters is reachable from the perimeter: the bottom board, the pier line, the penetrations and the crossover duct. Anything unreachable is reported as such.

Will bed bugs die out on their own in a home that has sat empty?

Do not count on it. The claim that they survive a year without feeding applies to cold conditions, roughly below 55 degrees Fahrenheit. At ordinary indoor temperatures the realistic range is one to four months, and an unheated home through a South Carolina summer is not cold.

Why did my bait stations stop working after a couple of months?

They may not have. Steady consumption alongside steady sightings usually means the supply was never interrupted, so you remove animals as fast as new ones arrive. That is a route problem rather than a product problem, and bait belongs after exclusion rather than instead of it.

Can you write me a termite letter for a sale?

No. We do not carry out termite treatment, we do not issue CL-100 wood infestation reports and we do not write bonds, so a closing needs a wood-destroying-organism company instead. We would rather decline than take a booking and disappoint you.

What is a marriage line and why do you keep checking mine?

It is the seam where the two halves of a multi-section home were joined on site. It runs the full length of the building, it was sealed by hand rather than in a factory, and the gaskets relax over the years. Its ends are a reliable mouse entry.

h1: Pest Control in Cayce, SC

hero.lead: Cayce operates roughly 283 miles of sanitary sewer main and serves more than 13,600 sewer customers against 6,556 households of its own. That buried network is where American cockroaches and Norway rats actually live. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions works the structure sitting on top of it, by scheduled appointment.

body:
Almost every pest page written for this city is really a page about the city next door with the name swapped. The two share a chamber, a school district and a greenway, so the confusion is understandable. It is still wrong.

We would rather build on the fact that makes Cayce unlike anywhere else we publish for. Its own budget book reports a utility serving more than 13,600 sewer customers through roughly 283 miles of sewer line. The census counts 6,556 households in the city limits. The utility is about twice the size of the town running it, and a sanitary sewer is the most consequential structure in urban roach and rat biology.

283 milesOf sanitary sewer main operated by the City of Cayce, plus about 222 miles of water line (City of Cayce FY2025 budget book)
13,600 vs 6,556Sewer customers against households in the city limits — arithmetic on two published figures, so read it as roughly double (City of Cayce FY2025 budget; Census QuickFacts, ACS 2020–2024)
26.8%Of the city’s 7,089 housing units went up in the 1960s, the heaviest decade; median year built 1969 (ACS 2020–2024 five-year, tables B25034 and B25035)

What does general pest control cover in Cayce?

  • Cockroaches — both species, diagnosed apart rather than lumped. See cockroach control.
  • Rodents — canine detection, trapping, and closing routes rather than refilling bait. See rat and mouse control.
  • Bed bugs — certified canine screening, treatment, then a verification pass. See bed bug control.
  • Ants, spiders, occasional invaders and exclusion — openings measured and closed in materials that survive teeth and weather, by our repairs crew.

Never on that list: termite treatment, CL-100 or wood infestation reports, bonds, fumigation, mosquito programmes, lawn work. If a closing needs a moisture letter, you want a different firm.

Why do Cayce and West Columbia keep getting treated as one place?

Proximity, shared river frontage, a joint chamber. They cooperate on plenty and are still not interchangeable. Every figure below is city-level, from one census table read twice.

MeasureCayceWest Columbia
CountiesLexington and RichlandLexington only
Land area, 202016.94 sq mi8.99 sq mi
Density813.7 per sq mi1,937.3 per sq mi
Change since the 2020 census−0.8%+5.9%
Median year built19691976
Heaviest construction decade1960s, 26.8%1950s, 17.9%

Nearly twice the land at 40-odd percent of the density, a county line its neighbour does not touch, and the only city we publish for whose population estimate has gone down.

A related error local copy repeats: Columbia Metropolitan Airport is not in Cayce. It sits in unincorporated Lexington County with a West Columbia mailing address. Being near it is true; containing it is not.

What does 283 miles of sewer have to do with the inside of a house?

More than any other feature of the built environment. A sanitary sewer is not hostile ground for an insect or a rodent. It stays dark, holds a temperature that never freezes or bakes, stays humid, and carries organic material daily. For two of the species we are called about most, that is not a pipe. It is habitat.

Then think about what a connection is. Each of those 13,600 customers marks a point where the buried network meets a building, by way of a service lateral. Every junction has a cleanout, and at the far end fixtures, floor drains and pipe penetrations. The network does not stop at the property line. It ends in rooms.

Rain is the third piece. Heavy rainfall lifts levels in sewer voids and in the separate storm-drain system, displacing whatever was living in the dry crown of the pipe. That is the mechanical reason sightings cluster during and just after a storm.

No roach or rat census exists for any municipal sewer, and we will not invent one. The mileage is the city’s; the argument joining it to your bathroom floor is ours.

American or German cockroach, and why does that matter so much here?

With a utility footprint this size, the answer decides whether the work happens in the kitchen or below the floor. Get it backwards and you lose months treating the wrong storey.

American cockroach — the one that comes up

An inch and a half, reddish-brown, a pale border on the shield behind the head, clumsy in flight. Its population lives outside the living space: sewers, storm structures, meter boxes, grease traps, wet crawl spaces, mulch. It walks in, onto the lowest occupied floor, at night. See the American cockroach profile.

German cockroach — the one already inside

Half an inch, tan, two dark bars lengthwise on the shield. It cannot survive outdoors in our climate, so somebody carried it in — groceries, a used appliance, a moving day. It breeds within a few feet of food, warmth and water. See the German cockroach profile.

Telling them apart on site

Size settles it instantly. After that: where, how many, when. One large insect crossing open floor after dark, especially after rain, reads as arrival from below. Small tan ones in daylight near a cabinet hinge mean an indoor population.

What does a dry floor drain do, and what should go down it?

Floor drain, sink, shower and laundry standpipe all rely on one small piece of engineering: a U-bend holding a couple of inches of standing water. That plug is the only thing between room and drain line. It blocks sewer gas, and it blocks anything that crawls. Spraying a baseboard does nothing about it, because the animals are not in that room.

It also evaporates. A trap under a fixture nobody uses empties within weeks in a conditioned building, faster where air moves across the opening. It can be siphoned out by a poorly vented neighbouring fixture, or wicked away by a rag over the bend. The line then stands open to the room with a municipal sewer at its far end — typically a guest bath, a garage or utility drain, or a standpipe left when the machines moved.

  • Pour water. A quart to a gallon down every unused drain, monthly. Free, and the highest-yield thing a homeowner can do about any of this.
  • Slow the evaporation. A few ounces of mineral or cooking oil poured in afterward floats on top and stretches the seal considerably. Ordinary maintenance, not a pest product.
  • Bleach builds no barrier. Disinfectant creates no seal and reaches nothing living sixty feet away in a main.
  • Check the hardware. Grates present and seated; many floor drains also carry a threaded plug in the body, and a missing one is a hole.
  • Trap primers exist — plumbing that feeds a trickle to a floor-drain trap on a schedule. Fitting one is a plumber’s job, not ours.

Why does a rat problem return after the outside work was done properly?

Recognise this pattern; it gets misread as failed treatment. Exterior work is done well: burrows addressed, gaps sealed, vegetation cut back, trapping run to zero. Weeks pass quietly. Then droppings appear in a base cabinet, with no fresh burrowing outside.

Activity inside and nothing outside usually means arrival from below grade. Norway rats burrow, swim strongly, and are documented sewer inhabitants worldwide, living above the flow line and in voids that open around failed joints. A residential lateral is typically four inches — several times the gap a rat needs.

What lets them out is a defect: an offset or cracked joint, roots splitting a section, a collapsed run under a slab, a cleanout with a broken cap. And the one nobody thinks of — an abandoned lateral, cut when a structure was replumbed and never plugged at the main.

Pipe vintage matters, kept general. Mid-century laterals were commonly vitrified clay — short sections, many bell joints, an invitation to roots — and, from roughly the 1940s to the 1970s, bituminized fiber conduit, which deforms with age. That describes how houses of that era were plumbed, not what lies under any Cayce street; no such inventory is published. Species detail is in our Norway rat profile.

You can check: cleanout caps in the yard and at the foundation, present and intact; floor drains holding water and keeping their grates; toilets firmly seated; the crawl space free of sewage odor, soft ground or standing water; and whether any drain has begun to gurgle. You cannot check the pipe itself. Nobody sees through soil. Confirming a broken or abandoned lateral takes a camera inspection, which is a plumber’s tool and a plumber’s report.

What does a median build year of 1969 give you?

An unusually concentrated middle. The 1960s alone account for 26.8 percent of the housing; with the 1950s they reach 43.6 percent, 3,091 units of 7,089. Just over 60 percent predates 1980, the oldest median stock in this metro.

Houses that age arrive with original drain-waste-vent plumbing and sixty-odd years of trades work crossing the sill line: central air added, a water heater replaced, a kitchen remodeled. Each cut a hole somebody else was going to seal. Against that, 17.1 percent of units have gone up since 2010, the 1990s the thin part at 5.6 percent. A plastic lateral laid in the past fifteen years is a wholly different inspection.

Where does our work stop and whose problem starts?

  • The public main, the manholes, the 283 miles. City of Cayce Utilities. An overflow, a surcharging manhole, a street defect — that call goes to the city.
  • The private lateral, cleanouts, vents, traps and fixtures. The owner’s, worked by a licensed plumber. Camera inspection, repair, relining, plugging an abandoned run.
  • The structure. Ours. Inspection and diagnosis, targeted treatment, canine screening, trapping, and sealing every opening in the envelope we can measure.
  • What we will not do. Put product into a sanitary sewer, open a main, or repair pipe. Anyone offering to treat a municipal sewer for your roaches is selling something that is not theirs.

Bed bugs: what does a canine screen answer that a walkthrough cannot?

Coverage, and low numbers. A visual check confirms a heavy infestation in a room somebody already suspects. It is weak on the two questions people need settled: is anything in the rooms that look clean, and did the treatment work? A trained team screens whole rooms in minutes on odor rather than sightlines — which is how you learn whether this is one bedroom or four. Our handler holds NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA credentials. More on the bed bug control page.

How does a Windsor company actually serve Cayce?

By appointment, on scheduled days. The honest figure is about 45 driving miles, roughly an hour and a quarter. Cayce is the nearest metro city we publish for and sits well inside our range — but an hour and a quarter each way is not emergency response, and we will not pretend otherwise. If a truck within the hour is what today needs, call a firm in town.

What suits the distance is the work described above: a booked inspection with time to open a crawl hatch, walk a perimeter, check every drain and write down what was found. We cover the whole city on both sides of the county line, plus West Columbia, Columbia, Lexington and Irmo. The full list is on the service areas page.

Licensing sits with Clemson University’s Department of Pesticide Regulation. The category covering this work is 7A. To hold it, a company carries a DPR business licence, keeps a Designated Certified Applicator posted at every location, and insures to a combined single limit no lower than $100,000, deductible capped at $1,000. That credential is issued statewide, so it does not care which of Cayce’s two counties an address falls in. Ask whoever you hire for their number, us included.

Frequently asked questions

One big reddish-brown roach appeared in the bathroom after a storm. Am I infested?

Probably not the way you are picturing. That fits an American cockroach arriving from below grade rather than a colony in your walls. Check whether the bathroom’s drains hold water and whether the outside cleanout cap is intact. Repeated sightings in one room point at one opening.

Can you treat the sewer to solve this?

No, and neither can anyone else you might ring. Mains and manholes belong to City of Cayce Utilities, which runs roughly 283 miles of them. We work your structure: finding where the network reaches into it, treating harborage we can safely reach, closing gaps. Street defects go to the city.

How would I know whether my sewer lateral is broken?

From the surface you would not, and be wary of anyone claiming otherwise. Signs that raise the question: slow or gurgling drains, sewage odor in a crawl space, unusually green ground along the pipe run, indoor activity with no exterior sign. Confirming it takes a plumber with a camera.

What should I pour down a floor drain we never use?

Water — a quart to a gallon, once a month. That refills the trap seal keeping the drain line shut off from the room. A couple of ounces of mineral or cooking oil added afterward floats on top and slows evaporation. Skip bleach; it builds no seal.

Part of Cayce is in Richland County. Do you cover that side?

Yes. Cayce spans both Lexington and Richland counties, one of the things separating it from West Columbia. It changes nothing for us. Pesticide licensing is issued by the state through Clemson DPR, not county by county, so one credential covers every address here.

Can you write a termite letter or a CL-100 for my closing?

No, and we cannot arrange one either. This company handles household pests, the two cockroach species, rodent work built on detection and exclusion, and canine bed bug screening with treatment. Termite bonds, wood-destroying insect letters, moisture reports, fumigation and mosquito routes fall outside that. Call a firm that specialises.

Tell us where the sightings are happening

Which room, which floor, what time of day, whether it follows rain, and roughly when the house was built. That is usually enough to say on the phone whether this is something below grade or already inside.

hero.lead: Cedar Creek’s covenants do not permit unattached outdoor structures, so the attached garage and the attic end up holding everything a shed would have held. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions treats those two spaces as the front line here, works outward from stored goods, and screens with certified detection dogs.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Family-owned · Roughly five miles south of Aiken · Garage and attic surveyed first

body:
The Property Owners Association Cedar Creek publishes its rules openly, and one line decides more about pest pressure here than anything else on the property: unattached outdoor structures are not permitted. It is an appearance rule and it does what residents wanted. It also means that across eight hundred-odd homes on half-acre to one-acre lots, there is nowhere outside the house to put a mower.

So the mower goes in the garage, with the fuel can, the kibble, the birdseed and eleven months of holiday storage in the cartons it arrived in. What will not fit goes up the pull-down stair. That single displacement is the whole pest story here, and nobody selling pest control in Aiken County has written about it.

800+Homes built of 1,100 planned, per the POA’s own FAQ at ccaiken.com
1/4 in.Opening a house mouse can pass, per CDC exclusion guidance; one half inch for a rat
1991The Arthur Hills course opened; it hosted the 1995 NCAA Division II men’s championship (Post and Courier)

What does the general program cover here?

One recurring service built on general pest control, with the survey weighted toward storage rather than floor area.

  • Ants: identified to species first, because odorous house ants and fire ants need opposite handling.
  • Cockroaches: two species, two different jobs, and the garage decides which one you get. See cockroach control.
  • Spiders and occasional invaders: silverfish in stored paper, camel crickets at the slab edge, millipedes after rain.
  • Rodents: canine screening, trapping and exclusion, treating garage and attic as one space. See rodent control.
  • Bed bugs: detection and treatment, weighted toward guest rooms used a few weeks a year. See bed bug control.
  • Exclusion carpentry: seals, thresholds and vent screens, specified on paper first. See repairs.

Not offered here: termite work of any kind, wood infestation reports, bonds, fumigation, mosquito programs or turf treatment.

Why does a rule about outdoor structures become a pest question?

Because storage does not disappear when the shed does. It relocates.

Where detached buildings are allowed, the messy half of a household lives thirty feet from the back door in an unheated box with no opening into the living space. Whatever establishes in there stays there, and a rodent population in a shed is cheap to fix.

Cedar Creek does not work that way. The same possessions sit on the other side of one interior door from the kitchen, sharing a slab, an attic and a wall assembly with the rooms people sleep in. That is no complaint about the covenant, which governs how the neighborhood looks. It is a consequence nobody mentions at closing.

So on most jobs here we spend longer in the garage than in the kitchen. If a technician walks the perimeter, lays a band down and never asks what is stacked along the garage wall, you bought a treatment rather than a solution.

What is out there, and what does each item attract?

Pet food

The POA permits three pets per household, so most homes have at least one. An opened sack of kibble is the most dependable rodent food source on any residential lot, and it sits at floor level.

Birdseed

Worse than kibble. Woven bags leak, the seed is oily, and spillage under a shelf goes unnoticed for months. It also feeds Indian meal moths, which move into the pantry.

Cardboard

Delivery boxes flattened for recycling, wardrobe boxes from the move, holiday cartons that come down once a year. This is the item that decides which species you get.

The second refrigerator

A spare fridge runs a compressor that stays warm year round and sheds condensate underneath: a permanent heated, damp, dark island in an unconditioned room, and a classic German cockroach starting point.

Why is cardboard the problem when a plastic tote is not?

People assume the difference is tidiness. It is not. Corrugated board is a manufactured pest habitat that happens to be a container.

PropertyCorrugated cardboardRigid tote with a seated lid
ShapeFlutes form dark channels that touch an insect on several sides at once, the exact tactile condition a German cockroach hunts for.Smooth walls offer nothing to wedge into. The only voids are gaps between stacked bins.
Moisture and foodPaper pulls humidity out of garage air and holds it, and the starch adhesive bonding flutes to liners makes the box itself edible.Does not absorb, and nothing in the container is food.
Egg casesA female German cockroach glues her egg case into a crevice. A flute suits perfectly, and it travels with the box.No crevice at the right scale, and nothing to glue to out of sight.

A mouse shreds a box into bedding overnight, and a stack’s contents stay unknown until every lid is lifted, which is why nobody lifts them. The rule is short: nothing stays in cardboard beyond a week, and kibble and seed go into gasketed containers.

German or American cockroach, and why does a garage favor one?

The American is a visitor

Large, reddish-brown and native outdoors here. It breeds in storm drains, mulch and crawl spaces, then comes in at slab level when weather pushes it. It reaches the garage first, because that room has a floor-level opening sixteen feet wide. See the American cockroach profile.

The German is a resident

Small, tan, and unable to overwinter outdoors in Aiken. It never walks in from the yard; it arrives inside something carried through a door, and cartons are the classic vehicle. It stays where there is warmth, moisture and tight harborage. See the German cockroach profile.

The covenant did not create American cockroaches; they were here first. What the storage pattern creates is German cockroach capability in a room otherwise too bare to hold them, with an interior door onto the kitchen. Remove the cardboard and dry the drip pan and the harborage layer is gone before anything is applied.

What is really happening at the garage door threshold?

The largest deliberate hole in the building is closed by a panel with a strip of rubber along its bottom edge.

  • The seal bridges, it does not fill. A garage slab falls toward the door and is never flat, so the astragal compresses over high spots and spans the dips. A quarter-inch void under one is invisible from standing height.
  • The corners fail first. Where the bottom seal meets the vertical jamb weatherstrip there is a small triangular gap on each side, and it is open on most doors we inspect.
  • Rubber is a consumable. Ultraviolet light across 232 freeze-free days a year hardens the astragal until it takes a set and stops rebounding.
  • The house door is a fire barrier, not a pest barrier. Code asks it to resist fire and, in newer editions, to self-close. Nothing requires it to be tight, and most have no sweep. A line of light under it at night is a line an insect walks toward.

Two more belong on the list. Brick veneer weeps are drainage and must stay open, so they take stainless covers, not sealant. A dryer vent needs a purpose-made rodent guard, never window screen, which packs with lint.

How do rodents move from the garage into the attic?

The specification is dimensional first. CDC exclusion guidance puts the working figures at one quarter of an inch for a house mouse and one half of an inch for a rat, closed in material that resists gnawing. Copper mesh or stainless wool packed and sealed holds; foam alone does not.

Up the wall cavity

An attached garage shares framed walls with the house. Where plumbing or wiring crosses a top plate the drilled hole is oversized and rarely sealed, making a stairwell between garage, stud bay and attic.

The attic as overflow

The same displacement fills the attic, and that version is worse because nobody goes up between one January and the next. Cardboard plus fiberglass batt is a complete nesting kit, and the way in is usually a gable vent with torn screen, a lifted soffit panel or a cracked stack boot. See the house mouse profile.

The pull-down stair

Its frame drops into a rough opening cut through the ceiling drywall, and the perimeter gap is almost never closed. That is an open channel from attic to hallway, and it leaks conditioned air, which is what draws insects to it.

We screen with certified dogs rather than extrapolating from one pile of droppings. We also say what the research supports: no field validation exists for canine accuracy in structural rodent work, so we quote no figure for it.

Where do bed bugs fit, and what does a dog answer?

The POA describes Cedar Creek as an active-lifestyle community that primarily attracts retirees while welcoming all ages. In practice that means guest rooms standing empty most of the year and filling when family visits, plus travel. Both are how bed bugs reach a house that has done nothing wrong.

A visual check finds a heavy infestation easily and misses a light one routinely. An adult is about the size of an apple seed and a first-instar nymph roughly a millimeter, sitting behind a headboard, in a screw hole or in a box-spring seam. A canine screen works on odor and covers those voids without opening them.

Pfiester, Koehler and Pereira, in the Journal of Economic Entomology in 2008, reported trained detector dogs indicating live bed bugs at a 97.5 percent correct rate with no false positives against other household insects. A controlled study, not a field guarantee, and handler and protocol matter as much as the dog. See the bed bug profile.

One correction: bed bugs do not survive a year unfed in a shut guest room. That figure belongs to conditions at or below roughly 55 degrees. In a warm house here an unfed adult manages one to four months.

What does a house of this era give you, and what does it not?

Honest limits first. The POA publishes no founding date, and no neighborhood-level housing data for Cedar Creek exists in any source we could reach: no median year built, no foundation-type breakdown, no lot-size distribution, no unit count beyond the POA’s own 800-plus toward a planned 1,100. Anyone quoting those figures is estimating. What is dated is the golf course, opened 1991 to an Arthur Hills design and host of the 1995 NCAA Division II championship, which brackets development to the early 1990s onward. So we describe what we find, and three things recur.

  • Air sealing helps, then concentrates the traffic. Far fewer random gaps through the wall than a 1950s house, so one unsealed hose bib or duct penetration carries everything.
  • Deep attic insulation hides evidence. Good thermally, bad diagnostically: you read an insulated attic by disturbance patterns, not by looking at a floor.
  • Soffit unclips and weatherstrip wears out. One dislodged length opens a whole soffit run, and twenty years of Aiken sun on a garage door is past a seal’s service life.

What can you change this weekend that beats another treatment?

An afternoon of your own labor will outperform an extra service visit, because harborage removal is permanent and a residual is not. Do these five things, and what is left is worth paying to solve.

  1. Decant the food

    Kibble, birdseed and grass seed into hard containers with gasketed lids, raised off the concrete.

  2. Retire the cardboard

    Empty every box that has sat a season into a rigid tote and send the board off the property. Do not stage it by the door. Later is how the stack got there.

  3. Open a lane along the wall

    Pull shelving four to six inches clear so the slab-to-wall joint is visible end to end.

  4. Deal with the spare fridge

    Slide it out, vacuum the coils, dry the pan, and check the floor beneath for staining.

  5. Fix the two door lines

    Replace the garage door bottom seal, then kneel in daylight with the door shut and check both corners. Fit weatherstrip and a sweep to the house door.

How do we work inside the POA’s rules?

Cedar Creek is self-managed: no management company, a resident-elected Board, dues of $600 semiannually for 2026, amenity use included, and design guidelines governing new construction.

  • Nothing we install adds a structure. Seals, sweeps, thresholds, mesh and vent screens fasten to the existing house, so none of it is an unattached outdoor structure or alters an elevation.
  • Anything visible is specified first. If a repair would read from the street, materials and finish go on paper before ordering, so an owner can take it to the Board.
  • Pets shape the method. With three permitted per household and leashing required on the roughly eight miles of trails, interior work is trapping and exclusion, never loose bait.
  • Common ground belongs to the association. We work the lot we are called to, and report anything on shared ground rather than acting on it.

Who has to be licensed before treating your garage?

Structural pest control here is regulated by the Department of Pesticide Regulation at Clemson University, which catches people out, since most states put it under agriculture.

  • Category 7A is the one that matters: industrial, institutional, structural and health-related work. Everything on this page sits in it.
  • Treating another person’s property for money in that category needs an individual commercial applicator license.
  • The firm needs a DPR business license, a Designated Certified Applicator attached to each location, and general liability coverage of at least $100,000.
  • Technicians under that applicator complete DPR Verifiable Technician Training and retrain annually. Ask any firm for its license number and the applicator’s name.

Where else do we work near Cedar Creek?

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · 803-226-3155 · Kim@ck9ps.com. Cedar Creek sits about five miles south of Aiken, a short run from our base, so same-week scheduling is normal.

Close by we cover Woodside Plantation and Houndslake, the other two large planned communities this side of town, and Montmorenci east of here where lots stop being subdivisions. The city-wide program is on the Aiken pest control page; full coverage sits under service areas.

Frequently asked questions

We have never seen a roach in the kitchen. Why look at the garage?

Because the kitchen is where you notice them and the garage is where they live. A population can hold in stacked cardboard beside a warm appliance for months before anything crosses the interior door, so by the time one appears on a counter the source is well established. Checking the storage wall costs nothing.

Are plastic bins really enough on their own?

They are not a treatment, but they strip out the harborage layer, which is the part a spray cannot reach. Cardboard hands an insect a warm, tight, humid, edible crevice at its own body scale. A rigid tote hands it none of those. Pair bins with gasketed containers and the garage stops being habitat.

Can you seal the garage without anything showing from the street?

In almost every case, yes. Bottom seals, threshold ramps, jamb weatherstrip, corner closures, vent screens and weep covers are either concealed or read as ordinary hardware. Where a repair would genuinely show, we write the specification and finish first so you can clear it with the Board.

Should I put bait stations in the garage?

Not as an opening move, and not where pets are. A baited rodent stays alive several days and grows steadily slower, which makes it easy for a dog or cat to catch, and the dose transfers. It also dies somewhere unreachable, often a wall shared with a bedroom.

How much of the attic actually has to be cleared?

Less than people fear. What matters is that stored items sit in rigid containers rather than boxes, that a walkable path exists along the decking, and that the hatch perimeter is sealed. You do not have to empty the attic, only to see the insulation surface where storage sits.

Do you offer termite inspections or a CL-100 for a sale?

No. Termite treatment, bonds, wood infestation reports and fumigation are outside what we sell, and we do not take those calls as a route into a general pest contract. Different licensing, different work. If a lender or closing needs that document, a firm certified for it should produce it.

Start where the storage is

Tell us what is stacked along the garage wall, whether a second refrigerator lives out there, and what went up the attic stair last January. We survey those spaces first.

h1: Pest Control in Charleston, SC

hero.lead: Charleston’s average overnight low is 61.1 degrees against 54.4 in Columbia. Inland, a building sheds its moisture after dark. Here it does not, and that one number explains most of what people call us about. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions covers Charleston by booked appointment out of Windsor.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · Kim@ck9ps.com · 127 driving miles, about 2 hours 42 minutes, scheduled work only

body:
Two things are true about this city’s buildings at once, and most pages on pest control here print only the pretty one. Charleston holds 7,753 dwellings put up in 1939 or earlier, the deepest pre-war stock of any place we publish for. Its median year built is nonetheless 1995, newer than Charleston County’s own median of 1991.

That is not a data error. West Ashley, James Island, Johns Island, Daniel Island and Cainhoy sit inside the municipal boundary, and 26.3 percent of the city’s housing went up after 2010. Charleston is at once the oldest housing market in South Carolina and one of the newest. Arrive expecting one and meet the other, and you have misread the building.

61.1°FMean minimum temperature, Charleston City station, 1991–2020 normals, against 54.4°F in Richland County (SC DNR State Climatology Office)
1995 vs 1991Median year structure built, city against county. The city is the newer of the two (ACS 2020–2024 five-year, table B25035)
7,753Dwellings built 1939 or earlier, 10.0 percent of 77,417 units (ACS 2020–2024, table B25034)

What we treat here, and what falls outside it

  • Cockroaches — the outdoor species and the indoor one, told apart before pricing. See cockroach control.
  • Bed bugs — screening by a certified canine team, treatment, and a return visit to verify. See bed bug control.
  • Rodents — detection, trapping, and shutting routes rather than topping up bait. See rodent control.
  • Ants, spiders, occasional invaders and exclusion — gaps measured and closed in materials chosen for this climate, by our repairs crew.

Outside our scope, said up front rather than at the end: CL-100 and wood-destroying insect reports, bonds, fumigation, moisture certificates, mosquito routes and turf work.

Why is the overnight low the number that runs this page?

Pull the 1991–2020 normals from the State Climatology Office and the surprise is which figure moves. Charleston City averages a mean maximum of 73.3 degrees; Columbia’s Richland County station averages 78.6. By day the coast is the cooler of the two.

Now the minimums: 61.1 degrees here, 54.4 there. Subtract each pair for the daily spread. Charleston swings 12.2 degrees, Columbia 24.2, Aiken County 22.4 on 75.3 over 52.9. Both inputs in each subtraction come from one table, which is why we show the arithmetic.

A twenty-four-degree swing is a drying machine. Warm air holds moisture, sheds some overnight as it cools toward the dew point, then takes it back by mid-morning, and framing, subfloor and insulation stay in a range where little happens to them. Twelve degrees does no such thing. Air over the peninsula sits near saturation through much of the night for much of the year, so timber under the floor never gets its recovery window.

Nor is it that more water falls. By the DNR’s own city station Charleston is the driest place in this comparison at 44.26 inches a year, under Aiken County’s 50.77. Less rain, wetter buildings, because what soaks in has nowhere to go after dark.

The consequence is a change in what a building tolerates. A torn vent screen, a downspout dumping at the footing, a bath fan venting into a soffit: on a Midlands ranch the nightly cycle burns that damage off. The same defect three blocks from the Ashley River compounds instead. Nothing here dries itself overnight, which is why a coastal envelope repair should not wait a year.

One more input, attributed carefully. The Post and Courier reports Charleston Harbor reaching flood stage 54 times in 2024, seventh-worst on record and still the calmest year since 2021. That reporting counted no insects. What repeated wetting of ground-floor voids does to pest pressure is our argument rather than a published finding, and we say so.

The large roach outdoors and the small one indoors are separate problems

Confuse them and a season goes into the wrong half of the building; with warm damp ground all year, the split is sharper here than inland.

 American cockroachGerman cockroach
Size and lookInch and a half, reddish-brown, pale shield marginHalf an inch, tan, two dark lengthwise stripes
Where it livesOutdoors, below grade: storm structures, mulch, meter boxes, wet crawl spacesIndoors only: within feet of warmth, food and water
How it arrivesWalks in at night, under a door or up a dry drainCarried in: groceries, cardboard, a used appliance
What the coast changesEverything. No hard freeze resets the outdoor populationLittle. February looks like August to it
Where work happensPerimeter, grade, drains, crawl, low-wall penetrationsInterior harborage, plus whatever reintroduces it

One large insect crossing a hall after dark, especially after rain, is nearly always an arrival rather than proof of a colony indoors. Several small tan ones by a cabinet hinge in daylight is the opposite finding, and a longer job. Detail sits in the American cockroach profile and the German cockroach profile.

What happens to a crawl space that never gets dry hours?

More than 15 percent of the municipal area is water, and the city sits in the Coastal Zone ecoregion, a 1,508,820-acre band running from saltwater influence inland. Ground moisture is the baseline here, not an occasional event.

Under a raised floor that means damp soil, joists cooler than the night air, and condensation on any surface below the dew point. A vapor barrier walked apart by four trades and never re-lapped stops working then, as does a vent packed with leaf litter.

A coastal crawl inspection is narrow: standing water and its high mark, barrier coverage and overlap, subfloor around plumbing penetrations, ducts sweating onto insulation, batts slumping because they hold water, the gap where sill meets masonry. On slab construction the same logic moves outward to expansion joints and the lowest few inches of wall cavity. Damp voids matter for one reason: they hold the outdoor roach population against the building. We inspect and report; we do not issue moisture certificates.

Two building stocks inside one city limit

Break the 77,417 units by era and the shape of the work appears. Every row comes from one census table; the era groupings are ours.

BuiltUnitsShare
2010 or later20,37926.3%
2000–200914,51318.7%
1980–199915,89120.5%
1950–197916,41621.2%
1940–19492,4653.2%
1939 or earlier7,75310.0%

A quarter of the city is younger than fifteen years. Daniel Island alone covers 4,000 acres, first developed for housing in 1996, and lies in Berkeley County rather than Charleston. Those addresses bring engineered lumber, sealed sheathing and mechanical ventilation, and they fail at points: a fan discharging into a soffit, a perished garage seal, one penetration foamed in a hurry.

A peninsula house of the eighteenth or nineteenth century fails everywhere at once instead. Framing that has moved for two centuries, soft lime mortar, later additions meeting original fabric at a joint nobody closed, openings never square to begin with. The checklist for the first is useless on the second.

Why sealing a building in the Old and Historic District is regulated work

On 19 October 1931 Charleston’s zoning ordinance created the Board of Architectural Review and the Old and Historic District, the first law of its kind in the United States. Extended since, it now covers more than 4,800 historic structures. If your address is inside it, the exterior is subject to design review, and some of what a pest company might casually screw to your elevation needs approval first.

  • Approval is a real step. Where an exterior change requires review, the application belongs to the owner and the decision to the city. We flag anything crossing that line rather than fitting it quietly.
  • Two designations, two boundaries. The locally legislated district and the federal Charleston Historic District are different maps. Landmark designation came in 1960, National Register listing in 1966, and that district starts south from Bee Street; the local one runs south from Fishburne and Line.
  • Reversible, and worked from the hidden face. Fixings into later material, existing holes reused, nothing bonded to original fabric. A cast vent grille takes its mesh from inside the crawl so the visible ironwork is untouched; masonry is addressed in the mortar joint. Nothing bright and new goes on a weathered elevation.
  • The piazza is the working edge. On a Charleston single house, one room wide with its gable to the street and the real entrance halfway down the long side behind a false street screen, the piazza is where the building meets outdoors. It sits south or west, and that is where door sweeps, floor gaps and column bases earn their keep.

Sympathetic exclusion holds for decades. A foam gun on a 250-year-old sill fails twice, as carpentry and as a scar. Our exclusion and repair work is built on that difference.

Rodents in a stock that shares its walls

Only 47.7 percent of Charleston’s units are detached houses. Buildings of five or more units hold 27,447 dwellings, 35.5 percent of the total, and older peninsula fabric adds party walls, shared cellars, common attics and chases running from one address into another.

There a rodent problem is rarely contained by a lease line. Route beats room: a chase behind a stack, a gap where a joist bears into a party wall, a ceiling void continuous over three storefronts because nobody fire-stopped it. Bait set in one apartment against a population using four fails, and not because the product is weak. Nobody mapped it.

Vacancy is the other figure: 9,390 units, 12.1 percent, highest of the cities we publish for. An empty unit reports nothing, gets no housekeeping and often has its water off, meaning dry traps and open drain lines. We work the structure rather than the unit, use canine detection to place activity, trap before considering poison, then close routes. Sign and biology sit in the Norway rat profile; treatment is rodent control.

Bed bugs, 7.8 million visitors, and what a dog settles

The College of Charleston’s Office of Tourism Analysis put 2024 visitation at 7.8 million people with a $14 billion economic impact. Accommodation and Food Services employed 45,049 across Charleston County in 2022, the second-largest sector there, and should add 8,686 jobs by 2032, up 19.3 percent.

At that volume arrivals are constant however well a property is run, so the question is not whether one gets carried in. It is how fast you find it and how confidently you can call a room clear. Visual inspection confirms what somebody suspects and is weak on the two questions that cost money: is anything in the quiet rooms, and did the treatment work?

A trained team answers those on odor rather than sightlines, covering a floor of rooms in the time a careful visual takes on two. Published work on canine bed bug detection exists; nothing comparable has been published for structural rodent detection, so no figure is quoted here. Our handler holds NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA credentials. Property detail is on hotels and hospitality.

How does a Windsor company serve a city 127 miles away?

Honestly, and by planning ahead. The drive runs about 127 miles and roughly 2 hours 42 minutes each way, so Charleston is a scheduled market for us and nothing else. We will not be at your door this afternoon, and any company that far out claiming otherwise is telling you something you can check on your phone.

It suits work booked ahead with enough on site to justify it: a canine bed bug screen of a hospitality or multifamily property, a whole-building rodent survey, a crawl and envelope assessment on an older house, visits written into a commercial program. Several properties can run together in a day. Need someone tonight, hire locally.

Along the way we also cover Orangeburg on the same I-26 corridor, plus Columbia and Cayce in the Midlands. Home ground is Windsor and Aiken County. The full list lives on the service areas page.

Licensing: Clemson DPR and category 7A

Structural pest control in South Carolina is licensed by Clemson University’s Department of Pesticide Regulation, category 7A. Holding it means a business licence from DPR, a Designated Certified Applicator named for each location, and general liability at a combined single limit no lower than $100,000, deductible no higher than $1,000. Licensing is statewide, so one credential covers Aiken, Charleston and Berkeley County addresses alike. Ask anyone you are considering for their number, us included.

Frequently asked questions

A big reddish-brown roach came in off the piazza last night. How bad is it?

Less bad than it looked. That size points to the outdoor species arriving from the yard, a drain or a void, not a breeding population in your walls. Note the room, the hour and whether rain preceded it. Repeat sightings in one room usually mean one opening.

Why does the house feel damp overnight when it has not rained in a week?

Because the temperature barely falls. The mean overnight minimum here is 61.1 degrees against 54.4 in Columbia, so air stays near saturation instead of drying surfaces. By DNR figures Charleston gets less annual rain than Aiken County. Damp buildings on this coast are a drying problem, not a rainfall one.

Our house is in the Old and Historic District. Does that limit what you can do?

It shapes it. The district dates from the 1931 ordinance and now takes in more than 4,800 structures, with exterior alterations subject to review by the Board of Architectural Review. We plan exclusion to be reversible and hidden, worked from inside where possible. Where a proposal needs approval, the application is the owner’s.

We are on Daniel Island in a house built after 2000. Does any of this apply?

The climate half applies entirely. Newer construction is tighter and better detailed, so it fails at single points: a bath fan into a soffit, a hardened garage seal, one hurried penetration. Both, and rooms are among the best uses of a booked visit. A canine team covers a great many in one session and answers what a visual check cannot: which rooms are genuinely clear. We schedule around occupancy and report findings room by room.

hero.h1: Pest Control in Crosland Park, Aiken, SC
hero.lead: Crosland Park went up in the early 1950s as slab-on-grade starter houses for Savannah River Plant workers, and a slab hands pests a different set of doors than a crawl space does. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions works this north-side Aiken neighborhood for ants, roaches, spiders, rodents and bed bugs.
