h1: Pest Control in Graniteville, SC

hero.lead: Graniteville is a cotton mill village William Gregg laid out in 1845, and part of that housing is still lived in. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions handles ants, roaches, spiders, rodents and bed bugs here, in cottages whose siding, piers and crawl spaces predate any idea of pest exclusion.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Family-owned · Windsor, SC · Horse Creek Valley and Aiken County

body:
Most pest problems we are called to in Graniteville are building problems wearing a costume. That is not a slogan here, it is the local condition. The village was purpose-built as company housing for a cotton mill in the 1840s, and part of that housing is still occupied.

So this page puts the buildings first, and reads our household pest control program against the actual construction of a Horse Creek Valley mill village.

26Carpenter Gothic worker cottages still standing on Gregg Street, out of 100 built between 1845 and 1849 (Graniteville Historic District NRHP nomination)
42%Share of Aiken County housing units over forty years old — county-level, not a Graniteville figure (SRSCRO Aiken–Augusta Regional Housing Study, 2025)
2,439Graniteville residents at the 2020 Decennial Census, down from 2,614 in 2010, in 1,220 households

What does general pest control actually cover in Graniteville?

A short, honest list, the same on Gregg Street as on Weldon Way.

  • Ants — interior trails, perimeter nests, and colonies in a softened sill.
  • Cockroaches — German in kitchens and baths, American up out of crawl spaces and drains. Two animals, two jobs. See cockroach control.
  • Spiders — usually a byproduct. Webbing tells you what else lives down there.
  • Occasional invaders — silverfish, camel crickets, earwigs, millipedes: the damp-crawl-space crowd, which here is large.
  • Rodents — mice and rats located, trapped and locked out. See rat and mouse control.
  • Bed bugs — canine detection and treatment. See bed bug control.
  • Exclusion and repair — closing what the inspection found, to a specification rather than a bead of caulk. See repairs.

What is not on that list stays off it: no wood-destroying insect reports, fumigation, lawn treatment or mosquito programs.

Why does a mill village built in the 1840s behave differently from a subdivision?

Because of how the houses were made, and the record of that is unusually good here. The National Register nomination for the Graniteville Historic District — listed 2 June 1978, reference 78002491, 55 acres at SC 19 and Gregg Street — describes the worker cottages plainly: board-and-batten siding, slate roofs, brick foundations, and vergeboard trim. Gregg built a hundred between 1845 and 1849. Twenty-six survive on Gregg Street, nine more mill houses on Canal, Church and Taylor Streets.

Board-and-batten is a seamed wall. Vertical boards, a narrow batten nailed over each joint. It works beautifully until the wood moves, and wood moves for a hundred and seventy-five years. Boards shrink, nails back out, battens split at the fastener. Lap siding leaves many small overlapping gaps that mostly still shed water; a battened wall leaves fewer, but continuous and vertical, grade to eave. A mouse never has to find the one bad spot. It follows the seam.

A brick foundation means piers, and piers mean a crawl space. A slab house has one plane between soil and floor. A pier house has an open volume under it, vented to the outside on purpose, with your subfloor as its ceiling and joists, ducts and plumbing hanging in it. Anything down there is already inside the envelope but for the last half inch of flooring.

The band joist and sill are the hinge. Water, waste, gas, electric, later cable and a heat pump line set all cross that band, each hole drilled by somebody solving a different problem. More findings cluster there than anywhere else in these houses.

To be straight: the Park Service documented the construction, not the consequences. The reading above is ours.

Those thirty-five cottages are not all of Graniteville. The rest is later mill housing, post-war building and newer construction, where the only honest guide is county-level: 42 percent of Aiken County units are over forty years old (2025 SRSCRO study).

Where does a mouse get into a house standing on brick piers?

A house mouse passes an opening about as wide as a dime; a rat needs nearer a quarter. Working rule: over a quarter inch is a mouse route, over half an inch a rat route. That is an ordinary dimension in a building this old. A split batten leaves it. So does a pier that has settled a fraction, dropping the sill and opening daylight at the seat. So does a corroded foundation vent, which the residential code already treats as a defect.

  • The siding-to-sill line — worst where grade or a flower bed has crept up against it.
  • Band joist penetrations — supply, waste, gas, service entrance, cable, heat pump line set. The line set is often worst: drilled last, sealed with foam.
  • The crawl space access door — wood on soil, rotted at the corner, held shut with a brick. A rodent door with a handle.
  • Pier line and skirting — skirting added later over open piers is rarely continuous and rarely fastened at grade.
  • Chimney and masonry joints — lime mortar erodes, and a hole at attic level runs straight into a wall cavity.
  • Roof trim junctions — vergeboard, fascia and rake on a steep Gothic roofline give a lot of end grain.

Closing them is a materials question. Half-inch woven hardware cloth in 19 gauge stops rats; quarter-inch woven in 24 gauge stops mice; sheet metal no lighter than 24 gauge on a wall or pipe barrier. Copper mesh and steel wool are packing behind a hard cap, never the cap. Foam is an air seal and has never stopped anything with incisors. Our house mouse profile explains why two traps under a sink do nothing.

German or American cockroach — which one turns up in this housing stock?

Both, and the difference decides the treatment. Misidentify it and you lose a season.

German cockroach

Small, tan, two dark stripes behind the head. It lives indoors permanently and never walks in from the yard — it arrives in something carried through the door, then breeds in warm harborage near food and water. In a mill cottage that means the void behind a cabinet run, the gap between countertop and plaster, an old refrigerator motor housing. The female carries her egg case until it nearly hatches, so treatment that misses harborage only buys weeks. German cockroach profile.

American cockroach

Much larger, reddish brown, flies clumsily, and it does not want your kitchen. It wants a warm damp void: a crawl space, a sewer line, a floor drain, a mulch bed. On a pier-and-beam house it commutes up through plumbing penetrations, so the ones indoors are strays rather than residents. American cockroach profile.

Why the split matters here

Chase an American cockroach with a German cockroach program and you bait a kitchen for months while the population sits under the floor. Chase a German cockroach with a crawl space treatment and you never touch it. The first job on a roach call is working out which compartment the animals live in.

What does moisture under an old crawl space actually change?

It changes which pests survive down there year round — an occasional sighting versus a resident colony.

Graniteville sits on the Aiken Plateau in the Sandhills and Upper Coastal Plain, not the Piedmont, whatever a template page tells you. Upland soils here are sandy, low in organic matter and fast draining, but the same regional description notes that depressions and low ground hold poorly drained soil — and this town is arranged around a creek. Horse Creek runs down the valley from Vaucluse; Bridge Creek fed the mill canal Gregg dug in 1846.

Under a house that shows up as a crawl that never quite dries: bare soil, a torn vapor barrier or none, blocked vents, a condensate line dumping underneath, a leak nobody sees because nobody goes down there. The result is a humid, dark, sheltered volume with a wood ceiling — prime habitat for American cockroaches, silverfish, camel crickets and ants in softened framing, and somewhere rodents overwinter without entering your rooms.

We will photograph what is down there, but a treatment does not fix a wet crawl space. Grading, drainage and a vapor barrier are a contractor’s trade. Where the fix is exclusion carpentry — a vent, an access door, a sealed penetration — that is our repairs crew.

Why do bed bugs behave differently in older rental housing?

Two reasons: harborage and turnover.

Older construction gives an insect the size of an apple seed an enormous number of hiding places within a few feet of a bed — plaster cracks, baseboard pulled from a settled wall, plank floor seams, the joint where old trim meets a corner. Newer drywall is not bed bug proof, but it is flatter and less generous.

Then tenure. The 2025 SRSCRO study puts the split at 68 percent owner-occupied and 32 percent renter-occupied across the Aiken–Augusta region — regional, not Graniteville, and labeled that way because no town-level tenure table was available. Where the rental share is meaningful, units change hands, furniture moves in and out, and a population that arrives in a sofa can be established before anyone reports a bite.

A canine screen and a visual inspection answer two different questions. The visual one asks whether a person can find evidence where a person can reach and see. In a heavy infestation that works. It fails where it matters most: early low-level activity, a cluttered room, a wall void, a house treated once and knocked down without being cleared. A dog is not looking for what can be seen. It reads odor from live activity, including the parts of a room nobody can open.

What that buys is scope — which rooms and units have activity and which do not. The clear ones matter as much as the rest: those are the ones you stop paying to treat. Every indication is confirmed by hand. See the bed bug profile.

Why we seal before we spray

Because on this housing type, chemistry alone is a subscription rather than a solution.

A product applied indoors kills what contacts it. It does not close the seam behind a split batten, re-screen a rusted vent, or touch the hole around a heat pump line set. Treat without sealing and you have created a vacancy, in a village where the surrounding population lives under the floor and behind the siding.

Sealing first inverts that. Every opening closed is permanent, needs no reapplication, and works on ants, mice, roaches and spiders at once, because they all use the same gaps. One sequencing rule people get wrong: never seal a structure that still holds an active rodent population. Clear the interior, verify, then close the envelope.

How a Graniteville job runs

  1. What you tell us on the phone

    What you have seen, where, and what has been tried. On an older house we also ask what is underneath — open piers, enclosed crawl or slab. That changes the visit before we load the truck.

  2. Exterior and underside first

    Perimeter, grade line, siding-to-sill joint, vents, access door, pier line, every service penetration. Where the crawl is enterable we go in, photographing as we go.

  3. Interior, compartment by compartment

    Kitchen and bath voids, plumbing chases, attic and trim junctions, and the rooms you reported. For bed bugs, or a rodent problem nobody can locate, this is where a detection team earns its place.

  4. Findings, then the plan

    You hear what was found and where, with photographs, before any plan is described. If part of it is a contractor’s job, we say so.

  5. Clear, close, verify

    Trapping or treatment first where an interior population is active, exclusion to specification second, re-check after.

Who is licensed to do this work in South Carolina?

Not the state agriculture department, which is what nearly everybody assumes. The regulator here is the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation, which surprises most homeowners who ask about it. Structural work is Category 7A.

A legitimate firm holds a DPR business license, has a Designated Certified Applicator at the location serving you, and carries general liability coverage of at least $100,000. Ask for all three. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions was founded by Kimberly Camera — twenty-eight-plus years in scent detection, including FEMA Urban Search & Rescue canine work, certified through NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA.

What the numbers on Graniteville do and do not tell you

Small unincorporated places are hard to measure, and we would rather show the seams than quote a figure that collapses under its own margin of error.

Population. The 2020 Decennial Census counted 2,439 residents in 1,220 households. The 2024 American Community Survey five-year estimate says 2,056, sixteen percent lower. We use the decennial figure, because it is a count rather than a model.

Housing age. There is no citable Graniteville median year built, and we will not estimate one and print it as fact. County-level is citable: 42 percent of Aiken County units are over forty years old, 17 percent are thirty to forty, and the county added 6,138 units between 2013 and 2023. Backdrop, not a town figure.

Home value. The five-year median home value estimate is $112,200, plus or minus $48,452 — directionally useful, not much more.

Subdivisions. We found no verified subdivision names from a source we would trust, so this page names none. Every street above comes from a National Register nomination or an official address.

One piece of context, stated once: the January 2005 Norfolk Southern derailment and chlorine release killed nine people, and Avondale Mills closed the following year, ending milling that had run here since 1849. Documented local history, not a pest matter.

Where we work around Graniteville and the Horse Creek Valley

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · 803-226-3155 · Kim@ck9ps.com.

Graniteville sits on U.S. Route 1 about five miles west of Aiken, in ZIP 29829 — Byrd Elementary and Leavelle McCampbell Middle on Weldon Way, Graniteville Elementary on Willis Circle, Midland Valley High on Mustang Drive, Gregg Park Civic Center at 1001 A Avenue. South down the valley is Warrenville, then Gloverville, Langley, Burnettown, Bath and Clearwater. Five miles east is Aiken and the Gregg Park area; southwest, North Augusta. See every area we serve.

Frequently asked questions

My house is one of the old Gregg Street cottages. Will treatment damage it?

It should not. An exclusion-first approach means most of the work is carpentry rather than chemistry: re-screening a vent, closing a penetration, rebuilding an access door. Where a repair would alter a historic feature, that is a conversation with you beforehand, not a surprise afterward.

Why do I only see big roaches after it rains?

That usually means American cockroaches living under the house rather than in it. Rain drives them out of soil, mulch and the crawl space, and they move up through plumbing penetrations. What you see are strays from a population below the floor, which is why kitchen baiting alone disappoints.

How small a hole does a mouse really need?

About the width of a dime, and a rat about a quarter. Working rule: seal anything wider than a quarter inch for mice and half an inch for rats. On a board-and-batten wall that dimension turns up constantly, at split battens and shrunken board edges.

Do you inspect the crawl space, or just the house?

The crawl space is where most findings are on this housing type, so yes, whenever it is safely enterable. We look at soil moisture, vapor barrier, vents, the pier line, insulation, plumbing and the underside of the subfloor. If access is unsafe we tell you, rather than guessing.

Can a dog find bed bugs in a house that was already treated?

That is where a canine screen earns most. A partial treatment often drops a population below what anyone can find visually without eliminating it, so the problem returns weeks later and everybody argues about whether it left. Odor from live activity is a different signal than visible evidence.

Is Graniteville too small for you to service regularly?

No. We are based at 320 Wendy Lane in Windsor, same county, an easy run up to the Horse Creek Valley. Graniteville, Warrenville and the rest of the valley communities are ordinary route work rather than a special trip, so scheduling is not the obstacle people expect.

Do you offer wood-destroying insect inspections or mosquito spraying?

No, neither. We sell general household pest control, cockroach work, rodent detection and control, and bed bug detection and treatment. Wood-destroying insect reports, moisture certifications, fumigation, lawn treatment and mosquito programs sit outside that, and we would rather refer you than oversell.

I rent. Should I call you or my landlord?

Start with your landlord or property manager, because in a connected building the treatment has to cover more than your unit to work. A German cockroach or bed bug population in one apartment is usually a building population, and treating a single unit moves it next door.

title: Greenville, South Carolina Service Area
description: Areas we serve in Greenville, South Carolina
h1: Pest Control in Greenville, SC

hero.lead: Four of Greenville’s old textile mills are apartment buildings now, and a mill converted into housing is the hardest structure in this city to treat one unit at a time. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions covers Greenville for roaches, rodents and bed bugs, by booked appointment.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · Kim@ck9ps.com · 123 driving miles, just under three hours

body:
Greenville was chartered as a village in 1831 and as a city in 1869, and for most of the century after that it made cloth. MetroConnects, which documents the Textile Crescent, records mill development beginning in 1873, sixteen county mills and two bleacheries at the 1930 peak, and thirteen still standing.

Standing, not spinning. Several were gutted and rebuilt as apartments, producing a building type nobody in this trade describes honestly. Everything below about pest control here starts from what happens when a loom floor becomes forty front doors.

42.6%Of city housing sits in buildings of five units or more: 16,788 of 39,373 units, against 41.8 percent detached (ACS 2020–2024 five-year, table B25024)
13 of 16County mills still standing from the 1930 peak, when sixteen mills and two bleacheries ran (MetroConnects, Textile Crescent)
1987 vs 1992Median year built, city against county: city housing is five years older (ACS 2020–2024 five-year, table B25035)

What is on our list in Greenville, and what is not?

The list is the same everywhere. Delivering it inside a hundred-unit building is not.

  • Cockroaches — German indoors, American out of drains and wet voids. Separate animals, separate programs. See cockroach control.
  • Bed bugs — canine screening across as many units as it takes, treatment, verification. See bed bug control.
  • Rodents — located, trapped, then shut out of the route they were using. See rat and mouse control.
  • Ants, spiders and occasional invaders — household work, done at the perimeter as much as indoors.
  • Exclusion and repair — openings measured and closed in lasting materials, by our repairs crew.

Asked for here and not sold: wood-destroying insect reports, moisture letters, bonds, fumigation, mosquito routes, turf work. A manager who needs a CL-100 before a sale needs another vendor, and we say so on the first call.

Why does a converted mill behave unlike any other address in the city?

Because it was never a residence. A cotton mill is a stack of enormous open floors on heavy timber posts and beams inside load-bearing masonry, built for machinery and daylight. Conversion drops partitions into that plate and threads water, waste, ductwork and wiring through a skeleton built for none of it.

Four of the ten major mills catalogued by the Post and Courier hold apartments now:

MillBuiltWhereNow
Mills Mill1897West Greenville village arts districtLofts at Mills Mill, converted in the early 2000s
Monaghan Mill1900Smythe StreetLofts of Greenville, 194 units, reopened 2006
Brandon Millearly 1901Draper StreetWest Village Lofts, converted 2016
Woodside Mill1902Woodside AvenueApartments, 309 units, 2021

Judson Mill, 1912, went mixed-use: apartments, restaurants, offices and a music venue. Poe Mill on A Street near Pete Hollis Boulevard burned in 2003, with a 482-apartment complex planned there. Dunean Mill on Emery Street still runs textiles.

Note the scale: three hundred and nine apartments is a small neighborhood under one roof and one set of shafts.

Where are the shared voids, and why do they decide the outcome?

Here is what a walkthrough of one apartment cannot show. This describes the building type, not one address.

The plate above the ceiling

Mill floors span far wider than any apartment. Partitions dropped into that space often stop at the new ceiling rather than the deck above, so a wall between neighbors has open sky above it. One plenum runs the length of several units.

The vertical core

Hoistways, stair towers and old chases that carried power or line shafting run the full height. Anything reaching a shaft is no longer confined to one floor. That is how a ground-level population becomes a fourth-floor complaint.

Plumbing that was never meant to be there

Kitchens and baths here are inserted work. Supply and waste get cut through timber and masonry that had no openings, and oversized holes get boxed rather than sealed. Those chases connect units both ways.

Timber and unpointed mortar

Exposed brick sells these apartments and open mortar joints are part of the look, while heavy timber checks and shrinks for decades. Both leave harborage in the middle of the living space.

One rule follows: treat the void, or repeat the treatment.

What does 42.6 percent multifamily do to the approach?

It makes the building the customer even when a tenant is the caller. Of 39,373 city housing units, 16,788 sit in structures of five units or more — 42.6 percent, against 41.8 percent detached. More people here live in an apartment building than in a house.

The rest follows: 41.1 percent owner-occupied, so renters hold 58.9 percent of occupied homes, with 1.95 persons per household and 9.9 percent vacancy. Those are city figures, ACS 2020–2024 five-year. The county runs 68.9 percent owner-occupied, and that number should never be quoted for a downtown apartment.

One inversion worth knowing: the city median build year is 1987 against the county’s 1992, so housing in town is five years older than the stock around it. Charleston runs the other way on the same table. The older, more heavily altered buildings in this metro are downtown, not at the edge. The commercial version of that is our multifamily and property management program.

Why is one unit’s German cockroach the building’s problem within weeks?

Start with the biology. The species does not live outdoors in our climate, so no yard in Greenville produces them. It arrives through a door in a box, a used appliance or a couch, then stays, because warmth, water and food are permanent indoors. It breeds where it hides, in gaps measured in millimeters.

Now put it in a converted mill. Nymphs need no hallway to reach the next kitchen; they follow the pipe chase and the plenum over the ceiling. Two kitchens are often closer inside a shared void than their doors are along the corridor.

Which is why the housekeeping lecture is wasted breath. Sanitation is a real risk factor and a dirty kitchen grows a bigger population, but a spotless apartment sharing a chase with an infested one gets roaches anyway. The unit of treatment has to match the unit of infestation. See the German cockroach profile.

How do rodents use a structure this size?

Vertically, the way it was built to be used. A mill moved material between floors, and a mouse reads the same shafts as a staircase. The animal nests in one place, feeds in another, and never appears in the apartment paying for the trap.

  • Openings are not a judgment call. A quarter-inch gap will pass a mouse and a half-inch gap a rat, which is an ordinary tolerance in century-old masonry.
  • Bait outside one door is not a program. It quiets that apartment while the population continues in the void, and the next call comes from another floor.
  • Waste handling is structural. A chute, compactor room or dumpster corral is a food source at a fixed address, setting the population level for the property.

Our house mouse profile covers the breeding rate that makes this a scoping problem before a trapping one.

How do you clear six leases of bed bugs at once?

Two questions a flashlight handles badly: which units are involved, which are clear.

A visual inspection can only confirm what somebody is able to see from wherever they can physically get to. That works on a heavy infestation in an uncluttered room, and fails where a multifamily building needs it most: a low-level population, a cluttered apartment, a wall void, a unit treated once and never verified. A dog works from odor given off by live activity instead of sightlines.

What that buys is coverage per hour. Screening the units around a reported one is affordable when each room takes minutes, and it is the only honest way to draw a boundary. Clear units matter as much as hot ones, because those apartments come off the treatment list. Nothing is treated on an indication alone; a handler confirms each one by hand. Our handler is certified through NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA. See the bed bug profile.

How do you seal a building made of heavy timber and brick?

Not the way you seal vinyl siding. Three differences run the job.

Mortar is the weak line, not the brick. Masonry from 1900 was laid in soft lime-based mortar, which erodes long before brick does, and an eroded joint or old anchor pocket opens a path into a wall cavity. Repointing is a mason’s trade; a hard modern mix on soft brick damages the wall.

Timber keeps moving. Posts and beams check and shrink for decades after a conversion, so a seal at a timber-to-masonry junction wants checking again later.

Metal at every penetration. Foam seals air and nothing else; teeth go through it in a night. Half-inch hardware cloth in 19 gauge stops rats, quarter-inch in 24 gauge stops mice, and copper mesh is packing behind a hard cap rather than the cap.

One rule gets broken constantly: never close an envelope that still holds an active interior population. Clear the inside, confirm, then seal.

Does Piedmont clay change the perimeter, compared with Sandhills sand?

It changes what the ground does with water, which is most of what a perimeter is about. The rest of our service area sits on Sandhills sand: quartz, nutrient-poor, permeable, rain draining straight down and away. Greenville County is Piedmont, its far north in the Blue Ridge.

SC DNR describes Piedmont soils as predominately loamy clay to clay in texture, with high cation exchange capacity and high water holding capacity, across rolling, weathered, often eroded hills between roughly 375 and 1,000 feet. The characteristic series is Cecil, sandy loam over red clay — and Cecil is North Carolina’s state soil, not South Carolina’s.

Clay that holds water sits against a foundation differently than sand that sheds it. Water leaves slowly, so a downspout discharging at the wall keeps that ground damp far longer than the same mistake would in Aiken County. Damp perimeter soil is where American cockroaches, millipedes, silverfish and ants build the outdoor population that later comes inside. DNR’s 1991–2020 county normals add 50.73 inches of precipitation a year onto ground that lets go of it slowly. The soil descriptions are published science; the perimeter argument drawn from them is our judgement, and we would rather label it than dress it up as a citation.

How does a company based in Windsor serve Greenville?

By appointment, with the distance in writing rather than left for you to discover. Windsor to Greenville is 123 driving miles, about two hours fifty-four minutes without stops. Call it just under three hours — the longest run of any market we publish, and longer in time than Charleston, because no interstate carries you the whole way northwest.

So this is scheduled work, not same-day coverage. If something needs a technician this afternoon, hire an Upstate firm. The distance suits the work described above: a building-wide bed bug screen, a roach program scoped across a block of apartments, twenty units lined up for access on one date. Those get booked weeks out anyway, and they are where an independent detection team is worth the mileage.

Greenville is the far corner of our map. The nearer part is the Midlands — Columbia, Irmo, Lexington — and the Aiken County ground around the shop, all of it on the service areas page.

One correction to finish on: local copy likes to hang the BMW plant on Greenville. That plant is in the Upstate, not in Greenville County.

What licensing should a Greenville property manager check?

  • The regulator is Clemson University, through its Department of Pesticide Regulation — not the health department, and not agriculture.
  • Category 7A is the structural one, taking in institutional and health-related pest work. Everything on this page falls under it.
  • The business holds the license, with a Designated Certified Applicator posted to the location serving your address. Employing a certified person is not the same thing.
  • Liability insurance has a floor of $100,000. Ask for the license number and the applicator’s name, from us and from anyone else quoting you.

The credential is statewide, so a Windsor company is licensed here on the same terms as a firm on Main Street. Distance is a scheduling fact, not a legal one. Our founder is Kimberly Camera, who spent more than twenty-eight years on scent detection work before this company existed, FEMA Urban Search and Rescue canine deployment among it.

Frequently asked questions

I live in a mill conversion and my neighbor has roaches. Am I next?

Possibly, and it is no comment on your housekeeping. German cockroaches move between apartments through pipe chases and the space above dropped ceilings, which in a converted mill runs past several units. Ask management to inspect the whole block of apartments at once, rather than treating one kitchen and waiting.

Can you screen a whole floor of apartments in one visit?

That is the format this work is built for. A canine team clears rooms in minutes rather than the long visual check each unit would otherwise need, so a full floor becomes practical in a day. You get a unit-by-unit result: where activity is, and which apartments can be left alone.

How long does it take you to reach Greenville?

About two hours fifty-four minutes, over 123 miles. We book Greenville work in advance and travel for it, which suits inspections, building-wide screens and property management programs. It does not suit an emergency this afternoon, and we will say so on the phone.

The brick inside my apartment is exposed. Is that a problem?

It is a harborage question, not a hazard. Old brick laid in soft lime mortar erodes at the joints, and open joints are narrow, dry, protected spaces of the sort roaches and bed bugs use. It does not mean anything lives there, only that the wall offers more places to sit than drywall.

My landlord treated my unit and the bugs came back. What went wrong?

Usually the scope rather than the chemistry. Where a population lives in a shared void and only one apartment was treated, survivors on the far side of the ceiling or chase move back in. Screening the neighboring units shows how far it reaches before anyone spends more.

Do you handle termites or mosquitoes in Greenville?

Neither, here or anywhere. What we sell is household pest control, the two cockroach species, rodent work built on detection, trapping and exclusion, plus canine bed bug screening with treatment. Termite letters, CL-100 reports, bonds, fumigation, lawn and mosquito programs are all outside it. We would rather refer you.

Related services

General Pest ControlCockroach ControlBed Bug ControlMultifamily & Property ManagementExclusion & Repairs

Tell us how the building is put together

Unit count, number of floors, whether it is a conversion, and which apartments have reported something. That is enough to scope a screen to the structure rather than the complaint.

faqs.a: Usually the scope rather than the chemistry. Where a population lives in a shared void and only one apartment was treated, survivors on the far side of the ceiling or chase move back in. Screening the neighboring units shows how far it reaches before anyone spends more.

faqs.q: Do you handle termites or mosquitoes in Greenville?
faqs.a: Neither, here or anywhere. What we sell is household pest control, the two cockroach species, rodent work built on detection, trapping and exclusion, plus canine bed bug screening with treatment. Termite letters, CL-100 reports, bonds, fumigation, lawn and mosquito programs are all outside it. We would rather refer you.

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions works on ants, spiders, cockroaches, rodents and bed bugs here — in the houses, and in the shared community buildings this place is organized around.

body:
The correction first, since most directory listings have it wrong. Gregg Park is not a City of Aiken neighborhood — it is a populated place inside the Graniteville census-designated place, in the Horse Creek Valley, about a mile and a half from the middle of Graniteville and some eight miles from downtown Aiken. Its residents are enumerated with Graniteville, and the civic center everyone here uses carries a Graniteville address at 1001 A Avenue.

It still gets written as an Aiken address, which is fair enough: the county is Aiken County and the mailing region is shared. It matters because the geography decides what this page is about. Gregg Park is a residential pocket arranged around a public recreation building, so this page reads our pest control program against a building the whole neighborhood uses, then against the houses nearby.

2,439People counted in the Graniteville CDP at the 2020 Decennial Census. Gregg Park has no separate published population — it is tallied inside that CDP
1.5 miDistance to Graniteville, the nearest named place; downtown Aiken is eight miles east (gazetteer coordinates 33.575, -81.793)
12.5 hrsPublished Monday-to-Thursday opening day at the Gregg Park Civic Center, 8:30am to 9pm — a pattern no house has

What does the household program include, and where does it stop?

  • Ants — the trail indoors, the colony outdoors supplying it, and the link between them.
  • Cockroaches — two species sharing little but a name and a shape.
  • Spiders — usually a readout of what else is available to eat.
  • Occasional invaders — silverfish, crickets, earwigs, millipedes.
  • Rodents — locate first, remove second, close the routes third.
  • Bed bugs — canine screening and treatment, homes and shared facilities alike.
  • Exclusion and repair — the physical work that follows the inspection.

Never sold here or quietly bundled in: wood-destroying insect reports, moisture letters, fumigation, turf programs, mosquito spraying.

Why is a shared building not simply a larger house?

Because most of what a residential program assumes stops being true at the door. The anchor institution here is the Gregg Park Civic Center at 1001 A Avenue, whose own published description lists a basketball gym, meeting and event rooms, full kitchen facilities, a picnic shelter and courts. That is a building type, described from the center’s own material — not a report about any address.

VariablePrivate houseBuilding the community shares
Who comes inThe same few people most daysDozens weekly, from unrelated households
What comes inGroceries, mail, a deliverySports bags, mats, folding gear, catering trays
A sighting meansAn inconvenienceA public conversation by the end of the day

What do propped doors, loading areas and a shared kitchen actually do?

Propped doors. A gym warms up, somebody wedges the exterior door, and it stays wedged until the last practice ends after dark. A held-open door defeats its sweep, closer and threshold at once, and after dusk it is a lit opening at ground level: American cockroaches, flies, wasps, rodents working the wall line. Nothing chemical competes with a doorstop.

The loading area. Deliveries stage on concrete, cardboard piles beside a dumpster, and the service door above rarely seals to its slab. Cardboard is the most reliable way to import a cockroach population: it arrives folded, warm and already occupied.

The shared kitchen. Rotating intermittent use is its own hazard: nobody owns the standard, crumbs go under the equipment rather than out of the building, and a refrigerator holds whatever the last rental left. The discipline is any food-service kitchen: pull the equipment, clean beneath it, keep drains and mop sinks wet. An evaporated trap is a sewer line with nothing in the way.

German or American cockroach, and which turns up where here?

German cockroach — kitchen and servery

Small, tan, two dark bars behind the head, permanently indoors. It never wanders in from the parking lot; it is carried in inside a box, a tote or a returned dish crate, then settles in warm harborage near food and water. German cockroach profile.

American cockroach — drains, voids, the gym floor at 7am

Large, reddish brown, a clumsy flier. It wants a warm wet void rather than your kitchen: sewer laterals, floor drains, mechanical rooms, mulch tight against the wall. The ones found in a big building are usually travelers that came up a drain or in under a door.

Telling them apart

Where, when, how many. Several small ones near food after dark is a resident German population needing harborage work. One large one crossing open floor after heavy rain points outward and downward instead.

How do rodents use a building that empties every night?

Comfortably, which is the point. Houses hold unpredictable humans at odd hours; a civic building goes fully quiet for twelve, with food debris, water and storerooms of undisturbed equipment in it. Then the seasonal shape: a hall runs hard through camp and the sports calendar, then sits lightly used for weeks. Evidence piles up in that gap, and whoever opens the storeroom in September thinks it happened overnight.

  • Storage rooms — stacked mats, bagged uniforms, boxes nobody moves year to year.
  • Suspended ceilings and cable trays — dark, warm, continuous, connected to every room on the floor.
  • Door thresholds — the gap under a metal door whose sweep has dragged across grit for a decade.

One rule specific to a place with children in it: no loose bait indoors, ever. Exterior work goes into tamper-resistant stations set away from play areas and recorded on a map; interior work is mechanical trapping in locked spaces or ceiling voids, checked on a schedule. Slower, and the only defensible way to do it. See rodent control.

Why put a detection dog through a hall where nobody sleeps?

Because a bed bug does not need a bed. It needs a ride, and a shared facility is where rides get exchanged. They arrive on bags — a gym bag on a bench, a backpack under a folding chair, a lost-property bin nobody has emptied since spring. With no sleeping host a facility is poor habitat, so a population rarely builds. What it is, is a transfer point: an insect leaves one household’s bedroom and departs in another family’s bag. That is how one household’s problem quietly becomes eleven households’ problem.

A visual inspection and a canine screen answer different questions. The visual asks whether a person can find physical evidence where a person can reach and see. In a hall of bleacher joints, chair stacks, mat rolls and upholstered seating, the seams run into the thousands and early activity hides in any of them. A dog works odor from live activity instead, including inside things nobody will disassemble.

What that buys is scope: which rooms have activity and, more usefully, which do not — so the clear ones leave the treatment list and the budget. See the bed bug profile.

What record should a facility manager be able to produce?

Assume a board member, a parent or an insurer eventually asks what was done. That is why our commercial programs are built around a file rather than a spray schedule.

  • A dated screening log, room by room — including rooms that came back clear. Negatives show later that something arrived after a given date.
  • Findings written separately from the sales proposal — what was found and where, photographed, whatever is recommended next.
  • Treatment records — product, target pest, location, method, date, applicator and license number.
  • Follow-up results and a written clearance standard — consecutive clear checks over a stated interval, not one visit.
  • A note for every reported sighting — who, where, when, what was done that day. The record that ends a rumor.

What about the houses on the streets around it?

They are Graniteville houses and get treated as such; the construction story of the valley belongs on the Graniteville page.

What belongs here is the traffic between the two. Wherever people gather, a few pests travel both ways with them. A cockroach rides home in a box of leftover supplies; a bed bug leaves in a bag and surfaces in a bedroom three streets away. Rodent pressure around a busy refuse area ignores property lines, and the closest houses feel it first.

Households get the ordinary sequence: perimeter, entry points, kitchen and bath voids, storage, interior. On housing age the only citable figure is county-level — 42 percent of Aiken County housing units are over forty years old, per the 2025 SRSCRO Aiken–Augusta Regional Housing Study — and it is backdrop, not a Gregg Park number.

Who is allowed to treat a building the public uses?

South Carolina puts structural pest control under neither a health department nor an agriculture department. It belongs to the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation, part of the land-grant university, which surprises almost everyone. Structural work falls in Category 7A, covering cockroach, rodent and bed bug jobs.

Before signing for a facility, ask three things: the firm’s DPR business license number, the Designated Certified Applicator assigned to the location serving you, and a certificate showing general liability coverage of at least $100,000. The cheapest diligence a volunteer board will ever do.

Our founder, Kimberly Camera, spent twenty-eight-plus years in scent detection before this company existed, FEMA Urban Search & Rescue canine deployment among it; teams certify through NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA.

What we can honestly say about Gregg Park, and what we cannot

No separate statistics exist. Population, households, housing values and tenure are published for the Graniteville CDP. There is no Gregg Park row in any of them, and we will not model one and print it as a fact.

No subdivision names. Not one plat name here could be verified from a source worth trusting, so this page names none; A Avenue comes from the civic center’s published address. The place name almost certainly honors William Gregg, who chartered the Graniteville mill in 1845, but no source says so outright — inference, not history.

Where we work around Gregg Park

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · 803-226-3155 · Kim@ck9ps.com.

It is a mile and a half to Graniteville proper, a short run down the valley to Warrenville. East along US 1 is Aiken; southwest, North Augusta. Every area we cover is listed here.

Frequently asked questions

Is Gregg Park in Aiken or in Graniteville?

Graniteville, for every purpose that matters. It is a populated place inside the Graniteville census-designated place, ZIP 29829, and its people are counted as part of Graniteville rather than separately. Aiken County is the county and downtown Aiken is eight miles off, which is why listings shorten it to an Aiken address.

Do you work on community buildings, or only houses?

Both. A hall, gym, clubhouse or church kitchen is handled as a commercial job: written findings, mapped station and trap locations, a documented follow-up schedule, and work timed around whoever uses the room. Scheduling around camps and weekend rentals is routine. Households get the residential program, and sequencing the two together beats treating either alone.

Someone mentioned bed bugs after an event in a hall we rent. What now?

Screen before you treat. Have the rooms checked, note which come back clear, and treat only what has evidence behind it. A hall is a transfer point rather than a habitat, so the likely outcome is a small localized finding or nothing at all. Treating a whole building on one report settles nothing.

Why do we see one big roach in the morning and never a group?

That pattern usually means American cockroaches living outside the room rather than in it — a floor drain, a sewer lateral, a mechanical space, mulch against the wall. They travel alone and get noticed crossing open floor. A resident German population looks different: several small insects near food and warmth after dark.

Do you provide termite letters or mosquito spraying for outdoor events?

No to both. Our work is household pest management, cockroach programs, canine and mechanical rodent work, and bed bug screening with treatment. Termite letters, moisture certificates, fumigation, turf spraying and event mosquito work are things we do not do at all, so a facility is better off with a specialist than with us learning on it.

We are a volunteer board with no budget for a monthly contract. Is one inspection worth it?

Often, yes. A single documented inspection tells you what condition the building is in, which rooms are clear, and which fixes are carpentry and cleaning rather than recurring chemistry. Plenty of facilities need three or four repairs and a changed routine far more than a monthly visit.

h1: Pest Control on the Hitchcock Woods Edge, Aiken, SC

hero.h1: Pest Control on the Hitchcock Woods Edge, Aiken, SC
hero.lead: Hitchcock Woods is 2,100 acres of privately owned forest inside the Aiken city limits, and a long line of houses backs straight onto it. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions works that boundary: ants, roaches, spiders, rodents and bed bugs, plus the carpentry that keeps a wooded lot out of your walls.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · Family-owned · Addresses bordering the Woods · Licensed through Clemson DPR

body:
A boundary with a working forest is not a problem you solve once. It is a supply line that reopens every night. That sounds bleak until you notice what it implies: the forest side is fixed, so everything worth doing sits on your side of the pins.

This page is about roughly thirty feet of ground. Fence base, firewood, compost, feeder, shed floor, gutter outlet, the dark space beneath the deck. Get those right and animals moving along the treeline keep moving. Get them wrong and your building becomes the most interesting structure on the line.

2,100 acresHitchcock Woods, called by the Hitchcock Woods Foundation the largest privately-owned urban forest in the country, inside Aiken city limits (Aiken County)
70 milesSandy trails, per the Foundation. Aiken County publishes 65 miles and seven perimeter entry points; we quote the landowner and note the gap
1,109 acresUrban watershed that discharged into the Sand River through a single 120-inch storm drain, before the city’s vaults were commissioned in 2022

What is Hitchcock Woods, and why is it a neighbor rather than a culprit?

Get the description right; plenty of local copy does not. This is a privately owned, nonprofit-managed urban forest, held by the Hitchcock Woods Foundation. Not a city park, not a state park, not a subdivision, and nobody lives in it. Thomas Hitchcock and William C. Whitney bought the first tract in the 1890s for the sandy footing it gave horses; the Foundation was established in 1939 on a gift of roughly 1,100 acres, and some 900 more have been added since.

The rules are unusually strict. Motorized vehicles and bicycles are both prohibited, and management aims at passive recreation to preserve the integrity and tranquility of the forest. Walking, riding, birding and dog walking outside hunt schedules are permitted. Admission is free; the best-known way in is at South Boundary.

None of that makes the forest a source of pests. Mature longleaf habitat with a burned understory supports a stable native community, and the Woods holds Certified Wildlife Habitat status. Healthy forest does not put a mouse in your pantry. A split bag of sunflower seed does.

What do we cover out here, and what will we flatly not do?

Everything below is general pest control, on a lot where the back fence is the treeline.

  • Ants: indoors, at the slab or sill, and in damp litter along the fence.
  • Cockroaches: two species with opposite biographies. See cockroach control.
  • Spiders and occasional invaders: crickets, millipedes, sowbugs and silverfish from ground cover.
  • Rats and mice: canine screening, trapping, permanent exclusion. See rodent control.
  • Bed bugs: certified canine screening and treatment. See bed bug control.
  • Exclusion carpentry: screening, closures, sweeps, skirting. See repairs and exclusion.

Now the refusals, because a forest-edge page that stays vague here is dishonest by omission. We are not a wildlife trapping or removal company. Our rodent work covers commensal rats and mice and stops there. We do not trap, relocate or haul away a raccoon, an opossum, a squirrel or a fox, and we will not take the job by calling an attic raccoon a rodent.

What we do is the part that lasts. Once a licensed wildlife operator has resolved the animal, or once it has left and that is confirmed, we close the opening so the next one cannot use it. Sealing a hole with something still behind it makes matters worse. Background on the species people call about: the raccoon and the Virginia opossum.

Off the menu as well: termite treatment, bonds, wood infestation reports, fumigation, mosquito programs and turf work.

What is the thirty-foot rule?

Draw a line thirty feet inside your property from wherever the forest begins. Everything in that band is yours to change, and nearly everything deciding whether an animal keeps walking sits inside it. The goal is not a sterile strip; bare scraped ground would be bad for the Woods and would not help you. It is to make your buildings the least rewarding structures on the line.

  • The fence base. A fence is a travel corridor, a hard edge to run against with cover both sides. Keep the bottom foot open enough to see through, and lean nothing against it.
  • Firewood. The most productive single change most people here can make. Split wood on soil against a wall is shelter, insulation and insect food in one heap. Use a metal rack eighteen inches clear of the ground, away from house and fence both.
  • Compost. An open heap at the property line is a feeding station with a view of your back door. Enclosed bin, lid, hardware-cloth floor, no meat or grease.
  • The bird feeder. You do not have to stop feeding. You do have to stop feeding at night. Fit a catch tray, sweep beneath it, keep it clear of the wall, and store seed in a lidded metal can.
  • The shed. A garden building on skids gives you a dry roofed void six inches above the sand, which is a den site by any reasonable definition. Skirt it or close it.
  • Downspout outlets. A spout dumping at the corner keeps one band of soil permanently damp, and that is where ground insects concentrate.
  • The deck. Handled below, because it is the largest single opening on most wooded lots and lattice does not close it.

Two things not to do. Do not push brush or clippings over the line, and do not burn your own pile at the boundary. That land is your neighbor’s, and it is managed with fire by people who plan it.

Where does a woodland rodent get in, and how big is the gap?

People picture a hole. Usually it is a gap that has been there since the house was built, and something worked out what it was for.

OpeningReal dimensionWhat closes it
Gap a house mouse will passAbout a quarter inch, roughly 6 mmQuarter-inch galvanized hardware cloth, cut oversize and fastened. Not foam
Gap a rat will passAbout half an inch, roughly 13 mmMetal at the perimeter with sealant behind it, never sealant alone
Crawl vent with rusted louversThe full opening, often 8 by 16 inchesNew screen fixed to framing inside the opening
Penetration at a hose bibb or line setHalf an inch to two inches of annular spaceCopper mesh packed tight, then sealed over
Void under an outbuilding on skidsFour to eight inches of open groundBuried skirt, twelve inches down and twelve inches turned out

Species changes the search. The house mouse needs almost nothing and nests a short trip from food. The Norway rat digs, and soil matters here: the deep upland sands of these ridges hold a burrow well and drain fast, so an entrance beside a footing stays open in wet weather.

On canine work we say the same everywhere. Dogs shorten the search. No field validation exists for structural rodent detection accuracy, so we publish no percentage, and every alert is confirmed by eye.

Why is bait the wrong tool on this boundary?

Two reasons, and the first is arithmetic rather than ethics. Rodenticide reduces a population, which is sensible inside a closed building where that population is finite. On a boundary it is not, because 2,100 acres sit on the far side of the fence and vacancy on a good edge never lasts. You are not clearing a problem, you are subscribing to one. Sealing is the only work that compounds.

The second reason is what else eats a slow rodent. Anticoagulants take days, and through those days the animal is alive, exposed and easy to catch, which is exactly why predators get dosed. Owls, hawks, foxes and neighborhood cats hunt the same edge you would be baiting. Laying out an open supply of slow poisoned prey against a fence line held as certified wildlife habitat works against the thing people value about living there.

Instead: trap where activity is measurable, in protected boxes, checked and logged so you get a count rather than a guess. Close the openings. Fix food and cover inside the thirty feet. Any exterior station stays tamper-resistant, secured and documented.

What does prescribed fire have to do with when you see things?

The Woods is managed with regular prescribed burns, carried out to keep conditions hospitable to a longleaf pine stand, a system that does not persist without fire. Burning inside a city limit, along streets of houses, is unusual and deliberate.

For a homeowner on the line the consequence is simple. Fire strips low cover off the burned unit, and animals using it shift elsewhere for a while. Elsewhere can be your fence run, your woodpile or your deck. Burn plans are the Foundation’s to publish, but the weeks after a nearby burn are a poor time to have stacked a fresh cord against the fence.

Crawl space, deck and gutter: three things a wooded lot punishes

  1. The crawl space is the room you never enter

    This is where a rodent problem is stopped or hosted, and most people have not looked into theirs in years. We check vent screens one at a time, the access door and frame, every pipe and wire penetration, and the insulation for sagging that says something lived in it.

  2. The deck is a roofed vacancy facing the forest

    Dry, dark, sheltered and hidden from predators describes an ideal den. Lattice excludes nothing. The fix is a skirt of quarter-inch galvanized hardware cloth fastened to the framing and carried into the ground in an L, twelve inches down and twelve out, so digging along the face hits wire.

  3. Gutters here carry a load that never ends

    A lot with a few trees drops its litter and finishes; a lot facing mature forest takes whatever the wind lifts off many acres. A packed trough holds a wet mat with standing water in it, a drinking source at roof height, and the overflow runs behind the fascia into the soil below.

German or American cockroach, and which came out of the treeline?

Nearly every roach question at a forest edge is really this one.

American cockroach: yes, that one is from outside

Big, reddish brown, called a palmetto bug locally. It holds genuine outdoor populations across South Carolina in leaf litter, hollow trees, mulch, woodpiles and drain lines, which describes the whole boundary band. It enters at a dried-out drain trap, a plumbing sleeve or a garage jamb, usually after heavy rain or a first sharp cold. One in the bathroom is a question about openings and moisture. See the American cockroach profile.

German cockroach: the forest had nothing to do with it

Small, tan, two dark stripes on the shield behind the head. It holds no outdoor population in this climate and did not walk across your yard. It was carried indoors inside something: a grocery box, a used appliance, secondhand furniture. It breeds in warm tight voids near food and water, and treating the yard accomplishes nothing.

The field test is where and when. Large ones at floor level near drains after a storm came from the litter; small striped ones behind a fridge arrived with an object.

What does a certified dog settle that a walk-through cannot?

Bed bugs are the one thing on this page the boundary has no bearing on. They travel with people and luggage, so a house on the fence line is at the same risk as one three miles away. That matters, because on a wooded lot people learn to blame the treeline for everything.

What a screen buys is a defensible negative. Visual inspection reads the seams a person can reach, and the evidence it finds persists for years after an infestation ends, so a stain proves only that something happened at some point. A properly imprinted dog works to the odor of live insects and viable eggs, and answers in the present tense across a whole floor.

Limits get stated up front. An alert marks odor at a location; it does not count insects or date an infestation. Sessions stay short, and every alert is confirmed visually. Canine bed bug detection has published field validation behind it, which is why we cite research there and not for rodent work.

Who is supposed to be licensed for this work in South Carolina?

  • The regulator here is the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation, which owns structural pest licensing statewide. Newcomers expecting a state agriculture department are often surprised.
  • The category covering household pests, cockroaches and rodents is 7A.
  • A company needs a DPR business licence and a certified applicator answerable for your address. Ask for the number, the name and a certificate of insurance, and treat hesitation as the answer.
  • Different work needs different credentials. Wildlife removal, wood-destroying organism reports and fumigation sit outside this page.

Which parts of Aiken do we cover here, and what do we not know?

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · 803-226-3155 · Kim@ck9ps.com.

The forest touches several distinct parts of the city and we work all of them. Winter Colony Historic District I adjoins it, and that district’s National Register nomination names the forest as a feature. Downtown Aiken sits at the head of the watershed draining through it. Houndslake lies southwest. The city-wide program is on our Aiken pest control page; the rest is under service areas.

Where the record is thin, we say so. Nobody publishes a count of houses on the boundary, or any study of pest pressure by distance from the forest, so a figure quoted for either was invented. Nor do we speak for the Foundation on hunt dates, burns or access.

Frequently asked questions

Can you get a raccoon out of my attic?

No, and we would rather say so than send a truck. We are not a wildlife trapping or removal service, and our rodent work covers rats and mice only. A raccoon, opossum or squirrel needs a licensed wildlife operator. Once it is gone and that is confirmed, we close the entry point behind it.

Is backing onto Hitchcock Woods bad for pest control?

It is a permanent condition rather than a bad one. Stable native habitat is not manufacturing your problem. What changes on a boundary lot is that vacancy never lasts, so removal alone never finishes. Sealing the building and fixing food and cover within thirty feet is what holds.

Should I clear the brush along my back fence?

On your own side, thin it and keep the fence base open and visible. Do not extend that past the property line, and do not dump clippings over it. Land beyond your pins belongs to the Hitchcock Woods Foundation and is managed deliberately, fire included.

Why not just put bait out along the boundary?

Because the supply behind the fence is effectively unlimited, so you buy the same result again every few months. It also places slow poisoned prey exactly where owls, hawks, foxes and cats hunt, at the edge of certified wildlife habitat. We trap where activity is measurable and seal the openings instead.

Do I have to take my bird feeders down?

Not necessarily. Feed by day, not by night. Fit a catch tray, sweep spilled seed, keep the feeder well away from the wall rather than under the eave, and store seed in a lidded metal can. If droppings turn up beneath it in the morning, bring it in for two weeks.

There is prescribed burning nearby. Will animals come to my house?

A burn strips low cover from one section for a while, and whatever was using it moves temporarily. If your boundary offers a woodpile, an open compost heap or an open deck, you are the obvious alternative. Have the last thirty feet in order and the shift passes you by.

Do you handle termite inspections or a CL-100 for a closing?

We do not. No termite work, no wood infestation reports, no bonds, no fumigation, no mosquito programs, no turf treatment. What we do is household pests, cockroaches, rodents, bed bugs and exclusion carpentry. A letter for a closing needs a firm holding that licence.

hero.h1: Pest Control in Houndslake, Aiken, SC
hero.lead: Houndslake is a fifty-year-old golf community in the 29803, and most of what gets into these houses was living in the landscape long before it reached a wall. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions reads the perimeter first — irrigation, mulch, shrub line, canopy — then deals with whatever is left.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Family-owned · A measured perimeter walk every visit · South and southwest Aiken

body:
The Azalea nine at Houndslake Country Club winds through the original homes. That one detail tells you more about pest work here than any survey would. The club and course opened in 1974, houses went up around them, and the shrubs planted along those first foundations have had half a century of a Sandhills growing season to do what shrubs do. A three-gallon holly set eighteen inches off the brick is now a mass leaning on the siding, over mulch nobody has pulled back.

So we start outside. It comes down to a band of ground about two feet wide running around the house, and what has been allowed to happen in it.

1974Houndslake Country Club opened, a Joe Lee design. The Post and Courier golf roundup lists it semi-private, 27 holes over three nines: Dogwood, Azalea and The Laurel
232Freeze-free days at AIKEN 4 NE, last spring freeze March 22, first fall freeze October 12 — eight months of a planting growing toward your wall
50.77 in.Aiken County average annual precipitation. Irrigation goes on top of that, over ground the USDA calls rapidly permeable sand for the first forty-four inches

Why does the pest problem here start outside the wall?

Because everything insects and rodents need is outdoors, and a mature golf community supplies it well.

Water on a schedule. Troup series soils here run sand from the surface to roughly forty-four inches before hitting clay, and the USDA calls them somewhat excessively drained. Water does not linger in that profile, which is why turf gets irrigated to stay green through July. Rain wets a wall and the wall dries. A head throwing on the same six feet of foundation every other morning never lets it.

Cover. Fifty-year-old plantings, layer on layer of pine straw and mulch laid over the last, ground cover run up to the brick. Underneath is a dark, humid, undisturbed seam at the height of your slab edge and weep holes. It is not that pests are drawn to the house. They already live against it.

Connection. Mature hardwood and pine canopy is most of what makes this neighborhood look the way it does, and where a limb rests on a roof it stops being a tree and becomes a bridge. Aiken has held Tree City USA designation for thirty-seven consecutive years as of its 2022 award. The canopy is an asset and also a route, and a route needs one limb.

We will not cast the golf course as a villain. Out-of-play ground on any course is rough, wood and water by design. We found no published habitat program for this club and will not invent one. The plain point is that your lot backs onto managed landscape rather than pavement, and managed landscape holds animals.

What clearances do we ask for, and what does each one buy?

The numbers we work to on a Houndslake lot. Each closes a mechanism, and most cost a Saturday with hand tools.

WhereWhat we ask forWhat the number does
The strip against the foundation12 to 18 inches of bare soil or washed gravel, nothing planted in itGives you a surface you can read. Rub marks, ant trails and a fresh burrow show on bare ground, not under pine straw
Mulch depth and setback2 to 3 inches maximum, held back off the slab edge, weep holes left clearMulch banked over the slab edge bridges the barriers the builder put there and holds damp against material meant to dry
Shrubs, plus any ivy or climbing cover12 inches of daylight between outer growth and wall; vines off the wall entirely, not trimmed at itSun and air reach the siding so it dries, the elevation becomes inspectable, and a covered runway to the soffit disappears
Limbs over the house6 to 8 feet of clear air between limb tips and roof edge, gutters and service wiresRemoves the bridge. The figure is generous on purpose: a climbing rat crosses a wider gap than people expect
Irrigation heads near the houseNone throwing onto siding or into the bed against the foundation; zones run early so surfaces dry by middayTurns a permanently damp band into one that dries daily — most of the ant and roach fight won with no product
Downspouts and gradeDischarge carried 4 to 6 feet out, ground falling awayStops a saturated corner, and corners are where burrows and small-ant swarms turn up

Two of those cause arguments. Nobody wants to cut a shrub that has stood since the Ford administration. Our position: keep the planting, just not touching the house. Move the bed line out, gain the gap.

What does irrigation do to ant pressure at the slab edge?

It relocates colonies, over and over, toward your house.

Household ants nest shallow — under a paver, beneath a landscape timber, in the top inch of damp mulch, in the seam where a walk meets the slab. Those sites get chosen because they hold warmth and moisture, and abandoned the moment they hold too much. Heavy rain floods a nest and the colony moves. Irrigation does the same on a timer, all summer. A nest three inches from your foundation that has to move has one dry cavity available: the void behind the veneer.

The odorous house ant is usually what people are describing when they call about tiny ants trailing a counter after a wet week. It nests readily in mulch and will site a satellite nest inside a wall — see the odorous house ant profile. Spraying a trail kills the ants you can see and settles nothing about the nest. Moving the mulch and fixing the head that soaks that corner takes the nest out of the running.

Mounds out in the turf are a separate conversation: lawn and turf treatment is not something we sell, and the rough belongs to the course.

Which cockroach walks in from the mulch bed, and which arrives in a box?

The cleanest illustration of the argument: the two species reach a house by opposite routes.

American cockroach — the landscape animal

Large, long-lived, genuinely at home outdoors in this climate. It breeds in warm damp organic material: deep mulch beds, leaf litter trapped behind shrubs, irrigation valve boxes, meter boxes, hollows in old trees. It gets in under a door, through an unsealed weep course, or up a floor drain whose trap has dried. One in a bathroom at night is an access and moisture story, not a housekeeping failure, and the fix is outdoors. See the American cockroach profile.

German cockroach — never from the yard

It does not live outdoors here and does not walk across your lawn. It is carried in: a grocery carton, a returned appliance, secondhand furniture, luggage. Then it stays close to heat and damp: inside a refrigerator compressor housing, or the cavity alongside a dishwasher. Nothing you do to the landscape touches it, which is why identification comes first. See cockroach control for how the programs differ.

Confusing the two wastes a season, because perimeter work steadily reduces American sightings and does nothing about a German population in a kitchen. We name the species on the first visit.

A limb on the roof is a road. Which rodent is using it?

Three commensal species turn up in Aiken houses and they behave nothing alike. The canopy question has exactly one right answer.

Roof rat — the one the canopy serves

The climber. It travels branches, wires and vine-covered walls, entering high and nesting high: attic insulation, the space over a tray ceiling, a soffit return. Noise overhead under mature trees is this animal first, and the branch touching the gutter is where we look. See the roof rat profile.

Norway rat — the ground floor animal

Heavier, a burrower, a poor climber. It digs along foundations, under slabs and stoops, under dense ground cover and beside the loose fill of an irrigation trench, and enters low. A canopy trim does nothing to it. Clearing the ivy bank and closing the bottom two feet does. See the Norway rat profile.

House mouse — already close by

Small range, small requirements, no need for a tree. A mouse works a territory often measured in tens of feet, so if one is inside, the source is on your lot, not across the fairway. It uses openings a rat could not, which is why our gap standard is a quarter inch. See the house mouse profile.

So a roof rat job is a roofline job and a Norway rat job a groundline job. We identify from droppings, rub marks, gnawing height and what a canine screening and trapping program turns up, and say which you have before anyone quotes repairs.

Which pests are on this program, and which do we refuse outright?

Our general pest control service, run as a perimeter program with the interior treated as a consequence.

  • Ants: identified to species, because the answer decides whether the work is in a mulch bed or a wall.
  • Cockroaches: both species, on two entirely separate programs, as above.
  • Spiders and occasional invaders: the crickets, silverfish and millipedes that live in leaf litter and come in when the litter reaches the door.
  • Rodents: canine detection, trapping and exclusion, roofline and groundline both.
  • Bed bugs: scent screening and treatment. See bed bug control.
  • Exclusion carpentry: closing what the inspection finds, to a written specification. See repairs and exclusion.

We do not offer termite treatment, termite bonds, wood infestation reports or CL-100 letters, fumigation, mosquito programs, or lawn and turf work. A page about mulch, irrigation and mature trees is precisely where a firm normally starts selling two of those. We are not going to.

Why would we rather change the landscape than sell you another spray?

Partly because it is honest and mostly because it works better. A residual product on a foundation has to survive ultraviolet light, rain and irrigation water. On a band of wall that stays wet under a shrub that never lets it dry, its useful life is a fraction of what the label contemplates. You then get quoted more visits to cover a condition a pair of loppers would have removed.

The test we would apply to any pest company, this one included, is what it says about the shrub. A firm that measures the gap, names the head to turn, points at the limb and then treats what is left is describing a shrinking problem. A firm that walks the perimeter with a wand and mentions none of it is describing a permanent one.

Which does not mean doing nothing. The claim is narrow: here the order should be conditions, then closure, then chemistry, and it gets run backwards because the third has a subscription attached.

What does a scent screen add to a bed bug inspection?

Coverage, and a per-room answer. A thorough visual inspection means dismantling a bed, lifting a mattress, pulling a headboard off the wall and working the seams. It is slow, and it only reports on the furniture you took apart. In a house with a guest room used a few weekends a year, the skipped room is the one that matters, because nobody sleeps there to be bitten.

A handler and a certified dog cover the house in one visit and settle the narrow question of whether anything is alive and where. Detection dogs on bed bugs have validation work in the published literature, which cannot be said of every canine service being sold. We run the dog again once treatment is finished.

One correction. The line about bed bugs surviving a year unfed comes from work at cool temperatures, near or below the mid fifties. In a heated Aiken house an unfed adult realistically manages weeks to a few months. Shutting a room up is not a treatment.

Which agency licenses the person treating your foundation?

  • Not a state agriculture department. South Carolina puts structural pest licensing with the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation, and people trained elsewhere get this wrong.
  • The certification category covering the household, rodent and cockroach work here is 7A.
  • The company needs a DPR business license, and each location must carry a Designated Certified Applicator. An applicator is certified as an individual; the business is licensed on its own.
  • General liability has to be carried at $100,000 or above.
  • Worth asking before anyone walks your perimeter: license number and category, whether the person walking it is certified, and who does the carpentry, to what written scope.

What we cannot tell you about Houndslake housing

There is no neighborhood-level Census data for this place. No build year, no breakdown of foundation types, no distribution of lot sizes. So we do not quote numbers we cannot source.

That matters because a confident figure is circulating. At least one directory states Houndslake homes were primarily built in the 1980s and 1990s, on a page that also puts the neighborhood in north-central Aiken, in the 29801, two miles from downtown. The club is at 901 Houndslake Drive in the 29803, on the south and southwest side, as Golf Digest, Visit Aiken and the Post and Courier confirm. A source that misplaces its subject by a whole ZIP code is not one we will repeat on a build era.

Where else do we work on this side of town?

Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · 803-226-3155 · Kim@ck9ps.com. Houndslake sits off Silver Bluff Road. We come in from Windsor, which is close enough to keep appointments inside the same week.

Close by we cover Woodside Plantation and Cedar Creek, and the Winter Colony in toward the center. Our city-wide program sits on the Aiken pest control page, and every place we cover is on service areas.

Frequently asked questions

Will cutting the shrubs back off the house really reduce what gets inside?

Yes, measurably, and it is the cheapest item on the list. Growth against siding keeps a strip of wall permanently damp and shaded, hides the openings we are looking for, and carries cover to the entry point. Open twelve inches of daylight along that wall and you remove the harborage, let the surface dry, and make the elevation inspectable.

My irrigation runs at night. Does that matter?

Late-night cycles are the worst option for a foundation, because the wall stays wet past sunrise. Early morning is better: the turf still gets its water and the siding, mulch and slab edge dry through the day. The bigger fix is aiming. No head near the house should throw spray onto the wall.

There is scratching in the attic. Do I have to take the tree down?

Almost never. Contact creates the highway, not the tree, so the work is trimming limb tips back six to eight feet from the roof edge, gutters and wires. Removing a mature hardwood is expensive and often misses the real route anyway, if the animal is climbing a downspout or a vine. We identify the route first.

Do you treat the lawn or the golf course?

No. Lawn and turf treatment is not a service we offer, and the course is the club’s ground. We work the structure and the band of landscape immediately around it, which is where pressure on your house originates. If you want mounds handled out in the turf, that is a lawn care company’s job and we will say so.

Termites, or a CL-100 letter for a closing?

Neither. Termite treatment, bonds, wood infestation reports and fumigation are not things we sell, and we will not treat the enquiry as an opening. Different license, different trade entirely. For a closing, a firm holding the correct category should issue the letter directly.

If we fix the perimeter, how often do you need to come out?

Less often, and that is the point. What sets the interval is pressure at the wall, not a subscription tier. Where the shrub line is off the siding, the mulch is thin and set back, the heads aimed away and the roofline clear, we are treating a much smaller problem, and we would rather quote that honestly.

Related services

General Pest ControlRodent ControlCockroach ControlRepairs & ExclusionBed Bug Control

Have the perimeter read before you buy another treatment

Tell us what you have seen and where, and we will walk the ground with a tape rather than a spray wand — shrub line, mulch depth, irrigation throw, downspouts, roofline. You get the list of what to change, the species named, and a plan that gets smaller instead of bigger.
