h1: Pest Control in Irmo, SC

hero.lead: Most people who say they live in Irmo are not inside the town limits, and most Irmo houses went up inside a single fifteen-year window. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions works both of those facts across the Irmo area, Lexington and Richland sides alike: ants and roaches, rodents, and bed bugs screened by certified dog.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · Kim@ck9ps.com · Straddling the Lexington–Richland line, northwest of Columbia

body:
Two things govern this page. The word Irmo covers at least three footprints, and the smallest is the one the Census measures. And the housing here never accumulated over a century the way older Midlands towns did. It landed in one push and is now aging on one schedule.

Both are matters of record, disagreements included, because anyone comparing quotes should know which Irmo each was priced for.

62.9%Of the Town of Irmo’s 4,876 housing units date from the 1970s or 1980s — 1,598 plus 1,467 (ACS 2020–2024 five-year, table B25034)
91.8%Detached single-family inside the town limits; structures of five units or more are 3.1 percent (ACS 2020–2024 five-year, table B25024)
12,204 vs 46,000+Town population, 1 July 2025 Census estimate, against 46,000 to 50,000 residents across about 33 square miles of Irmo Fire District (irmofire.org)

Which Irmo are we actually talking about?

Ask four people where the boundary runs and you get four defensible answers. Here is what the institutions say.

What somebody means by IrmoPeopleAreaSource
Town of Irmo, the municipal limits12,204 (2025 estimate)6.86 sq miCensus QuickFacts
Seven Oaks CDP, unincorporated15,9217.7 sq miCensus Reporter, ACS 2024
Irmo Fire District, founded 1963about 46,000 to 50,000about 33 sq miirmofire.org
School District Five, Lexington and Richlandnot publishedabout 196 sq milexrich5.org

Read the top two rows again: the unincorporated community next door holds more people than the incorporated town. The fire district, bounded by the county lines, Interstate 26, the Saluda River and Lake Murray, is five times the town’s size.

We work the fire-district version. If your mail says Irmo, we come. What changes is which numbers apply: every Census figure here describes the town only.

The county question splits the same way. The Town’s website gives its Woodrow Street address as Lexington County; the fire district states that all of the town lies within its district whether a part sits in Lexington or Richland. We follow the fire district. Irmo straddles the line.

The Okra Strut makes the point sideways: about 25,000 people by the Town’s count, historically up to 60,000, into a town of 12,204. Three sources give three founding years, so we say early 1970s.

What is on our truck here, and what is not?

  • Ants, spiders, silverfish and other occasional invaders — see general pest control.
  • Cockroaches, handled as two unrelated problems — see cockroach control.
  • Rats and mice, located, trapped, then shut out — see rodent control.
  • Bed bugs, screened by certified dog, treated as its own job — see bed bug control.
  • Exclusion and carpentry repair on vents, sweeps and penetrations — see repairs.

Outside our scope, stated once: no wood infestation report, no CL-100 letter, no mosquito programme, no fumigation, no lawn spraying, none of it subcontracted.

Why does a town built all at once fail all at once?

Table B25034 puts 1,598 of the town’s units in the 1970s and 1,467 in the 1980s. Only 160 units, 3.3 percent, predate 1970, and the estimate records zero from the 1950s and zero from 1939 or earlier. A town chartered on Christmas Eve in 1890 has no pre-war housing left inside its boundary.

There is a documented reason. The Town grows chiefly by annexation, and state law permits annexing only property already touching the boundary. A municipality that expands by absorbing finished subdivisions shows exactly this shape: a bulge where those subdivisions were built, a second wave of 957 units since 2010, nothing else.

Walking a street, the consequence is plain. Houses out of the same few years came out of the same catalogue: same siding, same window package, same insulation depth, same vent sizes, same shrubs at the same planted size. So the failures arrive together. Sealant has a service life, weatherstrip has a service life, screen rusts on a schedule. One neighbour finds mice behind a gable louver; the identical louver sits four doors along.

What happens where forty-year-old shrubs meet forty-year-old siding?

A house finished in 1978 was landscaped in 1978, with plants set close to the wall so the beds looked filled. Lexington County averages 51.98 inches of precipitation a year per the state climatology office. One-gallon shrubs are now woody and chest high, pressing on the cladding they were meant to soften.

  • Contact is a bridge. A branch touching a wall bypasses the ground entirely. We want eighteen inches of clear air between outermost growth and cladding.
  • The wall stops drying. Shaded, still air holds moisture against siding after rain, and damp turns an ant scouting trip into a colony.
  • Mulch has climbed. Four decades of topping up raises the bed. Leave six inches of foundation showing above it, and keep it shallow within a foot of the wall.
  • Limbs reach the roof. Trees planted small the same season now overhang the eave, and roof rats treat a branch as a ramp.

Cut the vegetation back and half the exterior work on a house of this age is done. We do not sell that, and we say it first, because it changes what the rest of the visit finds.

What have forty summers done to the windows and doors?

Assume nothing has been replaced until you have looked. With 81.6 percent owner-occupancy and 82 percent of residents in the same house a year earlier, original hardware is still in service here.

Sliders and their weep slots

Horizontal sliders of that era drain through small slots at the base of the outer frame. Grit and paint plug them, and a blocked weep is still an open slot at the height insects travel. Clear them; do not seal them. Later insert units, foamed into the old jamb rather than flashed, often leave a clear run into the wall cavity.

Sliding patio doors

Almost every plan of this vintage has one, and it is the weakest opening in the house. The pile weatherstrip on the interlock flattens, rollers drop, the bottom rail stops meeting the sill. Daylight at the corner of a closed patio door is an invitation.

Sweeps, thresholds, garage doors

Sweeps wear at the ends before the middle, so put a light outside a closed door at night and watch the corners. A sectional garage door’s bottom seal hardens and takes a set, and on settled concrete it opens at one corner.

What sits above the ceiling and under the floor?

An honest limit first: no source we could find breaks out crawl space against slab for Irmo, so we quote no share. What we can describe is how each looks at this age.

Attic insulation laid in the late 1970s went in at a depth nobody would specify now, and blown fiberglass has settled since. Settled insulation shows runways, and a track across a level attic floor stays legible for months, giving direction of travel. The pull-down stair opening is usually the largest unsealed hole in the ceiling plane, and an attic air handler puts duct connections and a condensate line through boots taped for air, never meshed.

Under a crawl space of the same period, rectangular foundation vents carry light screen that rusts out at the corners first, and the polyethylene ground cover, where one was laid at all, is torn and shoved aside. Plumbing and wiring cross the sill at holes drilled generously and closed casually. We photograph whatever we recommend closing.

Which cockroach is it, and does the build year matter?

American cockroach — vintage matters

Large, reddish-brown, what people call a palmetto bug. It lives outdoors in mulch, leaf litter, drains and sewer lines, which is what forty-year-old foundation beds provide. It enters by dried floor drain traps, unsealed plumbing sleeves, crawl vents and door bottoms, and on identical houses it uses identical routes. See the profile.

German cockroach — vintage is irrelevant

Small, tan, two dark bars behind the head. It sustains no outdoor population in this climate and does not cross yards. It is carried in by cardboard, groceries, a secondhand appliance or a moving load, then settles in the warm cavity nearest food. See the profile.

Why that decides the method

Perimeter product outside is aimed at the first and does nothing about the second. Worse, a repellent pushed into a German cockroach harbourage scatters it into adjoining voids. That job is baiting and harbourage reduction.

Why does exclusion look the same house after house?

Because the openings are the same openings. Gable louvers, crawl vents, dryer terminations and utility penetrations were specified together and age together. We still measure yours; we arrive knowing what to look at.

The size rules do not bend. Anything over a quarter of an inch takes a house mouse, over half an inch takes a rat, and both widen an opening that is close. So the order is fixed: cover with metal that teeth cannot work, then seal, then treat. Quarter-inch galvanised hardware cloth over vents. Copper mesh packed behind a hard cover, never as the cover. Foam belongs inside an assembly. Identification is on the house mouse profile; sealing goes through our exclusion crew.

Certified dogs work indoors to narrow down where activity is, rather than reasoning outward from one pile of droppings. The limit, stated up front: we publish no accuracy figure for canine rodent detection in buildings, because none has been validated in the field. The peer-reviewed work covers bed bugs.

What does a dog add in a house holding forty years of belongings?

Scale. A visual bed bug inspection is a sampling exercise dressed as a search: a person checks what a person can reach and move, in the time available, then calls the result a house. Irmo households average 2.54 people, the largest of the five Midlands cities we cover, and the homes are overwhelmingly owner-occupied. Furniture that has not shifted in fifteen years will not shift on a Tuesday.

A dog works odour, so reach and sightline stop being the constraint. It covers the primary bedroom, the guest room nobody has slept in since Christmas, the recliner and the sofa in the time a visual inspector spends on one mattress. Rooms that come back clear matter as much as the rest.

Limits go in writing before booking. An indication marks odour at a location; it counts no insects and dates nothing. Each is confirmed by hand, and an ambiguous spot gets monitors and a return rather than treatment on a maybe. Our founder, Kimberly Camera, brought a scent-detection career past its twenty-eighth year into this business, FEMA Urban Search & Rescue canine deployment included. See the bed bug profile.

Who may legally treat the inside of your house?

Not who most people assume. The regulator is neither a health agency nor a department of agriculture: structural pest licensing here runs through the Department of Pesticide Regulation at Clemson University, and household insect, rodent and bed bug work is Category 7A.

Ask any firm for three things before it treats your house, ours included. The DPR business licence. The certified applicator responsible for your address. A current liability certificate. Hesitation on any one has answered the question.

How does a Windsor company actually cover Irmo?

Straight answer on distance, since you can check it yourself. Our base at 320 Wendy Lane sits about 63 driving miles away, roughly one hour and twenty-two minutes, per distance-cities.com. Straight-line it is under 46 miles, but the road runs out to I-20 and back: Irmo is four miles further from us than Cayce as the crow flies, eighteen further to drive.

That is a scheduling fact, not a capability one. Irmo runs on our Midlands routing rather than same-day call-out, booked in blocks with a window we can keep. First appointments need somebody home; later visits generally do not.

Nearby we also cover Lexington, Columbia twelve miles southeast, and Cayce down the river. The rest is on the service areas page.

Frequently asked questions

My address says Irmo but I am told I am not in the town. Does that affect service?

Not ours. We work the wider Irmo area, which the fire district maps at roughly 33 square miles against the town’s 6.86. It does affect other things, such as which police force answers. Every housing statistic here covers the town limits only.

Is Irmo in Lexington County or Richland County?

Both, and the sources genuinely disagree. The Town’s own website gives a Lexington County location for its Woodrow Street offices, while the fire district says all of the town falls inside its district regardless of which county a part sits in. We follow the fire district.

Our whole subdivision went up at once. Does that really matter?

More than anything else about the building. Identical houses got identical vent sizes, weatherstrip and sealant, and those wear out on a shared timetable. When a neighbour finds an entry point, the same detail on your house is worth checking.

Big reddish roaches appear after heavy rain. What is that?

Almost certainly the American cockroach, moving in from outdoors when its harbourage floods. Mulch beds, leaf litter, drains and sewer lines are where it lives, and mature foundation plantings hold the damp it wants. Dry the perimeter and seal the route in.

Do I need to empty rooms before a canine bed bug screen?

No. Emptying and dismantling is what a thorough visual inspection demands, which is why they come up short in a full house. A dog works odour, so a crowded room argues for booking the screen, not delaying it. Indications get confirmed by hand.

Do you handle wood infestation reports for a closing?

No. We issue no CL-100 or wood infestation report of any kind, run no mosquito programme, do not fumigate and do not treat turf. Our work is ants and roaches, rodents, bed bugs, and the carpentry that shuts them out.

h1: Pest Control in Jackson, SC

hero.lead: Jackson is a town of long-held houses. The median resident is close to sixty, most households here are one or two people, and many of these homes have stayed with the same family for decades. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions works ZIP 29831 for rodents, roaches, ants, spiders and bed bugs, and does the sealing itself.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Family-owned · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · Kim@ck9ps.com · Southern Aiken County
badges: We do the crawl space work

body:
Jackson sits two miles northeast of the Savannah River, and the 2020 census counted 1,521 residents across three and a half square miles of Sandhills ground. Part of the town fell inside the original 1950 boundary drawn for the Savannah River Plant, and survived only because the construction parameters shifted while the surveyors worked. Households that expected to be moved were not.

You can see it in the buildings. This is owner-occupied ground, held a long time and mended a piece at a time. By median age it is also far older than Aiken County as a whole, and those two facts decide how a pest call ought to run here.

59.8 yearsMedian age in Jackson town, ACS 2024 five-year estimate, plus or minus 10.3 years, against 42.1 for Aiken County (Census Reporter)
1.8People per household in Jackson, plus or minus 0.7, on the same ACS 2024 five-year release (Census Reporter)
42%Aiken County units past forty years of age in 2023. A COUNTY number, and the only sourceable housing-age figure (SRSCRO Aiken–Augusta Regional Housing Study, September 2025, page 14)

What changes when the median resident is nearly sixty?

The figure is 59.8 years, from the American Community Survey five-year estimates, plus or minus 10.3. Read it as a range, as you should anywhere this small. Even the bottom of that range sits clear of the county median of 42.1, and household size agrees at 1.8 people.

You know the building better than we will. Somebody thirty years in a house knows which window sticks in August and which corner the ants use every spring. We ask for that before opening a toolbox.

A plan sold for its own sake is a poor deal. Closing the openings once usually costs less across five years than paying somebody to spray the same wall forever.

The work under the house is ours. This is not a comment on anyone’s capability. A crawl space is eighteen inches of headroom over a sand floor with nobody nearby if a knee goes. Plenty of people in their seventies could still do it; far fewer ought to do it alone. We bring coveralls, lights and a second technician.

What do forty years of small repairs leave behind?

A well-kept house of this age is not one building. It is thirty repairs made across five decades by different hands to different standards, and rodents read the seams.

  • Where two eras of siding meet. Vinyl or hardboard over original wood leaves the old wall standing inside the new one, and at corner boards and gable returns the two layers rarely close. A quarter of an inch is all a house mouse asks for.
  • Abandoned penetrations. Each time the plumbing was redone or a cable came through, a fresh hole was bored and the old one stayed open. A four-inch dryer duct in a hole cut to five leaves a two-finger ring.
  • Doors re-hung and never re-shimmed. A back door that settled three-eighths of an inch shows daylight at the strike side and both threshold ends. Half an inch on that line and a rat is through without touching the sides.
  • Accessibility retrofits. A ramp ledger, grab rail or lift bracket is lagged through siding into framing, and those bolt holes stay open. The ramp then makes a dry covered run along the wall, the protected route a rat prefers.
  • Brick veneer weep holes. The open head joints at the bottom course, about three-eighths of an inch wide, are drainage and must stay that way. Stainless weep guards shut them to rodents without blocking water; caulk only traps moisture.

Add the crawl space hatch, usually plywood cut to fit twice and held shut with a block. None of this is neglect; it is what maintenance looks like spread over forty years. The county figure gives it context: 42 percent of Aiken County housing units had passed forty years by 2023. County-level, because no town figure is publishable.

What is on our list here, and what is not?

  • Ants indoors and the outdoor colonies feeding them
  • German and American cockroaches, treated as two different animals
  • Spiders, silverfish, crickets and the rest of the occasional invaders
  • Rats and mice: canine detection, trapping, and sealing that lasts
  • Bed bugs, screened by a certified dog and handled separately
  • Hardware cloth, sweeps, weep guards and sealed penetrations, fitted by us

Boundaries stated plainly, because vagueness wastes your afternoon. We do not treat termites, we do not write the wood infestation report a closing needs, and we run no mosquito or lawn programme. Where a crawl space shows damage or a moisture condition we photograph it and say so, then leave it to a firm certified for that. Everything above sits under general pest control.

Why is rodent exclusion something we do rather than something we sell?

Because the part still working after we leave is labour, not product: hardware cloth cut oversize and fastened, copper mesh packed into a void and sealed over, mortar patched where a pier lost a joint.

Here is the practice we think is worst in our trade. A company inspects, writes a report full of recommendations, and hands it over for the homeowner to arrange. For a household of one or two people that report is a dead letter, because nobody wants to chase a contractor into a crawl space for a small job. So the mesh, sweeps and mortar ride in the van.

Detection comes first. Certified dogs locate live activity inside a structure rather than guessing from droppings in one corner, and nobody has field-validated an accuracy number for rodent work inside buildings, which we say out loud. Method on the rodent control page, carpentry on exclusion and repairs, the animal in the house mouse profile.

What actually happens on a first visit?

  1. We talk on the porch first

    What have you seen, in which room, at what time of day, since when. After decades in a house, your account beats anything we could infer in an hour.

  2. The outside, on foot and then on our knees

    The foundation line, every vent and door bottom, the weep course, and the band where water, power, gas and dryer vent come through. Openings get measured, not eyeballed.

  3. Under the house and into the attic

    Ours to do. You get photographs of what is down there, so nobody has to take a torch under a house to see what we are describing.

  4. Inside, at whatever pace suits you

    Under the sinks, behind the range, the water heater closet, the rooms nobody uses now. We ask before moving furniture and put it back where it stood.

  5. Findings written down, itemised

    What is there, what closes it, what each item costs, and what needs nothing. If the honest answer is one follow-up look in six weeks, the paper says that.

Kitchen roach or crawl space roach?

One word covers two species with nothing in common but the name. The answer decides the whole job, and both sit under cockroach control.

German cockroach: it was carried through the door

Small and tan, with two dark stripes running back over the shield. Outdoors in this state it barely persists at all, so it did not wander in from a yard. It arrived with something: a second-hand appliance, a carton, boxes from a relative’s house or a storage unit. In a settled household an outbreak usually traces to one recent arrival, and that source can often be found. See the German cockroach profile.

American cockroach: it came up a pipe or in from the crawl space

The big reddish-brown one, up to an inch and a half, that people here call a palmetto bug. It lives outside, in mulch, drain lines and the damp under a porch. Sandhills uplands drain fast, but the low pockets between them stay wet and suit it. In a two-person house check one thing first: a bathroom nobody uses lets its trap evaporate within weeks, and a dry trap is an open pipe from the sewer. A cup of water down each unused drain monthly costs nothing. See the American cockroach profile.

Why does a canine screen matter if you cannot strip the bed yourself?

Consider what a thorough visual bed bug inspection physically demands. Lift the mattress. Pull the box spring out and turn it. Tip the frame, take the headboard down, kneel to read the rail undersides and the tack strip at the carpet edge. That is an hour of awkward lifting, and telling somebody with a replaced shoulder to do it is not advice, it is a brush-off.

A trained dog covers a bedroom in a couple of minutes with the bed still made, reading odour from seams nobody could open anyway. It answers the present-tense question: is anything alive in here now. Old staining behind a headboard proves something happened once, not that it is happening.

Two things we make a point of saying. Bed bugs are hitchhikers with no connection whatever to housekeeping: they travel on luggage, a coat, furniture, home from a hospital stay. And bites are unreliable, since reaction varies enormously and some people show nothing. We check the recliner as carefully as the bed, because a chair somebody sleeps in most nights gets missed constantly. Detail on the bed bug detection and treatment page and in the bed bug profile.

Why is bait the wrong opening move where a pet lives?

Anticoagulant rodenticides work slowly by design. An animal that has fed spends days going dull and unsteady before it dies, which makes it the easiest meal on the property, and the dose travels into whatever eats it. A cat, a small dog nosing through the shrubs, a hawk working a field edge: all downstream of that decision. Audubon records over two hundred bird species at its sanctuary here, a reminder of what else hunts the same rats.

There is a plainer objection. A poisoned rat dies wherever it happens to be, usually inside a wall, leaving a smell for two or three weeks and nothing you can reach. Where the crawl space is not an option, that is a bad trade.

So the sequence runs the other way. Trapping goes indoors, out of a pet’s reach, and we ask where your animals sleep, feed and wander before a device is placed. Where exterior bait has any role, it belongs in locked tamper-resistant stations, once the building is sealed.

Who is licensed for this work, and what should you ask to see?

South Carolina puts structural pest regulation in an unexpected place: the Department of Pesticide Regulation at Clemson University, rather than a state agriculture department. Household and structural work falls in category 7A. Small animal work is a separate category again.

At your door you may ask three things, and an honest technician answers without hesitating. Does the company hold a current DPR business licence. Is this person certified, or working under a certified applicator. What is being applied, and may you see the label. Anyone who goes vague there has answered you anyway.

What we will not print about Jackson

  • No founding year. The town runs a 75th anniversary project with an exhibit at Town Hall, pointing at the Savannah River Plant era, but no source states an incorporation year, so neither do we.
  • No subdivision names. Not one could be verified. The roads we can source come from official addresses: Main Street, Town Hall at 106; Atomic Road, the middle school at 18731.
  • No housing-age table, no vacancy claim. Median year built and tenure split are not retrievable here, hence the county label above. Housing units come in at 1,090 against 1,026 households, but both margins run near a third of the estimate, so that arithmetic means nothing. One dollar figure is worth quoting: median home value, $199,800 plus or minus $35,310.
  • No flood statement. The county’s environmental review volume would not open for us, so we claim nothing about floodplain at any address here.

Where do we work around Jackson?

Our base is 320 Wendy Lane in Windsor. In town the fixed points are Atomic Road, the ABBE library branch and October’s Hook & Cook Festival. At the edge of the postal area sits Audubon’s Silver Bluff Center and Sanctuary, 4542 Silver Bluff Road: 3,410 acres along 2.6 miles of the Savannah River, some 50 acres of it ponds and wetlands.

Hold that against a town of fifteen hundred people. Managed forest, grassland and standing water on that scale, at the edge of the houses, keeps a permanent supply line running for everything that lives outdoors and occasionally comes in.

We also cover New Ellenton to the north, Beech Island up the South Carolina bank, Windsor to the east where we are based, and North Augusta. The whole list is on the service areas page, or tell us what the house is doing.

Frequently asked questions

I have been in this house thirty years with no roaches. Why now?

Something changed, and it is usually findable. A repair opened a route that used to be closed. A spare bathroom drain dried out and stopped sealing against the sewer. An appliance or a load of boxes came in. We would rather find that change than spray baseboards.

Will you actually do the sealing, or hand me a list of jobs?

We do it. Hardware cloth, copper mesh, door sweeps, weep guards and mortar travel in the van, and the work happens on the visit wherever it can. Larger carpentry is quoted separately, but you are never left hunting somebody willing to crawl under a house for a two-hour job.

Do I need a monthly plan?

Often not. Recurring service earns its place where pressure is constant, such as an ongoing German cockroach problem. For a settled house with a sealed envelope, repair plus one follow-up look is frequently the whole answer. We will say which case you are in, including when saying it costs us the contract.

I cannot strip the beds. Can you still check for bed bugs?

Yes, and that is exactly what a detection dog is for, since it screens a made bed in a couple of minutes with nothing dismantled. Where an alert needs confirming by eye, our technician does the lifting. Chairs and recliners are checked as carefully as beds.

We have a small dog. Is any of this safe around her?

It changes the order of the work, not the result. Traps go where she cannot reach them, loose bait goes nowhere at all, and exterior bait sits in a locked station only after the building is sealed. Tell us where she sleeps, eats and roams.

Do you handle termites or the report needed for a sale?

Neither. Termite treatment, wood infestation reports and bonds are not services we offer, and a closing therefore needs a company licensed to issue that document. If our work takes us under your house and we see damage, we photograph it and say so, which is not an offer to treat it.

Have somebody else go under the house

Tell us what you have seen and roughly when it started. We walk the foundation line and the utility band, go under and into the attic ourselves, and put the findings in writing with a price on each item. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions, 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856.

h1: Pest Control in Johnston, SC

hero.lead: Johnston handles fruit. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions works the buildings fruit passes through, from packing sheds and coolers to the houses around them. General pest control, rodent work, cockroaches split by species, canine bed bug screening. We work on structures, never on crops, and this page says where that line falls.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · Kim@ck9ps.com · Structures only, no crop work, no fumigation

body:
The town exists because of a railroad. When the Charlotte, Columbia and Augusta line pushed west in the late 1860s, Dr. Edward Jones Mims talked its president, William Johnston, into routing track through his plantation and agreed to name the town for him. It chartered on 22 June 1877, having outgrown the name Johnson’s Turnout.

Fruit came later and has not left. The town calls itself the Peach Capital of the World, the Ridge grows roughly 60 percent of South Carolina’s peaches, and the Johnston Development Corporation scheduled the 42nd Peach Blossom Festival for 2 May 2026. Fruit at commercial volume must be handled indoors. Those buildings are ours.

84,630 tonsSouth Carolina’s 2024 peach harvest, second nationally behind California. Clemson calls Edgefield a Ridge county
1,160 ±224Housing units in Johnston, ACS 2020–2024 five-year via Census Reporter. An error bar near 19 percent, so the town percentages below describe shape, not precision
94.56 sq miLand in ZIP 29832 against 2.7 square miles inside the town limits. Orchards sit outside that line; the buildings receiving fruit sit close to it

What does general pest control cover here, and where does it stop?

General pest control means ants, cockroaches, spiders, silverfish and occasional invaders, plus the sealing that decides whether they return. Three specialisms sit beside it: rodent detection with trapping and exclusion, canine bed bug screening, and cockroach work split by species.

Now the boundary, stated hard, because on the Ridge it matters more than anywhere else we work. We do not treat crops. Nothing we apply goes onto a tree, down a row or into an orchard block. We do not fumigate: not a building, not a load, not a bin of fruit.

We work on the building: floor, drains, walls, openings, stored equipment, the ground around it. Termites belong to somebody else, as do mosquito and lawn programmes.

What kind of building is a packing shed?

It is two buildings wearing one roof. For a few weeks it is one of the most demanding food environments in the county, then it sits dark until summer.

During the runThe rest of the year
InsideFruit moving constantly, culls accumulating, juice on rollers and floorAn empty floor and the residue nobody reached
WaterHydrocooler, dump tank, spray bars, drains carrying solids all dayDry traps, and a dry trap is an open pipe to the sewer
OpeningsDock doors up for hours, vehicles all day, lights on lateShut for months, nobody looking at the seals
Our workMonitoring, counts, quick response, working around productionInspection, drains, sealing, carpentry impossible in July

The second column is where the value sits, since structural repair is cheaper and better done when the line is cold. Programme structure is on our food processing page.

Where does the sugar go once the fruit is graded out?

A grading line exists to remove fruit, and everything it rejects is still sugar and water, fermenting within a day or two in July heat. Add drops from the yard and split fruit from the dump tank. Volume is not the issue. Residence time is.

House fly

The generalist that turns waste into more flies. It breeds in moist decaying organic material and in warm weather runs egg to adult in roughly a week to ten days, so a cull pile standing a fortnight is not attracting flies, it is producing them. See the house fly profile.

Small vinegar flies

The ones that ruin an inspection. They need no pile, only a film: residue on the lip of a bin, under a roller bed, inside a drain. You cannot spray these into remission, and a fogging quote is a repeat visit being sold. Ants are evidence the same way, since a trail ends at residue.

Waste handling fixes more of this than chemistry: culls moved daily, bins on hard standing, lids that meet.

One thing we do not sell. Yellowjackets and paper wasps work fallen fruit hard, and we are asked about them here more than anywhere else. A stinging insect programme is not part of what this company offers, and we will not imply otherwise by staying vague. That nest needs another firm.

What does a wash line leave in the building?

Permanent water for the season, in a structure dry the other nine months. Floor drains become the most productive habitat in the building, and the breeding medium is not the water but the organic film lining the pipe above the trap. That film feeds small flies and shelters American cockroaches.

Condensation is the second problem, since cold surfaces in a humid room drip onto pallets and cartons, and wet cellulose is habitat. Washdown is often mistaken for treatment: high-pressure water at a wall junction drives moisture into the cavity behind and moves insects instead of killing them.

What comes back inside on the bins and pallets?

Between seasons, field bins and pallets go outside: along a fence, under a shelter, stacked at a field edge, on the ground. Wood absorbs juice and holds moisture, the stacks make hundreds of protected voids, and nothing disturbs them for months. In spring the lot comes indoors.

What travels with them: rodents nesting in the voids, Norway rats at ground level and mice anywhere in the pile; wasps building where nobody goes; ants and American cockroaches from the litter beneath. Rodent detection at a shed is mostly yard work.

  1. Break the stacks two or three weeks early

    Not the morning of the first load. Whatever lives in them needs somewhere to go that is not the building you are opening.

  2. Look at the moment of lift

    The instant a bin leaves the ground is the only chance to see underneath it. Droppings, nesting material and egg cases vanish from view seconds later.

  3. Close the shed first, then load it

    Wash and dry the bins, then seal the building before stock goes in. Sealing afterwards traps what arrived.

German or American cockroach in a fruit building?

German cockroach, an arrival

Small, tan, twin dark bars behind the head, and it does not walk in from an orchard. It arrives inside objects: a carton, a returned tote, a used refrigerator, a bag from another building. Then it settles where warmth, moisture and a tight seam meet. The highest-yield inspection is often the break room, not the line. German cockroach profile.

American cockroach, a plumbing report

Large, reddish brown, and able to live outdoors. It comes up: from drains, cleanouts, the pit under a tank, mulch and pallet litter banked against a wall. One seen at six in the morning beside a floor drain is information about drainage and a gap at ground level. American cockroach profile.

Where do the crews stay, and how should that be handled?

Packing and harvest are seasonal, so people arrive on a schedule and leave on one. Where a grower houses crew, or a landlord lets rooms by the month, the question is bed bugs. Start with what it is not.

Not a hygiene failure, not a poverty indicator, not a reflection on anybody sleeping in the room. They are a furniture and luggage problem, arriving in a secondhand mattress or a couch left by a previous tenant. Blaming the occupants is counterproductive as well as wrong, because it makes people hide a problem until the building has it.

Johnston has unusual amounts of small multifamily for a town this size: about 16.6 percent of units sit in buildings of five to nine apartments. Shared walls change the scope, and screening one unit while ignoring the two either side is how a building keeps a problem it paid twice to remove. A dog reads odor from seams nobody will unpick. Treatment sits under bed bug detection and treatment.

What should be in the file when a buyer asks?

Fresh produce moves against a food-safety expectation whether or not anyone has audited you, and pest control shows up in that as paper.

  • A site drawing with every device numbered and placed, matching what is on the wall.
  • A dated record per visit: what was inspected, what was found, what was done and by whom.
  • Counts that trend. One reading says nothing; the same monitor over six visits says whether the programme works.
  • Structural findings dated when raised, with the material and dimension that closes each.
  • Applications logged by product, strength, placement, the pest targeted and who applied it.

What you will not get is a clause number. Schemes revise their codes and the numbering moves, so citing last year’s paragraph to a quality manager is worse than citing none. Global GAP is one certification that turns up on Ridge packing operations, and whoever oversees a packing house is not who inspects a dining room. Tell us which scheme holds you and the record is written for that reader. Kitchens sit on the restaurant and food service page.

Who licenses this work in South Carolina?

Not the agency most people guess. Pesticide licensing here runs through the Department of Pesticide Regulation, housed at Clemson University rather than a state agriculture department. The credential for work in and around buildings is Category 7A: health-related, institutional, industrial and structural. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions holds it. Its founder, Kimberly Camera, has twenty-eight years in scent detection, including work with FEMA Urban Search & Rescue.

Treating a growing crop falls under a different category held by different applicators, which is the regulatory form of the boundary above. Before signing with anyone, ask for the DPR business licence in the firm’s legal name, the Designated Certified Applicator for your location, and proof of financial responsibility.

What about the streets themselves?

Most of Johnston is not a shed. It is roughly a thousand households on an old grid, with a National Register historic district along Calhoun, Edisto, Lee, Mims, Jackson, Church and Addison Streets. The housing is old and settled: median construction year 1967, 15.3 percent predating 1940, 63.1 percent owner-occupied against Edgefield town’s even split.

What that produces is an unremarkable list: ants along a slab edge in spring, large roaches after a wet stretch, mice moving toward warmth as the ground cools. One note on what we do not print: Old Edgefield Pottery has published that it hopes to reopen in Johnston, and hoping to is not being here, so we will not call it a Johnston business yet.

We work from 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856, about 29 miles from Johnston in a straight line and further by road. Trenton sits between here and the Aiken County line, same Ridge belt, though no packing operation is documented there. Edgefield is the county seat, and we run south to Aiken and North Augusta. The full service-area list is here, or describe the building and what it is doing.

Frequently asked questions

Will you treat our orchard or spray the trees?

No. We do not apply anything to a crop, a tree, a row or a field, and we will not take that booking under another description. Our licence and our equipment are for structures. Orchard work is a separate trade.

Do you fumigate a shed, a load or a container?

No, and it is worth being blunt, because fumigation gets asked for by name around fruit. We do not offer it in any form. If a fumigant is genuinely what a job needs, that is a licensed specialty and we would say so.

The shed only runs a few months. Can you work around that?

Yes, but February should not look like July. Monitoring, inspection and canine screening fit around production with some scheduling; structural work does not. In-season visits are short and about counts. Off-season visits are when bin storage, drains, seals and exclusion get fixed.

We are getting wasps around the cull bin. Can you deal with it?

No, and we say so immediately rather than send somebody. Stinging insect work is not part of what this company sells, so a nest at a loading area or in a soffit needs a firm that does it routinely. The flies, ants and rodents stay ours.

Do you handle termites or write a CL-100 for a sale?

Neither. No termite treatment, no bonds and no wood infestation report, so a closing needs a company certified for that letter. If other work puts us under a floor and we see damage, we photograph it and pass it on.

Our tenants have bed bugs. How do you handle it without embarrassing anybody?

Quietly. We arrive unmarked where you ask, screen with a dog rather than pulling rooms apart, and discuss findings with whoever is paying rather than in a corridor. We would also ask to screen the neighbouring units, since shared walls decide the outcome.

h1: Pest Control in Kalmia Hills (Kalmia Hill), Aiken, SC

hero.h1: Pest Control in Kalmia Hills (Kalmia Hill), Aiken, SC
hero.lead: Kalmia Hills sits between two edges. Overhead is a loblolly and longleaf pine canopy with a kalmia understory beneath it. Along the southern boundary runs the Norfolk Southern line. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions covers ants, roaches, spiders, rodents and bed bugs across this north-side Aiken subdivision.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · Family-owned · North Aiken, ZIP 29801 · Aiken County and the CSRA region
badges: Needle duff and mulch at grade

body:
Start with the name, because plenty of listings get it wrong and the difference is not a quibble. Kalmia Hills, plural, is the subdivision. Kalmia Hill, singular, is a City of Aiken park at 3416 Summit Drive, and also a road. Both are real, for different things.

The subdivision took its name from the shrub. The Aiken Chronicles describes tall kalmia, mountain laurel, scattered through the understory below an overstory of loblolly and longleaf pine. That canopy is not scenery here. It is the biggest influence on what reaches a house; the rail line on the south boundary is second.

2 acresKalmia Hill Park, 3416 Summit Drive: two tennis courts and a walking track of three-sixteenths of a mile per lap (City of Aiken)
1969Year an area near Laurel Drive and the railroad track flooded for want of drainage, per Council Member Ed Girardeau (Aiken Chronicles)
50.77 inAverage annual precipitation for Aiken County, mean temperature 64.1°F: what a packed gutter must move

Kalmia Hills or Kalmia Hill, and does it matter?

It matters: a company that cannot name your street has not looked.

The nameWhat it actually names
Kalmia Hills, pluralThe subdivision. The Aiken Chronicles bounds it by Summit Drive west, Laurel Drive and Highland Park Avenue across part of the north, and Norfolk Southern Railroad property south
Kalmia Hill, singularKalmia Hill Park, an official City of Aiken park at 3416 Summit Drive, and Kalmia Hill Road, a real 29801 street
Kalmia ParkA social-app label no authoritative source uses, so neither do we

One of the original developers was Mattie C. Hall, 1885 to 1961, remembered locally as an antiques dealer, businesswoman and realtor. No platting date is published and we will not invent one. The city sold about four acres inside the subdivision in 2021, land since subdivided, so the housing here is not all of one age.

What does general pest control cover on these streets?

  • Ants indoors and at the foundation, including colonies working out of wet needle litter
  • German and American cockroaches, two unrelated problems in similar shells
  • Spiders, silverfish, crickets and other uninvited visitors
  • Mice and rats: canine screening, trapping, then carpentry that stays shut
  • Bed bugs, screened by certified detection dog, as its own service
  • Squirrel damage and roofline sealing, handled as exclusion rather than trapping

There is a hard edge to what we sell, better drawn here than on your doorstep. No termite work, no CL-100 or wood infestation letter for a closing, no fumigation, no mosquito program, no lawn treatment. If that is the need, we say so on the first call. The rest is general pest control.

What does a pine limb touching the roof actually do?

A branch resting on shingles is not cosmetic. It is a bridge doing three jobs at once.

It carries climbing rodents over your defenses

A roof rat is arboreal and never tests your door sweep, because it never comes to ground. It moves limb to limb onto the roof and hunts the softest half inch: a gable vent screen, a lifted shingle in a valley, the gap where soffit returns meet. See the roof rat profile.

It gives squirrels a reason to stay

Eastern gray squirrels take the same bridge to the same attic. The tell is timing and edge quality: daylight activity and a clean rounded hole at a fascia joint. Background on the eastern gray squirrel.

It keeps a stripe of roof damp

Shade and dropped needles leave a band that never dries between rains. Decking and fascia soften, and soft wood is how a half-inch gap becomes a two-inch one.

Our clearances are simple. Break contact, then build a gap: four feet minimum between any limb and the roof, six where the tree can spare it. Published guidance puts a climbing rat’s horizontal jump at roughly four feet from a standing start, so trimming back a foot buys nothing. Check what else reaches the roof: service drops land on the same fascia, and a rat walks a wire as readily as a limb.

Pruning is not our trade; we mark limbs and leave saw work to an arborist. Where four feet is unachievable without losing a tree, sealing the roofline does the job alone, which is exclusion and repair.

Roof rat, Norway rat or house mouse, and which route does which use?

 Roof ratNorway ratHouse mouse
How it arrivesDown from the canopy, along limbs, wires, fence topsAlong the ground, following cover and edgesEither, usually carried in cover near a wall
Where it entersRoofline: gable vent, eave, soffit corner, chimney chaseGround level: crawl vent, slab edge, utility sleeveAnything from about a quarter inch upward
Where it nestsAttic, upper wall voids, dense vine or shrub massBurrows at foundations, under decks and ground coverIndoors, a very short walk from food

Under a closed canopy we start at the roofline. On lower ground toward the rail boundary, with heavy cover at grade, we start at the burrow line. One neighborhood, two inspections. Compare the Norway rat with the house mouse, and see the method on our rodent control page.

We quote no accuracy figure for canine rodent detection: no field validation exists for that work in structures. The dogs shorten the search, and the evidence still gets confirmed by eye.

Should pine straw be lying against the foundation?

Pine straw is the regional mulch and under these trees it arrives free, which is why it ends up banked against the wall. The material is fine. The placement is not.

  • Depth is the variable. Two inches is mulch. Six inches of settled duff is habitat: steady temperature and humidity, no light, endless decomposing material. Crickets, sowbugs and ants set up there, and large outdoor roaches follow.
  • Duff under the shrubs counts. Kalmia holds a low dense skirt and needles collect beneath it, until the bed is one mat from shrub line to foundation. Firewood against a wall does the same with a roof on.
  • Sandhills soil hides it. The deep upland sands here run about forty-four inches before clay in the Troup series and drain rapidly, so rain vanishes and people assume the ground is dry. A needle mat holds its own water on top.

None of this means tearing out landscaping. Leave a six-inch bare band so the wall base can dry, thin the duff, and ground-level pressure drops before anything is applied.

What does the rail corridor on the south boundary mean, and what does it not?

The southern edge of Kalmia Hills is Norfolk Southern property, which deserves a straight answer rather than a scare. In habitat terms a rail corridor is a continuous strip of ground managed for track and drainage rather than appearance: ballast holding voids, a verge of volunteer weeds, occasional spilled material. None of that is a criticism of the operator. Keeping a line safe is a different job from keeping a lawn tidy.

  • What it genuinely is: an edge. Where managed ground meets unmanaged ground you get concentrated cover, food and movement, and rodents follow linear edges by preference. The first properties back from one see more activity at grade than mid-block, so be strict about cover, stored material and gaps within three feet of the ground.
  • What it does not mean: proximity does not give you an infestation. Nobody publishes pest pressure by distance from a rail corridor in Aiken, so any figure quoted was invented.
  • Where drainage fits: Council Member Ed Girardeau noted the property between Laurel Drive and the railroad track is very thin, and that an area near there flooded in 1969 for want of drainage. Low ground that holds water is worth inspecting anyway.

Why are gutters a pest question in a pine canopy?

A gutter that cannot carry water becomes a planter. Needles pack tighter than leaves and pack at the outlet first, until the trough holds a wet organic layer and every rain sheets over the lip.

Follow the water. It runs behind the gutter onto the fascia, paint fails, the board softens, and soft fascia is the easiest opening on the building for a squirrel or roof rat, directly under the limb that dropped the needles. The overflow lands in a stripe along the foundation, watering the harborage above on a schedule.

  1. Look up first

    On a canopy lot we start at the roofline: limb contact, wire drops, needles in valleys, staining down the fascia, gaps at soffit returns and vent screens. Then we ask where each downspout puts its water, since a spout emptying at the wall undoes everything done in the bed.

  2. Work the base of the wall

    Mulch depth, clear band, stored material, utility penetrations, any low run that holds after rain.

  3. Close before treating

    Metal at every opening, mesh packed and sealed over, sweeps and flashing renewed. A product has a service life; a closed hole does not.

German or American cockroach, and which one came in from outside?

American cockroach: it was living in the mulch

Reddish brown, up to an inch and a half, what people here call a palmetto bug. It keeps a real outdoor population in South Carolina: needle duff, leaf litter, tree holes and drain lines are where it lives. On a canopy lot it has no distance to travel, entering at a dried-out floor drain trap, a plumbing sleeve or a threshold gap. One in the tub is a plumbing question, not a housekeeping one.

German cockroach: somebody carried it in

About half an inch, tan, with dark stripes behind the head. It keeps no outdoor population in our climate. It arrives inside something, a box, a used appliance, a secondhand chair, then settles into warm tight voids near food and water. Treating the yard does nothing. Baiting, harborage reduction and sanitation are the work.

The test is direction of travel. Large roaches at ground level, near drains, after heavy rain or a cold snap, came from the litter outside. Small striped roaches in a kitchen cabinet, never seen outdoors, came in with something: cockroach control.

What can a detection dog settle that a walk-through cannot?

Tense. A visual inspection finds fecal spotting, cast skins and dead insects, and all three persist for years after an infestation ends. Staining on a mattress seam tells you something happened, not that anything is alive tonight. A properly imprinted detection dog works against the odor of live insects and viable eggs, so its answer is present-tense, and it covers rooms nobody mentioned.

The limits get stated in advance. An alert locates odor; it does not count insects or date an infestation. Heat and a tired dog degrade the work, so sessions stay short, every alert is confirmed by eye, and an ambiguous spot earns monitors and a second look instead of a sale. Kimberly Camera, who founded the company, has 28-plus years in scent detection including FEMA Urban Search & Rescue deployment; teams certify through NESDCA, WDDO, CPDA and ICRWDA. More on K-9 bed bug detection and the bed bug profile.

Plainly: neither the canopy nor the rail line bears on bed bugs. They travel with people and luggage, and the tightest house here is as exposed as any other.

What licence should a company here already hold?

The regulator is not where most people expect. Structural pest licensing in this state runs through the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation, and the relevant category is 7A, covering industrial, institutional, structural and health-related pest control.

Any firm you call should hand over a DPR business licence number, name the certified applicator responsible for your address, and produce a current certificate of insurance without hesitating. If any of the three needs a call to head office, you have your answer.

What the record does not say about Kalmia Hills

Plenty. No plat date or construction range is published, so we state none, and whether your house is slab, crawl space or pier we find out by looking. Summit Drive, Laurel Drive and Highland Park Avenue are documented as boundaries; no other street here appears in a source we would cite. Median year built, tenure and lot size do not exist at this scale. Aiken’s Tree City USA standing, 37 consecutive years as of its June 2022 award, is verified; a tree canopy percentage is not, so we describe what is over your roof instead.

What we can source: north Aiken, deep rapidly draining Sandhills sand, and about 232 freeze-free days recorded at AIKEN 4 NE, which gives outdoor populations little enforced pause.

Which nearby parts of Aiken do we cover?

We work out of 320 Wendy Lane in Windsor and cover the north side of the city: Crosland Park, whose playground was rebuilt alongside Kalmia Hill Park under the City’s $500,000 September 2021 playground initiative; Downtown Aiken; Gem Lakes; and Aiken as a whole. The rest is on our service areas page.

Frequently asked questions

Is my neighborhood Kalmia Hill or Kalmia Hills?

Kalmia Hills, plural, is the subdivision, bounded by Summit Drive, Laurel Drive, Highland Park Avenue and the Norfolk Southern line. Kalmia Hill, singular, is the City of Aiken park at 3416 Summit Drive, and a road name. Both are genuine names for two different things.

Do I have to cut my trees down to fix a rat problem?

No. The aim is breaking contact between limbs and the building, not removing the canopy. We work to four feet of clearance, six where the tree can spare it, and mark limbs rather than whole trees. Where that is impossible, sealing the roofline does the job.

Something runs across my ceiling at night. Rat or squirrel?

Time of day is the quickest tell. Squirrels work in daylight, loudest near dawn, and gnaw clean rounded holes at fascia and vent joints. Roof rats move after dark and leave rub marks along framing. Both reach the roof by the same bridge.

Is pine straw a bad mulch to use here?

Not in itself. Depth and placement decide it. Keep a six-inch bare band between mulch and wall, and hold beds to a couple of inches rather than letting needles build a mat. Settled duff holds moisture and steady temperature, which is what ants and roaches want.

Does living near the railroad mean I will get rats?

No, and anyone saying otherwise is guessing. A rail corridor is ground managed for track rather than landscaping, so it functions as an edge, and rodents travel edges. Be stricter about cover and gaps near grade on the closest properties. It predicts nothing about your house.

Do you handle CL-100 letters or wood-destroying insect work?

We do not. No termite work, no reports for closings, no fumigation, no mosquito programs, no lawn treatment. We do household pest control, cockroaches, rodents, bed bugs and exclusion carpentry. Anything outside that, we say so on the phone rather than sending a truck.

Related services

Exclusion & RepairsRodent ControlGeneral Pest ControlK-9 Bed Bug DetectionCockroach Control

Have the roofline and the ground line looked at together

Tell us the address and what you are hearing. On a Kalmia Hills lot we walk the canopy contact points, gutters and fascia, the mulch line and the attic before anyone mentions product, and the findings go to you in writing. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions, 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856.

Call 803-226-3155Request an Inspection

h1: Pest Control in Lexington, SC

hero.lead: Lexington is a town of young households, and the first question we get asked here is almost never whether treatment works. It is whether it is safe to have in the house. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions answers that with placement, exclusion and the printed label, not with adjectives.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Family-owned · 320 Wendy Lane, Windsor, SC 29856 · Labels supplied before we treat · Lexington and the Midlands

body:
Almost every competitor page here disposes of the child-and-pet question with one reassuring adjective, then a phone number. A real answer is a set of decisions: whether any material is used at all, where it goes, how long it stays wet, who can reach it, and what the label permits in a room where somebody sleeps. Those are checkable. Adjectives are not.

So this page is about product and placement in a house with a toddler on the floor and a dog following them around. Nothing here is a safety guarantee, because nobody honest issues one.

27,074Pupils in Lexington County School District One, in 32 schools, one teacher per 12.99 (NCES Common Core of Data, 2024-25)
2.42People per household in the TOWN of Lexington, across 9,778 households, 68.7 percent owner-occupied (ACS 2020–2024 via Census QuickFacts)
$100,000Minimum liability cover a structural pest control firm must hold in South Carolina, with a licence and a Designated Certified Applicator (Clemson Department of Pesticide Regulation)

What does general pest control cover in a house like this?

  • Ants, indoors and along the slab line
  • Cockroaches, the kitchen-breeding kind and the large kind that comes up a drain
  • Spiders and the harborage feeding them
  • Occasional invaders — silverfish, crickets, millipedes
  • Mice and rats — canine detection, trapping, closing the way in
  • Bed bugs: canine screening, with treatment quoted separately
  • Exclusion and repair carpentry, the part that lasts

We sell no lawn programs, yard fogging or moisture certificates, and nothing here is an offer of one. The parent page is general pest control; sealing work sits under repairs and exclusion.

Why is exclusion the safest thing we can do in an occupied home?

Because a closed gap needs no product behind it. A sealed opening cannot be tracked across a floor on a shoe or licked off a paw. It has no re-entry interval, no drying time and no expiry date, and it works the same in year four as on the day it went in. Every opening closed is a decision you never have to make again about treating a child’s room.

A family house also generates its own pressure, and most of it is fixable with no product at all. Dog food lives in the garage in the paper sack it came in, a high chair feeds crumbs into the toe-kick gap daily, and toy bins build harborage nobody moves for a year. That is not bad housekeeping. It is what a house with children does, and it is easier to design around than to spray around. Our order is fixed: find it, seal it, trap it, then ask whether anything needs applying.

Where do bait stations go when a toddler crawls the floor?

  • Exterior first, against the structure where activity was actually found, not spaced evenly for the look of it.
  • Locked and anchored. Keyed rather than opened with a common tool, and weighted so a dog cannot carry one off.
  • Away from where your family actually is — not the patio, the play set or the fence line the dog patrols, so we walk the yard with you first.
  • Never loose material — no open trays, nothing balanced above a crawl space.
  • Indoors, monitors before toxicant, so activity is located without anything edible entering the building.
  • Numbered on a drawing and counted every visit, so a missing one is noticed that day rather than found by a two-year-old.

Read tamper-resistant closely, because it has a definition. Consumer rodent baits must now be sold in or with a tamper-resistant station, and loose pellets are no longer a household product; both came from the EPA’s rodenticide risk mitigation decision. Resistant is the operative word: a box tested against a child and a dog, not one neither can defeat given time. It is a delay, not a wall, and placement does the real work.

Why will we not broadcast-spray the baseboard your child sits against?

Because it wets the one surface a crawling child and a sleeping dog occupy all day, and misses the insects anyway. A wet band along every baseboard is a habit inherited from the 1970s, not a technique. The insects are not on the open face of the trim. They are in the void behind it, in the hinge recess, in the gap where a pipe enters a cabinet. Wetting the visible surface puts material exactly where small hands go and leaves the harborage untouched.

The alternative is not exotic. Crack and crevice work puts a small amount through a pin stream into an opening narrower than a pencil, dusts go into wall voids that are then closed, and baits sit inside cabinets in placements the size of a rice grain. Vacuuming and steam do part of the job with no residue at all. Where something must go indoors, we name the rooms and the spots first.

What does re-entry mean, and what does a label really say?

A pesticide label is not packaging copy. Under federal law it is the enforceable instruction, and using a product in a manner its labeling does not permit is a violation in itself. If the label forbids something in a bedroom, no salesperson can authorise it.

What you are readingWhat it tells a parent
Signal word — Caution, Warning or DangerThe acute hazard tier of the concentrate as sold — a ranking, not a verdict on the dilution in a wall void.
Precautionary statementsHazards to humans, to domestic animals, and separately to fish and wildlife. Read the domestic animal line twice.
Directions for UseThe binding part. Where it may go, where it may not, at what rate and by which method — which settles crack and crevice versus broadcast.
Re-entry languageHousehold labels commonly keep people and pets off treated surfaces until dry, and require ventilation. Dry is a condition, not a clock.
First aidWho to call on exposure. Medical and veterinary questions are not ours to answer.

On drying time, distrust any flat number. A slick surface with a fan clears quickly; a porous one in a closed room on a humid Midlands afternoon takes far longer, because airflow, humidity and the surface decide it. Cover the aquarium and switch the air pump off first, and move caged birds and small mammals out of the area rather than covering them in place.

Why is rodenticide close to the last thing we reach for here?

Two mechanisms, both specific. The first is delay. Anticoagulant baits act over days rather than minutes, which is what makes them work on a wary animal. It also means a dog that gets into bait looks entirely normal that evening, and the next one. Nothing announces that anything happened.

The second is the relay pathway, usually left out. A rodent carrying a lethal dose keeps feeding for days and holds that load in its tissues. It slows down, and a slow rodent in daylight is the easiest thing on the property to catch. Whatever eats it takes the load with the meal. Dogs do this. So do cats, and the hawks and owls over the same yards. The harm moves up one link with nothing applied to the animal that suffers it.

Then the practical failure: a poisoned rodent does not go outdoors to die. It dies in a wall cavity, above a bedroom ceiling or under a tub deck, with no access panel, and you get weeks of odor and no confirmation anything is finished. So we run the order backwards from the industry norm: detection, exclusion, traps where no child or dog can reach them, bait last and outside in anchored locked stations. Anything used is recorded by name and registration number, so your veterinarian has a document rather than a guess. That work is rat and mouse control; the finding stage is canine rodent detection in Lexington.

German or American cockroach, and why it changes your kitchen

German cockroach — the resident

Small, tan, two dark bars on the shield behind the head. It lives and breeds indoors in warm damp seams: hinge recesses, a refrigerator motor compartment, the dishwasher void. If you have them, they are not visiting.

The work is bait into those seams in tiny amounts, monitors to measure whether numbers fall, and removal of clutter, cardboard and available water. Deliberately not a spray job: repellent products scatter a population into adjoining rooms and can put insects off bait that would have killed them, and resistance to household sprays is well documented. A technical reason to keep material off your counters, and a family reason too. See the German cockroach profile.

American cockroach — the visitor

Much larger, reddish brown, with a pale margin around the shield. It originates outdoors and below: drains, sump pits, crawl spaces and mulch beds. Most of what turns up indoors came up a drain or through a door gap.

So the response is largely not chemical: drains sealed and in use, sump lids fitted, sweeps corrected, mulch pulled off the foundation, downspouts moved off the slab edge, exterior harborage cut back. Treating the inside of a house for something that lives outside is how families end up with material in rooms for no benefit. See the American cockroach profile and cockroach control.

Bed bugs in a child’s room: why screen before you treat?

Because the alternative is taking the room apart. A thorough visual search means stripping the beds, standing the box spring on end, unbolting a headboard and reading every seam of every soft item. In a bunk room shared by two children that is a long afternoon, and they come home to a room in pieces. A certified team reads the room with the beds made and indicates points for a targeted look.

The second reason belongs on a safety page. A screen that identifies one affected room lets treatment be confined to it, and rooms that come back clear are not treated at all. Detection keeps the treated footprint small, and every alert is confirmed by hand first. Detail is on our Lexington canine bed bug detection page. It scales up: with 27,074 pupils moving between 32 schools and their households daily, monitoring beats routine application in a building full of children. That is the basis of our schools and student housing program.

What should you ask before anyone treats a room your children sleep in?

  • Show me the licence. Structural work here is regulated by the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation, not an agriculture department, under Category 7A. A firm needs a DPR business licence, a Designated Certified Applicator, and liability cover of at least $100,000.
  • Send the label before you come, not after. Labels are public documents; a firm that will not send one has told you something.
  • Where exactly is material going, and where is it not? Rooms and surfaces, and the re-entry instruction read out in the label’s own words rather than summarised.
  • What in this plan is not a pesticide? If nothing is sealed, trapped, vacuumed or corrected, ask why not.
  • If stations go in, where, how are they secured, and are they on a diagram?
  • What is the follow-up, and how will we know it worked? A counted device is evidence; a repeat visit with no measurement is a subscription.

One note on language. Federal rules bar a registered pesticide’s labeling from calling the product safe, non-toxic or harmless. If somebody says those words on your doorstep, the container in the truck will not repeat them. That gap between the doorstep and the document is the most useful thing a parent here can learn about this trade.

Where do we work around Lexington?

From 320 Wendy Lane in Windsor we cover the town, the neighbourhoods south of the water, and the cities next door: Irmo at the top of the lake, Cayce and West Columbia down the Congaree side. Lake Murray’s 620 miles of shore sit immediately north, and a lake property with a boathouse is a different inventory to a house on a quarter acre. Full coverage sits on our service areas page.

Frequently asked questions

Is pest control safe for my kids and my dog?

Nobody honest hands you a guarantee, and a firm offering one is selling rather than explaining. What can be committed to is practice: less material, none where sealing or trapping will do, what is used kept inside voids and locked stations, and the label supplied in advance and followed. Judge a firm on placement and paperwork.

Do we have to leave the house while you work?

It depends on what is being done and what that label requires. A crack and crevice treatment in a kitchen commonly asks only that people and pets stay off treated surfaces until dry, and that the room be ventilated. Whole-room heat work for bed bugs needs the household out for the day.

Can you do a job with no spray at all?

Often, yes. Exclusion, trapping, vacuuming, steam and monitors handle much of what a family home needs, and rodent work is mostly carpentry and traps. The honest limit is that some jobs still call for bait, German cockroaches being the clear case. Bait is a product too, but it sits in a crevice, not on a surface.

Someone quoted a treatment they called all-natural and child-safe. Is that a thing?

Those are doorstep terms with no regulatory meaning. Federal rules bar a registered pesticide’s labeling from describing it as safe, non-toxic or harmless, so the pitch will not appear on the container. A minimum-risk category exempt from registration exists, and some of those products are useful, but exempt from paperwork is a statement about paperwork.

If a mouse eats bait in the yard, can that reach my cat?

That pathway is real, and it is why we start somewhere else. A rodent carrying a lethal anticoagulant dose keeps feeding for days, holds that load in its tissues, and turns slow and easy to catch before it dies. Whatever eats it takes the load on. An actual exposure is a call to your veterinarian.

What do we do with the fish tank and the guinea pig?

Cover the aquarium and turn the air pump off before any indoor application, because a running pump draws treated room air into the water. Caged birds and small mammals are better moved out of the area than covered where they stand. Lift bowls, bedding and the toy box off the floor first.
