title: Carpenter Ant ID & Control
description: Carpenter ants are the large black ants that hollow out damp or damaged wood to nest. Identification and control across Aiken, Augusta and the Midlands.
h1: Carpenter Ant — Identification & Control

hero.lead: Carpenter ants are the large black ants that hollow out damp or damaged wood to nest. They do not eat wood, but their galleries can signal — and worsen — a moisture problem.

body:
How to identify the Carpenter Ant

Among the largest ants you will see indoors, 1/4 to 1/2 inch, usually black, with a smoothly rounded thorax and a single node at the waist.

Behavior & biology

They excavate smooth galleries in moist or decayed wood — around leaks, decks, and window frames — and forage widely at night, often for sweets and protein.

Why Carpenter Ants are a problem

Galleries weaken already-compromised wood, and their presence usually points to a hidden moisture issue. Large satellite colonies can develop inside walls.

Signs of an infestation

Large ants indoors (especially at night), piles of coarse sawdust-like frass, faint rustling in walls, and winged swarmers near windows in spring.

How we handle Carpenter Ants in the CSRA

Finding and treating the nest — plus correcting the moisture that drew them — is the durable fix. Start with our pest control service. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. Browse the full pest library.

description: The cat flea is the biting parasite behind most flea problems in CSRA homes — it infests pets and then the carpets, bedding, and yard.
h1: Cat Flea — Identification & Control

hero.lead: The cat flea is the biting parasite behind most flea problems in CSRA homes — it infests pets and then the carpets, bedding, and yard, and is stubborn because most of its life cycle is hidden off the animal.

body:
How to identify the Cat Flea

Tiny, dark, wingless insects that jump rather than fly, hard to catch and flattened side-to-side. Flea “dirt” (digested blood) looks like black pepper on pets and bedding.

Behavior & biology

Adults feed on pets and people, but eggs, larvae, and pupae develop in carpet, upholstery, and shaded soil — so treating only the pet leaves the home reinfesting itself.

Why Cat Fleas are a problem

Bites are itchy and cluster around ankles, pets suffer, and the hidden life stages make infestations persistent without a coordinated approach.

Signs of an infestation

Pets scratching, black flea dirt in fur and bedding, itchy bites around the ankles, and tiny specks jumping from carpet and furniture.

How we handle Cat Fleas in the CSRA

Success means treating the home environment and yard in step with your veterinarian treating the pet. Our pest control program handles the property side. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. Browse the full pest library.

Familiar gray (sometimes brownish) tree squirrels with a bushy tail, 9–12 inches in the body. In attics they are heard more than seen.

Excellent climbers, they travel branches and power lines to roof edges and gnaw entry points into attics, where they nest and cache food.

Rarely seen — a small burrowing mammal with velvety gray fur, tiny eyes, and large, outward-facing digging paws. Its work is visible even when it is not.

It lives almost entirely underground, tunneling continuously for insects and worms. It does not eat plants but disrupts roots as it digs.

Why Eastern Moles are a problem

Feeding tunnels raise unsightly ridges across the lawn and volcano-shaped mounds of soil, and the tunneling damages grass roots and garden beds.

Raised ridges snaking across the lawn, volcano-shaped soil mounds, and spongy ground where tunnels run just below the surface.

h1: Eastern Subterranean Termite — Identification & Control

hero.lead: The eastern subterranean termite is the most destructive structural pest in South Carolina, eating wood from the inside out and often going unnoticed until damage is significant.

body:
How to identify the Eastern Subterranean Termite

Workers are pale and soft-bodied; spring swarmers are dark with two pairs of equal-length wings. Mud tubes on foundations are the classic sign.

Behavior & biology

Colonies live in the soil and build pencil-width mud tubes to reach wood, maintaining contact with moisture. Swarms of winged reproductives appear in spring.

Why Eastern Subterranean Termites are a problem

They silently consume framing, subfloors, and trim, and the CSRA climate keeps them active much of the year. Untreated, they cause serious structural damage.

Signs of an infestation

Mud tubes on foundation walls and piers, discarded wings near windows after a swarm, wood that sounds hollow when tapped, and buckling paint.

How we handle Eastern Subterranean Termites in the CSRA

Early inspection is everything. We identify active termite pressure and coordinate targeted treatment — start with our pest control and commercial services. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. See more in our pest library.

Stocky black birds with an iridescent green-purple sheen and white speckles in winter; the bill turns yellow in breeding season. They fly in dense flocks.

They aggressively take over cavities — dryer and exhaust vents, signage, soffit gaps — and roost communally in large numbers, displacing native birds.

title: German Cockroach ID & Control
description: The German cockroach is the small indoor roach that infests kitchens and bathrooms and is the hardest to eliminate because it breeds so fast.
h1: German Cockroach — Identification & Control

hero.lead: The German cockroach is the small indoor roach that infests kitchens and bathrooms and is the hardest to eliminate because it breeds so fast.

body:
How to identify the German Cockroach

Light tan to brown, about half an inch, with two dark parallel stripes behind the head. Egg cases are small, tan, and purse-shaped.

Behavior & biology

It hides in warm, humid harborage near food and water — behind appliances, under sinks, in cabinet voids — and is active at night. One egg case holds dozens of young.

Why German Cockroachs are a problem

It spreads bacteria across food surfaces, triggers allergies and asthma, and multiplies rapidly, making a small problem an infestation within weeks.

Signs of an infestation

Pepper-like droppings in drawers and corners, discarded egg cases, a musty odor, and live roaches scattering when a light comes on.

How we handle German Cockroachs in the CSRA

German roaches need a targeted, sanitation-aware program rather than over-the-counter sprays. Our food-service and commercial pest control teams handle heavy accounts. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. See more in our pest library.

Gray with four dark stripes on the thorax and reddish eyes, about a quarter inch. Fast, erratic fliers that cluster at windows.

h1: House Mouse — Identification & Control

hero.lead: The house mouse is the small gray rodent that slips indoors through gaps as small as a dime and breeds year-round. Small size and fast reproduction make it a persistent problem.

body:
How to identify the House Mouse

Dusty gray to light brown, 2.5–4 inches in the body with a thin, nearly hairless tail about as long, large ears, and a pointed nose. Droppings are rice-grain sized.

Behavior & biology

Curious rather than wary, mice explore new objects readily, nest in shredded material near food, and can produce a litter every few weeks.

Why House Mouses are a problem

They contaminate far more food than they eat, gnaw packaging and wiring, and trigger allergies and asthma. A few mice become many quickly.

Signs of an infestation

Small dark droppings along walls and in drawers, gnawed packaging, nests of shredded paper or insulation, and a faint musky odor.

How to identify the Lone Star Tick

Reddish-brown; the adult female has a single distinctive white dot on her back. Nymphs are tiny and account for many bites.

Behavior & biology

It waits on grass and low brush at yard edges and trails, then latches onto passing hosts. It is active from spring through fall in the Southeast.

Why Lone Star Ticks are a problem

It bites people readily and transmits illnesses including ehrlichiosis and STARI, and its bite is associated with the alpha-gal red-meat allergy.

Signs of an infestation

Ticks found on people and pets after time outdoors, concentrated activity along brushy yard edges, tall grass, and wooded borders.

How we handle Lone Star Ticks in the CSRA

Perimeter treatment plus reducing brush and tall grass at yard edges cuts exposure. Our pest control program includes tick management. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. Browse the full pest library.

Heavy-bodied and brown-gray, 7–10 inches in the body with a shorter, thick tail, small ears, and a blunt nose. Droppings are capsule-shaped with blunt ends.

Ground-dwelling and neophobic — wary of new objects — they burrow, follow established runways, and gnaw constantly to keep incisors in check. They are strong swimmers and enter through sewer lines and gaps.

They contaminate food, gnaw wiring and structural materials (a fire risk), and carry pathogens. A colony grows quickly once a food source is established.

Capsule droppings, greasy rub marks along walls, gnaw marks, burrow openings near foundations, and nighttime scratching.

title: Odorous House Ant ID & Control
description: Odorous house ants are the tiny ants that trail across kitchen counters and give off a rotten-coconut smell when crushed.
h1: Odorous House Ant — Identification & Control

hero.lead: Odorous house ants are the tiny ants that trail across kitchen counters and give off a rotten-coconut smell when crushed. They are one of the most persistent indoor ants in the region.

body:
How to identify the Odorous House Ant

Very small, brown to black, about 1/8 inch, with an uneven thorax. The telltale sign is the coconut-like odor when one is squashed.

Behavior & biology

Colonies have many queens and nest in wall voids, under floors, and outdoors under mulch and stones. They forage in trails toward sweets and moisture.

Why Odorous House Ants are a problem

They contaminate food, form long persistent trails, and split into new colonies when disturbed by sprays — which is why over-the-counter products often make them worse.

Signs of an infestation

Steady trails along counters, baseboards, and plumbing lines, clustering around sweets and spills, and the coconut odor when crushed.

How we handle Odorous House Ants in the CSRA

Non-repellent baiting that the workers carry back to the queens is the fix. Our pest control program targets the colony, not just the trail. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. Browse the full pest library.

Very small, about 1/16 inch, pale yellow to light brown, often noticed only as faint trails toward food and moisture.

Colonies have many queens and nest in warm, hidden voids — wall cavities, behind appliances, in wiring runs. Disturbance with sprays triggers “budding” into multiple new colonies.

It contaminates food and sterile areas, spreads through large buildings, and is capable of transmitting pathogens in healthcare settings — a serious concern where sanitation is critical.

Faint trails of tiny yellow ants toward sweets, grease, and water, especially in kitchens, bathrooms, and facilities, with numbers that grow after spraying.

How we handle Pharaoh Ants in the CSRA

Pharaoh ants require a bait-only program — never sprays, which make them worse. Our healthcare and commercial teams manage them correctly. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. Browse the full pest library.

body:
How to identify the Raccoon

Stocky gray animals with a black mask and ringed tail, 2–3 feet including the tail. Tracks look like small handprints.

Behavior & biology

Powerful and dexterous, they tear open soffits and vents, use chimneys as dens, and forage at night in trash and pet food.

Why Raccoons are a problem

They cause significant structural damage, and their droppings can carry roundworm, a human health risk. A cornered raccoon can be aggressive.

Signs of an infestation

Loud nighttime movement overhead, torn soffits or vents, tracks, droppings in attics or on roofs, and sounds of young in spring.

How we handle Raccoons in the CSRA

Raccoons require humane removal — including any young — and secure exclusion of entry points. Our wildlife & pest control team manages it safely. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. Browse the full pest library.

h1: Red Imported Fire Ant — Identification & Control

hero.h1: Red Imported Fire Ant — Identification & Control
hero.lead: Red imported fire ants build dome mounds across CSRA lawns and deliver a painful, burning sting when disturbed. They are one of the most common yard pests in the region.

body:
How to identify the Red Imported Fire Ant

Small reddish-brown ants of varying sizes in one colony, building loose dome-shaped dirt mounds with no obvious central opening.

Behavior & biology

Colonies contain tens of thousands of ants and boil out aggressively when the mound is disturbed. They relocate readily and thrive in open, sunny turf.

Why Red Imported Fire Ants are a problem

Stings cause painful welts and pustules and can be dangerous to allergic people, children, and pets. Mounds damage lawns and equipment.

Signs of an infestation

Dome mounds in sunny lawn areas, especially after rain, and fast, aggressive swarming when a mound is stepped on or raked.

How we handle Red Imported Fire Ants in the CSRA

Fire ants need a yard-wide baiting and treatment approach, not just knocking down visible mounds. Our pest control program manages them across the property. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. See more in our pest library.

title: Roof Rat ID & Control
description: The roof rat is the sleek climbing rat that nests high — in attics, rafters, trees, and upper cabinets — rather than burrowing.
h1: Roof Rat — Identification & Control

hero.lead: The roof rat is the sleek climbing rat that nests high — in attics, rafters, trees, and upper cabinets — rather than burrowing. It is common in warmer parts of the CSRA.

body:
How to identify the Roof Rat

Slimmer and darker than the Norway rat, 6–8 inches in the body with a tail longer than the body, large ears, and a pointed nose. Droppings are smaller with pointed ends.

Behavior & biology

An agile climber that travels utility lines and branches to enter roofs and attics. It prefers fruit, nuts, and seeds and nests above ground.

Why Roof Rats are a problem

It contaminates stored food and attic insulation, gnaws wiring in ceilings and walls, and spreads disease. Because it lives overhead, activity is often heard before it is seen.

Signs of an infestation

Pointed droppings in attics and cabinets, gnawing overhead, nighttime scrabbling in ceilings, and grease trails along rafters and pipes.

How we handle Roof Rats in the CSRA

Our dogs confirm whether noises overhead are active rats and where they are traveling — see K9 rodent detection, backed by our rodent control service. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. See more in our pest library.

For trapping, code-grade exclusion and clean-up, see our rat and mouse control service.

title: Silverfish ID & Control
description: Silverfish are the wriggling, silvery insects found in damp bathrooms, basements, and attics, where they feed on paper, starch.
h1: Silverfish — Identification & Control

hero.lead: Silverfish are the wriggling, silvery insects found in damp bathrooms, basements, and attics, where they feed on paper, starch, and glue and quietly damage stored items.

body:
How to identify the Silverfish

Teardrop-shaped, silvery-gray, wingless, with three long tail filaments and a fish-like wriggling motion. About half an inch long.

Behavior & biology

They thrive in humid, dark spaces and feed on starches — book bindings, wallpaper paste, paper, cardboard, and dry goods — and reproduce slowly but persistently.

Why Silverfishs are a problem

They damage books, documents, wallpaper, and stored paper and fabric, and their presence signals excess moisture that invites other pests.

Signs of an infestation

Silvery insects in sinks, tubs, and boxes, yellowish stains and tiny scale-like debris, and feeding damage on paper and wallpaper.

How we handle Silverfishs in the CSRA

Lowering humidity and treating harborage clears them. Our pest control program addresses silverfish and the moisture behind them. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. Browse the full pest library.

title: Virginia Opossum ID & Control
description: The Virginia opossum is a nocturnal marsupial that shelters under decks, sheds, and crawlspaces and raids trash and pet food.
h1: Virginia Opossum — Identification & Control

hero.lead: The Virginia opossum is a nocturnal marsupial that shelters under decks, sheds, and crawlspaces and raids trash and pet food. It is a nuisance more than a destroyer, but an unwelcome one.

body:
How to identify the Virginia Opossum

Cat-sized with coarse grayish-white fur, a pointed pink nose, and a long hairless prehensile tail. It often “plays dead” when threatened.

Behavior & biology

Slow-moving and solitary, it dens in sheltered spots close to food and moves between sites frequently. It is a generalist that eats almost anything.

Why Virginia Opossums are a problem

It denning under a structure brings droppings, odor, parasites, and the risk of it getting into crawlspaces, trash, and pet food.

Signs of an infestation

Nighttime raiding of trash and pet bowls, denning under decks and sheds, droppings near entry points, and the occasional “dead” opossum that revives.

How we handle Virginia Opossums in the CSRA

Exclusion of the den site plus removal is the durable answer. Our pest & wildlife control program handles opossums. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. Browse the full pest library.

hero.lead: Yellowjackets are the aggressive ground- and void-nesting wasps that peak in late summer across the CSRA and sting repeatedly when a nest is disturbed.

body:
How to identify the Yellowjacket

Black and bright yellow, about half an inch, with a smooth, hairless body and a fast, darting flight. They are often mistaken for bees but lack the fuzz.

Behavior & biology

Colonies nest in ground holes, wall voids, and undisturbed cavities, growing to thousands by late summer and foraging aggressively around food and trash.

Why Yellowjackets are a problem

They sting repeatedly, defend nests aggressively, and pose a serious risk to anyone allergic — a real hazard near patios, playgrounds, and dumpsters.

Signs of an infestation

Heavy wasp traffic to a single ground hole or wall gap, aggressive activity around outdoor food and trash, and rising numbers into late summer.

How we handle Yellowjackets in the CSRA

Nests should be treated professionally, not swatted or poured into. Our pest control program locates and treats the nest safely. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule. Browse the full pest library.

body:
Every rodent job comes down to one question: how are they getting in? Bait and traps handle the animals already inside. They do nothing about the quarter-inch gap under the garage door corner, the failed crawl space vent screen, the dryer vent with no damper, or the gap where the refrigerant line enters the wall. Leave those and you are on a subscription — forever paying for the same population, rebuilt every season from outside.

We work the other way around. We find the entry points and the travel routes first, seal them to a specification that rodents cannot gnaw through, and use trapping and stations to clear what is already inside while that work happens. If you also want certainty about where the activity is — inside a wall, above a ceiling, in a specific section of a warehouse — that is what our certified K-9 rodent detection is for. This page is about the treatment and the repair.

1/4″The gap a house mouse can pass — and the maximum dimension the residential building code allows on crawl space vent coverings
25,000Droppings a single Norway rat produces in a year; a house mouse produces roughly 36,000
82%Of US homes with detectable mouse allergen in a national survey of 831 homes across 75 areas

What rodents do we actually have here?

Norway rat

Rattus norvegicus. Around a pound, coarse brown fur, blunt muzzle, small eyes, and ears too small to fold down over the eyes. The tail is shorter than the head and body. Droppings run up to three-quarters of an inch with blunt ends. A burrower and a ground-floor animal — crawl spaces, slab edges, dumpster pads, shed floors, sewers. Six to twelve young per litter, four to six litters a year, sexually mature at about three months. Needs a half-ounce to an ounce of free water a day. Travels an area roughly 100 to 150 feet across daily and rarely goes more than a few hundred feet from the burrow. Neophobic — it avoids new objects for days, which is exactly why pre-baiting matters. Norway rat profile.

Roof rat

Rattus rattus. Five to ten ounces, pointed muzzle, large eyes, ears long enough to pull down over the eyes, and a tail longer than the head and body. Droppings about half an inch with pointed ends. An excellent climber that nests above ground — attics, rafters, trees, ivy-covered walls — and uses overhead lines and fence tops as runways. Its documented US range covers the lower East Coast and Gulf states, which includes South Carolina. Three or more litters a year, five to eight young each, and it usually needs water daily. This is the species that drives soffit, roofline and attic work. Roof rat profile.

House mouse

Mus musculus. Half an ounce, five to seven inches including a nearly hairless tail, with a slightly pointed nose and large ears. Rice-grain droppings about a quarter-inch with pointed ends. Five to six young per litter, five to ten litters a year, sexually mature at six to ten weeks. Critically, it does not need free water — which is why mice colonize dry attics, wall voids and cabinets where a rat could not survive. Its home range is only 10 to 30 feet across, and it nibbles at many places each night rather than eating one meal. That single fact is why low-density trapping fails. House mouse profile.

What it probably isn't

Not every animal in the attic is a rat. Southern flying squirrels are nocturnal cavity-nesters and are constantly reported as “rats in the attic” because of the night noise. Eastern gray squirrels are a game animal in South Carolina with their own handling rules. Cotton rats and woodrats are native species that live in grass and woodland and rarely invade structures — cotton rats turn up under bird feeders, not in pantries. White-footed mice are the Peromyscus you are likely to see here. Identifying correctly matters, because the legal and practical handling differs.

How do rodents get in, and what actually closes it?

The numbers are not marketing. Seal every opening larger than a half inch for rats and larger than a quarter inch for mice — that is the figure in the standard wildlife-damage management handbooks and it is corroborated by UC IPM, which notes a rat will squeeze under a door with a half-inch gap.

The building code says the same thing in a different way. Section R408.2 of the International Residential Code requires under-floor ventilation openings to be covered so that the least dimension of the covering does not exceed one quarter inch, and lists what is acceptable: perforated sheet metal at least 0.070 inches, expanded sheet metal at least 0.047, cast-iron grating, extruded brick vents, hardware cloth of 0.035-inch wire or heavier, or corrosion-resistant mesh with a least dimension of an eighth of an inch. In other words, a code-compliant crawl space vent in your house is already a rodent barrier — and a rusted, torn or missing one is a code-level defect, not just a nuisance.

The rodent-proofing specifications we work to:

  • Hardware cloth for rats: half-inch by half-inch mesh, 19 gauge, woven — woven specifically, because non-woven breaks easily.
  • Hardware cloth for mice: quarter-inch by quarter-inch mesh, 24 gauge, woven.
  • Sheet metal: 24 gauge or heavier for wall and pipe barriers; 22 gauge or heavier for kick plates and door edging.
  • Masonry: concrete at least two inches if reinforced, three and three-quarter inches if not; brick three and three-quarter inches with mortared joints.
  • Doors: the gap between the door bottom and the threshold must not exceed a quarter inch, with flashing or a sweep closing to within an eighth of an inch at the edges.
  • Burrowing barrier: a curtain wall extending at least 36 inches below grade, or an L-footing with a one-foot horizontal outward extension, or a stone band of one-inch-plus gravel two feet wide and half a foot deep.

What rodents chew straight through — and what we will not use as a permanent seal: lead and aluminum sheeting, window screen, wood, rubber, vinyl, fiberglass, plastic and low-quality concrete or block. UC IPM's house mouse guidance is explicit that effective materials are metal or concrete, and that plastic screening, rubber, vinyl, expanding foam, wood and other gnawable materials should be avoided. Steel wool and copper mesh have a role as fillers behind a hard cap — steel wool rusts and can be worked loose, and neither is a barrier on its own. If someone sealed your house with a can of foam, it was not sealed.

Where we look, in order: crawl space vents and access doors; the garage door corner seals and threshold; utility, plumbing, HVAC line-set and electrical penetrations; dryer vents; gable and soffit vents; roof-to-wall junctions and the fascia return; plumbing chases; floor drains and sewer cleanouts; the attached-garage-to-house door; and, for roof rats, every overhanging limb, fence line and utility line that reaches the roof. Sewers are a genuine Norway rat pathway — a 2023 systematic review in Urban Ecosystems found sewers act as major reservoirs for urban rat populations, with rats moving between the underground system and the surface, and with higher presence in systems built of brick and clay, poorly maintained, and near residences and food establishments.

How our rodent service works

  1. Inspection and mapping

    Exterior perimeter, roofline, crawl space, attic, garage and interior. We record droppings by size and shape, rub marks, gnaw damage, runways, burrow openings, nesting material and food sources, and we photograph what we find. Droppings tell us the species; the travel routes tell us the entry.

  2. Confirm the species

    Norway rat, roof rat and house mouse need three different trap layouts and three different sealing priorities. Blunt-ended three-quarter-inch droppings and ground-level burrows mean Norway. Pointed half-inch droppings and overhead runways mean roof rat. Rice-grain droppings scattered widely mean mice. Getting this wrong wastes the first two weeks.

  3. Trap at real density

    The most commonly botched variable in the whole trade. Mouse traps go no more than about six feet apart — because a mouse home range is only 10 to 30 feet across and it feeds at many sites per night, so a trap eight feet away may as well be in another building. Rat stations and traps run within roughly 20 to 30 feet. Traps go tight to walls, behind objects and in dark corners; for roof rats they also go up, on beams, pipes, ledges and sills. Traps with wide trigger plates catch better.

  4. Pre-bait where it matters

    Norway rats avoid new objects for days. Traps are left baited and unset until the bait has been taken at least once — a minimum of three to five days, with feedings no more than 48 hours apart. Skipping this is why a DIY snap-trap line catches nothing for a week and then gets abandoned.

  5. Exterior stations, used correctly

    Where rodenticide is appropriate, it goes in tamper-resistant stations, secured, numbered and mapped, with placements recorded. It is not scattered, it is not used indoors as a first resort, and it is not the whole plan.

  6. Seal the building

    The actual fix. Vent screens, thresholds and sweeps, penetrations, soffit and fascia gaps, roof-to-wall junctions, and the crawl space envelope — all closed with metal, mesh or masonry to the specifications above. Where the scope is structural, our repairs and exclusion crew does the work.

  7. Clean up and verify

    Droppings, contaminated insulation and nesting material removed; damaged vapor barrier and ductwork documented. Then we come back and check — empty traps, no fresh sign, no new gnawing. If you want independent confirmation that a structure is clear, our K-9 detection teams can verify it.

Why does “just put out bait” fail?

Because bait removes individuals and does nothing to the two things that actually determine your rodent population: the food and shelter available, and the holes in the building.

Look at the reproduction numbers. Norway rats produce four to six litters a year of six to twelve young, reaching sexual maturity at three months. House mice produce five to ten litters a year and mature at six to ten weeks. A single surviving pair, or a single unrepaired gap that lets the neighbors' population walk in, rebuilds the infestation inside a season. Even the FDA Food Code frames the requirement as eliminating harborage conditions alongside control methods — the regulator itself treats bait as insufficient on its own.

There is a second reason to be careful with rodenticide, and it is one we would rather raise ourselves. Anticoagulant residues are widespread in wild raptors. A Cornell study published in Ecotoxicology in 2022 found 68 percent of 72 red-tailed hawks tested in New York carried anticoagulant rodenticide residues. A USGS study found 48 percent of 40 barred owls in Oregon and Washington positive for at least one anticoagulant, with exposure described as widespread rather than concentrated near development. Both studies are out of region — we could not find comparable Southeastern raptor monitoring data and we are not going to imply one exists. But the finding is enough to shape how we work: stations secured and mapped, product used where it is the right tool rather than as a default, and exclusion carrying the long-term result.

One thing worth knowing as a consumer: since the EPA's rodenticide risk mitigation decision, the second-generation anticoagulants — brodifacoum, bromadiolone, difenacoum and difethialone — are no longer registered for consumer products and are available only to the commercial and structural pest control markets. Consumer products must be ready-to-use bait stations with block or paste formulations, and pelleted consumer baits are no longer permitted. A licensed applicator can lawfully use products and placements you cannot buy, in tamper-resistant stations, with placement records.

What does not work

  • Ultrasonic and electronic repellers. In May 2001 the Federal Trade Commission sent warning letters to more than 60 manufacturers and retailers of ultrasonic pest-control devices, stating that efficacy claims must be supported by scientific evidence, and it brought enforcement actions against six companies between 1985 and 1997 and further actions in 2002 and 2003. UC IPM's 2025 guidance states there is little evidence that sound, magnetic or vibrational devices of any kind will drive established house mice from buildings. The handbook is blunter: advertising claims for many commercial devices are unsubstantiated by scientific research.
  • Expanding foam as a seal. Named explicitly by UC IPM among the gnawable materials to avoid. It stops air. It does not stop a rodent.
  • Glue boards as a control method. UC IPM notes adult rodents can often detect and avoid the glue, so what you catch is mostly juveniles — you miss the breeding adults driving the population — and animals caught on glue may not die quickly and need to be euthanized. There is also real non-target risk to lizards, snakes and songbirds. We use them for monitoring in specific situations, not as the plan.
  • Sanitation alone. The handbook is honest about this too: even the best sanitation will not eliminate house mice. It makes trapping and baiting work better and makes fresh sign visible. It is not a substitute for closing the building.
  • The fire statistic you have seen. You will find “rodents cause 20 to 25 percent of fires of unknown origin” on a great many pest control websites. We traced it to an uncited state health-department fact sheet, and we could find no NFPA or US Fire Administration data attributing any share of structure fires to rodents. So we do not repeat it. What is true and verifiable: rodent incisors grow about five inches a year, rodents gnaw constantly including on electrical insulation, and chewed wiring is a routine finding in established infestations. That is reason enough to take an attic or crawl space infestation seriously without inventing a number.

What is the actual health risk?

The CDC lists a long set of diseases transmitted directly by rodents — including leptospirosis, salmonellosis, rat-bite fever, sylvatic typhus, tularemia, hantavirus and lymphocytic choriomeningitis — and a second list transmitted indirectly through ticks, mites and fleas. Several of those are not US-endemic and have no business on a South Carolina page. The ones plausibly relevant here are leptospirosis, salmonellosis, rat-bite fever and LCMV.

Hantavirus deserves a straight answer, because it is the one people worry about. The CDC has recorded 890 US hantavirus disease cases in total since surveillance began in 1993, and 94 percent of infections occur in states west of the Mississippi River. The main US agent is carried by the deer mouse. House mice and commensal rats — the species actually infesting homes in Aiken and Columbia — are not reservoirs for it. Hantavirus is real, and it is not a meaningful driver of rodent risk in the Midlands. Anyone telling you otherwise is selling.

The better-supported concern is allergen. The National Survey of Lead and Allergens in Housing sampled 831 homes across 75 randomly selected areas and found detectable mouse allergen in 82 percent of US homes, with roughly 22 percent showing kitchen-floor concentrations above a level associated with allergy and asthma. Risk was highest in high-rise apartments and mobile homes. If someone in the house has asthma, the droppings in the pantry are not just unpleasant.

And the contamination math is worth seeing. One Norway rat eats about an ounce of food a day — 20 to 40 pounds a year — and contaminates roughly ten times that amount with urine and droppings. Grain-storage research cited in the standard handbook found that 10 to 26 rats contaminated 70 percent of stored grain within 12 to 28 weeks. In a crawl space, what we routinely find is nested-out batt insulation, torn vapor barrier and shredded flex duct. We will document what is in your building with photographs rather than quote you a percentage we cannot source.

When do rodents move in around here?

The South Carolina State Climatology Office puts Aiken's last spring freeze around March 22 and its first fall freeze around October 12, with Columbia stations ranging from late February to late October — a freeze-free season of roughly 226 to 261 days depending on the station. That is far longer than the seasons most national rodent advice is written for, and it means outdoor food and cover persist most of the year.

It does not mean rodents breed year round outdoors, and we are not going to say that. The wildlife-damage literature is specific: Norway rat breeding peaks in spring and fall, declines during the heat of summer, and often stops in winter depending on habitat. The honest version is that mild Midlands winters extend the productive breeding window at both ends compared with colder markets.

  • Late February to April. Spring breeding peak. Burrow activity along foundations, sheds and dumpster pads becomes visible as populations start to build.
  • May to August. Breeding slows in the heat. Outdoor food is abundant, so rats and roof rats work the landscape — fruit and nut trees, pet food, bird feeders, dumpsters. Structural complaints drop while exterior harborage builds.
  • September to November. The annual spike, and the reason we push exclusion in August and September. Fall breeding peak coincides with cooling nights and the collapse of outdoor food, right around those October freeze dates. Roof rats move into attics as the canopy thins.
  • December to February. Whatever got in is now inside and obvious — attic noise, pantry droppings, gnawed wiring. A heated, harborage-rich building is a habitat where winter breeding does not stop, so an untreated interior population comes into spring larger than it started.

The practical takeaway: seal before they need to come in. August through early October is the window, and UGA Extension gives the same advice for the same reason.

Why the CSRA and Midlands are different

The soil. The Sandhills run in a belt along the Fall Line through Aiken County and Columbia, with deep, coarse, excessively drained quartz sands — the Lakeland series carries sand thicknesses beyond 80 inches with rapid to very rapid permeability. In our field experience that soil is easy for a Norway rat to excavate and does not waterlog, so burrows under slabs, stoops, sheds and dumpster pads stay usable through the year. We will flag that as professional inference rather than published research, because no one has measured rat burrowing in Sandhills soil specifically. The countermeasure, though, is spec'd: a curtain wall 36 inches below grade, an L-footing with a one-foot outward extension, or a gravel band.

The housing. New construction across the South Atlantic is now about 86 percent slab, which means crawl-space housing here is disproportionately the older stock — the Aiken Winter Colony districts built largely between 1900 and 1930 with stables and outbuildings, the Graniteville mill village whose canal dates to 1846 and whose mill was completed in 1849, Old Shandon in Columbia established in 1893, and the Olympia and Granby mill villages. Pier-and-beam framing, vented crawl spaces, a century of utility penetrations and original millwork are exactly where rodent entry concentrates. If you own one of these houses, the exclusion scope is bigger and it is worth doing once, properly.

The agriculture and industry. Aiken County reported 1,132 farms and 138,479 acres in farms in the 2022 Census of Agriculture, with more than 4,000 acres of corn for grain, 8,000 acres of cotton, and a livestock inventory including nearly 3.6 million broilers. Grain handling, feed storage and poultry houses generate serious commercial rodent pressure, and the industrial and distribution footprint around Sage Mill, Graniteville and Beech Island adds warehouse and dock-door exposure on top of it.

The vegetation and the water. Ivy-covered walls, overhanging limbs and heavy shrub lines are roof-rat highways — the standard guidance is to remove vine-covered structures and trim limbs so they do not overhang or touch the roof. We will not quote you a specific clearance distance, because no extension source publishes one. Firewood goes at least a foot off the ground. Garbage goes in rust-resistant, damage-resistant containers with tight lids. Bird feeders and pet food left out are, in practice, the two most common reasons a property has rats at all.

Commercial rodent programs and audits

If you operate a food establishment, warehouse or plant, the standard you are held to is written down and it is worth reading.

The FDA Food Code, at 6-501.111, requires premises to be maintained free of pests by routinely inspecting incoming shipments of food and supplies, routinely inspecting the premises for evidence of pests, using control methods including trapping devices if pests are found, and eliminating harborage conditions. Section 6-501.112 requires dead or trapped pests to be removed from control devices and the premises at a frequency that prevents accumulation or the attraction of more pests. Section 6-202.15 requires outer openings to be protected by filling or closing holes and gaps along floors, walls and ceilings, with tight-fitting windows and solid, self-closing doors; where an opening must stay open, it specifies 16-mesh-to-the-inch screening or a properly designed air curtain. An active infestation can meet the Food Code's definition of an imminent health hazard, which is the mechanism by which a restaurant gets closed.

In South Carolina, retail food inspections are run by the South Carolina Department of Agriculture, not DHEC — that responsibility moved on July 1, 2024 when DHEC was split into the Department of Public Health and the Department of Environmental Services. Any vendor still telling you DHEC inspects your kitchen has not updated their materials since 2024.

For plants under third-party audit, we build the deliverable your auditor expects: a documented pest program, a site map with uniquely numbered monitoring and bait device locations, service reports, trend analysis, corrective actions, and applicator licensing, product labels and safety data on file. We describe it that way deliberately — we are not going to quote you SQF or BRCGS clause numbers we have not verified against the current standards, because a wrong clause number in front of a QA manager is worse than saying nothing. See our commercial programs, our warehouse and distribution program, and our nationwide K-9 rodent detection for audit-driven work.

Who licenses this work?

In South Carolina, pesticide applicators and pest control businesses are licensed by the Clemson University Department of Pesticide Regulation. Structural and household work falls under Category 7A. Commercial firms need a business license from DPR, a Designated Certified Applicator at each location, and comprehensive general liability coverage of not less than $100,000 combined single limit with no deductible over $1,000.

In Georgia, the Georgia Department of Agriculture regulates structural pest control through the Structural Pest Control Commission under the Structural Pest Control Act. The relevant operator category is Household Pest Control, and Georgia's own rules define it in a way that is unusually precise about rodents: it “does not include the control of mammals with the exception of commensal rodents and squirrels.”

What is included in a rodent service

  • Full interior, exterior, crawl space, attic and roofline inspection with photographs
  • Species identification from droppings, runways, gnaw marks and nesting sign
  • Entry-point map showing every gap that needs to close and why
  • Trapping at correct density — and elevated placements where roof rats are involved
  • Pre-baiting where the population is neophobic
  • Tamper-resistant, secured and numbered exterior stations where rodenticide is appropriate
  • Exclusion to hardware-cloth, sheet-metal and masonry specification — not foam
  • Sanitation and habitat findings: feeders, pet food, dumpsters, wood piles, vegetation contact
  • Droppings, nesting material and contaminated insulation removal
  • Follow-up verification, with K-9 detection available where you need independent confirmation

Where we work

We are based in Windsor, South Carolina, and run rodent service across Aiken, North Augusta, Graniteville, Vaucluse, Warrenville, Beech Island, Edgefield, Columbia, Lexington, West Columbia, Cayce and Irmo, plus Augusta, Evans and Martinez on the Georgia side — from Winter Colony houses and Horse District barns in Aiken to Hammond's Ferry and Riverside Village in North Augusta, the Graniteville and Vaucluse mill villages, Shandon, Rosewood, Earlewood and the Olympia and Granby mill villages in Columbia, the Riverwalk corridor through Cayce and West Columbia, and Lake Murray shoreline properties in Lexington and Irmo. See all areas we serve.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know whether it's rats or mice?

The droppings settle it. Mouse droppings are about a quarter inch, rice-grain shaped with pointed ends, and scattered widely. Rat droppings are much larger — Norway rat droppings run up to three-quarters of an inch with blunt ends, roof rat droppings about half an inch with pointed ends. Location helps too: mice range only 10 to 30 feet from the nest and turn up everywhere; Norway rats stay low; roof rats stay high. Send us a photo with something for scale.

Can you get rid of them without poison?

Often, yes — and in occupied homes with children, pets or asthma concerns we prefer to. Trapping at correct density combined with full exclusion resolves a great many residential jobs with no rodenticide at all. Where we do use product it goes in secured, tamper-resistant, numbered exterior stations. Tell us your preference at the inspection and we will build the program around it.

Why do I still hear them after treatment?

Two normal reasons and one bad one. Normal: a rodenticide-based program takes several days to work, and remaining animals move more as the population thins. Also normal: what you are hearing may be a flying squirrel or a gray squirrel rather than a rodent at all — the noise is very similar and the handling is different. The bad reason is an unsealed entry point still admitting new animals, which is exactly why we lead with exclusion instead of ending with it.

Will sealing the crawl space make it worse if something is trapped inside?

That is a real risk and it is why sequence matters. We clear the interior population first, or seal with a one-way arrangement where the situation calls for it, and we verify before final closure. Sealing a building with an active interior population is how you end up with an odor problem, and it is a mistake we design around rather than discover.

Is expanding foam good enough to close a gap?

No. UC IPM lists expanding foam among the gnawable materials to avoid. Rodent incisors grow about five inches a year and foam offers no resistance at all. Foam is a fine air seal behind a proper barrier — hardware cloth, sheet metal or mortar — but on its own it is a cosmetic repair that fails within a season.

Do ultrasonic plug-ins work?

No. The FTC warned more than 60 manufacturers and retailers about unsupported ultrasonic pest-device claims in 2001 and brought multiple enforcement actions before and after. UC IPM's current guidance states there is little evidence that sound, magnetic or vibrational devices of any kind will drive established house mice from a building. Save the money and spend it on a door sweep.

How many traps do I actually need?

Far more than most people use. Mouse traps should be no more than about six feet apart along active runs, because a mouse's entire home range is only 10 to 30 feet and it feeds at many sites each night. Rat traps and stations run within roughly 20 to 30 feet. A single trap under the sink is not a rodent program — it is a sample.

What about my bird feeder?

It is very often the answer. Bird feeders and outdoor pet food are documented rodent attractants, and cotton rats in particular are noted feeding beneath feeders. Keep firewood at least a foot off the ground, use rust- and damage-resistant garbage containers with tight lids, store pet food in sealed rodent-proof containers, and either take feeders down during an active infestation or move them well away from the structure.

Do you clean up droppings and contaminated insulation?

Yes. Droppings, urine-soaked and nested-out insulation, nesting material and damaged vapor barrier all get removed and documented, and we photograph the condition of ductwork and the crawl space envelope. That matters both for the health side — 82 percent of US homes carry detectable mouse allergen — and because leftover odor and pheromone continue attracting rodents to the same voids.

How is this different from your K-9 rodent detection?

This page is the treatment and repair: trap, seal, remove, verify. K-9 detection answers a different question — exactly where live activity is inside a structure when the evidence is ambiguous, or independent confirmation that a facility is clear after remediation. Homeowners usually need this page. Facilities with an audit finding, a trend report that does not match reality, or a recurring problem no one can locate usually need both.

h1: Repairs & Exclusion — Seal Pests Out for Good

hero.h1: Repairs & Exclusion — Seal Pests Out for Good
hero.lead: The lasting fix pests hate. We find and seal the gaps, cracks, and entry points that let rodents and pests in — and repair the damage they leave behind.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Certified K9 teams · Family-owned

body:
We’re a family-owned company, and we believe the best pest control is a building pests can’t get into in the first place. Meet the family behind Coastal K9 →

What exclusion & repair actually covers

Catching pests is only half the job. If the gaps, cracks, and damage that let them in stay open, they come right back. Exclusion and repair is the step that makes pest control permanent — and it is often overlooked by companies that just spray and leave.

The work that keeps pests out for good

We seal the entry points rodents and wildlife use — foundation gaps, utility penetrations, roofline and soffit openings, vents, and crawlspace access — using rodent-proof materials like steel mesh, hardware cloth, and durable sealants. We also repair the damage pests leave behind, from chewed insulation and fouled attic spaces to compromised weather seals.

Paired with our K-9 rodent detection, exclusion turns a temporary knockdown into a lasting fix. We find exactly where they are getting in, seal it, and restore what was damaged — so you are not calling someone back every few months.

How it works

1

Inspection

We find every gap, crack, and entry point pests are using.

2

Sealing

We close those openings with durable, long-lasting materials.

3

Repair

We fix the damage rodents and pests leave behind.

4

Protection

Your home is sealed to keep pests out for good.

Exclusion & entry-point sealing

Most pest problems come back because the door was left open — literally. Rodents and pests exploit gaps around pipes, vents, rooflines, garage thresholds, and foundation cracks. Our exclusion work finds and seals those entry points with durable materials, so treatment isn’t a revolving door. It’s the single most effective thing you can do to keep pests out.

Repairing pest & rodent damage

Rodents chew, insects tunnel, and moisture pests rot. We repair the damage that pests leave behind — from gnawed openings and damaged vents to compromised seals — restoring your home’s defenses and appearance.

Crawl space & attic

Attics and crawl spaces are where rodent and pest activity hides. We address entry points, vulnerable openings, and access points in these spaces so the parts of your home you don’t see stay protected.

What’s included

  • Full entry-point inspection
  • Gap, crack & void sealing
  • Garage, vent & roofline exclusion
  • Rodent and pest damage repair
  • Crawl space and attic protection
  • Durable, long-lasting materials

Why choose Coastal K9

  • Exclusion-first philosophy.
  • Stops problems from returning.
  • Durable, professional repairs.
  • Pairs perfectly with rodent and pest service.
  • Local, reliable craftsmanship.
Serving Aiken, North Augusta, the CSRA, and the Midlands — with capability for large commercial and multi-site work. See all service areas →

Frequently asked questions

What is exclusion?

Exclusion is sealing the physical entry points pests and rodents use to get inside. It’s the most effective way to make pest control last.

Do repairs really stop pests from coming back?

They dramatically reduce return problems. Treatment removes the current pests; exclusion keeps new ones from following the same paths in.

Do you fix rodent damage?

Yes. We repair gnawed openings, damaged vents and seals, and other damage rodents and pests leave behind.

Do you work in crawl spaces and attics?

Yes. These hidden spaces are common rodent highways, and we seal and protect them as part of thorough exclusion.

Can this be combined with pest or rodent service?

Absolutely — it’s the ideal pairing. We knock down the active problem, then seal the building so it stays solved.

What does exclusion and repair include?

Sealing the entry points pests use — foundation gaps, utility and pipe penetrations, roofline and soffit openings, vents, and crawlspace access — plus repairing the damage they cause, such as chewed insulation and fouled attic spaces.

Why is exclusion necessary after rodent control?

Because trapping or baiting removes the current rodents but leaves the openings they used. Without sealing those entry points, new rodents follow the scent trails right back in. Exclusion is what makes the solution permanent.

What materials do you use to seal entry points?

Rodent-proof materials built to last — galvanized steel mesh, hardware cloth, and durable sealants — chosen so rodents cannot gnaw or squeeze back through. Quick foam-only patches do not hold up; proper exclusion does.

Do you repair damage rodents have already caused?

Yes. Beyond sealing, we restore damage such as chewed or contaminated insulation and fouled attic and crawlspace areas, so your home is both sealed and cleaned up.

Is exclusion better than just setting more traps?

For a lasting fix, yes. Traps treat the symptom; exclusion removes the cause by closing off access. Combined with detection to find every entry point, it is the difference between a recurring problem and a solved one.

h1: K-9 Rodent Detection for Restaurants & Food Service

hero.h1: K-9 Rodent Detection for Restaurants & Food Service
hero.lead: Your health score is public — and permanent online. Our detection dogs find rodent activity before an inspector does, and before your customers notice, so you stay open, compliant, and trusted.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Certified K-9 teams · Family-owned · Serving the CSRA & Midlands

body:
In food service, a pest problem is never just unpleasant — it is a public health-score risk and a permanent online reputation risk. One failed inspection or one customer photo of a mouse can follow a restaurant for years. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions helps restaurants, kitchens, bars, and food-service operations across the CSRA and Midlands stay inspection-ready with canine rodent detection that finds activity early and precisely.

We are detection-first, which matters enormously in a kitchen. Instead of spraying broadly near food-contact surfaces and hoping, we send a trained dog to pinpoint exactly where rodents are active, then treat and seal only those areas. It is faster, cleaner, safer for your guests, and it produces the documentation your inspector and your auditor want to see.

35+Diseases rodents can spread, according to the CDC
½ inchA gap this small is all a rat needs to get inside
5–10Litters a single female mouse can produce in one year

Your health score is on the wall — and online forever

Rodents nest in the parts of a kitchen you cannot see: behind and beneath equipment, inside wall voids, above ceiling tiles, in dry storage, and along the dock. They are most active at night, after your staff has gone home, and a small problem becomes an established one quickly — a single female mouse can produce five to ten litters in a year.

That is why a reactive approach fails restaurants. By the time a customer spots a mouse or an inspector finds droppings, the population is entrenched. A detection dog finds active harborage fast, so you can correct it before it becomes a violation, a re-inspection, or a viral post — and before it ever reaches the dining room.

The pests we detect in food-service settings

Rodents are the headline threat to your health score, but food-service environments attract several pests we detect and control:

Norway rats

Burrowing rats that enter from below — foundations, docks, and drains. They contaminate food and gnaw wiring, and they need only a half-inch gap to get in.

Roof rats & house mice

Climbers and squeezers that nest above ceilings and in dry storage. Mice fit through a quarter-inch gap and reproduce rapidly, contaminating far more than they eat.

German cockroaches

The classic kitchen roach, thriving in warm equipment voids and spreading rapidly. We locate harborage so treatment is precise, not a broad spray.

Flies (drain & small)

Drain and fruit flies signal sanitation and moisture issues that also draw rodents. We identify the sources as part of a full-kitchen program.

The standards and regulations we build your program around

A food-service pest program has to satisfy the health department, your auditors, and your brand at the same time. Ours is built for inspection-readiness:

  • FDA Food Code & health inspections — Inspectors specifically look for pest evidence. Rodent droppings or activity can cost points, trigger a re-inspection, or drop a public score. Detection helps you find it first.
  • Third-party & brand audits — Franchise and food-safety auditors expect a documented pest-management program with trend records. Our reporting is built to support them.
  • HACCP prerequisite programs — Pest management is a prerequisite program under HACCP food-safety plans. Our documentation slots directly into your plan.
  • Food-safe, detection-first treatment — We confirm activity first so any treatment is targeted and minimal near food-contact surfaces — protecting both compliance and your guests.

How our restaurants and food service K-9 program works

Every food-service engagement follows a clear, documented workflow designed around your service hours:

  1. Assess

    We walk the kitchen, prep, dry storage, dish, bar, and dock areas to identify the zones rodents use and the gaps that let them in.

  2. Detect

    A certified detection dog screens those areas by scent — including the equipment voids and ceiling spaces a visual check cannot reach.

  3. Pinpoint & confirm

    The handler confirms live activity and maps the exact harborage and travel routes so nothing is guessed at.

  4. Exclude & treat

    We seal the entry points rodents use and apply targeted, food-safe control only where activity is confirmed.

  5. Verify

    A follow-up sweep confirms the activity is resolved — the proof you need for a re-check or an auditor.

  6. Document & monitor

    You receive a written report, and we can schedule recurring and pre-inspection sweeps so you are always inspection-ready.

What our restaurants and food service program includes

  • Kitchen, prep, dry-storage & dock detection targeting the areas rodents actually use.
  • Structural exclusion to seal the gaps and entry points that let them in.
  • Pre-inspection sweeps ahead of a health-department visit or third-party audit.
  • Re-check support if you have had a finding and need to prove correction.
  • Discreet, after-hours scheduling so service is never interrupted.
  • Cockroach and fly service for equipment voids, drains, and prep areas.
  • Recurring monitoring to catch new activity before it spreads.
  • Documented reports for your files, your inspector, and your auditor.

Why canine detection outperforms conventional pest control for restaurants and food service

Scattered traps and blanket spraying are exactly the wrong approach in a kitchen. Here is why food-service operators choose detection:

 Traps & blanket sprayingCoastal K-9 detection
Finding the sourceHit or missPinpoints active harborage by scent
Near food surfacesBroad chemical applicationTargeted, food-safe, minimal
Entry pointsUsually missedLocated and sealed with exclusion
Health-score riskReactive, after a findingProactive, caught before inspection
Odor issuesRodents die in wallsActivity found and removed at the source
DocumentationMinimalAudit-ready records and trends

Documentation that protects you

You receive documentation of every inspection and any corrective work — proof you can hand a health inspector or third-party auditor that shows a proactive, detection-first pest program.

In food service, that record can be the difference between a passing note and a violation, between a smooth audit and a failed one. It demonstrates diligence, supports your HACCP plan, and gives you a defensible history if a complaint is ever filed.

Signs your restaurant needs a sweep now

Do not wait for an inspector or a customer to find it first. Call if you or your staff notice:

  • Droppings along walls, in dry storage, under equipment, or in cabinets.
  • Gnaw marks on packaging, wiring, or door sweeps.
  • Greasy rub marks along baseboards and rodent travel routes.
  • Scratching or scurrying sounds at night after the kitchen closes.
  • A staff or customer sighting — even one is worth an immediate screen.
  • An upcoming inspection or audit you want to walk into with confidence.

Serving restaurants and food service across the CSRA & Midlands

Coastal K-9 serves restaurants, cafes, bars, breweries, food trucks, ghost kitchens, and catering operations across the CSRA and Midlands. That includes Aiken and the Whiskey Road and downtown dining districts, Augusta’s Broad Street, Washington Road, and Riverwatch corridors, North Augusta, Evans, Martinez, and the Columbia Vista, Five Points, and Devine Street areas.

As a local, family-owned company we schedule around your service — including after-hours and early mornings — and offer same-week response when you have a finding or an inspection coming up.

Why CSRA restaurants and food-service operators choose Coastal K-9

Restaurants across the region choose Coastal K-9 because we protect what matters most: your health score and your reputation. We are discreet, we work around service, and detection-first means targeted, food-safe treatment instead of blanket spraying near your food.

Our founder is FEMA-trained and NESDCA-certified, and we treat your kitchen the way we would want ours treated — thoroughly, quietly, and with the documentation to prove it.

Frequently asked questions

Can you inspect without disrupting service?

Yes. We schedule around your hours, including after-hours and early mornings, so a detection sweep never interrupts service or alarms customers.

Can you help before a health inspection?

Absolutely. Pre-inspection sweeps are one of our most requested services — we find and help you correct rodent activity before an inspector does.

We had a violation — can you help prove we fixed it?

Yes. We can inspect, support corrective exclusion work, and document that the issue is resolved, which is exactly what a re-check requires.

Is detection safer than spraying in a kitchen?

Far safer and more targeted. We find exactly where the problem is so any treatment is precise and minimal — not a broad application near food-contact surfaces.

How much does commercial rodent detection cost for a restaurant?

It depends on the size of your kitchen and how often you schedule, but detection-first is almost always cheaper than a failed inspection or a lost-reputation event. Call 803-226-3155 for a quote.

How do dogs find rodents a person cannot?

Detection dogs alert to the scent of live rodents, urine, and nesting material, locating active harborage inside walls, equipment voids, and ceilings that a visual inspection cannot reach.

Do you seal the entry points too?

Yes. Detection is paired with structural exclusion — sealing the gaps, penetrations, and door-sweep gaps rodents use — so the fix lasts.

How often should a restaurant schedule service?

Most operators do best with recurring monthly or quarterly monitoring plus pre-inspection sweeps, so activity is caught early and you are always inspection-ready.

Do you provide documentation for audits?

Yes. Every inspection and corrective action is documented in a format that supports health inspections, HACCP plans, and third-party audits.

Do you handle cockroaches and flies too?

Yes. Beyond rodents we address German cockroaches in equipment voids and drain and fruit flies tied to sanitation and moisture.

How quickly can you respond?

We offer same-week response across the CSRA and prioritize active findings and upcoming inspections.

What areas do you serve?

Restaurants and food-service operations across Aiken, Augusta, North Augusta, Columbia, Lexington, Evans, Martinez, and the greater CSRA and Midlands.

title: Rodent Control for Warehouses
description: In a warehouse or food facility, a rodent program built on bait stations alone is a program with no end date
h1: Rodent Control for Warehouses and Food Facilities: Why Detection and Exclusion Beat Bait
body:
Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions  |  Windsor, SC  |  September 15, 2026

In a warehouse or food facility, a rodent program built on bait stations alone is a program with no end date — you keep killing rodents, and rodents keep coming in, because nothing has changed about how they’re getting in. The approach that actually solves the problem is detection and exclusion: find precisely where the activity is and how they’re entering, then physically seal the building. K9 detection makes the first half of that realistic in a space far too large and too full of concealed void to inspect any other way, and exclusion makes the result permanent rather than perpetual.

Why do bait-only rodent programs never end?

Because bait addresses the symptom, not the cause. A bait station kills the rodents that find it, but it does nothing about the gap under the dock door, the unsealed utility penetration, or the damaged wall panel that let them in. As long as those openings exist, the surrounding rodent population continuously refills the building, and you’re locked into an indefinite service contract that manages the problem rather than ending it.

In a food facility, this is worse than merely expensive. A perpetual bait program means toxicant permanently present in and around a food environment, dead rodents in wall voids creating odor and secondary pest problems, and — critically — no actual reduction in the risk of a rodent turning up where an auditor or an inspector can see it. The presence of an active bait program is not evidence of control; it’s often evidence that the building is still open.

Why is a warehouse so hard to inspect conventionally?

Scale and concealment. A distribution center or food plant may be hundreds of thousands of square feet, filled with racking, pallets, equipment, drop ceilings, wall cavities, mechanical spaces, and utility chases — an enormous volume of space that rodents can occupy entirely out of sight. A visual inspection can only find droppings and gnaw marks where a person can look, which in practice means the accessible margins of a facility that is mostly inaccessible.

The result is that conventional inspection tends to confirm that rodents exist somewhere without answering the questions that actually matter: where is the activity concentrated, where are the harborage areas, and where are they entering? Without those answers, remediation is guesswork — and in a facility this size, guesswork is extraordinarily expensive.

K9 INSIGHT  An active bait program is not proof of rodent control — it’s often proof the building is still open. If rodents keep coming back no matter how many stations you service, the problem was never the rodents you’re killing; it’s the gap you never found.

How does K9 detection change the picture?

A trained rodent detection dog works by scent, so concealment doesn’t defeat it. It can detect live rodent activity inside wall voids, above ceilings, behind racking and equipment, and within mechanical spaces, and it alerts at the source — turning “there are rodents in this building” into “the activity is concentrated here, here, and here.” In a facility where a manual inspection of every void is flatly impossible, that is the difference between a plan and a guess.

The dog can also cover a large facility efficiently, which makes systematic sweeps practical rather than aspirational. We pair the detection work with a detailed structural inspection focused on the flagged areas, tracing activity to the actual physical openings — which is what converts detection into an actionable exclusion scope of work.

What entry points do we find in commercial buildings?

The same ones, over and over. Dock door gaps and worn dock seals are the most common by far — the gap under a poorly sealed overhead door is a highway. Then: unsealed utility and conduit penetrations, pipe chases, gaps around HVAC and refrigeration lines, damaged or missing door sweeps, floor drains and unsealed drain lines, gaps where walls meet floors and where panels have been damaged by forklift strikes, roof penetrations and vents, and openings created by previous maintenance work that was never sealed.

Remember the scale involved: a mouse passes through a gap the size of a dime, a rat through one the size of a quarter. In a large commercial building with decades of maintenance history and constant forklift traffic, there are typically many such openings — and finding all of them is exactly the work. Missing one keeps the door open.

Why does exclusion matter for audits and compliance?

Food facilities operate under third-party audit schemes and regulatory inspection, and rodent evidence is among the most serious findings possible. Auditors and inspectors don’t just look for live rodents — they look for droppings, gnaw evidence, and, importantly, for whether the facility has structural deficiencies that would allow rodent entry. A building with obvious gaps and an active bait program is a building that has not solved its problem, and experienced auditors know it.

Exclusion is what actually improves the finding. Sealing entry points, correcting the structural deficiencies, and being able to demonstrate a documented detection-and-exclusion program shows control rather than management. And in a food environment, reducing reliance on toxicant in and around the product is a meaningful benefit in its own right. If you have a specific audit scheme with defined requirements, those requirements should drive the scope — we’re glad to work to them.

What does a commercial detection and exclusion program involve?

It starts with a thorough K9 detection sweep of the facility, paired with a structural inspection that traces flagged activity to physical entry points, and produces documented findings: where activity was detected, and every opening we found. That becomes the exclusion scope — the specific list of gaps to be sealed, with the appropriate gnaw-resistant materials and repairs for each.

From there the exclusion work is executed, and the building is genuinely closed rather than merely serviced. Follow-up detection verifies the result and catches anything missed or newly created — important in an active facility where forklift damage and maintenance work continually create new openings. That’s the honest reality of a large commercial building: exclusion isn’t a single event, it’s a maintained condition. But it’s a condition you can actually achieve, which is more than a bait program will ever deliver.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does our warehouse keep having rodents despite a bait program?

Because bait kills the rodents that find it but does nothing about how they’re getting in. As long as the entry points remain open, the surrounding population continuously refills the building. A bait-only program manages the problem indefinitely rather than ending it — an active bait program is often evidence the building is still open.

How can a dog detect rodents in a large warehouse?

The dog works by scent, so concealment doesn’t defeat it. It detects live rodent activity inside wall voids, above ceilings, behind racking and equipment, and in mechanical spaces, and alerts at the source. That turns “there are rodents somewhere in this facility” into specific, actionable locations — which a visual inspection of a huge building cannot do.

What rodent entry points do you typically find in commercial buildings?

Dock door gaps and worn dock seals most often, plus unsealed utility and conduit penetrations, pipe chases, gaps around HVAC and refrigeration lines, missing door sweeps, floor drains, wall-to-floor gaps, forklift-damaged panels, roof penetrations, and openings left by past maintenance work. A mouse needs only a dime-sized gap.

Why does exclusion matter for food safety audits?

Because auditors and inspectors look not only for rodent evidence but for structural deficiencies that would allow entry. A building with obvious gaps and an active bait program hasn’t solved its problem, and experienced auditors know it. Exclusion — sealing entry points and correcting deficiencies — is what actually improves the finding.

Is exclusion better than poison in a food facility?

It addresses the root cause rather than the symptom, and it reduces reliance on toxicant in and around a food environment — a meaningful benefit in its own right. A bait-driven program also leaves dead rodents in wall voids, creating odor and secondary pest problems, while never closing the openings that let rodents in.

What does a commercial detection and exclusion program involve?

A K9 detection sweep paired with a structural inspection that traces flagged activity to physical entry points, producing documented findings and an exclusion scope: the specific list of openings to seal. The exclusion work is then executed with gnaw-resistant materials and repairs, and follow-up detection verifies the result.

Is exclusion a one-time fix?

In an active facility, exclusion is best understood as a maintained condition rather than a single event — forklift damage and ongoing maintenance work continually create new openings. But it’s a condition you can genuinely achieve and hold, which is more than a perpetual bait program will ever deliver.

Yes. Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions provides K9 rodent detection and exclusion for warehouses, distribution centers, food facilities, restaurants, and grocery operations across Aiken, Columbia, Charleston, Greenville, Lexington, and surrounding areas. Call 803-226-3155.

We’re a family-owned company serving CSRA homes and businesses, with the specialized experience to take on large-scale rodent mitigation nationwide. Meet the family behind Coastal K9 →

How to know if you have a rodent problem

Rats and mice are secretive, mostly nocturnal, and they nest inside the parts of your home you never see — wall voids, attics, crawlspaces, and behind appliances. Most homeowners notice the evidence long before they ever see the rodent itself. Watch for these signs:

  • Droppings along walls, in cabinets, pantries, or drawers.
  • Gnaw marks on wood, wiring, food packaging, or plastic.
  • Scratching or scurrying sounds in walls or ceilings, especially at night.
  • Greasy rub marks along baseboards and entry points where rodents travel.
  • Nests of shredded paper, fabric, or insulation in hidden corners.
  • A musky, ammonia-like odor that builds up near active nesting areas.

The problem with store-bought traps and bait is that they treat the symptom, not the source. Rodents keep coming back because the entry points are still open. Our detection dogs find exactly where rodents are living and traveling, so we can seal them out for good. Call 803-226-3155 to schedule an inspection.

Local rodent control for homes and businesses

Mice and rats don’t just raid the pantry — they chew wiring, contaminate food, and multiply fast. We handle rodent problems for CSRA homes and businesses from the first sign of droppings, combining fast knock-down with the exclusion work that actually keeps them out. Rodent control done right is about sealing the building, not just setting traps.

Nationwide rodent mitigation & Norway rat burrow work

Beyond the CSRA, Coastal K9 provides nationwide rodent mitigation and support for more than 15 companies dealing with large-scale infestations and severe Norway rat burrow problems. We specialize in the heavy, entrenched pressure that big facilities face — mapping burrow systems, breaking the breeding cycle, and building exclusion programs that hold up under real-world conditions.

Food processing & agriculture specialists

Food and agriculture sites carry the toughest rodent challenges and the highest stakes. We specialize in food-processing facilities and agriculture nationwide, delivering burrow mitigation, exclusion, and documentation that stands up to audits and protects both product and reputation.

Frequently asked questions

Do you handle large Norway rat burrow problems?

Yes. Norway rat burrow systems are a specialty. We map and mitigate burrows, break the breeding cycle, and seal the structure so the colony can’t re-establish.

Can you support food-processing and agricultural facilities?

Absolutely. We specialize in food processing and agriculture nationwide, and support more than 15 companies with large-scale rodent mitigation, exclusion, and audit-ready documentation.

What is exclusion, and why does it matter?

Exclusion is sealing the gaps, cracks, and entry points rodents use to get inside. It’s the part most treatments skip — and the reason problems come back. We make it central to every job.

Are your methods safe around kids and pets?

Yes. For homes we use family-safe methods and place control products where children and pets can’t reach them. For facilities we follow the appropriate safety and compliance standards.

How quickly can you respond?

We offer same-week service locally and scope larger facility and nationwide work on a timeline that fits the operation. Call 803-226-3155.

What are the first signs of a rodent problem?

The earliest clues are usually droppings along walls or in cabinets, gnaw marks on wood and wiring, and scratching or scurrying sounds in walls and ceilings at night. A musky odor and greasy rub marks near baseboards are also common.

How do dogs detect rats and mice?

Detection dogs alert to the scent of live rodents, their urine, and nesting material. That lets them locate active harborage and travel routes hidden inside walls, attics, and crawlspaces that a person could never inspect.

Isn’t it cheaper to just buy traps?

Traps and bait treat the symptom, not the source. If the entry points stay open, rodents keep coming back. Our dogs find where they are actually getting in and living, so exclusion is precise and the fix lasts — usually saving money over repeated trap-and-bait cycles.

Do you seal up the entry points?

Yes. Detection is paired with exclusion and repair work — we seal the gaps, cracks, and access points rodents use so they cannot return. That is what makes the solution permanent instead of temporary.

Why do rodents keep coming back after I set traps?

Because trapping removes a few individuals but leaves the entry points open. Rodents follow scent trails back inside. Locating and sealing those access points is the only way to keep them out for good, and that is exactly what our detection-and-exclusion approach does.

Are rodenticides safe around my kids and pets?

We minimize rodenticide use by detecting first and treating precisely. Where control products are needed, they are placed in targeted, tamper-resistant ways — and in many cases exclusion alone solves the problem without broad poison use.

We offer same-week appointments across Aiken, Augusta, Columbia, and the greater CSRA. Call 803-226-3155 and we will get a certified K-9 team scheduled quickly.
