h1: K-9 Rodent Detection for Warehouses & Distribution

hero.h1: K-9 Rodent Detection for Warehouses & Distribution
hero.lead: A rodent problem in a warehouse is a whole-facility problem. Our detection dogs cover large footprints fast — pinpointing activity that scattered traps and bait stations miss entirely.
hero.meta: Call 803-226-3155 · Certified K-9 teams · Family-owned · Serving the CSRA & Midlands

body:
In a warehouse or distribution center, rodents ride in on inbound freight and disappear into racking, palletized product, and structural voids. Across tens of thousands of square feet, a handful of bait stations covers almost none of it. Coastal K-9 & Pest Solutions gives large facilities across the CSRA and Midlands something traps never can: fast, systematic canine detection that pinpoints where rodents are actually active.

Detection-first is the difference between reacting to product damage and preventing it. Instead of waiting for a customer complaint or a failed audit, a detection dog maps activity across your footprint so exclusion and control go exactly where they are needed — and so you can prove a proactive program to every customer and auditor.

½ inchA gap this small is all a rat needs to enter your facility
35+Diseases rodents can spread, according to the CDC
HoursFor a dog to sweep what takes a technician days to search by eye

In a big facility, traps tell you where rodents died — not where they live

Bait stations and snap traps are reactive and only cover the few feet around them. In a facility measured in acres, that leaves enormous blind spots — and rodents nest in exactly the places traps do not reach: high in racking, deep in palletized product, above suspended ceilings, and inside structural voids and roof lines.

A detection dog systematically clears racking, pallet storage, mezzanines, and structural voids, mapping where rodents are genuinely active. That means your exclusion and control resources go where they will actually matter, and you find a problem while it is small — before it becomes damaged product, a rejected load, or an audit finding.

The pests we detect in warehouse and distribution facilities

Rodents are the primary threat to stored product and audit scores, but distribution environments face several pests we detect and control:

Norway rats

Enter from below through foundations, dock levelers, and utility penetrations. They contaminate product and gnaw wiring, and need only a half-inch gap to get in.

Roof rats & house mice

Climbers and squeezers that nest high in racking and above ceilings. Mice fit through a quarter-inch gap and are the most common stored-product rodent.

Stored-product pests

Indianmeal moths, beetles, and weevils that infest palletized goods. We help identify affected areas so infested stock is isolated quickly.

Birds

Sparrows and pigeons that enter through open dock doors and roost in rafters, fouling product and triggering audit deductions. We provide humane exclusion.

The standards and audits we build your program around

Distribution facilities answer to customers and third-party auditors. Our program is built to protect your contracts and your scores:

  • Customer & third-party audits — Retail and food customers require documented pest programs. Audits such as AIB and SQF (for food-grade facilities) scrutinize pest evidence and records closely.
  • FSMA & food-grade requirements — For facilities handling food, the Food Safety Modernization Act and food-grade standards demand proactive pest management and documentation. Detection strengthens both.
  • Inbound-freight control — Because most facility rodents arrive on incoming product, dock and inbound inspection is a core standard we build into every program.
  • OSHA housekeeping & safety — Rodent nesting and droppings are a housekeeping and safety issue. A documented program supports a clean, compliant facility.

How our warehouses and distribution centers K-9 program works

Every warehouse engagement follows a systematic, documented workflow scaled to your footprint:

  1. Assess

    We map your facility — racking, storage zones, mezzanines, docks, and utility runs — and review inbound patterns and any current concerns.

  2. Detect

    A certified detection dog systematically sweeps the full footprint by scent, covering in hours what would take a technician days to search visually.

  3. Map activity

    The handler confirms and maps exactly where rodents are active, so control resources are focused rather than scattered.

  4. Exclude & treat

    We seal the dock-door, penetration, and structural gaps rodents use and apply targeted control only where activity is confirmed.

  5. Verify

    A follow-up sweep confirms activity is resolved — documented proof for your customers and auditors.

  6. Document & monitor

    You receive audit-ready reporting with activity mapping and trends, plus a scheduled monitoring and inbound-inspection cadence.

What our warehouses and distribution centers program includes

  • Full-footprint detection across racking, pallet storage, and mezzanines.
  • Inbound freight & dock inspection to catch rodents at the point of entry.
  • Structural exclusion to seal dock-door, penetration, and roofline gaps.
  • Activity mapping so control resources go where they are needed.
  • Stored-product pest & bird service for palletized goods and rafters.
  • Scheduled monitoring to catch new activity before it spreads.
  • Audit-ready documentation for customers and third-party inspections.
  • Trend reporting that demonstrates a proactive program over time.

Why canine detection outperforms conventional pest control for warehouses and distribution centers

A few bait stations cannot protect a facility measured in acres. Here is why distribution operations choose detection:

 Bait stations onlyCoastal K-9 detection
CoverageOnly a few feet around each stationSystematic across the full footprint
Finding the sourceReactive, after damagePinpoints active harborage by scent
Inbound freightNot addressedDock and inbound inspection built in
Entry pointsUsually missedLocated and sealed with exclusion
Time to coverDays of visual searchingHours with a certified dog
Audit readinessSparse recordsActivity mapping and trend documentation

Documentation that protects you

Every sweep is documented — where the dog alerted, what was found, and what exclusion or corrective work followed. That record supports customer audits, third-party inspections such as AIB and SQF, and your own facility standards.

For distribution operations, documentation is not paperwork — it is how you keep a contract. A proactive detection record with activity mapping and trends is exactly what auditors and customers want to see, and it protects you if a load is ever questioned.

Signs your facility needs a detection sweep

In a large facility, early signs are easy to miss until product is damaged. Watch for:

  • Droppings in racking, on pallets, or along walls and utility runs.
  • Gnawed or contaminated packaging and product damage.
  • Sightings on security cameras, especially overnight.
  • Grease marks and runways along beams, walls, and dock edges.
  • Gaps at dock doors, levelers, and penetrations that invite entry.
  • An upcoming customer or third-party audit you want to pass cleanly.

Serving warehouses and distribution centers across the CSRA & Midlands

Coastal K-9 serves warehouses, distribution centers, third-party logistics (3PL), cold storage, and manufacturing-adjacent facilities across the CSRA and Midlands. That includes the industrial and logistics corridors around Aiken, Augusta, Grovetown, and Graniteville along I-20 and I-520, and the Columbia, Lexington, and West Columbia distribution hubs along I-77 and I-26.

As a local, family-owned company we can scale a program to a single building or a multi-site portfolio, with scheduled monitoring and on-demand response when a customer audit or a finding requires fast action.

Why CSRA warehouses and distributors choose Coastal K-9

Distribution operators across the region choose Coastal K-9 because a detection dog covers in an hour what would take a technician a full day to search by eye — and finds what the eye misses. That speed and accuracy protect your product, your contracts, and your audit scores.

Our founder is FEMA-trained and NESDCA-certified, we are local and responsive, and every inspection is detection-first — so control is targeted, documented, and cost-effective across even the largest footprints.

Frequently asked questions

How can a dog cover such a large facility?

A trained detection dog systematically works racking, storage, and structural voids far faster than a person searching by eye — often clearing in hours what would take a technician days, and finding hidden activity a visual check misses.

Can you check inbound freight?

Yes. Dock and inbound-freight inspection is a core part of a warehouse program, since rodents most often arrive on incoming product and pallets.

Do you seal entry points too?

Yes. Detection is paired with structural exclusion — sealing dock-door, leveler, penetration, and roofline gaps — so the fix is lasting, not temporary.

Can you support our AIB or SQF audit?

Absolutely. Every inspection is documented with activity mapping, corrective work, and trends, giving you audit-ready records for AIB, SQF, customer, and third-party inspections.

How much does warehouse pest detection cost?

It scales with facility size and monitoring frequency, but detection-first is highly cost-effective against the price of damaged product, a rejected load, or a failed audit. Call 803-226-3155 for a facility quote.

How often should we schedule?

Most facilities do best with scheduled monthly or quarterly monitoring plus pre-audit sweeps and inbound inspection, sized to throughput and audit cycle.

Do you handle stored-product pests and birds?

Yes. Beyond rodents we help identify stored-product pest activity in palletized goods and provide humane bird exclusion for dock and rafter areas.

How do the dogs find rodents in stored product?

They alert to the scent of live rodents, urine, and nesting material, locating harborage deep in racking and product that a visual inspection cannot reach.

Will detection disrupt operations?

Minimal disruption. We schedule around your operation, including off-shift, and a dog moves through the facility efficiently and safely.

Do you provide trend documentation over time?

Yes. Recurring programs include trend reporting that demonstrates a proactive, improving pest program — exactly what customers and auditors look for.

How quickly can you respond to a finding?

We offer same-week response across the CSRA and prioritize active findings and upcoming audits.

What areas do you serve?

Warehouses and distribution facilities across Aiken, Augusta, Grovetown, Graniteville, Columbia, Lexington, and the greater CSRA and Midlands.

Related commercial programs

Food Processing & ManufacturingRestaurants & Food ServiceMultifamily & Property ManagementAll Commercial Programs

Schedule large-footprint K-9 rodent detection and inbound inspection across the CSRA.

title: White-nose syndrome (WNS)
description: White-nose syndrome (WNS) is a fungal disease that attacks hibernating bats
h1: White-Nose Syndrome: The Fungal Disease That’s Devastated America’s Bats, and What’s Happening Here in South Carolina
body:
Detection before treatment. Every time. And verification before documentation. Every time. It starts with the dog. It lives with the handler. Every time.

This post is a departure from our usual tone. Most of our bat content is about appreciating a genuinely beneficial, misunderstood animal. This one is about a disease that has already killed millions of them, has been confirmed in South Carolina since 2013, and has pushed at least one of our state’s bat species toward local disappearance in the exact caves where SCDNR has been counting them for over a decade. It matters, and it’s worth understanding clearly.

What Is White-Nose Syndrome?

White-nose syndrome (WNS) is a fungal disease that attacks hibernating bats, caused by Pseudogymnoascus destructans (Pd) — a cold-loving fungus that thrives specifically in the cold, humid conditions found in caves and mines where bats spend the winter. It was first documented near Albany, New York, during the winter of 2006–07. According to the U.S. Geological Survey’s 2025 science strategy report, WNS has since been confirmed in 40 U.S. states and 9 Canadian provinces, and of the 47 bat species native to the U.S., Alaska, Hawaii, and Canada, 12 have been affected — including three endangered species and one proposed for endangered status. Millions of bats have died.

How It Actually Kills Bats: Questions & Answers

Q: Why does it only affect bats during hibernation? A: Because that’s the only time bats are vulnerable to it. During hibernation, a bat’s body temperature drops to nearly match the cold cave air — often just 2 to 10°C — and its immune system becomes suppressed, which is exactly the narrow window this cold-adapted fungus needs to establish an infection on the skin of the nose, ears, and wings.

Q: How does a skin fungus actually kill a bat? A: Indirectly, but effectively. A 9-year peer-reviewed study tracking little brown bats found the fungus causes roughly a 60% reduction in how long bats stay in each hibernation torpor bout, forcing them to arouse far more often than normal through the winter. Every arousal burns stored fat that’s supposed to last until spring, and infected bats were found to have no depot fat reserves left by March — well before insects return and flying is worth the energy cost. Separately, the fungus damages the wing membrane itself, disrupting circulation and normal skin function and promoting dehydration, which compounds the problem.

Q: How deadly is it, really? A: Among the deadliest wildlife diseases on record. The same peer-reviewed study documented hibernation mortality rates of 75 to 98% across four affected species — the little brown bat, northern long-eared bat, Indiana bat, and tri-colored bat — in the first several years after the fungus arrived at a hibernation site. Some previously common species have been reduced by more than 90% across large parts of their range.

Q: Where did this fungus come from? A: The leading evidence points to Europe or Asia, where the same fungus is present in bat populations but does not cause mass die-offs — those bats appear to have co-evolved some tolerance to it over a much longer shared history. North American bat species, encountering it for the first time in the last two decades, had no such resistance built up.

Q: Is this a risk to people or pets? A: No. White-nose syndrome only affects bats — it is not known to infect humans, pets, or any other animals. The precautions around decontaminating clothing and gear after visiting caves exist to avoid accidentally carrying fungal spores to a new site and infecting more bats, not because of any health risk to people.

White-Nose Syndrome in South Carolina

This isn’t a distant problem. Per SCDNR, white-nose syndrome was first confirmed in South Carolina in March 2013 at Table Rock State Park in Pickens County, and the fungus has since been detected in at least nine additional counties. The impact on our tri-colored bat population has been severe: SCDNR reports declines of up to 97% at major Upstate hibernation sites since the fungus arrived, with one major site losing 91% of its population in just three years — dropping from hundreds of bats to roughly 30.

There’s a genuine glimmer of hope in that same data, though: small numbers of banded tri-colored bats have been documented returning to that site in subsequent years, suggesting at least some individuals may be surviving exposure or developing resistance. SCDNR has also noted that South Carolina’s comparatively warmer, shorter winters may give our bats a somewhat better survival outlook than the 90-100% mortality rates seen in harder-hit Northeastern states — though it’s far too early to call that a solved problem.

What’s Being Done, and How You Can Help

  • Monitoring and testing. SCDNR biologists test hibernating bat colonies every winter (typically February and March, when symptoms are most detectable), sending samples to the National Wildlife Health Center and the Southeastern Cooperative Wildlife Disease Study for diagnosis.
  • Decontamination protocols. Anyone entering caves or mines — researchers, cavers, and rock climbers alike — is asked to follow USFWS decontamination guidelines to avoid unintentionally transporting fungal spores between sites on clothing, gear, or boots.
  • Vaccine and treatment research. Per USGS’s current science strategy, developing and optimizing a WNS vaccine and reducing environmental fungal levels are active, funded research priorities, though no cure or field-ready treatment exists yet.
  • Citizen science. SCDNR’s Bat Watch program lets South Carolina residents help by counting bats at known roosts, providing population data that’s genuinely difficult for researchers to collect alone. If you’re aware of a hibernating colony on your property, SCDNR wants to hear from you.
  • Supporting healthy roosts. While white-nose syndrome is specifically a winter hibernation disease, giving bats a clean, viable summer roosting option away from your home — like the bat house build we’ve covered separately — supports overall population resilience at a time when these species can’t afford additional pressure.

The CK9PS Bottom Line

We spend most of our bat content making the case for why these animals deserve a little more appreciation and a little less fear. White-nose syndrome is the other side of that coin — a real, documented, ongoing threat to the same bats doing free pest control over Aiken County every summer night. Understanding it doesn’t require panic. It requires the same thing everything else on this blog does: correct information, taken seriously, before deciding what to do about it.

Detection before treatment. Every time. And verification before documentation. Every time. It starts with the dog. It lives with the handler. Every time.

Know of a hibernating bat colony on your property, or found bats behaving unusually in winter? Contact Coastal K9 & Pest Solutions at 803-226-3155 or ck9ps.com — and consider reporting it to SCDNR as well.

  • Peer-reviewed: “Nutritional Capability of and Substrate Suitability for Pseudogymnoascus destructans” (PMC)

title: WHY IS AIKEN COUNTY SUDDENLY FULL OF BATS?
description: A field guide to your new dusk neighbors — plus the bug that loves to impersonate a bed bug
h1: WHY IS AIKEN COUNTY SUDDENLY FULL OF BATS?
body:
A field guide to your new dusk neighbors — plus the bug that loves to impersonate a bed bug

If you’ve been sitting on the porch around dusk lately and noticed little dark shapes swooping and looping over the yard, you’re not imagining it. This is peak bat season in Aiken County, and there’s a good reason your evenings suddenly have company.

Why So Many, Why Now

Two things are happening at once. First, it’s maternity season — roughly mid-April through August, female bats gather in tight-knit colonies to have and raise their pups. A hot attic, soffit, or church steeple works a lot like an incubator, keeping the babies warm while mom is out hunting. Second, summer nights in the Southeast mean an all-you-can-eat insect buffet, and bats are built for exactly that. A single bat can pack away hundreds of insects in one night’s hunting, and a nursing mother eats even more to keep up with the demands of a growing pup. Mosquitoes, moths, beetles — if it flies at night, a bat considers it dinner.

So the bats you’re seeing aren’t moving in. They’ve probably been in the neighborhood the whole time. You’re just noticing them now because maternity season means bigger numbers, more activity, and more of them out hunting at once.

Where They’re Actually Roosting

Bats used to rely almost entirely on natural roosts — loose bark on old oaks and beeches, hollow cavities in pines, bald cypress swamps, and cave-like crevices. A lot of that habitat has disappeared over the last couple centuries, so bats adapted, and human structures turned out to be excellent substitutes.

  • Attics and soffits — the most common household roost, especially for maternity colonies. Warm, dry, dark, and undisturbed.
  • Chimneys — usually older, inactive ones. Bats will almost never use a chimney that’s actively in service.
  • Behind shutters, fascia, and loose siding — common for smaller groups or bachelor males passing through.
  • Bridges, barns, and old outbuildings — a favorite for larger colonies, especially near water.
  • Tree cavities and loose bark — still the natural first choice when it’s available.

A bat doesn’t need much of a gap to get in — if you can fit a pinky finger into a crack or vent gap, a bat can probably use it. That’s why exclusion work is about sealing entry points, not about the size of the hole looking “bat-sized.”

How Many Species Are We Actually Talking About?

South Carolina is home to roughly 14 to 15 bat species, depending on the source and the most recent surveys — out of about 47 found across the entire United States, per the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources’ Bat Conservation Plan. The ones you’re most likely to actually cross paths with around an Aiken County home are the big brown bat, the evening bat, and the Brazilian (Mexican) free-tailed bat, with the occasional little brown bat showing up as well. The rest of the state’s bat roster — species like the hoary bat, the tri-colored bat, and the federally protected northern long-eared bat — tend to stick to more specific habitats like mature forests, swamps, or higher elevations upstate.

Every single one of them is doing your yard a favor. Bats are one of the more effective natural forms of mosquito and moth control you’ll find, no spraying required.

Now for the Plot Twist: Bat Bugs

Here’s where things get genuinely interesting from a pest ID standpoint. Bats carry their own parasite — the bat bug (Cimex adjunctus) — and it is close kin to the bed bug (Cimex lectularius). Same genus. Same general size. Same flattened, reddish-brown, oval body. To the naked eye, a bat bug and a bed bug look like the same insect.

They’re not, and the difference actually matters for how you treat the problem. Bat bugs feed on bats, not people, and they live in and around the roost — not in mattress seams. When a bat colony gets excluded from an attic (or just moves on), any bat bugs left behind can wander into the living space looking for a new blood meal, which is usually the moment someone finds one and assumes they have a bed bug infestation.

The Real Way to Tell Them Apart

It comes down to hair, and you need a hand lens or magnification to see it properly: bed bugs have short fringe hairs on the pronotum (the little plate behind the head) that are shorter than the width of the eye. Bat bugs have noticeably longer hairs there — as long as or longer than the eye itself — and their whole body reads shaggier overall. Pest professionals sometimes describe a bat bug as looking like “a bed bug that needs a haircut.”

This distinction isn’t just trivia. Treating a bat bug problem as if it’s a bed bug problem misses the actual source — the colony (or former colony) that’s still nearby. Get the identification wrong, and you can spray a bedroom repeatedly and never solve anything, because the real issue is thirty feet up in the attic.

What We Actually Do About It

Bats are protected wildlife in South Carolina, so this was never a spray-and-pray situation to begin with. When there’s a suspected roost, the process is inspection first — confirm species, colony size, and every entry point — then humane, one-way exclusion timed around the maternity season so pups aren’t trapped or orphaned. If bat bugs are the actual complaint, correct identification comes before any treatment plan, because the fix for a bat bug problem and the fix for a bed bug problem aren’t the same fix.

Detection Before Treatment. Every Time.
